Netanyahu may seek broad national government after election, sources in Ben-Gvir's camp believe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:43:09 UTC
20:43:09 KST

Sources close to Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir believe Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has already made a preliminary decision to try to form a broad national government after the election, even at the cost of leaving Ben-Gvir outside the coalition.
According to sources familiar with discussions in Ben-Gvir’s circle, Netanyahu’s change in messaging, from the “full, full right-wing government” slogan used in previous elections to the current emphasis on a “broad national government,” is seen as a sign that he is seeking to move in a more statesmanlike and centrist direction this time.
The sources claim that Ben-Gvir believes Netanyahu does not want to repeat a term in which he himself is positioned as the coalition’s leftmost member, with all his partners to his right. In their assessment, if election results allow it, Netanyahu would prefer to bring in a figure from the opposing camp, and in one possible scenario even former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, while leaving Ben-Gvir outside the government.
Ben-Gvir’s associates point to several signs that they say indicate this direction. One is Netanyahu’s use of the phrase “broad national government.” According to them, the choice of this wording, instead of the previous emphasis on a right-wing government, reflects a strategic shift.
They also point to Netanyahu’s political relationship with Ben-Gvir during the election campaign. Among other things, they cite the fact that Netanyahu did not appear with him at the Altalena event, as well as moves regarding surplus-vote agreements with right-wing parties, which they interpret as an attempt to create greater separation between the Likud and Otzma Yehudit.
From their perspective, these are not isolated incidents but part of a broader trend: an effort by Netanyahu to create greater room for maneuver ahead of the day after the election.
The assessment: Netanyahu will want to return to the center
The main argument among Ben-Gvir’s associates is also based on how they analyze Netanyahu’s political conduct over the years. They claim that the current coalition, in which all the partners are positioned to the right of Likud, was an exception and not necessarily Netanyahu’s natural preference.
They point to 2009, when Netanyahu brought Ehud Barak and the Labor Party into his government, while the National Union remained outside the coalition. According to them, National Union figures expected for an extended period to join the government but ultimately remained in the opposition.
They also note that in 2013, one of the first partners with whom Netanyahu reached agreements was Tzipi Livni. A government was later formed with Yesh Atid and the Jewish Home, while the haredi parties remained outside.
According to Ben-Gvir’s associates, beginning in 2015, Netanyahu’s room for maneuver gradually narrowed, partly because of political boycotts against him. That year, he was initially forced to establish a narrow government with 61 Knesset seats, and only later was Yisrael Beytenu added.
They claim that the peak of this pattern came after the 2019-2020 election cycles, when Netanyahu formed a parity government with Benny Gantz. Ben-Gvir’s associates note that in that government Netanyahu effectively abandoned advancing a broad judicial reform and agreed that the Justice Ministry would be placed under Avi Nissenkorn of Blue and White.
Judicial reform could also be abandoned
Ben-Gvir’s associates estimate that a move by Netanyahu toward a broader government would require him to give up some of the issues identified with the current right-wing government, foremost among them the continuation of the judicial overhaul.
According to their assessment, bringing a centrist party or a party from the opposing camp into the coalition would require significant compromises on issues related to the judicial system and would allow Netanyahu to present a more statesmanlike term in office.
The sources also link this to the assessment that this could be one of Netanyahu’s final terms as prime minister and that he may place greater weight on the legacy he leaves behind.
At the same time, Ben-Gvir’s associates acknowledge the argument working in the opposite direction. Netanyahu knows that Otzma Yehudit, if it joins a right-wing coalition, could provide him with a stable partner for a full term. By contrast, a government with Eisenkot could be more complicated and include significant ideological gaps.
Therefore, if the right-wing bloc wins 61 seats or more, leaving Ben-Gvir outside in favor of a government with Eisenkot could represent a gamble for Netanyahu: choosing a broader government that may nevertheless be less stable.
One scenario raised by Ben-Gvir’s associates is that Netanyahu may assume that even if a centrist partner later leaves the coalition, Otzma Yehudit could join at that stage and extend the government’s lifespan.
Their assessment is even more decisive in a scenario where the right-wing bloc fails to reach 61 seats even with Otzma Yehudit. In that case, Ben-Gvir’s associates are convinced that Netanyahu would prefer to bring in a party from the opposing camp rather than be dragged into another election campaign.
From their perspective, the central question ahead of the day after the election is therefore not only how many seats the right-wing bloc will win, but how much freedom of choice Netanyahu will have.
The more options available to him for forming a government, they believe, the greater the chance that he will return to the pattern that characterized him in the past: a broader coalition with a balancing force to the left of Likud, rather than a right-wing government in which he himself is the most moderate figure.

Putin’s Economic Growth Claims Diverge From IMF Data
Unknown

11:43:00 UTC
20:43:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed during the BRICS summit in New Delhi that Russia’s economy had outpaced global growth rates over the previous three years, assertions that diverge from official International Monetary Fund (IMF) and European statistical data, The Moscow Times reported.
Addressing leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday, Sept. 11, Putin contended that Russia’s gross domestic product expanded by 10.3% between 2023 and 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He attributed the performance to domestic structural realignment that he argued made Russia more resilient despite facing more than 30,000 international sanctions.
Putin further asserted that Western economies had suffered severe self-inflicted blowback, including mounting sovereign debt, widening budget shortfalls, and an 8% contraction in EU industrial production.
However, official data contradicts the Russian leader’s figures. According to Eurostat statistics, EU industrial output contracted in 2023 and 2024 before rebounding sharply in 2025, leaving a net three-year decline of approximately 0.6% rather than the 8% claimed by Putin.
Similarly, IMF figures show that the global economy grew by 10.7% from 2023 to 2025, marginally outpacing Russia’s 10.3% rate.
While the Russian economy expanded faster than the global benchmark in 2023 and 2024 on the back of historic wartime state spending, domestic growth decelerated to roughly 1% in 2025 as the global economy expanded by 3.5%.
Hard Times Ahead: Russian Attacks put Ukraine’s Finances Under Pressure
Stagnating momentum and widening fiscal deficits
Russia’s own official economic forecasts indicate that the growth divergence is set to widen further. The Russian Ministry of Economic Development projects GDP growth of just 0.4% in 2026, compared to the IMF’s global growth forecast of 3%.
Under those projections, Russia would substantially lag behind major economies such as the US at 2.3%, China at 5%, and India at 6.4%.
Moscow projects only modest acceleration in subsequent years, estimating growth of 1.4% in 2027, 1.9% in 2028, and 2.4% in 2029, representing cumulative growth of 5.8% over the three-year period.
The upbeat rhetoric at the summit also sits uncomfortably against recent domestic economic indicators. The Russian economy grew by 1.3% in the second quarter of 2026, while first-half growth reached just 0.6% – roughly half the pace recorded during the same period in 2025 and nearly seven times slower than the initial 2023–2024 wartime mobilization boom.
Fiscal pressures are simultaneously accumulating. On Sept. 3, Putin acknowledged that the federal budget deficit was expanding, with the January-July shortfall reaching 2.8% of GDP against a full-year government target of 1.6%.
Domestic supply constraints
Speaking at the BRICS Business Forum, Putin acknowledged that Russia has become the world’s most heavily sanctioned state, while claiming that the restrictions had ultimately strengthened national economic sovereignty and prompted a successful pivot toward non-Western trading partners.
Yet despite the official optimism, Western restrictions and persistent Ukrainian drone strikes against domestic energy infrastructure have exerted visible operational strains on the Russian economy.
Ukrainian strikes on refineries throughout 2026 have disrupted domestic processing capacity, prompting Moscow to enforce fuel export bans and compelling at least 26 major Russian airports – including St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo hub – to introduce severe refueling restrictions for commercial airlines.
Wartime labor shortages, persistent inflation, high central bank interest rates, and mounting fiscal deficits continue to weigh heavily on Russia’s economic outlook, even as the Kremlin continues to portray its economy as an insulated model for the Global South.

Pope Leo XIV marks 25 years since 9/11 attacks, calls for renewed commitment to peace
Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, called for a renewed commitment to peace on Sunday as he marked 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks on his home country.
The Chicago-born pope made his first public comments to commemorate 25 years since the attacks, speaking in English at the end of his traditional Sunday noon blessing from his studio window overlooking St. Peter's Square.
"Two days ago marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the United States of America," Leo said. "I renew my prayers for those who lost their lives and for those who continue to bear the wounds of that tragic day."
He added that "at a time when conflict and violence afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, I invite everyone to pray that the Lord will bestow his gift of peace upon the world."
Speaking in Italian, he added: "The memory of the tragic events of 25 years ago pushes us to renew our commitment to peace, above all with prayer."
On Sept. 11, 2001, the former Robert Prevost was in Rome attending a big assembly of his Augustinian religious order. At the time, he was the Chicago provincial leader of the Augustinians. Prevost was elected superior of the entire order on Sept. 14, his birthday, a position he held for two consecutive terms until 2012.
Vatican News on Sunday republished excerpts of his first homily as superior, delivered on Sept. 21, 2001. In it, the future American pope reflected on the attacks.
"We cannot fail to remember the tragic events that shook the United States on Sept. 11," he said in his homily. "The violence that the world witnessed last week in the United States is a tragic expression of a series of problems that are becoming increasingly acute everywhere.
"Hatred and violence will continue to grow as long as so many people are forced to live in extreme poverty and are oppressed by so many forms of injustice."
Two popes have visited Ground Zero: Pope Benedict in 2008 and Pope Francis in 2015.

Americans have worse view of Muslims 25 years after 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:33:09 UTC
20:33:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Americans have worse view of Muslims 25 years after 9/11
A study released earlier this month found that Americans' view of Muslims is today twice as negative as it was in the wake of the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago.
Multiple US-led wars fought in the name of countering terrorism, namely in Afghanistan and Iraq; prominent politicians building their brands on demonising Muslims and other marginalised communities; and the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, have all contributed to a negative image of Muslims among Americans.
A Pew research survey found that 43 percent of US adults believed that Muslims were less patriotic than other Americans and 42 percent said Muslims were having a negative impact on the country.
“9/11 gave a pass to further demonise Muslims and invade Muslim countries,” Mirvette Judeh, president of the Arab American Caucus of California, told The New Arab.
“9/11 gave governments a pass to surveille everyone. It destroyed our countries and destroyed our communities here. Whole communities were demonised and terrorized. I feel like the hate and fear have gotten worse,” she said.
In March 2002, six months after 9/11, 25 percent of adults surveyed by Pew said Islam was more likely than other faiths to encourage violence. In another survey this year, 51 percent gave the same response to the question.
Despite these highly negative views of Muslims 25 years after 9/11, a growing number of Muslim Americans are becoming more civically engaged, with many running for elected office and taking on other public roles.
“There’s optimism in the fact that our community is getting more comfortable being visible,” Amr Shabaik, legal director of the Los Angeles chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, told TNA. “Other communities have gone though this and have seen increased participation.”
Arguably the most prominent example of a successful Muslim American politician is New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who gave one of the main speeches at the 9/11 memorial on Friday.
Though there was a petition to prevent him from speaking at the event, the mayor was warmly received and stood out as the only senior elected official to stay at the ceremony after all of the names were read.
Among family members of the victims at the ceremony was Michael Massaroli Jr., who lost his father in the September 11 attacks. As the last one of the victims’ relatives to speak, he urged people not to spread hate in response to 9/11.
"I think the one parting thing I want to leave everyone with is that you do to my dad’s legacy and the legacy of all these victims no honour by using this tragedy to spread hate," he said. "I've had to grow up and spend the past 25 years seeing people use it to hate on our Muslim brothers and sisters, do hate on people who don't look like them, and that's wrong and that does no honour to the victims here."

Oktoberfest 2026: All the rules visitors need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:31:29 UTC
20:31:29 KST

Visitors are reminded to follow the rules while enjoying the event as it is meant to be, with a hearty "Ein Prosit der Gemütlichkeit!"
Next Saturday, when Munich Mayor Dominik Krause taps the first beer barrel on the city's Theresienwiese, the famous cry of "O'zapft is" will ring out once again as Oktoberfest 2026 kicks off.
From Saturday, 19 September to Sunday, 4 October, more than six million visitors are expected at Oktoberfest, Germany's world-renowned folk and beer festival.
But attendees will have to keep some important rules in mind.
Cannabis
Munich’s Oktoberfest is a cannabis-free zone.
Back in July 2024, the Bavarian state parliament passed the "Bayerische Cannabisfolgenbegrenzungsgesetz," banning the consumption of cannabis in certain places.
Anyone caught smoking cannabis on the festival grounds faces a fine of €1,500, while repeat offenders could have to shell out more than €5,000.
In the official final report for last year, Munich police recorded a total of 27 breaches of the cannabis ban at Oktoberfest. Simply possessing cannabis is allowed, as long as adults stay within the nationwide legal limit of up to 25 grams.
Smoking tobacco is permitted on festival grounds and in beer gardens, although a strict smoking ban has been in place inside beer tents since 2010. Most tents offer designated smoking areas or balconies, however.
There are potential fines of up to €1,000 for anyone who does not follow the rules.
Rules for children
As lively as the atmosphere may be between beer steins, music and candy floss, the law does not make exceptions for the youngest visitors.
Anyone strolling across the fairground with a pram or buggy should keep an eye on the clock. From Sunday to Friday, children in prams are welcome until 6 pm. After that it gets too crowded – and therefore too dangerous. The rules are even stricter on Saturdays and on 3 October, when prams and buggies are completely prohibited for safety reasons.
When it comes to youth protection, organisers have clear boundaries.
For the very youngest, the evening in the beer tent ends at 8 pm. Children under six, even when accompanied by their parents, must leave the tents at that time. For children and teenagers under 16, the rule from 8 pm is that they are no longer allowed on the fairground without a legal guardian. Those aged 16 or 17 may stay on the site until closing time without their parents – although in certain tents such as Käfer or the Weinzelt the night ends at midnight.
Anyone coming to the Wiesn by bicycle, e-scooter, scooter, skateboard or inline skates must leave them outside the entrance to the festival grounds. They are not permitted on the site itself.
Anyone who gets on an e-scooter or a bicycle afterwards should remember that the same alcohol limits apply as for motor vehicles. Starting at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5%, you risk a €500 fine, two penalty points on your license, and a potential one-month driving ban.
Cocaine
Cocaine is among the most commonly detected illegal drugs at Oktoberfest. In 2025 alone, around 100 people were caught using it.
The Bavarian State Office of Criminal Investigation (BLKA) reported in April 2025 that the number of cocaine offences in Bavaria had risen from 2,148 in 2020 to 3,972 in 2024 – an increase of almost 85% within four years. The agency said a "cocaine surge" across Germany was also being felt in Bavaria.
The figures are also rising in Munich. In 2025, 1,396 drug offences involving cocaine or crack were recorded, up from 1,227 in 2024 – an increase of 13.8%.
Drinking contests banned
Despite all the rules, people are of course allowed to enjoy themselves at Oktoberfest – but organisers draw a clear line between a lively atmosphere and a loss of control.
Drinking contests in which guests down their Maß as quickly as possible or encourage each other on to drink to excess are not welcome. Anyone who also starts clambering around on tables or benches and puts other guests at risk may find themselves being thrown out.
Oktoberfest visitors will also have to dig deep into their wallets in 2026, as beer is becoming increasingly more expensive.
A Maß now costs between €14.80 and €15.90. This puts the average price 2.38% above last year.
Visitors are also reminded to keep their hands to themselves and follow the rules while enjoying the event as it is meant to be, with a hearty "Ein Prosit der Gemütlichkeit!"

Carney pushes idea of making Canada 'associate member' of EU, WSJ reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:31:26 UTC
20:31:26 KST

Carney pushes idea of making Canada ‘associate member’ of EU: Report
BRUSSELS – Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney wants closer links with the European Union and is exploring whether his country could become an “associate member” of the bloc, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sept 13.
The EU, which has not been flexible about membership rules in the past, is open to the idea of granting Canada a yet to be created status of associate membership, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials both from the EU and Canada.
The Canadian embassy in Brussels and spokespeople at the European Commission did not respond to separate requests for comment.
Canada’s escalating trade war with the United States has added urgency to its strategic pivot towards other trading partners.
Canada’s relations with Washington have deteriorated sharply since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, with disagreements on trade and other issues.
The trade spat has led to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.
Canada and the EU are discussing ways to let Canada’s goods, services and workers involved in strategic supply chains such as energy, AI, defence and critical minerals move freely, thus effectively shifting the EU border, The Wall Street Journal said.
Canada and the EU are also talking about laying underwater cables, jointly constructing data centres, cloud storage and new satellite networks and infrastructure to ship Canadian energy to the EU, the newspaper said.
Carney has spoken regularly with several EU leaders, most notably French President Emmanuel Macron, about the possibility of letting Canadians live and work visa-free in the EU, WSJ said, citing two unnamed officials familiar with the matter.
Both leaders are set to meet later in September.
Macron’s press office did not respond to a request for comment.
The project to closely tie-up Canada and the EU is not such an easy feat, though, as fierce opposition to a more modest trade deal showed.
More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it. REUTERS

Nepal floods: 80 still missing after two weeks of disaster, says Isha Foundation

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:30:32 UTC
20:30:32 KST

77 pilgrims, 3 volunteers of Isha Foundation remain unaccounted for
Two weeks after flash floods struck the Nepal-Tibet border, 77 participants of a Kailash Manasarovar pilgrimage and three volunteers remain unaccounted for, the Isha Foundation said in a statement, adding that the figure has not changed since its previous update.The foundation said identification work at the disaster site was still under way and authorities had indicated that the process could take considerable time.According to the statement, Isha Foundation has remained in contact with Chinese, Indian and Nepali authorities, as well as embassies representing 19 countries in India, Nepal and China, to seek information about those affected and relay verified updates to families.
The death toll from flash floods in Nepal rose to 1,386 on Saturday as rescuers recovered more bodies from eight affected districts, authorities said.The floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 5,130 people remain missing, while 13,728 have been rescued so far.
Only 104 bodies have been identified and handed over to families. Meanwhile, 339 people are receiving treatment in 19 hospitals and 3,761 displaced people are staying in 37 holding centres.The foundation said identification details, photographs and other relevant material had been shared with authorities and search-and-rescue teams where required. It also said its volunteers had been in touch with the US state department and Global Affairs Canada, whose assistance in seeking information from Chinese authorities had been useful."Any new information that can appropriately be shared will be communicated to the affected families first and made public where it is legal, ethical, and appropriate to do so", Isha foundation said.Access to the affected site at Gyirong Port on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border remains restricted by Chinese authorities for rescue and forensic work, while access on the Nepal side is also restricted by Nepali authorities, the foundation said.“No private individuals or organisations have been allowed near the site,” it said, adding that Isha volunteers who had been stationed in Gyirong Town were asked by Chinese authorities to leave along with other non-official personnel.In Nepal, around 25 Nepali volunteers are supporting efforts on the ground, according to the statement. The team has been coordinating with hospitals, mortuaries, police and government offices and has shared information on missing individuals with the Nepal Police and Nepal Tourist Police.The foundation said contact had also been established with the Nepali Army and that details of those missing had been passed to personnel involved in search-and-rescue efforts.Following the floods, volunteers visited hospitals and mortuaries to gather information and understand identification procedures, the statement said. The team also visited a DNA centre to understand the requirements for identification, with the process being coordinated through the respective countries' consular services.
Isha said information received from embassies and authorities was being passed to the affected families, particularly emergency contacts, along with details of the next steps.The foundation said international media were granted access on the 12th day after the disaster, but that subsequent reports had not yielded new facts.It added that a volunteer team was responding to calls and emails through a dedicated hotline operating across eight countries. Families are also being assisted with practical arrangements, including the shipment of belongings left behind in Kathmandu.The foundation said it would continue coordinating with authorities and emergency services and share verified information with families as it becomes available.

UAE and Iran leaders meet at the BRICS summit for the first time since the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:29:40 UTC
20:29:40 KST

The talks follow the UAE’s suspension of trade and financial dealings with Iran in August and follow UAE's firm position that trust with Iran "is a mountain to climb" after Iran's attacks on the Gulf countries.
Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan met Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday during the BRICS summit in India, weeks after the UAE announced a suspension of trade and financial dealings with Tehran.
The talks mark the countries’ highest-level meeting since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, as the UAE has been making it clear through presidential diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash that "trust is the mountain we will have to climb," as "geography leaves us no alternative to engagement," but that those relations will need to be judged by actions and not words to rebuild the shattered trust.
The Abu Dhabi Media Office said the two leaders stressed the importance of supporting efforts to reduce tensions and strengthen regional stability.
On 19 August, the UAE’s foreign ministry announced that it had halted all trade and financial transactions with Iran until further notice, citing regional escalation.
The same statement reaffirmed the UAE’s commitment to dialogue and regional cooperation. Saturday’s account of the meeting did not announce a change to the trade restrictions or a specific agreement between the two countries.
Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz explained in a post on X that "despite all the bad blood between Abu Dhabi and Tehran, the emerging Gulf approach, and particularly the UAE’s, is increasingly clear: manage the Iranian risk rather than push Tehran into a corner."
"This does not mean trust. Rebuilding even a basic level of confidence between the two sides will take years. But from Abu Dhabi’s perspective, maintaining channels with Tehran is itself a form of strategic hedging. The UAE has little interest in becoming a frontline state in another regional war," the Israeli security analyst said.
Calls to protect trade and energy
Both countries are members of BRICS, the group of emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.
They backed the summit’s New Delhi Declaration, adopted on Saturday, which expressed concern over escalating tensions in the Middle East and called for “maximum restraint”.
The declaration urged the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect for national sovereignty and a lasting settlement through diplomacy. Leaders also called for cooperation to keep global trade, supply chains and energy moving, in line with international law.
Chinese President Xi Jinping urged BRICS to help bring peace to the region, saying China would work with other members towards that goal.
The declaration also criticised unilateral tariffs and sanctions and supported further work on international payments and trade using members’ own currencies.
Speaking on Sunday at the BRICS Plus outreach session, which brings members together with other invited countries, Pezeshkian said attacks on a country’s economic and energy infrastructure had consequences beyond its borders.
He said unilateral sanctions affected food security and people’s welfare, and called for greater use of national currencies and a stronger role for the New Development Bank, the lender established by BRICS countries.
Hormuz talks planned in Oman
Separately, Pezeshkian said Arab foreign ministers were due to meet in Muscat on Monday to sign an agreement establishing a joint Iran-Oman shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, disregarding the Gulf countries' united position that the strait must be open to free international navigation.
The UAE president's diplomatic advisor Anwar Gargash underlined days ago the country's firm position that it would not accept a single state's control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz and that it was unacceptable for oil tankers to be threatened and attacked while attempting to transit the key waterway.
“Our energy exports will not be held hostage, nor will our trade and economic activity,” Gargash said.
In an interview published on Saturday, Pezeshkian said the International Maritime Organisation would then be informed of the agreement.
Iran had already announced on 5 August that it had agreed the location of a proposed shipping route with Oman.
At the time, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the arrangement alone could not guarantee safe navigation while the US naval blockade and other actions against Iran continued.
Pezeshkian also said in Saturday’s interview that Iran would reopen the strait when the United States ended its blockade and attacks. His remarks did not set a date for reopening the waterway.
On Sunday, Qeshm governor Amir Teymouri said one person had been killed after a merchant vessel was struck near Iran's Hengam and Qeshm islands. He did not identify the source of the strike.

France climbs down in social media row with U.S. after ambassador’s appointment blocked
The appointment of French diplomat Aurélien Lechevallier as France’s envoy to Washington stalled following a diplomatic dispute between France and the U.S.
BRUSSELS — France has defused a social media row with the U.S. after an online spat over voting in the U.N. General Assembly reportedly led to the delay in the confirmation of Paris’ envoy to Washington.
In a statement on Friday reported by AFP, France’s mission to the U.N. in Geneva made amends for an online remark it posted in July questioning Washington’s commitment to human rights. “France and the United States recently adopted divergent positions during a vote at the United Nations General Assembly. This divergence concerned a single vote and did not relate to the defense of human rights,” the statement read.
“Differences in public opinion on a vote do not impede close dialogue with the United States and do not call into question our historic alliance, nor our ability to work together to promote peace, stability and prosperity, including within multilateral forums.”
Advertisement
AFP reported that the U.S. State Department responded positively to the apology. “We take note of France’s statement and appreciate it; we look forward to collaborating with them to promote our common values and interests,” a State Department official told AFP on condition of anonymity.
The appointment of French diplomat Aurélien Lechevallier as ambassador to the U.S. was blocked by Washington as a result of the spat, France24 reports.

2026-09-13
11:23:10 UTC
20:23:10 KST

The government is unlikely to meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England, Angela Rayner has acknowledged, saying there was only a “slim chance” enough houses would be built before the next election.
The manifesto pledge to build 1.5m houses by the next election was a “stretch target”, the communities secretary added, but said it was not being ditched and she was “definitely not giving up”.
The government’s target has been significantly hampered by inflation owing to the US war with Iran. Housebuilders have cut back the number of developments despite Labour’s planning reforms which were hoped to increase the numbers of new homes.
Rayner, who returned to the role after Andy Burnham became prime minister, acknowledged for the first time on Sunday that she could miss the target.
She told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “It’s a slim chance, but I’m definitely not giving it up. I think it’s really important that we keep a target that it was always a stretch target.”
Rayner said Burnham’s main focus was now on building council houses, suggesting that was taking priority over efforts to increase the overall target.
“The prime minister wants us to make sure we’re building council houses. He’s made that absolutely, fundamentally clear,” she said. “We’ve just announced £10bn into a social and affordable homes programme. We’re seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference.
“But the headwinds that are coming our way internationally and through those construction costs are having a negative effect on that target.”
Burnham recently backtracked on plans for cash from the 10-year affordable homes programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which he had suggested he was minded to do. Instead the £10bn will be spent on the mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.
The funds will build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing. London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.
Ministers are keen to find other ways to relax regulations for private sector builders, including instructing councils to give a “default yes” approach to housing developments that are within a reasonable walking distance of well-connected train and tram stations.

Voting under way in Sweden with far right eyeing first role in government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:17:15 UTC
20:17:15 KST

Voting is under way in Sweden in a high-stakes election that could lead to the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) entering government for the first time.
It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Polls suggest an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs.
Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (7am UK time). A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting.
Early indications of results will come at 8pm when the first exit polls are released, followed by a forecast from the broadcaster SVT an hour later. The first preliminary vote count is expected between 10.30 and 11pm. Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months.
The right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.
The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.
The rightwing coalition broke a longstanding taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.
SD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.
After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it has shifted much of the Swedish establishment to the right, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition wins, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.
SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Its controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them.
The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader, Magdalena Andersson, why she was so angry during a TV debate.
Another leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave.
Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.
“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”
Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for the Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.
The prime minister and leader of the Moderates, Ulf Kristersson, has put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused Andersson of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.
Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”

Russian drone hits train two km from Polish border, rail operator says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:16:51 UTC
20:16:51 KST

"We are continuing to monitor aerial threats, ensure the smooth running of trains and take every possible measure to ensure the safety of passengers and railway staff," Ukrzaliznytsia said.
A Russian drone struck the locomotive of a passenger train two kilometres from the Polish border on Sunday, Ukraine's state-owned rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) said.
The attack reportedly took place in Ukraine's Volyn region. There are not believed to have been any casualties from the incident.
"For the second day in a row, the enemy has been attacking the railways. Today in the Volyn region, two km from the border with Poland, the enemy struck the locomotive of a passenger train," Ukrzaliznytsia said on Telegram.
A tragedy was apparently averted thanks in part to an early warning. The team responsible for monitoring threats to the rail service detected the danger and alerted the train crew in good time, allowing them time to take measures to protect passengers and staff, per the company.
"We are continuing to monitor aerial threats, ensure the smooth running of trains and take every possible measure to ensure the safety of passengers and railway staff," it added.
The strike near the Polish border came as part of a broader Russian air offensive.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched more than 450 drones at Ukraine overnight, including jet-propelled drones and Banderol missile drones.
At least three people were killed and 36 people were injured in the overnight strikes.
Russian attacks also hit regions of western Ukraine bordering Poland.
The scale of the attacks meant that traffic at Polish–Ukrainian border crossings had to be temporarily restricted. Border Guard spokesperson Major Dariusz Sienicki told the PAP news agency that checks had been suspended overnight for safety reasons.
Border traffic has now returned to normal at Dorohusk, Zosin and Dołhobyczów. Processing at Hrebenne was also expected to resume.
The Border Guard did not record any direct threat at Polish crossings.
"We only received information from the Ukrainian side that a drone struck and destroyed a lorry at a distance of about 800 metres from the Jagodzin crossing," Major Sienicki said.
Russia 'knocking at the doors of the EU and NATO'
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric Russian strikes" were "not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."
"This is Putin’s terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he wrote on X, while also calling for further sanctions against Moscow.
"Make Moscow feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex," he urged.
Poland scrambled military aircraft
In response to the Russian attacks on western Ukraine, the Polish armed forces took steps to secure the country's airspace, with the deployment of Polish aircraft and other preventive measures.
Residents of the Lublin and Podkarpackie regions received a morning alert from the Government Centre for Security warning of a Russian air attack on Ukrainian territory and informing them about the activity of Polish military aircraft. The alert was cancelled at around 9 am, after roughly five hours.
Shortly before 10 am, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces announced that military aircraft were no longer operating in Polish airspace. It stressed at the same time that Poland's airspace had not been violated.
Poland's defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Polish defence systems had detected an early-morning attack using Geran-5 drones in western Ukraine.
"One of them struck 1 km from the border with Poland, another 5 km. The Polish airspace was guarded by F16 aircraft, helicopters, and the SAAB airborne reconnaissance aircraft. There was no breach of our border," he said.

Sweden began voting Sunday in a general election after a tight race that will see either the far-right enter government for the first time or the left-wing opposition reclaim power.
Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats was among the first to cast her ballot after polling stations opened at 8:00 a.m. local time.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Clad in a pale blue suit, the 59-year-old who in 2021-2022 became the first woman to serve as Sweden’s prime minister voted with her husband at a school in her home municipality of Nacka, south of Stockholm.
Opinion polls have long credited the four parties in her left-wing bloc with a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats.
But the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days of the campaign.
“It is now up to the Swedish people to decide which direction our country should take. Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats? Something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of cooperation?” Andersson told reporters after voting.
Her party, which governed the Scandinavian country for the better part of the 20th century and remains Sweden’s largest, has pledged to bolster the welfare state and help struggling households cope with rising costs.
Turnout Surges in Saxony-Anhalt State Election
‘Make Sweden great again’
Outgoing Prime Minister Kristersson has meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes’ everyday lives now that his government’s clampdown on organised crime and immigration has begun to show results.
Deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks have decreased significantly in recent years, and asylum applications are at a record low.
“We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people... to make Sweden great again,” Kristersson told AFP before the vote, borrowing US President Donald Trump’s famous catchphrase.
His three-party minority coalition cut a deal in 2022 with the Sweden Democrats giving them influence over government policy, in particular on immigration and crime, in exchange for their support in parliament.
Over the past two decades, far-right leader Jimmie Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream.
It is now hoping to enter government. Kristersson has promised the far right key cabinet posts if the right-wing wins the election.
“I think it’s a very important election this year, and hopefully a lot of people will realise that we have to change course... so that everyone will feel included in society,” store manager Linda Eriksson, 48, told AFP as she voted at a polling station.
Ingrid Rudien, a 64-year-old assistant secretary, said she hoped the country “can unite together as a nation even though we may have a close result”.
‘We’ve already won!’
Akesson was confident of victory at a final election rally on Saturday in the Swedish capital.
“We’ve already won!” the 47-year-old said to thunderous applause in Stockholm’s Kungstradgarden Park.
“Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish,” he said, surrounded by blue and yellow campaign posters blaring “Make Sweden Sweden Again”.
Agneta Andersson, a 78-year-old pensioner attending the rally, told AFP she was voting for the far right.
“Like Jimmie, I want it to be like it was when I was young, in the old Sweden. I can’t cope with all this violence in society.”
Voting stations close at 8:00 p.m. when exit polls were to be published, with the first reliable results expected several hours later.
Some eight million people are eligible to vote in the election, in a country of 10.6 million where voter turnout regularly tops 80 percent.
Around half of voters have cast their ballots in advance.
If the right wing were to win the election, the formation of a new government would be fairly straightforward.
But as the four left-wing parties are splintered ideologically, tough negotiations would be needed to form a government even if they hold a majority.

Rosh Hashanah 2026: Israel’s 78-year miracle was never supposed to happen - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:07:19 UTC
20:07:19 KST

As we start 5787, let’s take stock of the incredible times we live in.
In May 1948, a battered remnant of a people declared a state on a sliver of land no one else wanted. Five regular armies crossed its borders within hours. Twenty more governments wished it were gone.
The Jews inside had no oil, no great-power patron willing to fight for them, almost no heavy weapons, and a fifth column already shooting from behind. The smart money said the experiment would last weeks.
Seventy-eight years later, that experiment is a regional power, a technological engine, and the most successful national revival in modern history. The odds were not merely long. They were absurd. That is precisely why the story matters.
The first war was supposed to finish what the Holocaust began. Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq sent trained armies against a militia that had spent the previous decade smuggling rifles in crates of oranges.
Inside the new borders, thousands of Arabs took up arms against the government that had just offered them citizenship. The Jews absorbed 6,000 dead, 1% of the entire population, and still held the line. They have not lost a war since.
In 1967, they were outnumbered on three fronts and finished the fighting in six days. In 1973, they were surprised, bled, and then drove the attackers back across the canal and the Golan.
Every subsequent campaign has followed the same pattern: Israel is smaller, Israel is condemned, Israel survives and wins.
Survival was only the first miracle. The second was the ingathering. Nearly a million Jews fled or were expelled from Iraq, Yemen, Egypt, Libya, Syria, and Morocco. They arrived with suitcases and trauma.
Then came the remnant of European Jewry, the Soviet aliyah of the 1990s, the Ethiopians, the Indians. Israel did not merely house them. It turned refugees into citizens, conscripts, engineers, and rabbis.
No other country in the 20th century absorbed so many people, from so many civilizations, in such a short time, while fighting for its life.
The economic story is almost as improbable. For decades, the Arab League enforced a boycott designed to strangle the Jewish state in its crib.
Later came the BDS campaign, campus resolutions, and the ritual 69-plus-1 votes at the United Nations, the 22 members of the Arab League plus a rotating bloc of 48 African and Asian states that treat isolation of Israel as a standing agenda item.
Accusations escalated from “occupation” to “apartheid” to “genocide,” language borrowed from the worst crimes of the century and applied to a country that withdraws from territory, accepts cease-fires, and vaccinates its enemies. The intended result was pariah status.
Instead, Israel became the Start-Up Nation. A country with no natural resources except human capital now punches far above its weight in cybersecurity, medical devices, drip irrigation, desalination, and semiconductors.
Israeli firms list on Nasdaq in numbers that embarrass far larger economies. The same people who once rationed margarine now export intelligence software to governments that once would not stamp an Israeli passport.
Poverty has not disappeared, inequality is real, and the cost of living is high. None of that cancels the larger fact: a poor, blockaded state became rich by selling brains.
Wishes for the new year
Diplomacy followed the same improbable arc: the US, after early hesitation, became Israel’s indispensable ally. That relationship is now so deep that it survives administrations and wars.
Meanwhile, Israel quietly signed defense and commercial agreements from Colombia to Finland, India to Japan, and, most strikingly, with several Arab states that once led the effort to erase it.
The Abraham Accords did not end the conflict. They proved that the old consensus, no recognition until every Palestinian demand is met, was never as solid as its advocates claimed.
The least-noticed success may be the most Jewish. The study halls of Europe were ash. The great yeshivas of Lithuania and Poland existed only in memory and a handful of surviving rabbis.
Today, Israel houses the largest concentration of full-time Torah scholars in history.
The numbers dwarf anything that existed in Vilna or Pressburg. Kolels, women’s seminaries, and community kolels have multiplied. Hesed (kindness) networks, food, medical care, burial, and mental-health support operate at a scale the shtetl never imagined.
Observance is not uniform; Israel is argumentative by nature.
Yet the sheer volume of learning, the density of mitzvah performance, and the public presence of Jewish life exceed anything seen since Sinai, and, in raw numbers of people sitting before open volumes, arguably surpass it.
A people that was supposed to vanish rebuilt the very institutions the murderers tried to erase.
None of this was inevitable. It was the product of divine providence, Jewish resilience, improvisation, and a refusal to accept the verdict of demographics, geography, or the General Assembly.
Critics will always list the failures, the uncertainty in Gaza and Judea and Samaria that has lasted too long, political divisions, high costs of war, and the unfinished conflict with the Palestinians.
Those criticisms are not imaginary. They simply do not outweigh the central fact.
A state that should have died in 1948, or 1967, or 1973, or under the weight of boycotts and resolutions, is still here, still growing, still inventing, and still arguing about the meaning of its own existence.
The next 78 years are not guaranteed. Iran’s nuclear program, demographic trends, internal cohesion, mitzvah neglect, and the endurance of Western support all remain open questions. But the record already compiled is not a fluke. It is evidence.
Small peoples with a long memory and a short list of alternatives can rewrite the odds.
Israel did not merely survive. It turned the most lopsided bet of the 20th century into a massive success, and, for millions of Jews who had nowhere else to go, into a home.
That is not a miracle in the sense that it required no human effort. It is a miracle in the only sense that matters: it happened when every reasonable calculation said it would not.
As we start year 5787, let’s be grateful to God for the providential success we’ve enjoyed, the dedication and efforts of our leaders, soldiers, and civil servants who have made this country a success, and commit ourselves to greater Torah observance, dedication to helping our neighbors, and the growth of the Jewish nation.
The writer is a Zionist educator at institutions around the world and recently published a new book, Zionism Today.

Rosh Hashanah 2026: What does ‘shana tova’ mean in an Israel divided by politics? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:07:17 UTC
20:07:17 KST

What do we mean when we wish our friends, acquaintances, and passersby a shana tova (good year)?
If we are speaking on the personal level, the answer is simple: we are speaking of good health, happiness, prosperity, a good education for their children, satisfaction in everything they do, etc.
I suppose this also expresses the hope that we shall have a government that will enable us all to realize all these wishes, such as properly functioning health and education systems, and a solid economy. But all this is innocent and more or less politically neutral.
The moment we come to political issues, both short-term and long-term, we find ourselves in trouble, for here we are deeply divided in our beliefs and aspirations. Nothing exemplifies this division more clearly than the approaching general elections and the current election campaign.
For half of the Jewish population in Israel, the wishes for a good year are for the continued rule of the existing Right/religious coalition, at least for the time being, under its current leader – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
This half of the population is inclined to reject a negotiated settlement of the issues that are the cause of the war on seven fronts of the last three years, supports a major, revolutionary legal reform, and the weakening of the vestiges of Israel’s liberal democracy.
Much of this bloc also wishes Israel to become more religious, and large parts of it do not seek coexistence with Israel’s Arab population – whether citizens or only inhabitants – but rather its “voluntary” emigration.
For the other half of the Jewish population, getting rid of the current government and its head are considered primary goals – not only for ideological reasons, but also because it believes that this government is a badly functioning government in almost all spheres, but most notably health, education, economics, foreign affairs, justice, transportation, and environment.
This part of the population is inclined to believe that the use of military force must be accompanied by diplomacy and clear political goals based on non-religious realpolitik. It believes that the prime minister must be motivated exclusively by national interests rather than by an ambition to remain in power at any price.
Belief that government is tainted by corruption
It is also inclined to believe that the current government is more tainted by corruption and illegality than any previous Israeli government.
There is no doubt that each of the blocs believes that the victory of the other bloc in the election will be a catastrophe, so the “good year” of each side clashes with that of the other. If we wish a good year to whoever we happen to come across, we place ourselves in a stormy medley of irreconcilable contradictions.
Today’s government bloc believes that a government formed after the elections by the current opposition and supported by even a single Arab party – whether or not it includes Jews among its members – will be dangerous to Israel’s security and existence as a Jewish state in the religious sense.
Supporters of this bloc also believe that the return of today’s opposition to power will also cut short the current government’s efforts to do away with an alleged “deep-state” within Israel’s administration, its universities, its legal system, and even its military establishment – a deep-state which prevents the Israeli Right, and the various Jewish religious groups in the state, from effectively manifesting their numerical strength in the Israeli power structure and society.
Parts of the government supporting bloc even believe that certain elements in the opposition – primarily the Democrats and their leader, former IDF deputy chief of staff Yair Golan – are no less than traitors who collaborated with Hamas and other enemies of Israel.
On the other hand, the opposite bloc believes that a victory of the existing government bloc will bring about the end of Israel’s liberal democratic system and turn Israel into an authoritarian state, which disregards the international law on which the State of Israel was established 78 years ago, and is treated as a pariah state by its former friends in the enlightened world.
Furthermore, this bloc believes that Israel has been led for much too long by a man who started as a breath of fresh air, but today is not only flimsy with facts but whose cognitive and decision-making faculties are no longer as sharp as they were in the past, and is no longer surrounded by an entourage that elicits confidence and respect.
Netanyahu’s failure to appoint to the Likud list for the elections respected and inspiring personalities such as former chief of staff Gabi Ashkenazi, former Likud minister and confident Ron Dermer, and former Likud minister Yuval Steinitz (all of whom declined the offer), and the persons who were finally appointed (such as Yaakov Bardugo, a former TV presenter and commentator on channel 14), points to his declining power of persuasion.
The real danger, of course, is that even though there is still a small chance that one of the blocs will win a decisive victory, if neither side manages to form a government after the election – especially if the Arab parties win (as predicted) 13-15 Knesset seats – neither side will actually enjoy much of a good year.
Unless, under such circumstances, the two sides opt for a grand coalition (an unlikely occurrence) and the current government will turn into a transition government, with new elections for the 27th Knesset being called within several months, the situation will only get worse.
Such a development will be more favorably received by the current coalition than by the opposition, but it is still nobody’s vision of a good year.
Why is the vision of a grand Zionist coalition unlikely? First, because the current opposition bloc simply does not trust Netanyahu. Secondly, because a grand coalition would require rotation in the premiership, and as long as Netanyahu is on trial, he can serve as prime minister but not as a minister.
Thirdly, because neither of the two parties running in the elections that advocate such a government – Benny Gantz’s Blue and White, and the new union between Yoaz Hendel’s Reservists Party and Yaron Zelekha’s New Economic Party – are likely to pass the qualifying threshold.
So at the moment, let us stick to personal wishes of a shana tova to everyone, but especially to those wounded physically and/or mentally in the course of fighting during the last three years, and who are far from recovery, and to those who have lost loved ones on October 7, as hostages in the Gaza Strip, or in the fighting on seven fronts in the last three years and are still mourning.
In the final reckoning, we could all do with a better year.

Five sea turtles were released back into the sea on Friday at the Beit Yanai National Park beach after completing their rehabilitation process at the Israel Nature and Parks Authority’s National Sea Turtle Rescue Center.
About 250 people, mostly families and children, arrived at Beit Yanai National Park beach to watch the release of Miriam, Chapa, Matzav, Ran and Nidal, the five sea turtles that made their way back to the sea.
The turtles spent recent months at the National Sea Turtle Rescue Center receiving veterinary care after arriving with limb injuries caused by entanglement in plastic bags. Their rehabilitation has now been completed, and the turtles were released near the shoreline to help them reach the water quickly.
The Israel Nature and Parks Authority emphasized that anyone who finds an injured or dead sea turtle must report it to the authority’s hotline (*3639). The authority instructed the public not to remove strings or plastic waste from sea turtles, but instead to bring the turtle, along with the plastic bag or waste entangling it, to the rescue center for appropriate treatment.
The authority has received reports of numerous sea turtles washing ashore entangled in plastic bags. However, contrary to the authority’s instructions, some people who found the turtles removed the material themselves and returned them to the sea.
Around 50,000 visit nature parks during Rosh Hashanah holiday
The release took place as around 50,000 visitors toured nature reserves and national parks during the Rosh Hashanah holiday, with some visitors witnessing the return of the turtles to their natural habitat.
Among the most visited sites were Habonim Nature Reserve, Ashkelon National Park, Ein Hemed National Park and Yarkon Tel Afek National Park.
Around 2,600 people also chose to spend Rosh Hashanah Eve at the Israel Nature and Parks Authority’s overnight campgrounds, with the most popular locations being Tel Dan and Achziv.

Territorial disputes remain the central obstacle preventing Ukraine and Russia from reaching an agreement to end the war, US presidential special envoy Jared Kushner said on Sunday during the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) forum in Kyiv.
Addressing conference participants, Kushner explained that while mediators have assembled frameworks covering nearly all other facets of a prospective settlement, the division over front lines and sovereign borders has stalled diplomatic efforts.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He stated that Russian President Vladimir Putin had detailed Moscow’s specific territorial objectives during recent Kremlin consultations, but Ukraine firmly refuses to make concessions or pull back its military forces.
“The main issue will be territories, and that is precisely where the sides have not yet reached an agreement,” Kushner said, as reported by Ukrinform.
“President Putin laid out his position regarding what he wants to achieve. If Ukraine wanted to retreat to that line, we would have already prepared and agreed on the remaining terms of the deal. Currently, Ukraine does not want to do this.
And our task as mediators is to figure out how we can find a creative solution that does not contradict their desires, helps them achieve their goals, and compels Russia to end the conflict so both sides can move forward within a framework that prevents a recurrence.”
Russia Fired 2,100 Drones and 78 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
Kushner did not address the widespread war crimes committed by Russian occupation forces or the legal question of Russian accountability for launching the full-scale invasion. Instead, he characterized both nations as enduring “a lot of pain” and asserted that both Kyiv and Moscow harbor a determination to bring fighting to an end.
“[US] President [Donald] Trump is very, very committed to this cause. Steve [Witkoff] and I are very committed. President Zelensky is very committed. From what we have seen and heard, President Putin is also very committed to this cause,” Kushner claimed. “It is simply a matter of finding the right formula that will hopefully satisfy everyone to move forward.”
Pre-winter ceasefire uncertainty and security guarantees
Asked whether a cessation of hostilities could be achieved before the onset of winter, Kushner gave a cautious response, acknowledging that diverse ideas have been floated by multiple actors without achieving a diplomatic breakthrough.
Kushner detailed that diplomatic discussions over recent months have concentrated extensively on future security architecture and security guarantees designed to assure Ukraine that any cessation of combat represents an enduring peace rather than an operational pause for Moscow to regroup.
He stressed that sovereignty, security, and economic prosperity form the three non-negotiable pillars of any just outcome for Ukraine.
Kushner revealed that during previous trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi, delegations from Ukraine, the US, and Russia finalized practical mechanisms for conflict prevention and ceasefire verification involving military personnel. He stated that this monitoring structure is engineered to take effect the moment political leadership resolves the territorial dispute.
“We have developed a monitoring mechanism that involves the military, and everyone agrees that once there is a definitive resolution regarding frontlines or territorial issues, a mechanism will exist that everyone can hopefully abide by,” Kushner explained.
“I think this is something that satisfies both sides, representing genuine progress in that regard.”
Post-war prosperity as an incentive for lasting peace
Outlining subsequent stages of the US diplomatic initiative, Kushner argued that long-term stability must be anchored in economic prosperity and mutual financial incentives.
He contended that both Ukraine and Russia should leverage a post-war settlement to attract international capital, create jobs, and raise living standards, suggesting that societal economic interest in stability serves as the most effective defense against renewed conflict.
“When you end a war, people must have something to look forward to,” Kushner said, asserting that President Trump shares this philosophy.
“Both countries need to consider how they can seize this opportunity after the war to attract investments, create employment, provide greater prosperity, and increase incomes. That is what motivates societies to invest in and feel enthusiastic about peace. In many ways, it becomes your greatest security guarantee. If everyone lives well and maintains a personal stake in security, it will hopefully produce something durable and sustainable.”
Kushner’s remarks arrive following multi-stage consultations held in Kyiv on Sept. 6 alongside fellow envoy Witkoff and European national security advisers, which succeeded a three-hour meeting with Putin in Moscow. During those talks, Putin insisted on achieving his stated war aims, with Kremlin insiders reiterating that Moscow will refuse any frontline ceasefire until Russian forces capture the entire Donbas.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior Ukrainian officials have categorically dismissed territorial concessions as unacceptable capitulation, maintaining that restoring territorial integrity and securing legally binding Western defense guarantees remain indispensable to any durable settlement.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Dover unrest exposes serious flaws in Britain’s handling of far-right extremism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:00:06 UTC
20:00:06 KST

To anybody watching the videos of a group of masked men, all wearing black, descending on the port of Dover last weekend, it was immediately obvious that something novel and disturbing was happening: a mass intimidation in uniform not seen in Britain since the 1930s.
Yet to the police and the rest of the UK’s intelligence apparatus, the arrival of the men chanting “stop the boats” was a surprise, despite the fact that residents of a village 18 miles away tried to report that dozens of men were congregating there on the Friday, threatening to go to Dover and “attack Muslims”.
Intelligence specialists describe the events in Dover and the day after in Portsmouth as protests, as if they are on a par with cardboard-carrying campaigners marching on an approved route. The same definition was used by Kent police and Sarah Jones, the policing minister, on Monday. “Protest activity,” she told MPs.
Such semantics are important to the state, though they appear to misunderstand the recent events. In a democracy, it is argued it is not the job of MI5 and police to spy on campaign groups, as undercover police did so zealously on leftwing groups from the 1960s to the 1990s, sending reports to the Security Service.
Nigel Brookes, an assistant chief constable at Kent police, said this week: “The right to peaceful protest is an important part of our democracy and applies irrespective of the political views being expressed.” No arrests were made in Dover, though traffic was halted for several hours before the masked men dispersed.
The contrast with Palestine Action is sharp. The group was designated and banned as a terror organisation after some members broke into RAF Brize Norton and sprayed two military planes with red paint.
Terror arrests in Great Britain were at record levels for the year to March as thousands of mostly elderly supporters were arrested, many holding placards reading: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
Monitoring every protest group would be too intrusive, it is argued. Yet Patriot Platform, created in June by the far-right agitator Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, is clearly somewhat different, with its emphasis on recruitment of “English men”, vetting, uniforms and hostility to migrants arriving in the UK by small boats.
“In the next three or four weeks, we are going to ask you to be part of one of the biggest pushbacks this country has seen from its men since world war two. Are you up for it or what?” Thomas was reported by Searchlight as having said at a “national recruitment day” event at Burton Dassett, south of Coventry, last month.
The language is calibrated, not explicitly racially charged or inciteful. Those dressed in balaclavas and black were careful to avoid violence in Dover, though there were clashes the night after in Portsmouth. Police used batons and synthetic pepper spray to control people blocking the road away from the port, down which 120 disembarked migrants were expected to be taken for processing.
It appears that the aspiration is to agitate or provoke at a level just below the criminal threshold: grey zone tactics. In Dover, protesters were handing out a “legal reference sheet” justifying their right to obstruct the highway outside the port where migrants on boats are taken to and processed, citing the rights to freedom of expression and freedom of assembly under the Human Rights Act.
The question is, where is this heading? That is difficult to predict, but it is the job of intelligence to discover and assess genuine risks to the public and the country. Perhaps it is reasonable for masked gangs to block roads and turn up outside newspaper offices, but there is the possibility that intimidatory actions could escalate. The situation at Portsmouth, a day after Dover, was notably more tense, and the RNLI, the lifeboat charity, has stepped up security at south coast sites.
Nick Lowles, from the campaign group Hope Not Hate, said: “One of the ways in which the police were able to swiftly shut down far-right activity during the riots in 2024 [after the Southport attack] was making arrests.
“This time, the police response exposes serious failings in the authorities’ approach” to intimidatory far-right activity, he added. Being caught by surprise in Dover was flat-footed at best.
