Amit Shah says decolonising knowledge not about erasing history, but reclaiming India's narrative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:39:00 UTC
19:39:00 KST

Amit Shah says decolonising India’s history means presenting it from an Indian perspective
NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday said decolonisation of India's history and knowledge does not mean erasing the past, but presenting historical truth authentically and from an Indian perspective.Shah made the remarks while inaugurating the 'Ganesh Gyanarthi' exhibition at the Asiatic Society of Mumbai. He said India's knowledge traditions, manuscripts and archives should be preserved and taken to people across the country and the world.“Decolonisation does not mean erasing history. From our perspective, it means presenting historical truth to the world in an authentic manner and from an Indian perspective,” Shah said, as cited by news agency PTI.He said the British had intertwined knowledge and power and argued that the task now was to free knowledge from that framework.“Today, we are moving forward to liberate knowledge from that and towards decolonisation,” Shah said.
‘True knowledge is never held hostage by an ideology’
Shah said knowledge should remain free from ideological constraints and criticised the colonial interpretation of India's intellectual traditions.“True knowledge is never held hostage by an ideology. Knowledge itself is an ideology.
If you bind it in any way, you change the very meaning of knowledge. Knowledge should be free and uninhibited, and its declaration should also be free and uninhibited,” he said, according to ANI.“India's knowledge was not being written in India's voice. India's knowledge was being written in the language of a colonial perspective,” Shah said.
He said the focus should now be on using the wealth and collections preserved at the Asiatic Society for the creation of a “Great India”.“Rather than going into why the Asiatic Society was formed, who formed it, and for what purpose, we should move forward in the direction of how the wealth, knowledge, and collections gathered here can be used in the creation of a Great India (Mahaan Bharat),” he said.
Shah highlights manuscripts, proposes wider knowledge network
Shah highlighted the rare manuscripts preserved at the Asiatic Society, including an illustrated copy of the Mahabharata and texts related to Jainism and Buddhism.“A great deal of things are lying here, including an illustrated copy of the Mahabharata. Such texts of Jain Kalpasutra and Buddhism are hardly available anywhere else; such texts are lying here. Much knowledge is present here that should have come out a long time ago,” he said.Shah called on the new committee to expand the institution's reach by bringing scholars from Maharashtra and across India to study its collections. He also proposed bringing libraries and institutions preserving heritage across the country onto a common platform under the Asiatic Society.He suggested creating a shared pool of knowledge that could be made available to students, researchers and scholars.
Shah further proposed a campaign to collect ancestral documents preserved in villages and households across Maharashtra and link them with the Gyan Bharatam manuscript survey.“Because within these manuscripts lies immense knowledge, and there is a need to conduct research on this knowledge. A great power to take the nation forward lies within them,” he said.Referring to Nalanda, Shah said attempts to destroy physical repositories could not eliminate knowledge preserved through memory and tradition.“One can burn the library of Nalanda... but the knowledge that resides in people's minds as memory and tradition (Smriti and Shruti)—no one can destroy that knowledge,” he said.Shah said the Asiatic Society should work with the government and institutions across India to preserve and share India's knowledge traditions. He urged the new team to use Indology for the welfare of the country and the wider world.

Trump’s 51st state threat backfires as Canada turns to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:34:11 UTC
19:34:11 KST

After decades in which the United States was its main economic and strategic partner, Canada is beginning to reconsider the direction it wants to take. According to The Wall Street Journal, amid the trade war, President Donald Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state and strained relations with Washington, Prime Minister Mark Carney is pursuing a significant rapprochement with Europe — including exploring a model that would allow Canada to integrate more deeply with the European Union.
According to the American newspaper, shortly after Canada and the U.S. became embroiled in a bilateral trade war, Carney began calling European leaders and asking to take Canada’s relationship with the European Union to the next level. For months, he spoke with leaders across the continent and even with members of some of Europe’s lesser-known royal families in an effort to explore how his country could become more closely integrated with the 27-member bloc.
In fact, the Journal reported, the threat to turn Canada into the 51st U.S. state pushed America’s northern neighbor so close to Europe that leaders began half-jokingly referring to it as the European Union’s newest member. According to people familiar with the matter who spoke with the American newspaper, Carney instructed his special envoy to Europe to explore the most ambitious options available, short of full EU membership.
Working groups are still hammering out the details, but Carney has even floated a new designation for Canada to European leaders: “associate member of the European Union.” Officials on both sides told the Journal that the EU, which is not known for flexibility in enforcing its membership rules, is open to the idea.
European and Canadian officials are exploring ways Canada could informally integrate into Europe’s market in areas such as energy, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and, with greater urgency, defense. In practical terms, that could eventually allow goods and workers in those sectors to move freely between Europe and Canada. According to two people familiar with discussions between Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron, they even discussed the possibility of allowing Canadians to live and work in Europe without a visa.
In the energy sector, Carney is promoting the construction of pipelines that would allow Canada to redirect to Europe gas that currently flows through the United States. Officials are also considering expanding the transportation of goods via Arctic shipping routes. The initiative comes after decades in which the Canadian economy became increasingly integrated with the U.S. economy.
The White House is betting that the two countries’ mutual dependence will draw Canada back to the negotiating table more willing to make concessions. Carney, however, believes he can fundamentally change that dynamic.
But such a new alliance would also have consequences: Canada may be reluctant to surrender any degree of sovereignty in order to integrate with the European Union. Countries that trade freely with the EU, for example, generally contribute money to its budget, accept its workers and comply with its regulations.
In private discussions, according to the Journal, some of Europe’s most senior officials have expressed concern about the challenge of reconciling Carney’s ambitions with reality. During their meetings, EU officials have tried to determine whether the Canadians are merely using Europe as leverage in their negotiations with Washington. On Thursday, Carney is expected to address the European Parliament and lay out his vision for strengthening ties with Europe.
Trade war and 'annexation' in a social media post
About two-thirds of Canadian exports currently cross the U.S. border, but two and a half weeks ago, in a sharp response to the sweeping tariffs Trump imposed on Canada, the country announced that it would impose tariffs of up to 50% on imports from the United States. The measures cover about $20 billion worth of goods and some 700 products. Tariffs of 50% will be imposed on steel, dairy products, electrical appliances and agricultural equipment, among other goods.
The previous weekend, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian goods following the collapse of talks on a trade agreement between the two countries. The Canadian tariffs took effect Sept. 8 and are expected to drive up prices for American consumers. Canada is the United States’ second-largest trading partner after Mexico. In the first half of 2026, about 14% of all U.S. exports went to Canada.
Three days after Canada’s announcement, Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America,” marking a further escalation in relations between the two countries.
“The lake change, 'Lake of America', was something I've been thinking about for a long time,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both.”
Asked why he was so intent on antagonizing Washington’s allies, Trump replied: “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They're nasty people.”
"People oftentimes they'll ask me who's the worst to deal with on trade, and I said that's easy, Canada. They are the worst to trade, and they feel entitled, and just we can't have that," he added
Over the past month, Trump has published a series of posts attacking Canada after declaring his desire to “annex Canada and make it the 51st state” and even depicting the country as part of the United States.

China, Russia, India push for inclusive global growth at BRICS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:32:41 UTC
19:32:41 KST

BRICS leaders have concluded two days of talks in New Delhi focused on inclusive global growth, after reaching a rare agreement calling for calm in the Middle East.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged cooperation within the bloc on Sunday, addressing leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The power of BRICS lies in our diversity and cooperation,” Modi said. “We have tried to push inclusive global growth.”
Putin said the bloc was working to create a “new, more just, multipolar world order”.
Xi warned that a “world without rules is like an intersection without traffic lights; chaos and disorder are inevitable”.
Modi has said the bloc represents 50 percent of the world’s population, 40 percent of global GDP and more than 25 percent of global trade.
“We may be rooted in different realities, but together we rise through cooperation and blossom for humanity,” he said.
Created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers, BRICS is seeking to expand its global role while addressing conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
'Maximum restraint'
The Middle East conflict dominated Saturday’s opening talks, with leaders, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, issuing a joint statement after intense diplomatic efforts by host India.
“We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in the Middle East/West Asia,” the statement said, calling for “maximum restraint”.
The agreement followed a failure by BRICS foreign ministers to reach a joint statement in New Delhi in May, when Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
Modi maintains relations with both Iran and US ally Israel, while carefully managing India’s ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war partly by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s full-scale war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
'Advancing together'
Xi's participation in BRICS was also important because it was his first visit to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
His visit came six years after a deadly military clash along the disputed Tibetan border between China and India, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
"Although our two countries are different in many respects, they are fully capable of complementing each other's strengths, supporting one another, achieving mutual success and advancing together," Xi said as he met Modi, according to a video released by New Delhi.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border.
In a statement released after the meeting, India's foreign ministry said that the two leaders had expressed their commitment to finding a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution to the boundary dispute.
Deep mistrust remains, with a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry complicating ties.
"Both sides should... work hand-in-hand to promote high-quality major financial cooperation, advocate an equal and sustainable global order, and foster an economic globalisation that is open and inclusive," Xi said.
Xi's visit was the target of protests by dozens of Tibetans in New Delhi, exiles like their Buddhist leader, the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959.

Reform UK’s £72m donations may be caught by new bill, Rayner suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:31:44 UTC
19:31:44 KST

Reform UK’s record £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires could be caught in a new bill which will apply retrospectively, a cabinet minister has suggested.
Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week to restrict domestic donations in the elections bill after two donors – Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend.
Several MPs said they believed the government should have adopted an amendment by the Labour MP Stella Creasy to the representation of the people bill. Creasy’s amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it had the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote after the government said it would ask a taskforce to look at the proposal.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, said the bill would have restrictions on foreign donors and that the government was examining rules on domestic donations. The bill will go to the House of Lords this week.
The two donors who gave Reform UK £36m each have both previously been based outside the UK. Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. It is unclear when Delo returned to live in the UK and whether Harborne remains a resident of Thailand.
As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March. Reform UK has said it is confident the donations have been made within the law.
“All donations to Reform UK comply strictly with Electoral Commission rules and UK law,” a spokesperson said. “Both men are British citizens who are fully entitled to support political change in their own country, despite the establishment’s desperate attempts to silence opposition.”
The restrictions came after recommendations in a review of overseas donations by the former permanent secretary Philip Rycroft.
The government has said the rules will apply from the date the Rycroft review was published – 25 March – if donors were registered as overseas electors, or if they were not registered then it would date back to 6 July which is the date the government announced its response to the review.
Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme that the government had been clear in its intentions since the review was published and had always said the changes would be retrospective.
“We’re really clear on that. And that legislation is going through parliament at the moment. And we’ve also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy,” she said.
Rayner – the minister responsible for the bill – said it was not targeted at individual donors or parties. “I’m not going to get into individual donors and their money … People can see the 17 recommendations which the government has accepted.
“This was before these donations came through, to be fair. We didn’t know that donors were going to be putting that money in, and this isn’t about individual donors to a political party. This is an issue that has been raised about protecting our democracy from foreign interference, and the government is taking action on that.”
Reform’s economy spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the two donors were well aware of the law. He said: “[Ben Delo] has actually returned to the UK in part so that he can comply with the changes to law.
“Now, look, it might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform. Nothing would surprise me, but as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law.
“And I just say it’s a huge vote of confidence in Reform. It’s a breakthrough moment, really, for the party. It means that we will be battle ready if Andy Burnham calls an election, and we can compete now finally on a fair, even playing field with the two old parties.”

Try These 3 iOS 27 Safari Settings to Get More Out of Apple’s Browser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

At Apple’s recent hardware event, the software powering its foldable iPhone Duo stood out, with translucent Liquid Glass effects and vertically stacked icons. But you don’t need to snatch a folding smartphone to reap the benefits of Apple’s iOS 27 updates.
When iOS 27 leaves beta on Monday, Siri AI’s standalone app and smartphone search integration will likely be the most immediately obvious change for many iPhone users. But it’s worth digging even deeper to uncover helpful additions to key apps, like Apple’s Safari browser, as well as revamps to underutilized apps, like Shortcuts.
The version of Safari available in iOS 27 looks fairly similar to the last iteration, with a few key updates tucked away in the settings. These Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer (they're also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27).
Notify Me
If you’re shopping online and want a quick price-drop notification, you can use the “Notify Me” feature to scan a webpage on a certain cadence and look for changes. First, head to the page you want to track and tap the three-lined hamburger menu icon in the top right corner of Safari. About halfway down, you’ll see this option listed.
“Safari can let you know when a website updates the content you’re interested in,” reads the feature’s description. Here you’ll find an open text box where you can describe what change in content you want Safari to scan for, as well as how often you want it to check.
For example, my couch is broken, so I’ve been eyeing a few different replacement options. I have two final contenders from CB2, but both are out of my price range. So, I set up a “Notify Me” for Safari to scan the pages each day for a significant discount. Whichever one goes on sale first will likely be what I decide to get, and now I don’t have to refresh the pages manually every day.
While many other browsers have similar shopping features, like the price-tracking bell in Google Chrome, I appreciate how this feature stretches beyond just buying stuff. You can also use Safari to scan for ticket drops, privacy policy changes, and other content updates.
Describe an Extension
If you’ve experimented already with the “Describe a Shortcut” feature for iPhone automation, then “Describe an Extension” for Safari will seem familiar. It's located under the same settings menu as the “Notify Me” tool, just a little further down.
The feature asks you to type what you want the extension to do, then generates a custom option. Some of the suggested prompts in Safari revolve around boosting productivity, like “display a reading time estimate as a badge on the extension,” maintaining better focus, like “make the web page grayscale,” and more random ideas, like “show a colorful and explosive firework every time I tap.”
It took only a few seconds for each of those three examples to generate. Safari also suggests pre-made extensions during the process that could fit what you’re looking to do. As I scrolled through the internet with all three of the new extensions activated, everything worked as expected. While I’ll likely only keep the grayscale one to help me focus while reading online articles, the fireworks felt whimsical in small doses.
Organize Tabs
I am a glutton for mobile tabs, especially on Safari. I’m rarely ever exiting out of anything and always just pop open something new, which leaves me with hundreds upon hundreds of loosely connected, completely unorganized tabs—until now.
This feature is in the wider browser tab view accessible by tapping the two overlapping squares at the bottom-right corner of your screen. Swipe to a tab group brimming with websites and look for the three-lined button in the top-left. Here’s where you can choose to allow Safari to “automatically create topics” based on those tabs.
It takes a few seconds to organize everything after you activate this feature, but it did a great job of finding helpful trends in those 500+ tabs. For example, it grouped all the WIRED articles I had open and created a tab topic for upcoming San Francisco event pages and comedy clubs I was considering checking out.

Ukraine Warns Putin 'Knocking On NATO's Door' After Russian Drones Hit Sites Near Polish Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:26:43 UTC
19:26:43 KST

Two Russian drone strikes hit near the Polish border early on September 13, Ukrainian authorities have reported, attacks that Kyiv said was Moscow "knocking on the doors of the EU and NATO" and urged further sanctions.
The first strike hit a petrol station near the Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine, in the country's Volyn region. The checkpoint was temporarily closed but has since reopened, with no casualties reported in the incident.
The second, also in Volyn, struck the locomotive of a passenger train just two kilometers from the Polish border, Ukrainian Railways reported. According to Oleksandr Shevchenko, a local transportation official, the train was traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw.
As Ukrainian Railways said that a threat-monitoring group was able to warn the train's crew of the attack in advance, no casualties were reported. Video footage spread over Ukrainian social media showed people running from the blast at the railway station.
Air-raid alerts were issued in several eastern districts of Poland around the time of the strikes.
While there were no reports of violations of Polish airspace, Jacek Goryszewski, spokesman for the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces, said the "threat to Poland was real."
In separate incidents on September 13, Romanian authorities reported a drone entering the country, and Lithuania called on residents in the capital and neighboring regions to preventively seek shelter after issuing an alert of possible drone sighting.
The country's main airport in Vilnius was shut down and NATO jets were scrambled. The alert was called off within an hour.
The strikes in Ukraine come as Russia has stepped up its attacks on civilian and logistics infrastructure across the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a total of 2,100 drones, 1,700 gliding bombs, and 73 missiles were launched at targets across Ukraine in the past week.
"Russia's barbaric strikes at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn are not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X on September 13. "This is Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO."
He urged European leaders to "throw the full weight" of sanctions against Russia.
"Make Moscow feel the consequences of its terror. Not just half-decisions, but uncompromising, powerful steps. Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex," he wrote.
Earlier this month, Germany officially blamed an incident on Moscow in which explosive-laden drones interrupted flights at Leipzig Airport. At the time, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europeans are faced with a hard truth that this is the new normal."
"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every single day, laying down their lives to keep this aggression from expanding," Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram on September 13.
"Russian terrorism is a shared threat to many, but it can and must be defeated right here in Ukraine," he added.
According to Ukrainian authorities, the latest Russian attacks on Ukraine had also targeted the country’s western regions of Ivano-Frankivsk, Ternopil, and Lviv, as well as the key southern region of Odesa.
Regional authorities in the Odesa region said nine people had been injured after a drone struck several residential buildings. A warehouse in the region was also reportedly targeted.
Rescuers previously completed work at the site of the drone strike on a 25-story residential building in Odesa on the night of September 12. Two people were killed and more than 20 injured in that attack.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that its overnight strikes targeted "logistics centers through which military cargo is delivered and distributed, as well as energy facilities that support their operation."
The ministry also reported strikes on railway infrastructure in western Ukraine.
Russia denies targeting civilian areas despite widespread evidence of such attacks that have killed thousands of people since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Celine Dion’s return to the stage underscores a remarkable comeback after Stiff Person Syndrome forced her to cancel shows.
Celine Dion on Sept. 11 fulfilled her dream of returning to the stage after years battling a rare neurological disorder with a sell-out concert in an arena west of Paris.
The 58-year-old French Canadian singer appeared visibly moved as she opened her first full concert in six years with her 1990s French-language ballad “On ne change pas” (‘One Doesn’t Change’), singing to a crowd of around 30,000 people.
She paused briefly overcome by emotion, before enthralled fans chanted her name at the end of the opening number.
Her return to the stage underscored a remarkable comeback after Stiff Person Syndrome forced her to cancel shows and cast years of uncertainty over whether she would ever perform again.
“Finally — it’s amazing we are all together,” she said, speaking in English and French to fans who had packed the Plenitude Arena on the western edge of Paris for the sold-out opening night of her 26-show run.
“The path was rockier than expected,” she said. “But I held on to a faint ray of light in the distance, deep in the mountains. Tonight, I want to sing for you, sing for myself, sing for life,” she added.
The largely female crowd sported sequined dresses and tops, glittered cheeks, and T-shirts emblazoned with the star’s image or nods to her biggest hits.
Just hours before, one of the best-selling singers of all time greeted admirers outside her luxury hotel a short walk from the Arc de Triomphe.
Paris spared no effort in welcoming Dion, drawing thousands of fans from across the world, including some who flew in from as far away as the French Polynesian island of Tahiti.
Dion has regularly stepped outside the Royal Monceau hotel to greet waiting fans, at times breaking into song and dance with them well into the early hours.
On Sept. 11, hundreds turned out for a free singalong in the city’s northeast, swaying and warbling along to some of Dion’s best-known tunes. Over her four-decade career, Dion has sold around 260 million albums in English and French, with hits including “It’s All Coming Back to Me Now” and “Because You Loved Me.”
In December 2022, she revealed that she had been diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome, a rare and incurable autoimmune disorder that can cause severe muscle stiffness and agonizing spasms.
Dion has described the condition as making her feel as though she is being strangled, with cramps so intense they have left her with broken ribs.

5 key points from Anthropic CEO’s call to slow frontier AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:23:37 UTC
19:23:37 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for the development of the world’s most advanced artificial intelligence systems to proceed at a more controlled pace, arguing that safety measures are struggling to keep up with rapidly expanding capabilities.
In his essay, We Must Pace the Frontier, Amodei outlines emerging risks and proposes a three-stage framework involving independent evaluators, coordination among democratic countries and eventual global agreements.
 
Here are five key points from his proposal:
1. AI is beginning to accelerate its own development
Amodei’s central concern is recursive self-improvement — the growing ability of AI systems to help design, train, and improve the next generation of models.
He argues that this feedback loop could sharply accelerate advances in AI capabilities, leaving researchers with insufficient time to understand how increasingly powerful systems behave or ensure that they remain under human control.
 
2. Warning signs have moved beyond hypothetical scenarios
Amodei cites incidents in which groups of AI agents displayed unintended, coordinated behavior, including conducting cyber operations outside their assigned tasks and attempting to interfere with systems evaluating their performance.
While those incidents caused limited harm, he argues that similar behavior by more capable systems could have severe consequences. He warns that within six to 12 months, an advanced but misaligned swarm of agents might be capable of establishing a persistent botnet across the internet and causing massive economic damage.
 
3. ‘Pacing’ AI does not mean stopping progress
Amodei distinguishes his proposal from a complete moratorium on AI research or model training.
His aim is to keep improvements in AI capabilities from moving faster than work on alignment, interpretability, testing, and operational security. Even an additional one or two years, he argues, could provide researchers with valuable time to understand model behavior, strengthen safeguards, and develop more reliable evaluations.
 
4. Anthropic will invite independent evaluators inside the company
The first and most immediate part of the plan involves embedding third-party evaluators within frontier AI companies.
Anthropic says external reviewers will receive access similar to that given to employees conducting internal risk assessments, including access to relevant tools, workspaces, and development processes.
The evaluators would verify whether the company is honoring its safety commitments, investigate incidents, and publish key findings without editorial control from Anthropic, subject to limited legal, security, and confidentiality restrictions.
 
5. AI safety ultimately requires international coordination
Amodei proposes coordination first among frontier AI companies operating in democratic countries, supported by governments and common safety standards.
At the international level, he advocates seeking verifiable agreements with China and other governments. Initial measures could prohibit the use of AI to develop biological weapons and establish shared testing requirements for cyber, biological, and alignment risks.
More ambitious agreements could impose limits on recursive self-improvement or the overall pace of AI development. Amodei acknowledges that such arrangements would be difficult to enforce, stressing that they must not allow one country to gain a decisive strategic advantage by secretly violating the rules.

Kremlin hints at returning to tripartite Ukraine talks in October
Unknown

2026-09-13
10:23:00 UTC
19:23:00 KST

The Kremlin said Sunday that three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. on ending Europe's worst conflict since World War II could be held in October, Russian media reported.
"We do not rule out such a possibility; we are talking about the foreseeable future," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists, according to Russia's Ria Novosti and Tass news agencies.
Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled efforts to end the more than four-year war, with U.S. negotiators visiting Kyiv and Moscow, and U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin speaking by phone.
Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed, while U.S.-led efforts stalled.
In an interview released Saturday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G-20 summit for talks.
But Peskov immediately ruled it out as "impossible," speaking to AFP in New Delhi Saturday, repeating Moscow's demand that a meeting only take place in the Russian capital.
Zelenskyy's chief of staff also said Saturday Ukraine expects talks on a peace settlement to resume next month.
"We are preparing for October," Kyrylo Budanov told journalists, confirming the talks would take place in a three-way format. He did not give a precise date or location for the meetings.
U.S. negotiators visited Moscow and Kyiv last weekend to explore a peaceful resolution to the war in Ukraine. They also discussed the possible resumption of the three-way dialogue, suspended for months.
Negotiators conduct the talks and must consult their heads of state throughout the process. A direct meeting between the presidents of the U.S., Russia and Ukraine is only expected at the end.
The U.S. last mediated in February, during direct talks between Russia and Ukraine in Switzerland. Budanov was part of the Ukrainian delegation at the time.
Putin, however, has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face meeting with Zelenskyy to broker an end to the conflict, which has killed thousands and crippled both countries' economies.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have escalated long-range strikes against each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.
Previous rounds of talks have foundered, with Moscow so far unwilling to drop its demands to end the fighting, including that Ukraine cede territory in the east not captured by Russian troops.
On Sunday, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov told journalists, including AFP, there is so far no "coordinated package" on which to base negotiations.
"Currently, the idea is to agree on the territorial issue. But there are also many other questions," he added.

Russia Faces Shortage of Chinese Drone Jet Engines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:22:00 UTC
19:22:00 KST

Russia is experiencing operational disruptions in obtaining Chinese-manufactured jet engines for its long-range strike drones following coordinated diplomatic and intelligence interventions by Ukraine and its international partners, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
Speaking at the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) conference in Kyiv, Deputy Head of the Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) Vadym Skibitsky underscored the critical necessity of expanding multilateral sanctions targeting supply chains that sustain Moscow’s aerial bombardment capabilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“That is why I emphasize once again: international sanctions are needed. Today, the Russian Federation has certain problems with jet engines for drones. We are talking about engines from China. This is the result of our actions and the actions of our partners,” Skibitsky stated.
The intelligence official noted that Beijing is acutely aware of the regulatory and economic risks facing its domestic industrial sector if it deepens its commercial and logistical entanglement with Russia’s wartime defense industry.
Skibitsky added that Ukrainian military intelligence has mapped the full network of Russian enterprises and joint production ventures operating alongside Chinese suppliers. However, he cautioned that targeting these installations directly remains an operational challenge due to geographic depth.
“Unfortunately, they are located far from our border – at a distance of over 2,000 kilometers. Hitting such targets is not easy. This is possible only with long-range strike assets, particularly unmanned aerial vehicles,” Skibitsky explained.
Drones Target Nizhnekamsk Hub and Slavyansk Refinery in Russia
Manufacturing bottlenecks
In recent weeks, the Russian military has increasingly relied on turbojet-powered loitering munitions and hybrid drone-missiles as its primary aerial strike vector against Ukrainian urban centers and critical infrastructure.
The primary platforms deployed include the Geran-4 and lower-cost “Banderol” loitering munitions.
Despite their heavy operational deployment, Ukrainian technical analysts indicate that Moscow is grappling with inventory constraints.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian presidency on defense technology, stated that Russian forces currently lack sufficient stockpiles of jet-powered Shaheds to stage the mass saturation raids seen earlier in the war, when hundreds of propeller-driven drones were launched simultaneously.
Instead, Beskrestnov noted that the Russian military is fielding newly produced jet drones literally straight off the assembly line to sustain continuous pressure against Ukrainian air defenses.
Air defense challenges posed by turbojet systems
The deployment of turbojet engines represents a major evolution from earlier propeller-driven Shahed models powered by internal combustion engines.
Equipped with miniature aircraft-grade turbine engines, the newer drones operate at altitudes of several kilometers and achieve speeds between 400 and 600 kilometers per hour, nearly three times faster than piston-engine variants.
Their increased velocity and cruising altitude allow them to outpace Ukraine’s primary fleet of propeller-driven anti-drone interceptors, effectively functioning in an air defense profile more comparable to low-altitude cruise missiles.
While Ukrainian air defenses routinely intercept over 90% of slower Shahed variants, interception rates for jet-powered drones have hovered near 60%, forcing the Ukrainian military to commit high-end surface-to-air missiles and combat aircraft to counter the threat.
Technical teardowns of captured munitions have repeatedly identified Chinese-sourced components within the guidance and propulsion systems of Russian drones.
Chinese manufacturers – such as Shenzhen-based Telefly Telecommunications Equipment – have supplied microturbine engines and electronic sub-assemblies to Russian defense contractors.
Although Western sanctions have targeted shell companies and intermediaries facilitating component transfers through Hong Kong and third countries, Ukrainian defense officials have reiterated that throttling the flow of foreign turbine engines remains pivotal to containing Russian long-range aerial assaults.

The Royal Albert Hall's official website states that "flags are permitted at the Proms but are traditionally part of the Last Night celebrations provided they do not interfere with the smooth running of the concert."
Brexit turns 10
Ten years on from the UK's historic Brexit referendum, the nation's decision to leave the European Union appears as divisive as ever.
The vote has received renewed attention over the last two years as the ruling Labour party embarked on a campaign to rebuild relations with the EU under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who pledged to "put Britain at the heart of Europe."
Starmer had agreed a Brexit "reset" with Brussels in 2025 that he said would slash "red tape and bureaucracy" as part of a drive to tackle the cost-of-living crisis and create new jobs.

Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles hit Russian chemical plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:20:19 UTC
19:20:19 KST

- Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant in Volgograd, Russia, with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles overnight on September 10-11, 2026.
- The U.S.-sanctioned facility produces combustion catalysts and other chemicals used in Russian aviation, shipbuilding and defense manufacturing.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a Russian chemical plant in Volgograd overnight on September 10-11, 2026, using FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missiles, according to Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that manufactures the weapon. Fire Point said the missiles hit their target directly and sparked a large fire at the facility.
The target, Volgogradpromproekt, is a specialty chemicals producer in Volgograd’s Kirovsky district. The company is under U.S. sanctions for supporting Russia’s military-industrial complex. It manufactures ferrocene-based combustion catalysts along with other chemicals, including organophosphorus compounds, flame retardants and resins, and Ukrainian monitoring groups say its products feed into Russian aviation, shipbuilding and defense manufacturing.
Ukrainian OSINT group Exilenova+ published satellite imagery it said showed one of the missiles had destroyed a roughly 20-by-15-meter section of the plant’s main production building. That damage estimate comes from the group’s own imagery analysis and has not been independently confirmed by other sources.
“Flamingos paid a little visit to Volgograd last night,” Fire Point said in a statement. “Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective.”
Russian officials offered a more limited account of the strike. Volgograd region Gov. Andrey Bocharov said only that debris from the attack had landed on the grounds of an industrial facility in the southern part of the city, a description that stops short of Fire Point’s claim of confirmed direct hits.
Defense analysts at Defence Express have suggested a reason Ukraine chose a large cruise missile over a cheaper drone for this particular target. The combustion catalysts Volgogradpromproekt produces are used in manufacturing solid rocket propellant, a component needed for missiles including Russia’s Iskander and Zircon systems. An FP-5, carrying roughly a metric ton of explosives, can do far more damage to a hardened industrial target than a drone strike, which may explain the choice of weapon for a plant that had not previously appeared on lists of well-known Russian defense contractors.
The FP-5 Flamingo is a ground-launched cruise missile that entered service in August 2025. Fire Point says it can carry a payload of up to 1,150 kg (2,535 lb) to targets as far as 3,000 km (1,860 miles) away, operating day or night and resisting electronic jamming.
The company describes it as the largest missile in its class while emphasizing that it remains relatively simple and inexpensive to build, with reusable launchers instead of costly dedicated launch platforms.
The strike on Volgogradpromproekt was one of several Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory reported the same night. Fire Point said its FP-1 drones separately struck an oil refinery and an Ozon logistics warehouse in Saratov, with the warehouse covering roughly 85,000 square meters and reportedly capable of storing more than 30 million items. A refinery in Volgograd was also targeted in a separate drone attack that night, according to local reports.

Danish drama wins big at Venice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

Danish director May El-Toukhy (R) and Danish actress Mathilde Arcel pose on the red carpet following the closing ceremony of the festival.
"Woman Unknown,” a drama about Denmark in the aftermath of the Nazi occupation directed by May el-Toukhy, won the prestigious Golden Lion at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Sept. 12.
The Maggie Gyllenhaal -led jury announced the winners, which included a best actor prize for John Malkovich for his performance in the dark CIA comedy “Wild Horse Nine.”
Malkovich was not in attendance at the ceremony, but he sent a video message, explaining that he is shooting in Montreal.
“I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” Malkovich said.
El-Toukhy, who was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year, is the eighth woman to have won the festival’s top prize.
“To me personally, ‘Woman Unknown’ is about the female body as a battleground,” el-Toukhy said. “At the same time the film tells the tale of women who are unseen, invisible and voiceless.”
She thanked Gyllenhaal for using her voice to shine a light on unequal opportunities for women in moviemaking.
The film, which does not yet have distribution in North America, is centered on a young nanny and housemaid who is about to marry her wealthy employer in the immediate aftermath of the war. But she harbors a secret past intimate relationship with a German soldier that threatens to upend her reputation. The lead, Mathilde Arcel, won the festival’s best actress prize.
Arcel was visibly emotional as she accepted the award, which she placed on the floor as she spoke as she said it was very heavy.
“This is my first lead role in a movie and my first time at a film festival,” she said. “I’m extremely honored.”
South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s poetic portrait of class and labor, “Possible Love,” won the Silver Lion grand jury prize. “Possible Love” is Lee’s first film in eight years, following his acclaimed “Burning.”
“We are living in an era where the meaning of labor is fading and human connections are increasingly becoming severed,” Lee said through a translator. “I made this film to ask what cinema can and should do in times like these. I take this award as a sign that you want me to keep asking these questions.”
“NAZA,” a harrowing documentary about military strategies employed in the war in Gaza from Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was awarded a special jury prize.
“It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the people, the Israeli politicians, the journalists back home who are attacking this film, denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said. “It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film.”
The was added to the main competition late — at the request of the filmmakers — and debuted late in the schedule as well, but its impact was felt as it received a record-breaking standing ovation, lasting some 25 minutes, after its premiere.
Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years, “NAZA” features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders including intelligence officers and soldiers give who insight into the war in Gaza and what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians.
The jury gave the Silver Lion for directing to Ilya Krzhanovsky for his film “Dau,” a project about the Soviet physicists who built the atomic bomb that has taken over 20 years to make. Krzhanovsky, who renounced his Russian citizenship in protest of the war in Ukraine, dedicated the prize to Ukrainians, including his mother who was born there.
French director Stéphane Brizé’s won the screenplay prize for his corporate drama “A Good Little Soldier.” Malou Khebizi was given the Marcello Mastroianni award for emerging actor for her role in Cédric Kahn’s “A Place to Heal,” which is set in an adolescent psychiatric ward in a public hospital.
The jury this year included “The Voice of Hind Rajab” director Kaouther Ben Hania, English composer Daniel Blumberg, French filmmaker Xavier Giannoli, Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat and Hong Kong filmmaker Johnnie To.
Malkovich’s Oscar chances just went up
Aside from Malkovich’s win, the starrier, Hollywood films playing in competition were shut out of the awards, including “Primetime,” “Bunker” and “Ink.”
Some look to the Venice Film Festival awards for early indications of who might be in with a shot at Oscar nominations and wins. In recent years, Venice has launched winning best actor campaigns for people like Brendan Fraser and Adrien Brody.
Malkovich has yet to win an Oscar.

Sweden votes in tightest election in decades as far right eyes historic government role
The vote could see the Sweden Democrats enter government for the first time, giving the party direct influence over policy it has spent years building from the sidelines
Polls opened at 8:00 am across Sweden, with opposition leader Magdalena Andersson among the first to vote at a school in her home municipality of Nacka. Her Social Democrats, the country's largest party, have pledged to strengthen the welfare state and ease the cost of living for struggling households.
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, the leader of the right-wing governing coalition, has focused his campaign on the results of a crackdown on organized crime and immigration. The Prime Minister says he wants to "make Sweden great again," a phrase borrowed from Donald Trump.
Kristersson said his coalition can "unify parties, voters and issues into joint action." However, one of his pledges, if his bloc wins, includes formally bringing in the far-right Sweden Democrats into government, for the first time.
Critics say this move would further tighten immigration rules and pressure minority communities to conform to Swedish cultural norms.
Kristersson's minority government, made up of the Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals, has relied on Sweden Democrats support in parliament since 2022. The Sweden Democrats have previously pledged to ban the niqab and burqa if they enter government.
Their leader Jimmie Akesson says such dress "reflects values that I don't think belong in Sweden." In response to the pledge by the Prime Minister, Akesson declared "we've already won" at a final rally Saturday in Stockholm, where he said Sweden is "becoming safer, better, and more Swedish."
Andersson, who served as Sweden's first female prime minister from 2021 to 2022, has criticized the government's approach as making the country "harder" and "poorer."

Turkey detains 26 people after raids targeting LGBTQ+ groups
ISTANBUL, Sept 13 - Turkish authorities have detained 26 people and searched the offices of six LGBTQ+ associations in a series of raids that followed allegations of prostitution and obscenity, prosecutors said.
The crackdown is part of a campaign that the government says is aimed at protecting family values.
The Istanbul chief prosecutor's office said operations were carried out across 12 provinces against 38 suspects over the weekend, with authorities seizing drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm.
Ankara-based LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL said at least 50 activists had been detained - a higher figure than that given by the chief prosecutor's office - including more than 10 who were taken in police raids on their homes.
In addition, it said authorities blocked access to dozens of websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTI+ organisations, activists and rights advocates.
Dubbed "My Family is Safe", the government's crackdown comes as President Tayyip Erdogan promotes a "Decade of Family and Population", an initiative designed to tackle falling birth rates and an aging demographic.
Rights groups have accused the Turkish government of increasingly targeting the LGBTQ+ community in recent years through a hardening of rhetoric and restrictions.
"The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the Turkish Human Rights Association said on X.
The prosecutor's office said evidence indicated that children and underage youths were being inappropriately influenced on issues relating to sexual orientation and gender identity.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said investigations coordinated by prosecutors in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin involved judicial proceedings against 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses across 15 provinces. REUTERS

Carer’s allowance scandal victims could wait until 2054 for justice, charities warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:12:47 UTC
19:12:47 KST

Unpaid carers who were pursued for bills for thousands of pounds after welfare officials unlawfully changed benefit rules could wait years before learning whether they will get the money back, campaigners have warned.
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is working through 200,000 cases where carer’s allowance benefit recipients were incorrectly given overpayments. An estimated 25,000 carers could receive full or partial refunds.
However, several months into the two-year reassessment exercise just a tiny fraction of the caseload has been processed – and at current rates charities say the project will not be completed until 2054.
Campaigners are concerned by the slow pace of progress and worry that unless it speeds up some unpaid carers may die, or become untraceable after stopping their claim for carer’s allowance, before they are repaid.
The reassessment followed an official review, which concluded systemic DWP failures caused hundreds of thousands of carer’s allowance recipients unknowingly to run up debts as high as £20,000 through no fault of their own.
The review was triggered by an award-winning Guardian investigation, which revealed how years of government neglect and mismanagement forced unpaid carers into severe financial hardship and emotional despair and resulted in hundreds of millions of pounds being misspent.
Ministers promised in December 2024 to end a scandal they consider to be an inheritance from the previous government, but nearly two years on MPs and campaigners have repeatedly expressed doubts about the speed of the response, the DWP’s appetite for change and its handling of the process.
Although the DWP has hired more staff and taken steps to try to stop overpayments, more than 30,000 more overpayments were made in 2025-26, including 78 for over £20,000. Last year official figures revealed 144,000 carers were still paying off carer’s allowance overpayment debts accrued over several years.
There was fury early this year when it emerged the DWP had slapped overpayments on 1,400 carers for allegedly breaking carer’s allowance rules, even though officials knew the decisions to issue penalties were based on faulty and discredited guidance.
The reassessment process, which started in April, is looking specifically at cases where the DWP breached the law by failing to allow carers with irregular wages from part-time work to average their incomes over a year, unfairly exposing them to being penalised for breaching earnings limits.
Last week Stephen Timms, the welfare minister, told MPs so far 3,000 cases had been reviewed as part of the £75m reassessment programme, and the DWP was on track to complete the process in the planned timescale.
Carers UK said it was concerned that, so far, just 1.5% of the total projected caseload had been processed, and at current rates the reassessment would take 27 years to complete. It is unclear whether any carers have been repaid.
“We are seriously concerned by the pace of progress of the reassessment exercise and would like to see a clear and realistic plan for speeding it up, to ensure that carers who have been wrongly given overpayments over the last decade get a swift resolution,” said Emily Holzhausen, the director of policy and public affairs at Carers UK
She added: “Many carers who are owed a refund or the writing off of their overpayment debt to DWP have already been waiting for years – some for over a decade – to get justice and fair treatment from the department.
“For those who still don’t know whether their case will be reassessed and when, a lengthy reassessment process will only compound the worry and uncertainty they are facing. We cannot risk carers being left to wait for years for a resolution to an injustice which was not their fault.”
A DWP spokesperson said: “We are on track to complete the carer’s allowance reassessment exercise within the three years previously announced.
“To support the exercise, we have been recruiting and training new Decision Makers in a rolling programme, ensuring we take the time to get things right.
“We have plans in place to increase resource at a steady pace over the course of the exercise.”

A kingdom within a republic: Inside Uganda’s Buganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:12:15 UTC
19:12:15 KST

A kingdom within a republic: Inside Uganda’s Buganda
The kingdom’s traditions and institutions have endured through colonial rule, independence and decades of upheaval
Kampala, Uganda – Uganda became independent from British colonial rule in 1962, but independence did not mean the end of its traditional kingdoms. The new republic inherited a political landscape in which old monarchies and the modern state had to find a way to exist alongside each other.
More than six decades later, that history is still visible in Buganda, where a centuries-old monarchy exists within the modern Ugandan state.
The Buganda Kingdom is headed by a king, known as the Kabaka, and has its own traditional institutions, including the Great Lukiiko, which the kingdom describes as its parliament, and an administration headed by the Katikkiro, or prime minister.
These are institutions of the kingdom, rather than of Uganda’s national government. Under Uganda’s constitution, traditional and cultural leaders cannot exercise the administrative, legislative or executive powers of the state.
Buganda says its traditional territory covers about 61,000 square kilometres (24 square miles) and is home to roughly 12 million people.
The kingdom’s own history dates its establishment to the late 14th century, while oral traditions trace its origins further back to the 13th century and the figure of Katu Kintu.
The beginnings
As written records from that era do not exist, the precise timeline of how the early chiefdoms were unified into one of East Africa’s most powerful kingdoms remains a matter of historical interpretation.
According to Ugandan historian Semakula Kiwanuka, the kingdom emerged as local clan structures gradually moved from fragile entities towards a centralised authority.
“This consolidation was not necessarily driven by economic motives,” Kiwanuka said. “Oral traditions suggest that the strongest chiefdom brought its neighbours under its authority, establishing the foundation of the kingdom.”
Buganda’s oral traditions attribute the earliest unification efforts to Kabaka [King] Katu Kintu. But Kiwanuka said Kintu’s historical existence remains unverified, as the name is also shared by a figure in Buganda folklore.
Official kingdom accounts offer another version of the kingdom’s early history.
Owek Israel Kazibwe Kitooke, Buganda’s minister of information and official spokesperson, said from the kingdom’s administrative headquarters in Kampala that Kabaka Chwa I formed an alliance of five clans in the early 14th century: The Ffumbe, Lugave, Nnonge, Njaza and Nnyonyi.
As the kingdom expanded, six additional clans joined. According to Kitooke, Kabaka Chwa brought the constituent groups together through a council of clan leaders who served as royal advisers. He said the principles established through that system later evolved into the kingdom’s constitution.
Pillars of governance
Buganda’s system of governance rests on three primary pillars, according to Kitooke.
The first is the royal lineage. According to Kitooke, the reigning Kabaka selects an heir from the royal family, who is then tutored by senior clan elders in diplomacy, statecraft and traditional customs.
The second pillar is the clan system.
Clans are identified by traditional totems drawn from the local environment, including the civet, squirrel, goat and raven. Kitooke said respect for nature and the surrounding ecosystem remains central to Buganda’s cultural identity.
The third pillar is the people.
Citizens are not excluded from the kingdom’s institutions. The Kabaka appoints ministers, leaders and officials from among the wider population, allowing subjects to serve the monarchy in leadership roles, according to Kitooke.
Islam and the colonial era
During the 19th century, Islam reached Buganda under Kabaka Muteesa I, who welcomed Arab traders from the north. According to Buganda’s historical accounts, the Kabaka regularly hosted traders at his palace and observed Ramadan in 1877 after adopting the faith.
His successor, Kabaka Mwanga II, who also embraced Islam, ruled from 1884 to 1888 and again from 1889 to 1897. Mwanga II resisted British colonial expansion and fought against imperial forces.
“The name Buganda signifies a bundle of bound sticks,” Kiwanuka said, explaining the kingdom’s endurance. “Our people hold diverse religious beliefs, Christianity, Islam and traditional religions, but they share the view that their unity is the source of their strength.”
The kingdom was placed under a British protectorate in 1894. British officials used the name “Uganda” for the wider territory, a name derived from the Swahili rendering of Buganda.
Defeated by the British, Mwanga II was captured and exiled to Seychelles, where he died in captivity. Buganda’s historical records commemorate him as a martyr king.
According to the kingdom’s oral history, the traditional men’s attire, which resembles the Arab thobe, was inspired by clothing worn by Arab merchants who visited the kingdom and developed trade relations with it.
Independence
Uganda’s self-government arrangements took effect in March 1962, before the country gained independence from Britain on October 9 that year.
Under the 1962 Independence Constitution, Buganda retained a special federal position within the new state, with certain legislative powers assigned to its government. The central government retained most legislative powers.
But the relationship between the kingdom and the central government soon became turbulent.
In 1966, Prime Minister Milton Obote ordered a military assault on the Buganda royal palace, suspended the constitution and abolished the traditional kingdoms.
“We never forgave him,” Kiwanuka said.
“We lived through the regime of Idi Amin and witnessed the dismantling of cultural institutions, yet the kingdom remained resilient, rallying around the king,” he added.
The monarchy was restored in 1993, when Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II was enthroned as the 36th Kabaka.
Today, Uganda’s Constitution recognises traditional and cultural leaders and allows their institutions to exist according to the customs and traditions of the communities they represent. But it separates those institutions from the powers of the state. Traditional leaders cannot exercise the government’s administrative, legislative or executive powers, and they cannot participate in partisan politics.
The culture of the kingdom
For Buganda, the monarchy is about more than the Kabaka and the institutions around him.
The kingdom has insisted on preserving its political identity at times and its cultural identity always, Kitooke said.
“Our traditions are summarised in key matters, including the way of life at home, where we learn the etiquette of speaking to people, receiving guests, and the rules of hospitality, what to say, what to refrain from saying, and so forth,” he said.
He added that traditions also help maintain social cohesion, including visiting family and extended family, maintaining kinship ties, reaching adulthood, marriage and the payment of a bride’s dowry.
“The council of elders oversee family matters, promote unity and help resolve disputes between spouses,” he said. “These are very important; they are all part of our way of life.”
The kingdom and the republic
The Kingdom of Buganda celebrates its national day one day before Uganda’s national day. Neither the historian nor the minister offered an explanation beyond the fact that the kingdom itself is older than the Ugandan state.
On the coexistence between the kingdom and the state, Kitooke said the restoration of cultural rights was accompanied by an effort to preserve them within the laws of the central government.
“When our cultural rights were restored, we were keen to preserve them within the laws of the central state,” he said. “And the authority granted to the kingdom is a traditional cultural authority, and we do not play direct political roles. However, on the ground, we are actively engaged in political work through our institutions.”
For Kiwanuka, the Kabaka’s influence extends well beyond the palace.
“The Kabaka is the most popular figure in the kingdom, and even on the national level,” he said. “When he steps out of his palace, which is located one mile from the seat of the government, you can see tens of thousands of people lining up to welcome him.
“And if he were to say now that ‘we shall fight,’ then we will fight,” Kiwanuka said.

Lithuania issues possible air alert warning over potential drone sighting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:12:00 UTC
19:12:00 KST

Lithuania’s authorities have issued an all-clear (code white) following an earlier air alert warning over a potential drone sighting, which later turned out to be a flock of birds.
“The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: AIR ALERT IS OVER (WHITE). You may leave safe places or shelters,” the authorities said in an emergency message on Sunday afternoon.
The yellow air alert over a potential drone sighting was issued on Sunday at around 13:00 local time in Vilnius and the surrounding region, as well as the Trakai and Elektrėnai regions. Flights at Vilnius Airport were temporarily suspended.
The yellow alert meant there was no danger yet, but people were advised to locate their nearest shelter in case the threat level was elevated to code red.
The authorities later clarified that NATO jets confirmed the radar sighting was a flock of birds.

US approves $140 million Black Hawk helicopter sale to Argentina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:09:53 UTC
19:09:53 KST

- The U.S. approved a possible $140 million sale of four UH-60L Black Hawk helicopters to Argentina's Army, notified to Congress on September 10, 2026.
- The helicopters would be the Argentine Army's first Black Hawks, replacing an aging fleet of roughly 50 Bell UH-1H Hueys.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible $140 million sale of four UH-60L Black Hawk helicopters to Argentina, a deal that would give the Argentine Army its first Black Hawks. The approval, notified to Congress on September 10, 2026, follows through on a purchase Argentine officials confirmed earlier this year.
The package includes the four helicopters, two spare T700-GE-701D engines, and a long list of supporting gear: identification and navigation systems, a rescue hoist, a fast-rope insertion and extraction system, an internal auxiliary fuel tank, training equipment and spare parts. Sikorsky, the Lockheed Martin subsidiary that builds the Black Hawk in Stratford, Connecticut, would serve as the main contractor. The approval covers a potential sale rather than a signed contract, and the final price could come in lower depending on exactly what Argentina orders.
The helicopters are meant to replace Argentina’s aging fleet of Bell UH-1H Hueys, roughly 50 of which remain the Army’s primary helicopter type. The Army first tried to buy three secondhand Black Hawks through a tender launched in December 2024, but canceled that process in January 2025 after budget cuts. In June 2026, Lt. Gen. Oscar Santiago Zarich, the Argentine Army’s chief of staff, said the service would move ahead with an initial order of four Black Hawks still in U.S. service, with officials describing plans to grow the fleet further over time.
Argentina isn’t entirely new to the aircraft. A single VIP-configured Black Hawk has served the country’s presidential fleet since 1994, though it was transferred to the Argentine Air Force in 2024. The Army itself has never operated the type.
The UH-60L is an earlier version of the Black Hawk than the UH-60M now built for the U.S. Army and most export customers. Sikorsky runs a separate modernization program that fits older UH-60Ls with a digital cockpit and updated avionics closer to UH-60M standards while keeping the original airframe, an option Argentina could pursue later if it wants to extend the helicopters’ service life.
The purchase fits a pattern of incremental, budget-constrained modernization across Argentina’s armed forces, which have also recently picked up secondhand F-16 fighters from Denmark and P-3 Orion maritime patrol aircraft from Norway.
The State Department said the sale would not require additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Argentina and that no offset agreement has been proposed so far. Argentina has not set a delivery timeline, and the sale still needs to move from this approval into a finalized contract.

Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:09:00 UTC
19:09:00 KST

Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
September 13, 2026
At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday.
The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 miles) east of Australia.
The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities.
The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae.
Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea."
Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials.
In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts move toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors."
"To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of those missing and those we have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," the statement continued.
Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui.
"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel."
Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities
Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized."
French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted.
It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor.
"He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge.
"There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added.
Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort.
A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning.
The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning.
Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island.

President Xi Jinping on Sunday proposed five initiatives on greater Brics cooperation in areas of artificial intelligence, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry, smart manufacturing, and talent development.
Xi made the proposals when attending the second and final day of the Brics summit in New Delhi.
   
He stressed that greater Brics must make greater impacts, achieve greater development, and lay a solid foundation for practical cooperation.
Brics should leverage strengths in being rooted in emerging markets and connected with the Global South, uphold openness and cooperation for mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, keep industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded, and foster integrated markets, Xi said.
He also noted that Brics should build innovation incubators, upgrade traditional industries, develop emerging industries, and make forward-looking plans for future industries.
For his part, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for cooperation within the bloc, which he has said represents 50 percent of the world's population, 40 percent of global GDP and more than 25 percent of global trade.
"The power of BRICS lies in our diversity and cooperation," Modi told leaders on the final day of talks.
"We have tried to push inclusive global growth," Modi said.
"We may be rooted in different realities, but together we rise through cooperation and blossom for humanity," he said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, said the bloc was working to create a "new, more just, multipolar world order". (Xinhua/AFP)

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) lauded Taiwan’s efforts in cancer research and treatment in a video address marking the 20th anniversary of the Taiwan Society for Molecular Medicine on Sunday.
Lai said the government is actively implementing various strategies, including boosting funding for cancer screening from NT$2.8 billion (US$88.48 million) to NT$6.8 billion and expanding screening items, target groups, and age ranges, according to the Presidential Office. The measures are expected to benefit nearly 6 million people, the president said.
Lai said Taiwan also began including next-generation sequencing (NGS) in National Health Insurance coverage in May 2024, covering 19 types of cancer. In December of the same year, the government expanded coverage to include seven types of single-gene testing, he added. This September, applicable cancer types were broadened, allowing more cancer patients to benefit, the president said.
“Through NGS, we aim to more comprehensively map the genetic profile of cancer cells, helping doctors identify appropriate treatments for patients and turning relevant medical data into the basis for new drug evaluation and improved therapies,” Lai said.
At the same time, the Cancer New Drug Fund has been allocated NT$10 billion over the past two years to help economically disadvantaged cancer patients access innovative treatments and reduce their financial burden, Lai said. Taiwan possesses strong biomedical R&D capabilities and a comprehensive healthcare system, he added, and the government will continue to invest resources and improve policies in the field.
Molecular medicine will continue to transform approaches to disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, he said.
