The sources said the two crew members initially expressed reservations about appearing on the program, with one even raising concerns that he could be explicitly ordered to take part in the report.
At the same time, three of the sources said military officials were concerned that classified details about the rescue operation could be disclosed. The sources said senior Defense Department officials insisted that the crew members be interviewed, but after the two voiced concerns, Hegseth met with them and asked them directly whether they wanted to participate rather than forcing them to cooperate. Following the conversation, according to the report, one of the crew members, identified by the call sign “Bravo,” agreed to be interviewed, while the other, identified as “Alpha,” refused.
CNN said its latest report highlights how the Defense Department under Hegseth has sought to shape the narrative surrounding the war with Iran as public criticism of the administration over the issue grows.
“This entire story is a complete lie,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in response to CNN’s questions about the report. “The decision to participate in the interview was each pilot’s alone — because it is their story.”
“The Department took great care to ensure operational security, sources, and methods were protected,” he added. “To suggest otherwise is to denigrate every member of our military who participated in and supported the interview.”
Iran succeeded in shooting down an F-15E in April, the first U.S. fighter jet downed in the country during the war. Two crew members, a pilot and a weapons systems officer, were aboard. The pilot was rescued hours after ejecting from the aircraft, while the weapons systems officer managed to evade capture by Iranian forces in the mountains for more than a day before he too was rescued.
CNN also reported on the battle among media outlets seeking interviews with the two crew members since their aircraft was shot down, saying “the competition was intense.” According to the network, a “60 Minutes” producer contacted military sources on the day of the rescue in an effort to secure the interview. The program’s executive producer told staff that landing the interview was a “top priority,” and according to three sources who spoke with CNN, she dealt directly with Hegseth and other senior administration officials in an effort to secure an exclusive for the program.
As noted, the report said military officials were concerned about details being disclosed while the campaign was still underway. Two sources who spoke with CNN said active-duty service members expressed concern that featuring the incident on the program was an attempt by the Defense Department to use the heroism of U.S. troops in the successful operation for political purposes. According to the sources, political appointees at the department insisted that the interview go ahead despite those reservations.
According to one source familiar with the production of the program, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine also expressed concern that the interview could reveal military tactics, even inadvertently. He ultimately decided to participate in the report himself.
In the first preview of the interview aired by the network, “Bravo” is seen sitting silently as the interviewer asks him: “Did you ever have any doubt that the US military was coming for you?”

The problem is Putin. He is not going to stop the war until the pressure becomes much greater. Ukrainians are applying pressure heroically. Background

Whereas previously the main objective was to destroy oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, today Ukraine's strategy is increasingly focused on systematically destroying the entire economy that supports Russia's war machine. This concerns not only the energy sector, but also logistics, the financial sector, and enterprises that support the operation of the military-industrial complex.

The refinery is involved in supplying fuel to Russian military forces. The facility has been attacked by drones repeatedly. Egyptian president calls for greater BRICS cooperation to strengthen economic resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:02:28 UTC
18:02:28 KST

Sahin Demir
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Sunday called for deeper cooperation among BRICS members and partner countries to build more resilient economies amid rapid changes and challenges facing the global economy.
Addressing an open session of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, Sisi said economic resilience requires diversifying sources of growth, strengthening supply chains, investing in people and technology, and expanding cooperation among Global South countries.
He said Egypt attaches importance to cooperation in innovation and artificial intelligence, as well as technology transfer and localization, to enable developing countries to benefit more from technological transformation.
On sustainability, Sisi called for expanded cooperation in clean and renewable energy, greater efficiency in the use of resources, and easier access for developing countries to financing and technology.
He also highlighted Egypt’s investment in ports, transport corridors, and logistics networks, saying the Suez Canal remains at the heart of this system as one of the world’s most important international trade routes.
“Economic resilience cannot be separated from our ability to ensure food and energy security, maintain the smooth flow of trade and investment, and address supply-chain disruptions,” he said.
Sisi called for increasing trade and investment among BRICS members and partners and encouraging joint projects to strengthen economic integration and reduce the impact of external shocks.
He also called for strengthening the role of development finance institutions, particularly the New Development Bank, in financing infrastructure and development projects and expanding developing countries’ access to concessional financing.
The Egyptian president said BRICS, through the diversity of its members and partners, has an opportunity to build a practical model of cooperation among Global South countries based on resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability.
The remarks came on the final day of the two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi. The expanded 11-member grouping comprises Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

Full text of Chinese President Xi Jinping's speech at Session II of the 18th BRICS Summit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
17:01:36 CST
18:01:36 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers a speech when attending the second day of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Sept. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Yan Yan)
NEW DELHI, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sunday delivered a speech at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.
The following is the full text of the speech:
Cementing the Foundation for BRICS Cooperation and Bolstering the Strength of the Global South
Statement by H.E. Xi Jinping
President of the People's Republic of China
At Session II of the 18th BRICS Summit
New Delhi, September 13, 2026
Your Excellency Prime Minister Narendra Modi,
Colleagues,
I thank Prime Minister Modi and the Indian government for hosting this meeting.
We meet at a time when changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the world. The Global South, with its collective rise, has become a key driver of world multipolarity. At the same time, the international landscape is volatile and fraught with risks and challenges. To bring stability to the world and make it a better place, BRICS countries must seize the historical initiative, rally the Global South, be an active, stabilizing and positive force in international affairs, and advance the well-being of all humanity.
A world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed. Fairness and justice is a universal aspiration, and international rules must be written by all countries. The logic of "might makes right" does not hold, and should have been discarded long ago. Global South countries should jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs, safeguard the basic norms of international relations including sovereign equality, noninterference in internal affairs, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and ensure that international law and international rules are applied to all, free from double standards.
All countries, regardless of their size, strength or wealth, are equal members of the international community. Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the United Nations, support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, and ensure the equal participation of all countries in international affairs. We should see to it that the reform of the World Trade Organization proceeds in the right direction, uphold such principles as the most-favored-nation treatment, and actively explore new rules for the future. We should support the operation and development of the New Development Bank to facilitate Global South cooperation. The international financial architecture must be reformed and improved to increase the representation and voice of developing countries.
"To achieve great things, one should always put the people first." Global South countries should stay committed to a people-centered development philosophy and strive to deliver on the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Since China launched the Global Development Initiative five years ago, we have implemented over 2,000 projects in partnership with others, and provided training for more than 200,000 professionals, benefiting people in more than 120 countries. China is opening its door ever wider to the world. We have granted zero-tariff treatment for all the 53 African countries having diplomatic relations with China. We will continue to broaden independent and unilateral opening up, and share the opportunities of China's development with other countries.
As global challenges keep surfacing, we should adopt a holistic approach to address both the symptoms and root causes. Global South countries should jointly advance security governance and tackle both traditional and nontraditional security threats. We should improve global climate governance, and urge the full and effective implementation of the Paris Agreement. We should take a people-centered approach, develop AI for the positive and for good, and work faster to evolve a consensus-based global AI governance framework, so that new technologies can light the way toward shared prosperity.
Colleagues,
To accomplish great things and achieve major progress, the foundation of greater BRICS cooperation must be cemented. We should leverage our close ties with fellow emerging markets and Global South countries, uphold open cooperation for mutual benefit, safeguard stable and smooth industrial and supply chains, and foster a large integrated market. We should build incubators for innovation, upgrade traditional industries, develop emerging industries, and deploy future industries. To this end, I wish to put forward five initiatives:
First, the open source and inclusive AI initiative. China will be a pioneer in establishing a BRICS AI open source community, support the cooperation in developing and applying large language models, hold specialized AI seminars and training courses, and build an open ecosystem for AI.
Second, the trade and investment facilitation initiative. China proposes to establish a BRICS special economic zone partnership, under which countries can set up an intelligent portal, coordinate policies, and build a new frontier for open development. In an effort to cultivate new drivers of economic and trade cooperation, China will hold the BRICS Forum on Trade in Services next year. We welcome your active participation.
Third, the digital industry cooperation initiative. China will push for establishing a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform, and conduct digital skills training, technological exchange and industrial alignment, so as to jointly enable the development of the digital economy.
Fourth, the intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative. China stands ready to assist fellow BRICS countries in building smart factories and developing standards and norms, and jointly promote manufacturing transformation and upgrading.
Fifth, the science and technology talent development initiative. China proposes to set up a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance for joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards. China will launch a BRICS youth exchange program for scientific and technological innovation, so as to cultivate more high-caliber talent.
Colleagues,
This year marks the launch of China's 15th Five-Year Plan for economic and social development. It is both a blueprint for China's development and a cooperation list for the rest of the world. China will continue to advance high-quality development, expand high-standard opening up, implement the Global Development Initiative, and promote high-quality Belt and Road cooperation to share opportunities and prosper together with all countries. Let us work as one to promote greater BRICS cooperation and write a new chapter of strength through unity for the Global South!
Thank you.

France apologises for diplomatic spat with US to lift block on new ambassador to Washington
The French UN mission said it regretted an online post criticising a US vote at the UN General Assembly in a move that should clear the way for the new French ambassador Aurélien Lechevallier to take up his post in Washington.
The French UN mission said it regretted an online post criticizing how the United States voted during a UN General Assembly meeting, with US officials telling AFP on Saturday that Washington appreciated the statement.
France's permanent mission to the UN published the apology Friday, saying it regretted a post on X criticising the United States' commitment to human rights.
"France and the United States recently took different positions on a vote at the United Nations General Assembly. This difference concerned one vote, and not the defence of human rights," the mission said in an English statement on its website.
"Public differences of opinion on one vote do not stand in the way of close dialogue with the United States, and do not call into question our historical alliance, nor our ability to work together to advance peace, stability and prosperity, including within multilateral forums," the statement continued.
Read moreUN leadership candidates outline visions ahead of secretary-general race
The mea culpa was well-received by Washington, which has been holding up the appointment of France's next US ambassador as a result of the dispute.
"We note and appreciate France's statement and look forward to working together to further shared values and interests," a US State Department official told AFP on condition of anonymity.
The US State Department has held up the approval of Aurélien Lechevallier, French President Emmanuel Macron's choice as France's next envoy to Washington, replacing Laurent Bili.
Lechevallier is currently French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot's chief of staff.
US approval of a choice of French envoy is usually a formality but has remained in limbo since the dispute.
On July 24, the US was one of 10 countries to vote in the UN General Assembly against extending Volker Turk's term as UN human rights chief, joining the ranks of North Korea, Russia and Nicaragua, among others.
Read moreUS walks out of UN Security Council meeting as France condemns rights vote
"The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore," the French mission wrote in a post on X after the United States strongly opposed another term by Turk, who has repeatedly questioned US policies under President Donald Trump.
The criticism was met with immediate backlash from Washington, with the US representative walking out of a UN Security Council meeting days later when France's ambassador took the floor, in protest of the comments.

World's first museum devoted to prehistoric flying reptiles opens in NW China's Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
17:01:16 CST
18:01:16 KST

Visitors view pterosaurs replicas at a science museum in Hami, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Sept. 13, 2026. A science museum focused on pterosaurs, a winged reptile closely related to dinosaurs, opened on Sunday in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwest China.(Photo by Polat Niyaz/Xinhua)
URUMQI, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- A science museum focused on pterosaurs, a winged reptile closely related to dinosaurs, opened on Sunday in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwest China.
The world's first of its kind, this museum is located in a national geopark in Xinjiang's Hami region, a location renowned for abundant pterosaur fossil discoveries.
With an exhibition area of about 4,600 square meters, the Hami Pterosaur Museum consists of six oval-shaped halls in a staggered layout. Seen from above, it resembles a clutch of pterosaur eggs resting in the desert.
Fossils on display include specimens recovered during more than two decades of rescue excavations by researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). Also on display are the world's first 3D preserved fossilized pterosaur eggs and embryos, along with large pterosaur specimens making their public debut.
This is the first time all of these specimens have been displayed together. The exhibits present a panoramic recreation of pterosaur life and evolution during the Cretaceous period roughly 130 million years ago, the museum said.
Xu Xing, head of the CAS institute, said the museum not only highlights China's leading role in global pterosaur research but also offers the public a window to experience scientific discovery up close and appreciate the wonders of ancient life. ■

‘A Way for Russian Occupiers Go Home’: Ukraine Intel Reveals Why Kerch Bridge Still Stands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

The bridge that Russian President Vladimir Putin built to cement Russia’s grip on occupied Crimea remains a powerful symbol of Moscow’s occupation. But as Ukraine intensifies its campaign to isolate Russian-occupied Crimea, striking railways, roads, ports, fuel facilities and other logistics nodes across the peninsula, one of the most recognizable symbols of Moscow’s occupation remains intact.
Why?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Major General Vadym Skibitsky, deputy chief of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR), offered a rare explanation during a panel discussion at the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference this week.
According to Skibitsky, the answer is partly practical: the Kerch Bridge is simply no longer as important to Russia’s military supply logistics as it once was.
“It’s really not so strategic an object for the Russian Federation today,” Skibitsky said.Ukraine has already destroyed or disrupted numerous other logistics routes across occupied Crimea, he pointed out, while Russia has increasingly shifted the movement of military supplies toward the land corridor running through occupied southern Ukraine.
Most military cargo, including weapons destined for Russian forces fighting in Ukraine now moves through Russia’s Rostov region and then along the so-called land bridge through occupied Ukrainian territory, according to Skibitsky.
Political weight
Despite the logistical shift, the Kerch Bridge has long been one of the most politically and strategically significant pieces of infrastructure linking Russia with the Ukrainian peninsula it illegally annexed in 2014.
UN Warns Ukraine Faces Toughest Wartime Winter Yet
“For Russia, for Putin, the Kerch Bridge is a symbol of the occupation of Crimea,” Skibitsky emphasized.
With that in mind, he offered another reason for keeping it standing – with a pointed message to Russian forces on the peninsula.
“It’s maybe one of the ways for Russian occupiers to return home.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, damaging it in major attacks in 2022 and 2023 and again targeting the crossing in subsequent operations. But Ukraine’s strategy toward Crimea has increasingly expanded beyond the bridge itself.
Skibitsky also recalled that the bridge had previously been a focal point of Western fears of escalation. He noted that several years ago, during discussions around Ukrainian operations against the crossing, some European countries raised concerns that destroying it could provoke a major Russian escalation, including nuclear threats.
Today, however, HUR assesses that the bridge’s military significance has diminished. The discussion over the Kerch Bridge led directly to a broader question: whether Vladimir Putin could actually use nuclear weapons if Russia faced a major military setback.
Any Russian use of nuclear weapons, including tactical nuclear weapons, would have consequences extending far beyond Ukraine and could reshape security calculations in other regions of the world, he said.
For that reason, Russia’s nuclear rhetoric remains a tool of pressure, but the Kremlin also has to consider the international consequences of crossing that threshold.
Missiles, drones and the wider threat
Skibitsky then outlined what HUR considers one of Ukraine’s most immediate military threats: Russia’s expanding missile and drone campaign.
“It’s not a risk, it’s a real threat,” he said.
According to HUR’s assessment, Russia’s defense industry plans to produce at least 100 ballistic missiles in September. Russia is also using North Korean ballistic missiles against Ukraine, Skibitsky said.
Asked how Ukraine could counter the threat, he described a multi-layered strategy. The first element is obtaining more interceptor missiles from Ukraine’s partners. The second is striking the factories and enterprises producing Russian ballistic missiles.
“We absolutely know all enterprises, factories, companies that are involved in the production of such ballistic missiles on the territory of Russia,” Skibitsky said.
The third is attacking the launchers themselves. According to Skibitsky, Russia can deploy between 17 and 19 ballistic missile launchers in regions including Kursk and Voronezh for strikes targeting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.
And the fourth element is sanctions – particularly restrictions preventing Russia from obtaining foreign navigation systems and electronic components needed for its weapons industry.
Skibitsky also addressed cooperation between Russian and Chinese companies supporting Russia’s industrial capabilities. HUR, he said, is aware of enterprises involved in joint production with Chinese companies. But many are located more than 2,000 kilometers from Ukraine, making them difficult to reach even with Ukraine’s expanding deep-strike capabilities. That makes international sanctions particularly important, Skibitsky said.
He pointed to problems Russia has encountered obtaining Chinese-made jet engines for certain unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) programs as evidence that pressure on supply chains can work.
Another unusual part of the discussion centered on Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon. Asked why facilities apparently associated with civilian businesses were being targeted, Skibitsky said HUR does not consider every such site purely civilian.
“Wildberries and Ozon and other such centers in the Russian Federation are really involved in the logistics system of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation,” he said.
According to Skibitsky, disrupting these networks is part of a much broader Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s military logistics. Ukraine first focused on logistics in occupied Crimea and other occupied territories, seeking to break supply routes supporting Russian forces in the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson directions.
The campaign has since expanded as Kyiv attempts to identify and strike the wider logistics infrastructure sustaining Russia’s war.

About 500 people marched through central Kaunas on Saturday for the city’s second Pride event, calling for equal rights for LGBTQ+ people and protesting hatred and discrimination.
Participants marched from St Michael the Archangel Church along Laisvės Avenue and back, carrying LGBTQ+, Palestinian, Ukrainian and European Union flags. Many wore Pride symbols and carried signs calling for equality and greater recognition of LGBTQ+ rights.
A banner at the front of the march read “We were, we are, we will be”, a slogan repeatedly chanted by participants. The march ended with organisers reading a community manifesto.
Kaunas Pride organisers called for greater representation of LGBTQIA+ people in Lithuania’s education system, legal recognition and protection of same-sex families, and accessible, inclusive health care, including for trans people.
They also called for implementation of an April 17 Constitutional Court ruling concerning the right of same-sex couples to family life, as well as equal access to marriage, partnership and adoption rights.
The organizers said transgender people should have simpler procedures for changing their names and gender markers, stronger protection from discrimination and hate crimes, and access to non-discriminatory health care.
“LGBTQIA+ people are still not consistently protected by law,” the manifesto said, while calling for “respect, legal recognition and protection”.
Beata Starodubova, a Kaunas Pride spokeswoman, said organisers were also seeking greater LGBTQ+ representation in schools and access to appropriate medical services outside the capital.
“We are protesting transphobia and homophobia,” she said.
The march also expressed solidarity with Palestinians and other marginalised groups. Two Palestinian flags were carried at the front of the procession, and participants chanted “No pride in genocide”.
Starodubova said the organisers support Palestinians as part of their broader opposition to oppression.
A 35-year-old participant from Latvia, Metra, carried Palestinian and Ukrainian flags. She said she wanted to show solidarity with people facing oppression.
“We understand what it means to be oppressed,” she said.
Meanwhile, medical psychologist Bernardas Liukaitis, 24, said LGBTQ+ people can support Palestinians’ fight for freedom irrespective of conservative attitudes to homosexuality in Muslim societies.
“We can still speak out for people’s right to live,” he said. “People here are speaking for freedom.”
Counterprotest and police presence
The march was accompanied by a counterprotest and religious gathering.
About 10 Catholics gathered near the intersection of Laisvės Avenue and Vytauto Avenue, where they prayed the Rosary and sang hymns throughout the march.
At Kaunas City Municipality, 13 people demonstrated against what they called “LGBT ideology,” holding Lithuanian flags and signs opposing LGBTQ+ issues in schools. They shouted “shame” at marchers.
Police deployed larger-than-usual forces to maintain public order and monitored the event. Authorities said they had no information about planned provocations before the march and hoped the event would proceed peacefully.
There were some arrests during the event, according to the report.
Organisers had expected fewer participants than at the first Kaunas Pride in 2021, when about 3,000 people attended. The permit for Saturday’s event allowed up to 5,000 participants.
Starodubova said the lower expected turnout reflected the event’s political purpose.
“Protest is protest, not just a march or a celebration,” she said.
The Kaunas Pride march was first held in 2021.

Feature: First-ever Wushu Festival brings Chinese martial arts to heart of Russia's capital
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
17:00:52 CST
18:00:52 KST

by sportswriter Vladislava Chugueva
MOSCOW, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- In the heart of Moscow, beneath the open sky of the Muzeon Park of Arts, the rhythmic clash of wooden weapons and the flutter of silk fans marked the opening of the capital's first-ever Wushu Festival on Saturday.
More than 30,000 spectators and about 830 athletes from multiple Russian cities gathered to celebrate a martial art that has traveled far from its Chinese roots to become one of Russia's most popular Eastern disciplines.
The festival was organized by the Moscow Department of Sport, the "Moscow Sport" non-profit organization, the Moscow Wushu Federation and the Moscow Mayor's project "My Sports District."
A BRIDGE OF CULTURES
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Zhang Wei, Minister-Counselor of the Chinese Embassy in Russia, noted that wushu embodies deep Eastern philosophical wisdom about the "unity of heaven and man."
"As a bridge linking the hearts of people of both countries, wushu has already taken root in Russia and is developing actively," Zhang said. "We sincerely celebrate the achievements of Russian athletes at international competitions".
Sergey Sanakoev, Deputy Chairman of the Russian-Chinese Friendship Society, echoed the sentiment, saying that wushu can help deepen cross-cultural communication. "Wushu is deeply loved in Russia. I am confident that this festival will serve to further popularize it, drawing more and more people, both young and even older, into this beautiful art and sport," he said.
WUSHU, EMBODIMENT OF CHINA
For Radik Zaripov, a world champion in traditional wushu, the festival was a celebration of both the sport and the culture behind it. "I think Chinese culture itself, all of its richness, is embodied in this sport," he said. "Knowledge, culture, philosophy and atmosphere are passed down from generation to generation. I believe wushu is the very embodiment of China."
Zaripov recalled a phrase from one of his coaches to describe what wushu means to him: "Martial arts came into my life like spring and stayed there forever."
He added that the core lessons wushu imparts are discipline, spirituality, empathy, culture awareness and respect for traditions, expressing hope that wushu would gain greater popularity once it joins the Olympic family.
Maxim, a father whose son practices wushu, watched the performances with admiration. "My son does wushu, and we have a great appreciation for Chinese culture," he said excitedly. Asked what he would say to parents considering enrolling their children in a wushu class, he replied: "I would advise them not to hesitate and to make the right decision quickly. Wushu gives a child discipline, strength and flexibility."
A CELEBRATION OF SKILL AND SPIRIT
Among the participants of wushu competitions were young girl athletes from Oryol, Vika and Sonya, both of whom have practiced wushu for nine years. While preparing for their performance, they recalled their travels to China's Shanghai and Shandong. "It was very beautiful, and we were very well received," Vika said. "There are many seasoned athletes there."
When asked whether they want to become coaches in the future, they smiled: "It is only a dream for now. We want to earn higher ranks, and then plan for the future."
Vanya and Semyon, two young boys who came from Voronezh, called the festival the biggest event they had ever participated in. "It was really cool. This is the first time I've performed on such a scale," Vanya said, while Semyon admitted he was nervous at first before "everything fell into place." Vanya added that he has already visited Shaolin and other sites in China and now hopes to compete at the national level in Russia.
Apart from age-group wushu contests, the festival featured a performance by Shaolin monks, along with a dragon dance show and an attempt to set a record for the largest wushu training session.
The first Moscow Wushu Festival may have been a debut, but it already carried the weight of something much larger: a bridge built not on words, but on a shared love for sports and respect for heritage. ■

Chinese scientists find ‘extremely high-value’ underwater gold mine in Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:08 UTC
18:00:08 KST

Chinese scientists find ‘extremely high-value’ underwater gold mine in Pacific
Survey team says the ores, formed when super-hot water shoots from the seabed, are richer in gold and silver than those found on land
According to a report by state broadcaster CCTV on Friday, the discovery was made during a joint scientific expedition involving several Chinese academic institutions.
The ores within this seabed hydrothermal field – an area where hot, mineral-rich water shoots out from openings on the ocean floor – are exceptionally rich in precious metals. Silver, in particular, reaches more than 1kg (2.2lbs) per tonne of ore at its highest grade, while the average metal content exceeds that of typical terrestrial deposits.
“The [large seabed mining area] has extremely high exploitation value,” said Song Shiji, vice-dean of the Institute for Ocean Engineering at Tsinghua University and one of the lead scientists on the project.
These multi‑metal deposits form when super‑hot, metal‑rich water jets out of the seabed and hits near‑freezing seawater. The sudden cooling makes the metals bind with sulphur and drop out as solid sulphide minerals – mostly copper, zinc and lead, but often with some gold and silver as well.

Warning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still can | John Harris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:05 UTC
18:00:05 KST

Imagine this. Quite by chance, your TikTok feed presents you with footage of the fascists who recently took part in highly organised shows of strength in Dover and Portsmouth (and, on Wednesday, outside the London offices of the Daily Mail, demanding a new house for the mother of their leader, Daniel “Tommo” Thomas). For as long as the images hold your attention, you see and hear flashes of explanation, but then, as usual, you scroll away to someone leaping off a tall building, a fight on the London Underground, or a trick-performing dog.
Hypothetically, TikTok users are able to skip through 260 videos in under 35 minutes. And it’s this distracted, quick-fire way that so many people receive information that may be responsible for a worrying statistic from YouGov last week. Its poll on the Dover and Portsmouth events showed that 53% of people aged 18-24 years old simply didn’t have a point of view on whether the masked demonstrations were “a legitimate way of protesting”. Further, 43% of those of all ages were either unaware of the story, or not following it at all.
Those figures probably highlight one of the most worrying aspects of the times we live in: the decline of reading. Millions of us know what that phenomenon feels like: trying desperately to keep your attention glued to a book or news article with the nagging certainty that you will be tempted back to the more ephemeral attractions offered by your phone. But a background in the pre-digital world helps people not just follow national and global events, but clarify and contextualise them. In this case, at the risk of sounding hopelessly pompous, the fear many of us felt as we watched what happened in both ports was surely full of the perspectives gleaned from years of soaking up books and newspapers – and the sense that history often either repeats itself, or rhymes.
Black-clad – let’s be honest: uniformed – men who want to “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British”, while claiming to be protecting women and girls: the whole spectacle was pitched halfway between Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts – and, therefore, Hitler and the Nazis – and the Ku Klux Klan, with the seemingly ubiquitous balaclavas lacing everything with a flavour of the Troubles. But if you receive most of your information in the form of a distracting and seemingly infinite jumble of random moving images, what would you know about most of that?
All this crossed my mind thanks to an excellent new book marking what may well be a transformative moment for societies all over the world. The New Dark Ages is the work of the Times columnist James Marriott, and subtitled The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society. Presumably to accommodate itself to the changes it describes, it is short: 208 pages. But it is also full of insight and urgency.
In the 20 years since the UK’s National Literacy Trust began looking at children’s and young people’s reading, there has been a 36% fall in the number who say they enjoy reading in their spare time, to its lowest level on record. In 2024, the Guardian reported a survey by the Reading Agency charity, which found that 35% of adults said they were now “lapsed readers”, meaning that they used to regularly read for pleasure, but “rarely or never” did any more.
The Atlantic magazine recently ran an article baldly headlined The End of Reading Is Here, whose author, Rose Horowitch, made plenty of sobering claims. “The literate era will prove to be a brief interlude between the oral and digital ages,” she wrote – and drew on no end of evidence and anecdotes. A program director at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, for instance, ran focus groups asking high-school students about recreational reading. The conclusion: “most thought of it as an alien practice”. When Marriott first wrote about this, he says, “some professors reported that it was not that the young men and women in their classes were unwilling to read, but that they seemed almost unable to”.
In Britain, more than 320 newspapers closed down between 2009 and 2019, a statistic the book follows with a stark suggestion: “It is increasingly possible to get through life without any exposure to the news at all.” In the wake of the 2016 Brexit referendum, I met people who said they had simply stopped paying attention to current affairs because they were so maddening: now, I wonder if what was really powering this switch-off was technology. The resulting ignorance – a strong word, but it feels justified – is firewalled by phone screens: it feels as if the only stuff that can break through has to be angry, paranoid and visually shocking.
And because of the decline of reading, the people who purvey all the nonsense and poison can be increasingly confident that fewer and fewer people will come across anything halfway critical or analytical. In that sense, the screen age is exemplified by – oh yes – Donald Trump, who, according to an economic adviser in his first term, “won’t read anything – not one-page memos, not the brief policy papers, nothing”. His style of speechmaking is equally non-literate: as Marriott writes, “he doesn’t supply evidence for his ideas. Rather than organising his information analytically via clauses and subclauses in the manner of literate communication, he merely piles up assertions”.
His proposed election bribe of $5,000 is one surreal example, but there are plenty of others. I recently watched an online video of Sean Duffy, the former Fox Business host who is now Trump’s secretary of transportation. He was rejoicing in the administration’s quest to do away with start-stop ignition buttons in cars – mainly, I sensed, because of some weird quasi-Freudian attachment to the phallic(ish) shape of traditional keys. Written down in an attempt at coherent argument, his case would have looked ridiculous. But folksily barked out as Duffy’s “pet peeve”, I could imagine it being warmly greeted by exactly the people it was aimed at. The same, of course, applies to any number of much more malignant Trumpian positions and passions: climate denial, brazen racism towards Somali-Americans, unapologetic Islamophobia and the idea that the US is about to be overrun by criminals and the occupants of other countries’ prisons and mental institutions.
“Mass literacy is a recent phenomenon,” Marriott writes. “So is mass democracy. We simply don’t know whether one can survive without the other.” Meanwhile, on millions of screens, fascist faux-militias, populists and other merchants of loathing and absurdity blur into acrobatic skateboarders, arguments on the tube and dogs that do tricks. That strips them of context and thereby normalises their rise – and inch by inch, we move towards a future with echoes of the past that too many people will have failed to understand. And this time, there will be no books to burn, because we will have stopped reading them.
John Harris is a Guardian columnist

‘Really helpful’: the AI bootcamps aimed at addressing UK youth unemployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

In a youth centre opposite Preston bus station, the UK government is trying to address two of the greatest challenges facing the national economy: AI and youth unemployment.
The hope is that one will solve – rather than cause – the other. In a room at the recently opened Vault, a community hub in the Lancashire city, an “AI bootcamp” is under way – part of a trial in the north-west to give 16- to 24-year-olds AI training.
The bootcamp tutor is standing in front of a video screen and guiding the five attenders sitting around a long table on laptops through a task designed to emphasise the importance of glitch-free data in AI models.
“Does that make sense?” he asks. The room nods.
Everyone attending these sessions is either a 16- to 24-year-old not in education, employment or training – Neet, for short – or likely to join that bracket.
Youth unemployment is a problem in the UK. Nearly a million young people are Neet – just over one in 10 people in that age group. The advent of AI, either a threat or boon to the job market depending on your perspective, is now another factor to take into consideration when tackling the youth joblessness crisis.
Khudeija Rafique, who is attending the course, sees potential in the new tech. “It would be really helpful with whatever job I would like to go into,” the 18-year-old from Burnley says.
These taxpayer-funded bootcamps are a pilot scheme, open to 70 people who will undergo a three-week programme specially designed for Neets to learn how to build AI tools, understand how businesses use AI, and learn to use the technology responsibly. The retailer JD Sports, food company Heinz and IT firm Agilysys are among the partners offering AI apprenticeships specifically designed for the attenders to join at the end of the course.
There are two types of apprenticeship available: one for aspiring content creators to become AI marketing specialists, another to join IT helpdesks that need AI expertise. If a boot-camp trainee gets an apprenticeship, they will be going to an organisation that wants these skills and has an AI-focused role to fill.
“This is an opportunity to bridge a gap, to improve productivity and bring AI into organisations,” says Lauren Monks, an executive at IN4 Group, the company contracted to run the programme.
Amid general concerns about the availability of entry-level jobs and whether AI is stifling that market, being on top of the technology can be an advantage if you’re seeking your first job.
This is common advice from graduate recruiters, but experts say it can apply to Neets as well, depending on what sector of the economy they are joining.
Remy Simms, 17, is interested in applying for the content creator apprenticeship and says the Preston course has “changed my opinion” on AI. “It shows that you can work with AI and you don’t have to work against it,” he says. “I’ve got a better understanding of it and I know more about how it works.”
Alan Milburn, a former Labour cabinet minister, warned in a recent report that the country was “at risk of a lost generation” without government action on the Neet crisis. Milburn’s prescription goes a lot further than AI bootcamps – he calls for reform of the welfare system, for instance – and his report points out that work programmes by successive governments have failed to answer the problem.
Concerns about AI’s impact on employment have focused on the graduate job market so far, not on school leavers and non-graduates, amid expectations that it will be able to do the “grunt work” associated with junior employees in areas such as banking, consulting and law.
The impact on non-graduate work was unclear, according to Dr Bouke Klein Teeselink, who is researching AI and the future of work at King’s College London.
“We don’t have really good insights into how AI affects the non-graduate market compared to the graduate market,” he says, but suggests this scheme could help answer the puzzle of getting more young people into the labour market.
The key test of the bootcamps and ensuing apprenticeships, Teeselink says, would be the thoroughness of the AI training and whether these newcomers made a real difference to their employers’ productivity. “I hope the policy will be rolled out in a way that allows the government to answer both those questions,” he says.
So will the bootcamps make a difference to Neet numbers? Experts say there is no single cause of the crisis and any comprehensive solution must be multi-faceted.
Chris Goulden, the deputy chief executive of the Youth Futures Organisation, a non-profit that researches how to help young people find employment, says he does not believe AI is a driver of Neet numbers. The country still needs to increase the amount of apprenticeships it offers, and guide children who are not on a pathway to university into vocations, he says.
“Our sense is that AI is not driving the increase in Neets since the [Covid] pandemic,” he says. “It’s more to do with mental health issues and a general slowdown in the economy. But that’s not to be complacent, because AI is doing new things every day and it’s going to affect lots of jobs.”
Goulden says if the “first rung of the ladder” is being taken away by AI, it is logical to give young people a foothold in the technology. “Teaching young people to use AI is part of how we prepare them for the future,” he says.
In Preston, the bootcamp attenders are keen to take the next step.
Asked whether he wants the content creator or the IT helpdesk apprenticeship, 16-year-old Hamid Muhammad-Asif, from Blackburn, says: “I’m happy with both.”

Religious Vance seeks to avoid Maga schism as he keeps the faith for 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

US vice-president JD Vance has worn his religion on his sleeve since converting to the Catholicism in 2019. He recently published a book, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, and memorably met the late Pope Francis at the Vatican on Easter Sunday in 2025, a day before the pontiff died.
But his religious identity could take on new weight as he positions himself for a presidential run in 2028, in which a successful campaign would make him only the third Catholic president in US history. Vance’s winding spiritual path – combined with his avowed evangelical roots – have the potential to stymie him, as he seeks to retain the Christian nationalist voters that have sustained Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement while wooing fellow Catholics.
His presidential ambitions and religious convictions were both on show in a keynote speech to the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday evening, where he invoked scripture and the Apostle Paul in paying homage to the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated last year.
“We live in the city of man, not the city of God,” Vance said. “But I believe that our founders built this nation on a promise that echoes our creator.”
The address amounted to “the beginning of 2028 Republican primary competition”, according to Larry Jacobs, a political scientist at the University of Minnesota.
“Vance has thrown his hat in the ring,” he said. “One of the dimensions that JD Vance is bringing to the Republican ticket is the white Christian nationalism. He is trying to put together a coalition that will support him, and he wants the white Christian nationalists to be a key part of that.”
One impediment to that, some religious analysts say, is his conversion to Catholicism – something they believe could leave him with an identity crisis that alienates both evangelicals and Catholic voters.
Both ways
Vance expounded on his beliefs and the evangelical influences that shaped his upbringing in a recent interview with Bryce Crawford, a 22-year-old Christian podcaster with 929,000 subscribers on YouTube.
Commentators say his dilemma was crystallized when Crawford asked for his views on “end times”, an event signifying the second coming of Christ that is much discussed in evangelicalism, but much less so in Catholicism.
Vance expressed a long-held fascination with “end times” beliefs – saying that he had owned a John Hagee bible, which emphasizes end times teachings – before subtly trying to sidestep the issue.
He said: “What I’m trying to focus on is doing as much of God’s work as possible right now, and if that leads to the end times, OK. And if that leads to, you know, us building a better world that thrives and survives for a very long time after I’m gone, that’s great too.
“I just think you’ve got to kind of try to have an attitude of the end times may be coming. In fact, they are coming. It’s just a question of whether they’re coming thousands of years down the road, or a few months down the road, and we’ve got a lot of work to do right now. I‘ve got to try to do the work I can right now.”
The response showed Vance trying to “have things both ways”, suggested Robert Jones, president and founder of the Public Religion Research Institute.
“It reminded me of the kind of conversation that young evangelical men would have sitting around in their dorm room at university,” argued Jones, who comes from an evangelical Christian background. “He’s basically saying, ‘I have no stake in the debate.’
“Anyone schooled inside that evangelical debate would find that position either dismissive of theological of deep theological concerns, or deeply uninformed about them.”
After Pope Leo XIV criticized the Trump administration over the Iran war this year, Vance risked upsetting Catholic voters by telling the pontiff to be “careful” if he was “going to opine on matters of theology”.
The exchange followed an earlier difference of opinion with Pope Francis, in February 2025, when Vance invoked the medieval Christian concept of “ordo amoris” – which translates from Latin as order of love – to justify the Trump administration’s hardline policy of detaining and expelling undocumented people.
“You love your family, and then you love your neighbor, and then you love your community, and then you love your fellow citizens in your own country,” he wrote on social media. “And then after that, you can focus and prioritize the rest of the world.”
The late pope wrote an open letter rejecting the idea and citing the parable of the Good Samaritan.
‘A huge threat’
Daniel Hummel, director of the Lumen Center, a Christian research group in Madison, Wisconsin, said Vance’s public statements highlighted potential pitfalls as he tries to win over both evangelicals and Catholics.
“Vance is a recent Catholic convert, and he still talks a lot like an evangelical,” he said.
That, in itself, could be sufficient to antagonize even conservative Catholics, warned Hummel. “There’s a certain way that Catholics, even conservative Catholics, who might actually disagree with the pope – his view on the Iran war, or something – but respect the pope and would never speak ill of whatever he says, versus an evangelical tradition, where … it’s fine to tell Christian leaders to stay in their lane.”
Vance, who has said he drifted from his evangelical upbringing into atheism by the time he joined the US Marines Corps, may face a further barrier to his political ambitions through a lack of clarity around his religious views.
“It’s pretty clear to me that he understands himself to be a Christian, who is being driven into politics in part because of his Christian faith,” said Hummel. “But it’s unclear to me – even as someone who observes him regularly – what exactly is the content of that Christianity.
“It’s unclear sort of where he’s actually drawing his ideas from when it comes to political theology or how he understands the relationship between religion and politics.
“I think that’s a huge threat to him, because he’s with communities that have strong opinions on these things, and talk about them in very certain ways. So there’s a danger he’ll either commit too much to one side, or the other, and then alienate the other side.”
Authenticity
Jacobs, the University of Minnesota political scientist, said Vance – once a fierce critic of Trump, and warned that he could be “America’s Hitler” – could be derailed by less abstract factors than theological differences.
“The challenge with Vance is authenticity,” he said. “The thing with Trump is the guy resonated authenticity with a variety of Americans, even if the reality behind the scenes would suggest otherwise. He came off as someone who meant what he said.
“But JD Vance too often comes off as someone who is playing the political game.”
Jones said Vance’s appeal to Christian values was underpinned by demographic factors that showed self-identified Republicans to be “more than two-thirds white and Christian”. “A majority of them explicitly support this Christian nationalist movement,” he said.
Vance’s interview with Crawford revealed a further “deeply troubling” trait in his religious beliefs, according to Jones, when the vice-president professed to seeing God’s actions in small coincidences.
The vice-president cited the failed assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. Shots fired by a lone gunman left Trump with a grazed ear, but killed one rallygoer and critically injured two others.
Vance appeared to attribute that to divine providence, noting that Trump had bowed his head slightly to look at a chart on immigration at the instant the bullet passed. If Trump had been killed, he argued, millions of Americans would not have accepted the election result, and the US would have been irreparably split.
Jones said: “A view like that, un-interrogated – especially from a leader as high up as he is – is quite dangerous, because it is always interpreted as the hand of providence when it is something that favors you.
“If Trump had been killed that day, he even says he would not have taken that as the hand of God. He would have taken that as a grand conspiracy. So that tells you right there that the hand of God will only be seen in things that benefit you.”
The Guardian contacted Vance’s office for comment.

A Lithuanian hotelier bringing cold pink soup to Cambodia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Silvija Andruškevič, a graduate of Simono Konarskio Gymnasium, now runs a hotel on Cambodia's Koh Rong island where Lithuania's cold pink soup, šaltibarščiai, is also part of the menu. "Now I can confidently say that this is my place," she says.
Silvija Andruškevič began her travelling adventures while she was still at school. At first, she travelled to neighbouring countries, but later ventured further afield. Eventually, tourism became her profession.
"Later, I became increasingly interested in more distant countries. I also worked in tourism – I was a guide and a resident representative for a tourism company in Poland.
"I had the opportunity to work in Kenya, Bulgaria, the Philippines and Croatia, so these were my longest and most significant trips away from home, as I lived in each of those places for six months," Silvija recalls.
It was during these trips that she developed an increasing affection for Asia. Later, drawing on her experience in information technology and the opportunity to work remotely, she began considering living outside Europe.
"I really enjoyed it and also fell in love with Asia and its culture. I wanted to go and live there for a while one day. Later, I found a job I could do remotely, as I was also working in information technology, so it wasn't difficult for me.
"I travelled to Thailand with some friends. After the trip, they had to return to Lithuania while I was going to stay. But things worked out differently: I was offered a job in Cambodia managing a hotel owned by Polish people. I accepted the offer and left," she says.
The difficult start
Silvija's first few months in Cambodia were nothing like the dream of a tropical holiday. She took on the role of hotel manager and was effectively responsible for everything. The owners lived in Poland, so most of the responsibilities fell to her.
"The beginning in Cambodia was very difficult. I wasn't happy because there was so much work – I sometimes had to work 16 hours a day. The climate was difficult; it was hot. The first six months were very hard. There were many days and nights when I cried.
"I would ask myself: why did I come here? But it was also because the hotel was fairly new and everything had to be put in order and organised, as I was the main manager. I managed the hotel from A to Z," she says.
Over time, however, the situation began to change. Once the hotel had been put in order and the most difficult period was over, Silvija began to see her surroundings in a completely different way. What had initially seemed like a difficult place to live gradually started to look more like a paradise island where she could build her future.
"It's paradise on Earth. It's a beautiful place, there are wonderful people here, and there is also a very large Polish community. I also started looking at it from an investment perspective and realised that it was a good place to build a life of my own," the Vilnius native says.
Her own hotel and a new chapter in life
After a year and a half working at the Polish-owned hotel, Silvija began looking for her own place in business. Initially, she planned to build a hotel of her own. But life offered her another opportunity – to buy an existing hotel run by a well-known figure in the restaurant business.
"I found someone who could replace me because I already knew that I wanted to leave and hand over the management of the hotel to someone else. I started looking around the island and thinking about the opportunities it offered for further personal growth," she says.
At that point, an opportunity arose to buy another property. The hotel belonged to someone involved in the restaurant business. After several years of doing business on the island, he decided to sell the property. Silvija knew the hotel and thought very highly of it, so she decided to buy it.
"I was here and I really love this hotel because it's wonderful, and it also has very good food. I realised that it was a very good opportunity, because the price also seemed much more attractive than in Europe," she says.
Lithuanian šaltibarščiai on the hotel menu
Despite being thousands of kilometres from her native Vilnius, Silvija says she wants to preserve elements of Lithuanian and European traditions. One of these will be the food. At her new hotel, she definitely plans to serve Lithuanian šaltibarščiai, a cold beetroot soup particularly well suited to Cambodia's hot climate.
"I'm changing the menu at my hotel now, and I definitely want to include šaltibarščiai because some dishes are difficult to make here. For example, I could eat cepelinai every day, but I doubt the local cooks would be able to make them. Šaltibarščiai, on the other hand, are perfect for this kind of weather because it's constantly hot here and they are refreshing, so they will definitely be on the menu," she says with a smile.
Business is not the only area in which Silvija has become involved in life on the island. Local people live much more modestly than residents of European cities. Together with others living and working on the island, she helps children and the local school while also trying to create jobs for local people.
"Local people on the island mostly live modestly. There is also a big difference between life in the city and in the provinces. On the other hand, these people don't need much. We try to help local people by providing them with jobs, organising various initiatives and charity drives, and helping the school. Recently, drinking water was brought to the school, and repair work will also be carried out there now," she says.
Other Europeans living on the island are also involved in helping the community. One of Silvija's friends, who is from Poland, set up a Lions International club there and started a project to build a kindergarten.
"It's an international charity organisation, and it has now started a project to build a kindergarten on the island. So we try to help local people in whatever ways we can," Silvija says.
Helping does not always mean large, organised initiatives. Sometimes it starts with a very simple gesture. Silvija recalls an incident she noticed while riding a scooter. She saw children walking along the tarmac without shoes. She knew that their flip-flops often wore out, so she simply went to a shop.
"I know more or less all the children in my small village. Quite often, their flip-flops wear out. Once, while riding my scooter, I noticed that the children were simply walking barefoot on the tarmac, so I quickly went to buy them some flip-flops. But things like that actually happen quite often in everyday life. We buy them a drink or even a chocolate bar, because, like all children, they enjoy those things," she says.
Over the past year, Silvija's business activities in Cambodia have expanded significantly. Alongside running the hotel, she has also become involved in tourism. She was invited to help set up a travel agency and became its director. As she explains, the new business also complements her main venture.
"We now organise trips to Cambodia, mainly from Europe, but we also arrange excursions for local residents. We organise transport to the island as well as stays on the island itself. This is one of the new areas of my business, and it greatly helps my main venture – the hotel – because I can promote my hotel through the agency," Silvija says.
The agency operates through an officially registered company and is overseen by the Ministry of Tourism. Appropriate licences are required to operate such a business. Silvija says her business partner has many years of experience in Cambodia's tourism sector and good contacts within the ministry.
"My business partner has very good contacts at the Ministry of Tourism. He is an adviser to the ministry and ran this company in Cambodia for more than 20 years. During the Covid-19 pandemic, the business slowed down somewhat, so he was looking for partners to revive it," she adds.
As Silvija explains, Cambodia does not have the four seasons familiar to Europeans. The year is broadly divided into the dry and rainy seasons. However, the latter does not necessarily mean endless downpours. Silvija points out that temperatures remain around 30C even during the rainy season, while rainfall is often short-lived.
The term "green season" is increasingly being used instead of "rainy season" to encourage tourists to visit Cambodia at this time of year.
"You don't see the sun, but you can still get a tan through the clouds, so quite a lot of people actually prefer this so-called 'rainy season'. We now call it the 'green season' to change the perception somewhat and make people less afraid of the rain. 'Green season' sounds friendlier," Silvija says.
Attracting more Lithuanians and Poles to Cambodia
Silvija, who is from Vilnius, says she would like to use her connections in Central and Eastern Europe to promote Cambodia in Lithuania and Poland. In her view, both markets still have considerable potential because Cambodia is not as popular a destination there as, for example, Thailand.
At present, the largest groups of foreign tourists are French, British and American. According to Silvija, particularly large numbers of French visitors come to Cambodia, partly because of the country's history.
"There is now a direct flight from Prague to Cambodia, which is also a big development for us. From December to April, during the peak tourist season, there will be flights from Prague, which will also help promote this market. In general, we get a lot of French, British and American visitors. Cambodia was once a French colony, so the French have developed a particular fondness for the country," she explains.
Although travelling from Europe to Cambodia can be expensive, particularly because of the cost of flights, expenses once in the country can be considerably lower. Silvija says the country remains affordable for the average tourist.
"Cambodia is still very attractive in terms of prices; it is quite cheap. For €5-7, you can have a very good meal. You can find a hotel for around €40 a night, depending on the location and region. It is slightly more expensive on the islands, but on the mainland it is genuinely quite cheap, and you can find practically everything at an affordable price," she says.
Although tourism is one of the country's most important economic sectors, it is not the only area in which Cambodia is developing rapidly. Increasing amounts of investment are coming from other Asian countries.
"Tourism is the main sector, but other sectors are also developing very quickly in Cambodia. Japan is now building a seaport – the largest in Cambodia. The Chinese are building roads, while South Koreans are also investing heavily in the beauty industry because Korean aesthetic medicine is quite popular. So all these countries are also actively investing in Cambodia. Various factories and companies are being opened – the country really is developing rapidly," she says.
In her view, the changes taking place in the country will mean Cambodia increasingly comes onto the radar of Europeans.
'This is my place'
For Silvija, promoting Cambodia is not simply a business task. As she admits, after spending many years in the country, she increasingly feels that she has chosen to build her life there. Whenever she returns to Europe, she finds herself comparing life there with her everyday life in Cambodia.
"It's not even a task, but probably my destiny – to show people this country, because it really is wonderful, very friendly and safe," she says.
Although the beginning was full of doubts, Silvija no longer hesitates when asked whether Cambodia has become her home. She has a business there, plans new investments and helps the local community. She has also brought her brother Jokūbas to live with her.
"Now I can confidently say that this is my place. Considering all the plans for the hotels, I will probably have to spend the next 15 years in Cambodia," Silvija says.

Nepal flood survivor says rescue efforts must continue

Nepal flood survivor says rescue efforts must continue
Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in darkness inside a flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water for 10 days while praying for rescue
For 10 days, Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in darkness inside a flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water and losing all sense of time as he desperately prayed for rescue.
When a disaster response team finally pulled him to safety on September 4, Sah’s first question showed how deeply the ordeal had disoriented him.
“When I was rescued I first asked, how many days has it been?” Sah, aged 30, said in an interview, while on his way back home in Saptari district on Sunday.
“He said that it has been 10 days. I thought it had been just a few days.”
Sah’s extraordinary survival was a rare ray of hope after a disaster that killed at least 1,429 people and left more than 5,640 missing, the majority in Nepal.
Family, friends and neighbours celebrated Sah’s return with garlands and a cake, and his home was adorned with balloons and colours.

Niger military government reshuffles army command weeks after deadly mutiny
New chief of staff appointed after failed mutiny tested military rulers’ grip on power.
Niger’s military government has named a new chief of the armed forces as it reshuffled its top military command following a failed mutiny late last month.
A decree read on state television on Friday announced that General Mamane Sani Kiaou, previously the army’s chief of staff, would take over as head of the armed forces, replacing General Moussa Salaou Barmou.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Niger military accuses France of orchestrating failed coup: What to know
- list 2 of 2France denies Niger’s accusation it orchestrated failed military mutiny
Both men had held senior posts since a July 2023 coup brought a group of army officers – led by General Abdourahamane Tchiani – to power.
No reason was given for Barmou’s removal.
General Abdourahmane Abou Zataka has been promoted to succeed Kiaou as army chief of staff, according to the same decree.
Regional broadcaster RFI reported that General Ismael K Sidi Omar has also been named the new second-in-command of the general staff. Sidi Omar previously commanded Base 101, RFI reported, the airport base at the centre of the mutiny, and remained loyal to Tchiani throughout the crisis.
The mutiny that began on August 28 lasted almost 24 hours, drawing in fighting at the presidential palace, Niamey’s international airport and a nearby military base.
Mostly young soldiers took fellow servicemen hostage and opened fire on several sensitive sites, according to Niger’s Ministry of Defence.
Military government forces needed support from Russia’s Africa Corps, a state-backed force that has replaced the mercenary group Wagner in several African countries, which stepped in with ground and air support.
Dozens of mutineers were killed or arrested, along with three members of the presidential guard, though the government has not disclosed an overall death toll or said what charges detained soldiers might face.
Analysts and diplomats told The Associated Press news agency that the mutineers appeared driven by anger over worsening attacks by armed groups and poor conditions within the military.
Kiaou is a field commander who has led operations against armed groups in Niger’s western Tillaberi region and the southeastern Diffa region, and helped negotiate the withdrawal of French and United States troops after the coup.
State media reported he recently completed a tour of the country’s main garrisons intended to restore unity among the ranks.
Tchiani’s government seized power in July 2023 from elected President Mohamed Bazoum, who remains in detention, arguing the civilian government had failed to contain armed groups and violence.
Since then, Niger has cut military ties with France and the US and drawn closer to Russia, even as the security situation has continued to deteriorate.
Niger has accused France of being behind last month’s mutiny, an allegation the French government dismissed as “pure fantasy”.

Russians receive new batch of tanks with upgraded anti-drone protection
Russian forces have received a new batch of T-90M Proryv and T-72B3M tanks. The vehicles have been equipped with upgraded anti-drone protection.
Source: Russia's state-owned corporation Rostec
Details: The tanks, manufactured at the sanctioned Uralvagonzavod plant, have been fitted with all-round protection. The Russians claim that the system protecting the tanks from attack UAVs has been upgraded to "provide the vehicle with maximum protection".
"Additional protection is being developed, primarily against unmanned aerial vehicles. Certain innovations are also being introduced in the additional equipment section, which helps operate in combat conditions," the corporation said.
In a video posted by Rostec, the tank turrets are covered with screens made of metal cables, grilles and chains. Additional protection has also been installed on the sides.
The Russians claim that each tank must travel at least 100 km before being sent to the front line so that the vehicles can be tested and any defects eliminated.
Russia did not disclose the number of tanks or the front to which the vehicles were sent.
Background:
- In September 2025, OSINT analyst Jompy spotted hundreds of T-72A hulls near Uralvagonzavod. The plant is one of the key players in Russia's tank industry and manufactures T-90M tanks and BMPT armoured fighting vehicles, but in recent years has focused mainly on repairing and upgrading T-72B tanks to the T-72B3M version.
- Defence Intelligence of Ukraine also reported that more than half of the Russian companies belonging to the key armoured vehicle manufacturing concern are still not under sanctions.

Swedes vote in tight election that could bring far-right into government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
08:41:21 UTC
17:41:21 KST

Swedes began voting on Sunday in a closely contested general election that could see the far-right Sweden Democrats enter government for the first time or the left-wing opposition return to power.
Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats was among the first to cast her ballot after polling stations opened at 8 a.m. local time.
The 59-year-old former prime minister voted with her husband at a school in her home municipality of Nacka, south of Stockholm.
Polls had long given the four-party left-wing bloc a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the Sweden Democrats. But the gap narrowed to a virtual dead heat in the final days of the campaign.
“It is now up to the Swedish people to decide which direction our country should take,” Andersson told reporters after voting, warning that the election could produce a government dominated by the Sweden Democrats.
Far-right seeks historic government role
Kristersson’s government has relied on Sweden Democrats support since 2022, giving the far-right party significant influence over immigration and crime policy.
The party, led by Jimmie Akesson, has roots in the neo-Nazi movement but has moved into the political mainstream over the past two decades. Kristersson has pledged to offer the party cabinet posts if the right-wing alliance wins.
Kristersson has highlighted falling levels of deadly shootings and bombings linked to organized crime, as well as record-low asylum applications, while promising to improve everyday life for Swedes.
“We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people ... to make Sweden great again,” he said before the vote.
Welfare, crime and the cost of living
Andersson’s Social Democrats, Sweden’s largest party, have campaigned on strengthening the welfare state and helping households cope with rising living costs.
Akesson, meanwhile, expressed confidence in victory at the party’s final rally in Stockholm on Saturday, telling supporters: “We’ve already won!”
Around 8 million people are eligible to vote in the election, with turnout in Sweden regularly exceeding 80 percent. About half of voters have already cast ballots in advance.
Polling stations close at 8 p.m. local time, with exit polls expected shortly afterward and reliable results several hours later.
A right-wing victory could make government formation relatively straightforward. If the left wins a majority, however, negotiations could prove more difficult because of ideological divisions among the four parties.

Astrological forecast for the week of September 14–20: great ambitions, strong passions, and tests of power
Kyiv • UNN
Astrologer Kseniia Bazylenko forecasts an active week with an intensification of issues surrounding power, finance, and negotiations. Ukraine may face international pressure and news in the defense sector.
The week from September 14 to 20 promises to be very energetic and eventful. On the one hand, it gives us an excellent opportunity to move forward, put plans into action, and take on matters that we have long been postponing. On the other hand, this very week will bring the themes of money, power, ambition, jealousy, difficult negotiations, and hidden processes into particularly sharp focus. Astrologer Kseniia Bazylenko told UNN readers exclusively about what the stars and planets predict for this week.
Details
Astrologer Kseniia Bazylenko notes that the Moon continues to wax, which means that now is a good time for growth, launching new ventures, and taking active steps. The important personal planets are not currently creating a difficult retrograde backdrop. We should take advantage of this, because the situation will begin to change as early as October, when we will face the retrograde cycles of Venus and, later, Mercury.
At the beginning of the week, the harmonious interaction between the Sun and Mars provides additional strength. We may feel more energy, confidence, and a desire to act. Therefore, my first piece of advice is very simple: do not put off until later what can be started now. But I certainly would not call this week calm
Black Moon in Capricorn: trials involving power and ambition
One of the most important astrological events of this period will be the transition of the Black Moon, or Lilith, into the sign of Capricorn. We may have begun to feel its influence in recent weeks, and ahead lies approximately nine months of a new cycle
According to her, the Black Moon is not a planet but a calculated astrological point. In the astrological tradition, it is associated with our shadow manifestations, temptations, extremes, and situations in which it is particularly easy to lose our sense of proportion. Capricorn, meanwhile, represents power, status, career, major ambitions, hierarchy, and responsibility.
On a personal level, the next nine months may become a kind of test of our ambitions. What do we seek, and what price are we prepared to pay to achieve it? Are position, money, status, or the desire to control others becoming more important than our own principles? This period may be particularly revealing for managers, business owners, and people with significant powers. In mundane astrology, the spotlight shifts to the state and government institutions. Abuses of power, non-transparent agreements, struggles for positions and influence, corruption scandals, and weak points in large systems may come to the surface more often. The Black Moon in Capricorn seems to illuminate the summit of the system—and reveals not only its strength but also what has long remained in the shadows
Venus and Pluto: when feelings become too intense
Another of the week's main aspects, according to the astrologer, is the square between Venus and Pluto, which will manifest particularly strongly on September 15.
And this truly is an aspect of great passions. Venus is in Scorpio, so feelings are already becoming deeper and more intense. Pluto can amplify them to extremes. Strong attraction may coexist with jealousy, resentment, possessiveness, and a desire to control the person we love. So take care of your relationships. This especially applies to young couples, where intense emotions can very quickly turn a minor argument into a serious conflict. Do not test love through jealousy, and do not try to hold on to another person through the force of your emotions
