Yemeni army rosters filled with 'ghost names,' leaving Mocha vulnerable to Houthi takeover - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
07:03:32 UTC
16:03:32 KST

Yemeni battalions stationed in the port city of Mocha were left largely unprepared to fend off a takeover by the Iran-backed Houthis on Thursday, with much of the force’s roster filled with “ghost names” of soldiers that did not actually exist, according to a Saturday CNN report.
A Western source with knowledge of Yemeni anti-Houthi operations told CNN that the “ghost names” received salaries, making the army seem much stronger than it was on paper. In actuality, the army was only around 20% of what it appeared to be, according to the source.
Blame for the apparent lack of military resistance to the Houthi takeover has been split between Yemeni leaders, the United States, and Saudi Arabia, with multiple sources telling CNN that different parties were responsible for the failure.
'A Saudi-American f*** of epic proportions'
One regional CNN source described the fall of Mocha as “a Saudi-American f*** up of epic proportions” caused by delayed decision-making by Washington and Riyadh.
“The failure this time is not with the Yemenis,” the source told CNN on Friday. “There was not one airstrike throughout the day yesterday (by Saudi support forces), although there were minute-by-minute updates.”
Another source stated that the Saudi military had been put on high alert due to the possibility of a Houthi advance weeks ago, but failed to prepare for the attack. Key air command personnel for directing combat aircraft allegedly were not deployed.
“The Saudis threw the Yemenis under the bus,” the source told CNN.
According to the report, a senior Yemeni official said he had warned US Central Command (CENTCOM) repeatedly “that the situation was becoming critical.”
The source told CNN that CENTCOM assured him that the US was “watching the situation closely and that Saudi air support was coming,” but the air support did not show up.
On Thursday, the day of the Houthi attack, CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper was in Saudi Arabia for coordination meetings, two sources told CNN.
While CENTCOM did not confirm that the visit occurred, CNN cited a US official as saying that in recent weeks American military personnel have been working with a newly established joint forces command that was formed after it was suspected that Iran was intensifying efforts to support Houthi attacks.
Some say divisions between Yemen's leaders are to blame for fall of Mocha
DC-based Mohammed al-Basha, who has served as an advisor to the US government on the Arabian Peninsula, argued to CNN that internal divisions among Yemen’s leadership were to blame for the failure to defend Mocha.
“This goes back to a deeper problem in the anti-Houthi coalition,” Basha told CNN. “There is no political cohesion.”
“There’s no united command and control in Yemen,” he continued. “I think everybody was aware of the Houthis’ push towards the west coast. The writings on the wall were very clear.”
When asked what may come next, Basha predicted that the Houthis would continue pushing eastwards, further into Yemen, telling CNN that “We are seeing today, via satellite and via OSINT (open-source intelligence) photography… that the Houthis are mobilizing.”

Berlin woman attacked with broken glass bottle after wearing Star of David necklace, police say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
07:03:20 UTC
16:03:20 KST

The Berlin police opened an investigation on Saturday into a suspected antisemitic attack after a 43-year-old woman was targeted by two men who noticed the Star of David necklace she was wearing, directed antisemitic insults at her, and assaulted her with a broken glass bottle.
According to a police statement, the incident occurred at around 2:30 a.m. between Thursday and Friday on Torstrasse in the Mitte district of central Berlin. Two men, whose identities have not yet been determined, approached the woman after noticing the Star of David she was wearing.
They then hurled antisemitic insults at her, and at one point, one of them attacked her with a broken glass bottle.
Woman suffered cuts before suspects fled scene
The woman attempted to defend herself and suffered several cuts to one of her hands. The two suspects fled the scene following the attack.
Emergency responders treated her at the scene before taking her to a hospital for further care. Police did not provide further details at this stage regarding the woman’s condition or a description of the suspects.
The investigation has been transferred to the Berlin Criminal Police’s State Security Division, which handles offenses with political, extremist or antisemitic backgrounds. German authorities have not yet announced any arrests in the case.
The attack joins a long list of antisemitic incidents recorded in recent years in the German capital. According to Berlin authorities, 2,268 antisemitic offenses were recorded in the city in 2025, up 24.3% from the previous year. Sixty-four of the cases were classified as violent offenses.
Berlin reports continued rise in antisemitic incidents
In June, another investigation was launched after a 47-year-old man wearing a kippah was attacked in the Charlottenburg neighborhood. According to police, the suspect directed antisemitic insults at the man and his two children, spat at them and struck the man in the face. Police also transferred the investigation to the State Security Division.
A report by the Berlin public prosecutor’s office published in July said that 820 proceedings with an antisemitic background were opened during 2025, compared with 756 in 2024.
The prosecutor’s representative responsible for combating antisemitism warned that the number of incidents remains high and that attacks of this kind harm not only the direct victims, but also undermine the sense of security of the city’s Jewish community.

Kiev strikes emergency fuel convoy to Europe’s biggest nuclear plant – Rosatom

Kiev strikes emergency fuel convoy to Europe’s biggest nuclear plant – Rosatom
Ukraine has carried out a series of strikes on tankers delivering emergency diesel fuel to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), killing two Russian servicemen and wounding multiple others, Rosatom CEO Aleksey Likhachev has said.
The attacks took place on Friday in the immediate vicinity of the plant’s perimeter and targeted fuel trucks transporting diesel needed for the facility’s emergency power systems, Likhachev said in a statement on Sunday.
Two Russian servicemen were killed and “a large number” were wounded, some seriously, according to the Rosatom chief. He said the troops had been involved in securing a “strictly civilian mission” to maintain fuel deliveries to the nuclear facility.
Likhachev accused Kiev of knowingly targeting the tankers despite being aware of their cargo and its importance to nuclear safety.
The incident comes just days after the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) warned that the ZNPP’s diesel reserves had been critically depleted during nearly three weeks without external electricity. The plant lost its sole remaining power connection on August 20 and had to rely entirely on emergency generators until a temporary IAEA-brokered ceasefire allowed repairs to be carried out and the line to be reconnected on September 7.
Even after external electricity was restored, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi stressed that replenishing diesel remained essential because the plant could again lose grid power due to unspecified “military activity” in the area.
During the latest blackout, the plant had reduced the number of operating generators from four to two to conserve diesel and began running some cooling pumps intermittently. The generators provide electricity for essential safety systems, including pumps cooling all six reactors and their spent fuel pools.
Likhachev accused Kiev of deliberately increasing the risk of a nuclear emergency at Europe’s largest nuclear power plant.
“The Kiev regime has openly embarked on a path of provoking a nuclear incident at Europe’s largest nuclear power plant, with unpredictable consequences,” he said, arguing that any such event could affect areas far beyond the immediate vicinity of the facility.
The Rosatom chief called on the IAEA to “strongly condemn” the attack and explicitly identify those responsible. He also urged Kiev’s Western backers to distance themselves from what he described as the Ukrainian government’s “most horrific crimes.”
The IAEA has repeatedly warned about military activity around the ZNPP and nearby Energodar. In its latest update before Likhachev’s statement, the agency reported hearing explosions, drones and sustained gunfire in the area and said the plant’s power situation remained “increasingly fragile.”

Mystery son and disputed heir: Uganda’s king buried amid succession dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
07:00:59 UTC
16:00:59 KST

Mystery son and disputed heir: Uganda’s king buried amid succession dispute
The 34-year-old monarch’s death has opened a rare challenge to the traditional process of choosing Tooro’s next king.
Fort Portal, Uganda – When King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV of Tooro was buried on September 12, the ceremony unfolded under the shadow of a bitter dispute over who should succeed him.
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a 56-year-old news anchor and editor at Uganda Broadcasting Corporation, had been selected by the royal clan to succeed Oyo. During the burial at the Karambi Royal Tombs in Fort Portal, he formally assumed power by casting nine coffee berries into the king’s grave, part of the traditional handover ritual.
But the succession remains contested.
Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa, and his sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, have opposed Kijanangoma’s selection, saying the late king’s will named a son as his heir.
Oyo never married and was not publicly known to have children. After his death, Tooro’s Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki announced that the king had left a son whose identity would be revealed at an appropriate time. The child has not been publicly identified.
Oyo’s family says a 2022 will named a son whom he described as his lawfully recognised biological son as heir to the throne. But Babiito clan elders, who are responsible for guarding the Tooro royal lineage, determining succession and safeguarding the kingdom’s traditions, say Oyo had not introduced the child through the customary process and instead backed Kijanangoma as his successor.
“The will is not a determinant of who is supposed to be a king; it is a document that expresses one’s wish,” said Reverend Father Charles Oyo, a Babiito clan elder. “The Musuuga [Babiito clan leader] is above the will.”
Princess Komuntale has accused the elders of trying to take over the throne.
“King Oyo was a very peaceful man, a very humble man,” she said. “I just don’t want these evil vultures to come and steal what he worked so hard for. I continue to stand with my brother.”
The dispute has divided opinion over who should be regarded as Oyo’s legitimate successor. The Ugandan government also became involved in talks aimed at resolving the dispute before the burial.
The child king
Oyo’s own path to the throne began when he was just three years old.
He became king in 1995 after the death of his father, Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III, and was recognised as the world’s youngest reigning monarch.
As a child, Oyo was homeschooled, with the palace serving as his classroom. When he later joined primary school, childhood friends remember him as a kind and warm person.
During school holidays, he sometimes sneaked out of the family’s private residence in Buziga, Kampala, to play football in the neighbourhood.
Martin Odong, a radio journalist and childhood friend, remembers him as “friendly, social and compassionate”.
Oyo would stop football games to check on an injured player, regardless of which side they were playing for, Odong said.
His love of football continued into adulthood. He promoted local tournaments, including the Tooro Kingdom MTN Masaza Cup, which was suspended as his health deteriorated.
Oyo died on August 27, aged 34, in the United States while receiving cancer treatment. His body was returned to Uganda for nine days of mourning before his burial at the Karambi Royal Tombs, which coincided with Empango, the anniversary of his coronation.
At St John’s Cathedral, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa remembered her son as someone who had always protected her.
“He was my shield who always stood for me,” she said.
She recalled praying for his life when she was in hospital.
“When I was in the hospital, I said, ‘God, please leave my son alone; take me first,’” she said. “He [God] decided to take him [King Oyo] first. I said, ‘Why? Because he was closer to You than me.’”
Princess Komuntale described her brother as a “funny person” who “always brightened my day”.
Although he was younger than her, she said, he often behaved like the older sibling and protected her and their mother after their father “left to be with the Lord”.
Father Charles Oyo remembered him as a “handsome king who loved his kingdom so much”.
He said Oyo died just as he was “beginning to demonstrate his abilities and capacity as a king”.
A king without political power
Uganda is a constitutional republic, and its traditional kings have no formal political authority. But the kingdoms retain cultural influence and command loyalty among many of their communities.
Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967. They were restored in 1993 under President Yoweri Museveni.
Oyo was guided by regents while he was a child and took on the full responsibilities of the monarchy as an adult.
His unusual position meant he met presidents, royalty and other world leaders from a young age. Among them was former South African President Nelson Mandela, who reportedly wanted to meet the young king during a visit to Uganda. Oyo, however, was more interested in playing with his toys behind the VIP tent.
As an adult, he used the platform of the throne to promote issues beyond the kingdom.
In 2020, he climbed the Rwenzori Mountains to draw attention to climate change and the retreat of the glaciers there.
He also supported a campaign to plant 10 million trees across Tooro over five years.
He promoted healthy living and took part in cancer awareness runs. Komuntale called him her “best workout partner”.
Before his death, Oyo had allocated land and begun fundraising for a paediatric hospital in Kyenjojo district. Clan elders have since appealed to the government to complete the project and establish a specialised cancer facility and an international stadium in his memory.
His final months
Oyo’s illness was kept largely private.
According to his sister, he began experiencing pain in his back and rib cage last year. The family initially thought it might be linked to strenuous exercise or ulcers.
He later travelled to Kenya, where he was diagnosed with angiosarcoma, an aggressive form of cancer, before travelling to Germany for treatment and eventually to the US.
“He told us to keep it private, and we respected that,” Komuntale said.
She said that shortly before his death, Oyo spoke to key workers in Uganda about returning home. He wanted to celebrate Empango, the anniversary of his coronation, with his people.
He never made it home.
For Komuntale, the king remained her younger brother even after he became one of Africa’s most recognisable traditional rulers.
She remembered playing dodgeball with him and his love for his three dogs.
“Even though you were crowned a king, you were still a kid who loved to play,” she said.
“I will keep your legacy, what you loved, and we will talk about you every day.”

Middle powers guarding Europe’s eastern flank – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Ukraine and Poland, two Central and Eastern European states whose regional influence has often been underestimated, illustrate how middle powers can shape outcomes once reserved for great powers, Maksym Khylko and Adam Reichard write for the New Eastern Europe Magazine, partners of LRT English.
In January 2026, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney used the podium of the World Economic Forum in Davos to warn that the world was living through “a rupture, not a transition” in the international order, in which great powers increasingly treat economic interdependence, tariffs and supply chains as instruments of coercion.
His central claim – that middle powers are not powerless but must act together or risk being “on the menu” rather than at the table – has become a reference point for a broader debate about the future of democracies in the changing world order.
Scholars and analysts from Central and Eastern Europe have converged on a similar diagnosis. In a special 2026 edition of New Eastern Europe dedicated to this new disorder, Andreas Umland argues that the world as we know it is nearing its end and is increasingly being displaced by a system that presents itself openly as non-liberal, if not outright anti-liberal, reflecting the shifting preferences of powerful leaders.
Wojciech Michnik links this trend to the fate of European security, arguing that the sense of Europe adrift in the emerging order stems from both external shocks and internal shortcomings: on the one side, the United States is signalling that Europe is no longer the central theatre of American strategy; on the other, Europeans themselves remain divided over how far they are willing to go in assuming strategic autonomy.
Paul Bell frames the resulting predicament starkly, describing Europe as sandwiched between autocrats who, for their own distinct purposes, are each working to weaken it, undermine European policy and democratic values.
The case for European strategic autonomy rests on a structural observation: no single EU member state, and arguably not the Union as a whole in its current institutional configuration, possesses the sovereign capability to guarantee its security, prosperity or technological relevance if the assumptions underlying transatlantic and global economic integration continue to erode.
Discussing EU strategic autonomy as independence (disengagement from external dependence), as responsibility (binding more closely with like-minded partners to jointly resist coercion), and as hedging (preserving room for manoeuvre between rival powers), Daniel Fiott argues that the EU’s ability to resist being wedged apart by Washington or Beijing depends less on a top-down Brussels-led strategy than on internal binding efforts among member states.
When considering the role of middle powers in this context, the Central and Eastern European states play key roles: Ukraine’s resistance to the Russian invasion has served as the external shock that pushed EU member states towards a more responsibility-oriented posture, while Poland has played an important role in anchoring the Union’s defence posture around this model of autonomy, particularly at the initial stage of providing assistance to Ukraine and, in parallel, unprecedented investments in its own defence.
Ukraine, Poland, and the EU: middle powers in practice
The concept of the middle power has a long lineage in international relations theory, dating to debates at the founding of the United Nations, when Canadian and Australian diplomats sought recognition for states that, while lacking great-power capability, made disproportionate contributions to the war effort and collective security architecture.
A middle power is generally understood as a state occupying an intermediate position in the international hierarchy: it lacks the capacity of a great power to determine systemic outcomes unilaterally, but possesses sufficient economic, military, diplomatic or normative resources to shape outcomes within a region or issue-area, typically through coalition-building and multilateralism rather than coercion.
Eduard Jordaan’s influential distinction between “traditional” middle powers – wealthy and stable democratic states, which tend to legitimise the existing order – and “emerging” middle powers, which are often semi-peripheral, more assertive regionally, and less committed to defending a status quo that historically marginalised them, remains analytically useful today.
This distinction helps to comprehend the phenomenon of the rise of authoritarian and illiberal middle powers, in particular in the Middle East and Asia, which combine regional assertiveness with a transactional, sovereigntist posture toward international institutions.
Thus, the challenge facing the EU is not simply that great powers behave without constraint, but that the “middle tier” of the international system, once assumed to be a natural constituency for a rules-based order, is itself becoming ideologically heterogeneous and, in some cases, corrosive of that order. Against this backdrop, it is in the EU’s vital interest to support the development and cooperation of democratically-oriented middle powers. Ukraine and Poland are critical cases in this regard.
Over the last four-plus years, Ukraine has offered a vivid illustration that a middle power can confront a far greater one and avoid defeat. Despite Russia’s overwhelming advantages in population, military-industrial capacity and nuclear status, Ukraine has not only resisted conquest since February 2022, but has imposed disproportionate costs on the aggressor, including long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory that have unsettled Moscow’s calculations and prompted the previously sceptical Donald Trump to change his stance on Kyiv’s chances.
While Ukraine’s resilience has depended on external support, its agency in whole-of-society mobilisation, drone-warfare innovation, and asymmetric strategy has been decisive.
In the first weeks after the invasion, Poland became the main logistical corridor for western arms transfers, delivering some of Ukraine’s earliest heavy equipment. At the same time, Poland absorbed the largest share of Ukrainian refugees, funding reception and integration at a scale unmatched elsewhere.
This response was driven not only by threat perception and humanitarian imperative, but it also demonstrated Poland’s ambition to assert regional leadership. The country positioned itself as a key player in shaping the West’s response, providing lethal aid even before the invasion, and pressed larger western allies towards firmer positions.
That early solidarity has since been reinforced by a genuine structural transformation: Poland’s defence budget has roughly tripled over the past decade, reaching the highest ratio in NATO – nearing five per cent of its GDP this year. The Polish armed forces have more than doubled since 2014, with plans to reach 300,000 personnel by 2035, making Poland the EU’s largest land force.
The EU’s collective response serves as a good example of what middle powers can achieve by acting together. When the US sharply curtailed assistance to Ukraine in early 2025, European aid did not collapse.
Funding channelled through EU institutions rose from roughly half of total European assistance in 2022 to nearly 90 percent by 2025, substituting for the American shortfall. The fact that a coalition of middle and small powers sustained Ukraine’s war effort without its largest former patron demonstrates that acting together, middle powers can substitute for the protection a single great power once provided.
Great powers are also starting to recognise the growing influence of middle powers. Through much of 2025, President Trump’s statements towards Ukraine were often dismissive, yet by mid-2026, following Ukrainian successes and the EU’s demonstrated capacity to sustain support independently, his rhetoric shifted.
During this year’s G7 and NATO summits, Trump had begun praising Ukraine’s resilience, aligning more closely with European positions. This shift should not be assumed irreversible, but it is consistent with a basic realist logic: demonstrated resolve and capability, not appeals for sympathy, alter a great power’s calculus of respect.
A shared, secure future, not a contentious past
The clearest emerging illustration of complementary middle-power roles is in missile and drone defence, where Ukrainian experience and Polish industrial capacity are becoming genuinely interlocking assets.
Following Trump’s announcement at the July 2026 NATO summit in Ankara that Washington would allow Ukraine to license-produce Patriot interceptor missiles, Poland proposed a trilateral framework with the US and Ukraine, under which production and maintenance would take place on Polish soil, drawing on an existing agreement Warsaw had signed with the US, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden to host a European Patriot PAC-3 service centre.
Polish officials have framed this explicitly as a way of combining Ukrainian operational knowledge with a secure, allied manufacturing base close to, but outside, the range of the heaviest Russian strikes, addressing both Kyiv’s need for scale and Washington’s concerns about producing sensitive systems inside an active war zone.
A parallel dynamic is underway in counter-drone defence. Ukraine’s forces have developed some of the world’s most combat-tested methods for intercepting mass drone and missile salvoes, downing over a thousand Shahed-type drones with a reported roughly 95 percent success rate using low-cost interceptor systems.
This expertise is highly valuable for Poland’s Eastern Shield programme and the broader European “drone wall” initiative launched with France, Germany, Italy and the UK after Russian drones repeatedly violated Polish and other allied airspace in 2025.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has explicitly offered to help Poland and other partners build “a joint, truly reliable shield against Russian aerial threats”, based on Ukraine’s battlefield experience, while Polish and Ukrainian manufacturers already cooperate on joint training and production projects.
This critical cooperation, however, is being tested by an historical dispute which Europe can least afford at this moment.
In mid-2026, a diplomatic crisis erupted after Zelensky renamed a military unit in honour of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) – commemorated in Ukraine as a symbol of resistance to Soviet domination, but remembered in Poland chiefly as the perpetrator of the 1943–44 mass killings of Polish civilians in Volhynia (Wołyń) region.
This moved was followed by the decision of the Polish president, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour (which the previous president Andrzej Duda had awarded in 2023).
This episode provides fertile ground for Russian influence campaigns to exploit growing anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland – sentiment already layered over the longer-running dispute over Ukrainian agricultural exports and EU accession terms. Ahead of Poland’s 2027 elections, these tensions risk complicating Ukraine’s membership process through bilateral “memory politics”.
This dispute is one that Europe cannot afford, given that no other European state could replace Poland’s role as NATO’s principal logistics hub for Ukraine in the foreseeable future.
Ukraine’s continued resistance is equally crucial for Polish security on NATO’s eastern flank. Thankfully, both governments appear to have shown that they can step back from the brink: Zelensky’s decision to open historical archives on the Volhynian tragedy and authorise broader exhumations, and quiet diplomacy between the two presidents at the Ankara NATO summit, suggest that the relationship’s structural logic still outweighs its emotional politics.
But this cannot be left to improvised de-escalation after each flare-up. Given how much depends on both countries’ security, Poles and Ukrainians have a direct interest in quarrelling less over an unresolved and painful past and cooperating more deliberately around a common European future, treating historical reconciliation as a standing diplomatic project rather than a recurring source of crisis.
Middle powers guarding Europe’s eastern flank
Against the backdrop of Russia’s war against Ukraine, the volatility of American policy under Trump, and the strengthening of authoritarian and illiberal tendencies globally, the EU has been compelled to demonstrate that an alliance of medium and small powers can be an equally strong actor.
This does not require uniform contributions from every state, but rather a smart division of responsibilities and specialisations, within which countries apply their comparative advantages to promote shared European values, security, and prosperity.
Ukraine and Poland have adjacent, mutually reinforcing niches within this division of responsibilities. Ukraine has become the EU’s frontline of defence with advanced experience in modern warfare, drone technology and societal resilience under existential pressure.
Poland has established itself as the logistical and political hinge connecting that frontline to the rest of the EU, while rapidly building its own military-industrial base needed to convert battlefield lessons into deployable European capability.
Their further strengthening and success as middle powers are crucial for Europe to achieve genuine strategic autonomy.
What both governments and societies now owe each other, and the EU as a whole, is the discipline to keep that cooperation from being derailed by unresolved historical, political and even economic disputes, at precisely the moment when their own security and that of the whole of Europe’s eastern flank depends on getting it right.
Maksym Khylko is the chairman at the East European Security Research Initiative, and Associate Professor at the Institute of European Studies and International Relations, Faculty of Social and Economic Sciences, Comenius University.
Adam Reichardt is the editor-in-chief of New Eastern Europe and the co-host of the Talk Eastern Europe podcast and YouTube channel.

Russian Attacks Kill 9, Injure Dozens in Ukraine as Moscow Says It Hit Ships, Plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Russian airstrikes in several Ukrainian regions on Saturday killed nine people, injured dozens and damaged residential buildings and infrastructure across the country, local officials said.
The civilian death toll has risen sharply in Ukraine over the past two months as Russia steps up attacks on power plants and other infrastructure. Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia, and both sides have targeted each other's shipping.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, writing on Telegram, said Russia had deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since early morning.
“Basically, the Russians have expanded the war away from the front, where they have no success, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war,” Zelensky wrote.
“Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance,” Zelensky added.
The city council in Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine's frontline “fortress cities” that Russia wants to capture, said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period. Four people were injured.
“These are not military targets,” the council said. “They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business.”
The governor of Ukraine's Zhytomyr Region west of Kyiv, Vitaliy Bunechko, said a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zvyahel. Bunechko said two gas stations also came under attack, as well as an unidentified “enterprise with foreign investment.”
Earlier, Zelensky reported attacks on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, his hometown.
The governor of Zaporizhzhia Region, Ivan Fedorov, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi Rih's military administration, said two people were killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles.
The Russian military said its forces hit Ukrainian steel maker Zaporizhstal in the city of Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro and several plants in Kryvyi Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex.
Reuters could not independently verify accounts from either side.
In the Black Sea port of Odesa, Regional Governor Oleh Kiper said nearly 40 people had been injured in attacks that extended from overnight well into Saturday evening.
The Russia-installed head of areas of eastern Donetsk Region under Moscow's control said three people had been killed in Ukrainian drone attacks.
In Moldova, on Ukraine's western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed.
Russian drones have regularly entered Moldovan airspace despite official protests. During one instance this week, the departure of Zelensky's aircraft to Norway was delayed.
Russian strikes on Ukrainian port
The Russian Defense Ministry said Russia's forces have maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, hitting a cargo ship in Odesa it said was carrying goods for military use.
Earlier in the day, the ministry said its forces struck two cargo vessels overnight in the port of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine's military said it hit one of Russia's largest synthetic rubber producers in Tolyatti in the Samara region, causing a fire. The Tolyattikauchuk plant specialized in the production of synthetic rubbers and fuel additives that are used in fuel for Russian missiles, it said.
Russian regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said industrial facilities in Samara region had been attacked by Ukrainian drones, without specifying which they were or whether they had been damaged, Interfax news agency reported.
Ilya Sukhikh, mayor of the city of Tolyatti in Samara region, said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The military will conduct a three-day joint precision munitions live-fire exercise from Wednesday to Friday at the Jiupeng base in Pingtung to assess long-range precision-strike capabilities and test new equipment.
The exercise will include routine live-fire operations involving fighter jets, Patriot and Sky Bow air defense missiles, and the Navy's Hsiung Feng II and III anti-ship missiles, per CNA. The Army will deploy High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems and ALTIUS 600M loitering munitions. The retired Chi Yang-class frigate Lan Yang will serve as the target.
The exercise will test integrated strike capabilities across air, sea, and coastal domains. The Navy will also conduct wartime transition drills.
Three warning zones have been designated. The first lies in waters east of the coastline from Taimali in Taitung to Eluanbi in Pingtung, according to CNA. The second extends from the Taitung-Pingtung boundary eastward to waters off Green Island and Orchid Island. The third is located in waters east of Chenggong and Taimali in Taitung.

Tallinn strengthens cooperation with South Korea in innovation and entrepreneurship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:42:54 UTC
15:42:54 KST

This week, a Tallinn delegation visited South Korea on a business mission aimed at expanding cooperation in innovation and entrepreneurship. The visit focused on creating new opportunities for Tallinn-based companies in the Korean market and promoting Tallinn among Korean businesses as a gateway to Europe.
“South Korea’s experience shows that a complex geopolitical situation does not necessarily prevent a country from attracting foreign investment and developing its economy. On the contrary, a strong innovation ecosystem, international partnerships and support for entrepreneurship can provide an important competitive advantage. I am pleased that Tallinn has established meaningful cooperation with the Seoul Business Agency, enabling us to help Tallinn companies enter the Korean market while supporting Korean start-ups in finding opportunities for growth in Tallinn and the wider European market,” said Tallinn Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan.
A central part of the visit was Try Everything, a major start-up and innovation event in Seoul, where Tallinn hosted its own programme and exhibition stand. The programme was opened by Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan and Estonian Ambassador to South Korea Tanel Sepp. Tallinn presented its business and innovation ecosystem and the opportunities it offers international companies to test and validate solutions, find partners and enter the European market.
Five Tallinn-based companies participated in the business mission: 5.0Robotics, SafePAS, Digiotouch, UP Catalyst and Creatomus Solutions. At Try Everything, the companies presented their solutions and met potential partners, customers, investors and representatives of innovation organisations.
One concrete outcome of the mission was the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Digiotouch and the Korean company ZEP Co at the Estonian Embassy in Seoul. Digiotouch develops an AI-powered meeting automation solution, while ZEP Co creates interactive digital environments and metaverse solutions. ZEP Co was also selected for Tallinn’s Test in Tallinn innovation programme, through which the company’s solution will be piloted in Estonian schools.
The Tallinn delegation also met representatives of the Seoul Metropolitan Government’s Digital City Bureau. Discussions focused on exchanging experience in smart-city development and digital innovation, using digital-twin technology, and improving urban safety, resilience and crisis preparedness.
During the visit, the delegation toured Pangyo Techno Valley, one of South Korea’s leading technology and innovation clusters, the MARU360 start-up and entrepreneurship centre, and the internationally recognised robotics company ROBOTIS. The company is best known for its DYNAMIXEL intelligent robotic actuators and its humanoid and service robots. ROBOTIS presented its latest robotics developments, including a humanoid robot currently under development, while the parties discussed rapid advances in robotics and artificial intelligence. Although ROBOTIS technologies are already available in Europe, Tallinn could potentially become the location of the company’s future European headquarters.
The visit took place within the framework of Tallinn’s cooperation and delegation exchange with the Seoul Business Agency. The partnership aims to give Tallinn companies more opportunities to explore Korea’s innovation ecosystem, establish contacts with local partners and enter the Korean market. At the same time, Tallinn is introducing Korean companies to opportunities to test and develop new solutions in the city and use it as a launchpad for entering the European market.

One dead, 102 rescued after Indonesian ferry goes missing in Java Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:36:40 UTC
15:36:40 KST

More than 100 people missing after Indonesian passenger ship capsizes
Search and rescue are ongoing after Virgo Transport 8, with 243 people on board, lost contact with its operator.
Rescuers in Indonesia say six people have been killed and 130 were missing after a passenger ship capsized in the Java Sea.
The Virgo Transport 8, with 243 passengers and crew on board, lost contact with its operator in the early hours of Sunday, according to Basarnas, Indonesia’s search and rescue agency.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Trump may be BRICS’s best recruitment agent
- list 2 of 2BRICS meets in India: What’s on the agenda, why it matters
It had sailed from Surabaya on the Indonesian island of Java on Saturday and was heading for Banjarmasin, a port city on Borneo.
Basarnas said in its latest update that six people were killed and 130 were missing. It said 107 people had been rescued.
There were 213 passengers and 30 crew members on board, the agency added.
Indonesia’s Ministry of Transportation said in a statement that the ship had capsized.
The ship encountered rough weather, said I Putu Sudayana, head of the local search-and-rescue office in Banjarmasin.
The ferry’s last known position was in the Java Sea, about 81 nautical miles (equivalent to about 150km) from Banjarmasin, the AFP news agency reported.
Rescue ships and a helicopter have been searching the area, where Sudayana said waves as high as 2.5 metres (8.2ft) have hampered the operation.
“It is extremely risky for vessels. Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 metres (131ft) long, is at great risk,” Sudayana told reporters, referring to the country’s search-and-rescue agency.
Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington, reporting from Indonesia’s capital, Jakarta, said authorities have yet to determine the cause of the sinking.
An investigation is under way, Washington added, with authorities examining factors including the weather and possible technical failures.
People in Indonesia, an archipelago of 17,000 islands, rely on ferries as a key mode of transport, with sea routes more affordable and readily available than air travel.
Last month, a fire on a ferry sailing between Bali and Lombok killed one person and left five missing. In July, a ferry carrying more than 70 people sank near Selayar Island, south of Sulawesi.

China-Laos "Peace Train-2026" joint exercise conducts full-process drills
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:35:51 CST
15:35:51 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Search-and-rescue drones took to the skies for wide-area reconnaissance, tracked unmanned vehicles advanced to transport the injured, triage operations quickly got underway inside field medical tents, and critically injured personnel were swiftly evacuated to a medical train.
On Saturday, the China-Laos "Peace Train-2026" joint humanitarian medical rescue exercise, held in Lao capital Vientiane, entered its full-process drill phase. A realistic rescue operation unfolded in an intense yet orderly manner.
"Commanders of the Chinese and Lao medical service units, a large number of casualties have been detected in this area. Please proceed immediately to the disaster site to conduct search-and-rescue operations and prepare for casualty reception and treatment."
As the forward joint command post issued the order, Fu Lei, a member of the Chinese directing team, closely monitored the command screen and assessed the situation in real time.
The joint search-and-rescue team arrived at the disaster site equipped with drones, robot dogs, and other specialized equipment. Participant Tu Long used data relayed by the unmanned equipment to pinpoint the locations of the injured and advanced with a mixed Chinese-Lao search-and-rescue squad to carry out the rescue operation.
"Twenty casualties located; one is in critical condition."
The joint search-and-rescue and medical teams worked closely together to manage the influx of casualties. Unmanned transport vehicles were used for emergency evacuation, while field ambulances and casualty transport vehicles conducted forward reception and transportation.
Medical staff officer Xu Wen and his team members verified handover forms, rapidly registered casualty information, checked vital signs, conducted triage based on injury tags, and organized evacuations in an orderly manner.
Inside the field medical tent, a joint Chinese-Lao team specializing in critical trauma care raced against time to provide emergency care to a casualty who had been trapped under rubble for 26 hours. Other casualties, after receiving stabilization treatment, were evacuated to the medical train.
Notably, the medical train employed a self-developed command and decision-support system for casualty reception and treatment, integrating artificial intelligence large-model technology throughout the process.
The system provided precise and intelligent recommendations for command and dispatch, triage, and treatment plans, enabling end-to-end information management from the initial reception of casualties through to their final treatment.
Serving as a "mobile ICU," the intensive care unit is equipped with 10 electric double-decker lifting hospital beds, as well as mobile ventilators, portable ultrasound machines, and ECG monitors. It can accommodate 21 patients with moderate to severe injuries or illnesses.
"We extended the chain of care from casualty collection points and field medical tents to the medical train's treatment carriages," said Ma Dan, a surgeon. "We focused on practicing the seamless integration of anesthesia, surgery, and intensive care under realistic conditions, gaining valuable experience in how China and Laos might jointly respond to mass-casualty emergencies, such as those caused by natural disasters, in the future."
Wu Jiajia, deputy leader of the "Peace Train" medical team, noted that through the practical training, medical personnel from both sides gained a deeper mutual understanding and further enhanced their coordination and medical support capabilities. ■

In Indonesia, a vessel carrying 241 passengers that disappeared at sea is being searched for – CNN
Kyiv • UNN
The Virgo Transport 8 lost contact in the Java Sea while en route to South Kalimantan. No casualties have been reported.
Indonesian rescuers launched a search operation on Sunday after a passenger ship carrying at least 240 people lost contact in the Java Sea while sailing from East Java to South Kalimantan on the island of Borneo. CNN reports, according to UNN.
Details
The Search and Rescue Office in Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province, said it had received a report that the vessel "Virgo Transport 8" lost contact while sailing to the city from Surabaya, Indonesia's second-largest city, in East Java province.
According to preliminary data, the vessel's last known location was in the Java Sea, approximately 148 kilometers (92 miles) from the pier in Banjarmasin. According to the vessel's passenger manifest, there were 241 passengers on board.
No casualties have been reported so far.
Arianto Ardi, head of the Banjarmasin rescue service's operations center, confirmed that contact with the vessel had been lost and said that rescue units had been dispatched to the scene.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson are battling for the premiership. Kristersson has said that, if he wins, the far right could join his government.
Swedes are heading to the polls on Sunday to elect a new parliament, in a closely fought election that could deliver fresh gains for the far right and potentially bring it into government for the first time.
Conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is seeking another term in office, but his chances of staying in power could depend on the Sweden Democrats, the far-right party that already supports his minority government.
Kristersson’s main challenger is his predecessor, Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson, with opinion polls pointing to an extremely tight contest between the country’s rival political blocs.
The prime minister currently leads a minority government made up of his centre-right Moderate Party, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals. The coalition relies on the backing of the Sweden Democrats, which have become increasingly influential in Swedish politics.
Kristersson has said he could go a step further after the election and form a governing coalition that formally includes the Sweden Democrats. Such an outcome would mark a historic breakthrough for the far right, giving the party direct access to government for the first time and underlining its growing role in shaping Sweden’s political agenda.
Around eight million people are eligible to vote in the Nordic country of roughly 10.6 million. More than half have already cast their ballots in advance, reflecting Sweden’s traditionally high voter turnout.
Polling stations will remain open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Two exit polls are expected as soon as voting ends, with more reliable partial results due several hours later.

Fashion consultant says school clothes should show a child's personality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Fashion consultant says school clothes should show a child's personality
Fashion consultant Karolin Kuusik says that although many schools today use uniforms, children's clothing should still reflect some of their own style and personality. Small details can make an outfit look more academic and polished.
"Clothing should express at least a little of the child's own wishes, style and character. For example, I have a daughter who absolutely refuses to wear skirts and always goes to school in trousers, and a son who says you can never have too many stripes," Kuusik said.
Kuusik noted that colors are great, but the child must feel what suits them. "Some want to stand out more, some less. The idea of a polo shirt is that it's made from T‑shirt or sweatshirt fabric, but has a touch of neatness — something for teachers and something for kids. It covers everything. Polo shirts are very trendy this autumn," she emphasized.
For both boys and girls, trousers are the main item, Kuusik said. "Soft, pleated trousers are in fashion. Pleated skirts are also trendy and very school‑like, and you can add personality to them. If a skirt feels too proper, you can pair it with a sweatshirt or wear it with cool white socks."
A practical item is a vest. "A vest can be worn in layers — underneath you can put a white T‑shirt, which adds neatness and a black‑and‑white contrast."
"The preppy style — which in some ways is a grandfather style — is very fashionable right now and looks very youthful today," Kuusik added.
Preppy style is clean, elegant and academic, originating from the dress traditions of elite U.S. schools and universities.
"If you put a button‑down shirt under a sweatshirt, you immediately get an extra layer that adds a touch of neatness," Kuusik said.

“The loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement said.
The office said a full investigation would be conducted to establish the facts and prevent a recurrence.
It also urged ship owners to prioritise safety, ensure vessels are seaworthy and properly equipped, and maintain reliable communication systems.
“Ignoring strong marine warnings puts lives at risk,” it said.

Indonesia rescuers search for 140 people from stricken ferry

Indonesia rescuers search for 130 people after ferry sinks
Published September 13, 2026last updated September 13, 2026
An Indonesian passenger ship carrying 243 people sank in the Java Sea on Sunday after it was hit by bad weather, local authorities said.
Officials said six people had died, while 107 were brought to safety and some 130 passengers were still missing.
"We have carried out efforts to search for victims to the fullest extent. There were passengers who ... had already been successfully evacuated by the units at the scene," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, told reporters.
The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Indonesia's second-largest city of Surabaya to Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province on Borneo island.
It departed on Saturday at 10:13 a.m. local time (0330 UTC), but the ship's operator lost contact with the vessel early Sunday amid bad weather. It was scheduled to arrive in Banjarmasin at about 2 p.m. local time on (0700 UTC) Sunday.
Search operation underway
Search and rescue teams launched an operation after the operator alerted authorities. Ships and a helicopter were deployed to the vessel's last known location.
"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in an earlier video briefing.
The ship's last known position was in the Java Sea, roughly 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin, according to the Associated Press.
Sudayana added that authorities were mobilizing all available personnel and equipment given the large number of people aboard. The agency was coordinating with maritime authorities while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area, he said.
Indonesia, a nation of roughly 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for transportation, with sea travel often cheaper and more accessible than flying. But safety enforcement across the country's maritime sector has been inconsistent, contributing to a comparatively high rate of accidents.

Ahmad Adil
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
- BRICS agrees on a bloc-integrated early warning system for response to infectious diseases, says Indian premier
 
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said Global South countries' confidence in BRICS has increased amid rising tensions across the world.
 
Delivering an opening statement at the expanded session on the second day of the BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi, Modi said: “We have tried to promote inclusive global growth through the BRICS.”
 
“We believe that the benefits of developed solutions in the BRICS should not only be limited to the BRICS. They should be made adaptable and accessible according to the needs of the Global South,” he said.
 
Noting that the “number of tensions in the world is constantly increasing,” Modi said the pandemic, climate disaster, and supply chain disruption have “shown that in today’s interconnected world, no crisis is limited to one area. That is why we have focused on increasing resilience in all areas.”
 
Addressing the BRICS leaders, Modi said: “The confidence of the countries of the Global South has increased in the BRICS.”
 
“Their voice is heard in the BRICS. Their experience is respected. And solutions are not only made for them, but are made together with them,” he added.
 
The BRICS bloc has been holding the annual summit of its leaders, including those of its partner nations, in the Indian capital since Saturday.
 
Modi was addressing the session on “resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability.”
 
Stating that the power of BRICS “is in our diversity and cooperation,” Modi said: “We may be rooted in different realities, but together we rise through cooperation and blossom for humanity.”
 
“Our diversity, our identity, our cooperation, our inspiration, and our progress should be useful to the entire humanity,” he said.
 
Regarding the number of countries participating in the BRICS summit, Modi said: “This is proof of the increasing power, attraction, and unparalleled faith of BRICS.”
 
 BRICS agrees to establish early warning system
 
Modi said the bloc has “focused on increasing resilience in all areas.”
 
“We have agreed on a BRICS-integrated early warning system for the prevention and response of infectious diseases. Early warning data integration guidelines have been prepared for disaster management,” he said, adding that the BRICS logistic supply chain cooperation framework will help our supply chains become more reliable and resilient.
 
He also said the BRICS Incubator Network “will connect our startups and incubators to each other through innovation,” and the network on digital agriculture will create new opportunities for farmers.
 
Noting that the "weaponization of technology and critical minerals can be a barrier to our sustainable development," Modi said, adding: "We have focused on inclusivity in the adoption of technology."
 
The weekend summit in New Delhi is attended by the Chinese, Russian, and Iranian presidents, among others, and comes at a time when the US-Iran war has been ongoing for around seven months, while the Russia-Ukraine war has continued for more than four years.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The winter will be hard – I have nothing new to add to that. But we have no other plan than to get through this winter with dignity,” Koretskyi said.
Koretskyi noted that Russian forces continue to subject Ukrainian power infrastructure to sustained aerial attacks, making total physical defense unfeasible. However, he emphasized that structural lessons drawn from the previous heating season have significantly bolstered state readiness.
“Russia may view the current period and the winter season as an opportunity to exert rapid pressure on Ukraine,” Koretskyi explained, adding that the government intends to navigate the coming months through internal coordination and continued assistance from international partners.
Decentralization and multi-tier response plans
According to the prime minister, the core of Ukraine’s winter energy strategy centers on the decentralization of critical utility and life-support networks across regions, cities, and oblasts to prevent localized damage from triggering systemic grid collapses.
Russian Attack Halts US-Owned Oleina Sunflower Oil Plant in Dnipro
Koretskyi stated that the scale and destruction of Russian strikes have multiplied over the past two months, creating additional strain on the national economy. Despite the escalation, he maintained that the government possesses the resources, reserves, and operational readiness necessary to address winter disruptions.
Koretskyi referenced his administrative experience managing energy operations during previous wartime campaigns when he served as head of national oil and gas company NJSC Naftogaz of Ukraine.
Fuel stockpiles and municipal heating preparations
Koretskyi’s assessment follows official confirmations that Ukraine reached its natural gas storage targets for the 2026–2027 heating season approximately one month ahead of schedule.
On Aug. 28, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal announced that Ukrainian underground gas storage facilities had accumulated 14.6 billion cubic meters of natural gas, fulfilling baseline requirements for the autumn-winter season.
The milestone was achieved through coordinated extraction and storage by domestic producers, the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine (GTSOU), and Naftogaz.
Concurrently, the Ministry of Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport reported in late August that roughly 100,000 residential buildings – representing approximately 70% of the government’s seasonal target – had completed winterization procedures, alongside preparations for 12,400 boiler houses and 11,700 kilometers of municipal heating networks.
The government previously allocated nearly Hr 6.8 billion ($152 million) for energy infrastructure repairs, backup generation, and physical barriers, prioritizing autonomous backup power for municipal water and heating services during potential grid outages.

Forget low-calorie food, Chinese youth turn to tasteless, chewy snacks to lose weight
One individual even admits to chewing on dog chew sticks to help alleviate severe exam anxiety
Young dieters in China are increasingly turning away from low-calorie foods in favour of a new trend: chewy snacks.
On social media, they are sharing their new-found favourites, including beef jerky, frozen buns, and even baby teething biscuits – each characterised by their toughness and chewiness.
Many prefer chewy foods as a way to keep their mouths busy and trick their brains into feeling satisfied, reducing the urge to eat more.
For these dieters, taste is not the top priority; instead, the focus is on the toughness of the snacks. The harder to chew, the more effective they believe it is.
One 37-year-old netizen from Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, using the handle @yigexiangmujingli, has taken to munching on dangshena root thought to bolster the spleen and lung in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) – as her chewy snack of choice.
She shared with the SCMP that while she maintains a workout routine, she struggles with self-control around food. Hence, she seeks chewy snacks that keep her focused at work without adding weight to her body.

'Woman Unknown' wins Golden Lion award at the 83rd Venice Film Festival while 'Naza' wins special jury prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:04:20 UTC
15:04:20 KST

El-Toukhy's drama depicts the life of a young nanny and housekeeper who marries her wealthy and older widower employer, but harbours a shameful secret that threatens to unravel her new life and status in the post-World War II anarchy.
“Woman Unknown,” a drama about Denmark in the aftermath of the Nazi occupation directed by May el-Toukhy, won the prestigious Golden Lion at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Saturday.
El-Toukhy was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year.
Her film centres on a young Marie, played by Mathilde Arcel, whose Best Actress win makes it a rare double victory. Marie is a nanny and housemaid who is about to marry her wealthy employer in the immediate aftermath of the war. But she harbours a secret past intimate relationship with a German soldier that threatens to upend her reputation.
South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s poetic portrait of class and labour, “Possible Love,” won the Silver Lion grand jury prize, the runner-up award. “Possible Love” is Lee’s first film in eight years, following his acclaimed 2018 title “Burning.”
“NAZA,” a harrowing documentary about military strategies employed in the war in Gaza from Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was awarded a special jury prize.
“It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film,” Abraham said.
The film was added to the main competition late — at the request of the filmmakers — and debuted late in the schedule as well, but its impact was felt: It received a record-breaking standing ovation, lasting some 25 minutes, after its premiere.
Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years, “NAZA” features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders including intelligence officers and soldiers give who insight into the war in Gaza and what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians.
The jury gave the Silver Lion for directing to Ilya Krzhanovsky for his film “Dau,” a project about the Soviet physicists who built the atomic bomb that has taken over 20 years to make.
Krzhanovsky, who renounced his Russian citizenship in protest of the war in Ukraine, dedicated the prize to Ukrainians, including his mother who was born there.
The Maggie Gyllenhaal-led jury announced the winners in a ceremony on Saturday night, which included a best actor prize for John Malkovich for his performance in the dark CIA comedy “Wild Horse Nine”.
Malkovich was not in attendance at the ceremony, but he sent a video message, explaining that he is shooting in Montreal.
“I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” Malkovich said.
Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine was also met with a standing ovation, lasting well past 10 minutes. The dark comedy follows two CIA agents travelling to Easter Island shortly before Chile's 1973 military coup.
The film's stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell's performances were among the elements that drew attention at the premiere.
McDonagh has previously premiered two films at the festival, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin.
He has previously won screenplay prizes for both films, while Colin Farrell received an acting award for the latter.
“Unknown Woman” star Mathilde Arcel was visibly emotional accepting the best actress award, which she said was very heavy and decided to place on the floor while she spoke.
“This is my first lead role in a movie and my first time at a film festival,” she said. “I’m extremely honoured.”
French director Stéphane Brizé’s won the screenplay prize for his corporate drama “A Good Little Soldier.”
Malou Khebizi was given the Marcello Mastroianni award for emerging actor for her role in Cédric Kahn’s “15/18 (A Place to Heal)” which is set in an adolescent psychiatric ward in a public hospital.

Musk, Altman, Hassabis back Amodei’s call to slow pace of AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:00:36 UTC
15:00:36 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Some of the most prominent figures in artificial intelligence have backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call for the industry to slow the pace of frontier AI development and introduce stronger safeguards.
Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis voiced support for Amodei after he published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” in which he argued that the AI industry should slow down and outlined a three-part plan for doing so.
“Dario is right,” Musk said in a brief response to Amodei’s post on US social media company X.
Altman also agreed with the proposal, saying pacing the frontier had been a major subject of recent discussions at OpenAI.
“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks,” he said.
Altman particularly endorsed Amodei’s proposal to give independent evaluators extensive access to advanced AI systems.
“Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon,” he added.
Hassabis said Amodei’s essay pointed “towards the right path forward,” while acknowledging that details of the approach still needed to be worked out.
“The direction is correct for meeting this critical moment,” he said.
Hassabis linked Amodei’s proposal to Google DeepMind’s recent call for an industry-wide standards body for frontier AI.
In an essay released Saturday, Amodei expressed concern about whether humans will be able to maintain control over AI models capable of improving themselves. He also pointed to a recent incident involving AI agents that independently carried out cybersecurity attacks as another reason for concern.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”
“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious. … They include the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he added.
Earlier this week, an Anthropic researcher announced that he was leaving the company because of concerns that Anthropic and rival firms were not developing AI systems responsibly.
Jacob Coxon, who had also worked at Anthropic competitor OpenAI, said the companies appeared to be prioritizing competition with one another over ensuring the safety of their AI products.

Beijing pushes AI-assisted chip design as part of self-sufficiency drive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13

Beijing pushes AI-assisted chip design as part of self-sufficiency drive
Agentic AI is creating a ‘paradigm shift’ in semiconductor design, chairman of domestic EDA leader Empyrean Technology says
Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly taking the wheel in designing China’s next-generation semiconductors, as Beijing and domestic technology firms accelerate efforts to integrate AI into chip design software to bolster national self-sufficiency.
Empyrean Technology, China’s top maker of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, has been accelerating the chip design process by using AI-optimised algorithms and agentic tools, according to company chairman Liu Weiping.
By applying an AI agent to its simulation and layout tools, the company slashed the time needed for a circuit layout task from four weeks to just one week, Liu said.
Agentic AI has brought a “paradigm shift” to chip design, moving away from “humans operating tools” to “humans commanding agents”, Liu said at the 2026 International Integrated Circuit Innovation Expo in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
This shift would also apply to the business model of the industry, which was changing from the traditional software licence model towards a new model based on token consumption with agentic EDA, Liu said.
Empyrean was developing an agentic EDA platform, which the company considered core to its future strategy, that would allow its own agentic tools to work with its partners’ agents, according to Liu.
