A rescue official said emergency crews faced waves of up to 2.5 metres as they fought to reach the ferry amid "extremely risky" conditions.
One person has died and 102 were rescued on Sunday from a ferry that went missing off of the Indonesian island of Java, rescue officials said.
The vessel, which was carrying 243 people, had been sailing between the islands of Java and Borneo when it encountered bad weather.
"We have carried out efforts to search for victims to the fullest extent. There were passengers who...had already been successfully evacuated by the units at the scene. We can inform you that the total number of evacuated passengers is 103 people," local search and rescue chief I Putu Sudayana told reporters, adding that one of the passengers had died.
Sudayana said rescuers faced waves of up to 2.5 metres as they fought to reach the ferry amid "extremely risky" conditions for vessels.
"Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 meters long, is at great risk," he said, referring to Indonesia's Search and Rescue Agency.
It comes after a speedboat carrying eight people, including five journalists covering the recent eruption of Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatoa, went missing earlier this week. The search for the vessel remains ongoing.
The Southeast Asian nation is made up of more than 17,000 islands, with boats providing a common and important form of transport.

Syria temporarily raises fuel prices amid global supply pressures
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:48:40 CST
14:48:40 KST

DAMASCUS, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Syria on Sunday temporarily raised fuel and cooking gas prices, citing rising global energy and shipping costs as well as reduced domestic refining capacity.
The country's Permanent Committee for Pricing Petroleum Products and Mineral Resources issued a new temporary price bulletin, raising the price of 95-octane gasoline from 152 new Syrian pounds (about 1.25 U.S. dollars) to 195 pounds (about 1.60 dollars) per liter, an increase of 28.3 percent.
The price of 90-octane gasoline rose from 147 pounds (about 1.21 dollars) to 185 pounds (about 1.52 dollars) per liter, up 25.9 percent, while diesel climbed from 125 pounds (about 1.03 dollars) to 175 pounds (about 1.44 dollars) per liter, marking the steepest increase of 40 percent.
Cooking gas prices also rose, though more moderately. The price of a household gas cylinder rose from 1,470 pounds (about 12.05 dollars) to 1,600 pounds (about 13.12 dollars), an increase of 8.8 percent.
The Energy Ministry said the increases were temporary and reflected an exceptional rise in the cost of procuring petroleum products from international markets, alongside the major overhaul of the Banias refinery, a key supplier of fuel to the domestic market.
The latest increases came just over a week after another adjustment took effect on Sept. 4, when gasoline and diesel prices were each raised by five pounds per liter, while household and industrial gas prices remained unchanged. ■

Preservation and development of Old Sofia – focus of KvARTal Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:43:09 UTC

Author
Yoan Kolev
News
Preservation and development of Old Sofia – focus of KvARTal Festival
Sunday 13 September 2026 08:11
Sunday, 13 September 2026, 08:11
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
Font size
In 2016, a new festival was born in the center of Sofia in the small streets surrounding the mosque, the Central Market Hall, and the Central Mineral Baths, an area that surprises visitors with its remarkable buildings and an atmosphere preserved from the last century. "KvARTal Fest" was one of the first attempts to answer the question, "Why haven't we noticed them until now?" while aiming to showcase the district's cultural and historical potential.
Today, in 2026, KvARTal Festival is a beloved and eagerly awaited event held around the Day of Sofia on September 17th.
This year’s program - running from September 18 to 20, features over 60 locations: galleries, studios, cultural spaces, spots for dining and tasting the flavours of Old Sofia, pedestrian festival zones, music stages, installations, exhibitions, tours, a children’s architecture zone, workshops, and other initiatives dedicated to history, architecture, and cultural heritage. We spoke with the festival’s initiator, Martina Stefanova, about the eleventh edition.
Martina Stefanova
PHOTO Yoan Kolev
“The festival aims to invite visitors to the capital and Sofia residents to the old historic city, in order to experience it through flavours, history, and various educational programs. It is a festival where we get to feel the city and come to love our history, because without history, there is no future.”
This year, the festival’s main theme focuses on the future of Sofia’s historic center and the preservation of its cultural heritage. Prior to the festival's opening, the "Future of the Old City" forum will take place on September 16. Architects, experts, and professionals in the sphere of cultural heritage will participate in the event. Representatives from all relevant institutions have been invited to discuss topics such as 20th-century architecture, archaeology, the city's mineral water heritage, including its baths, as well as the future of museums.
PHOTO Martina Stefanova
"It is important that we are announcing two new initiatives this year," Martina Stefanova says. "The first is 'Adopt a Building,' which we will present to companies and citizens wishing to donate for the restoration of a historic building. The other key initiative is the 'Neighborhood Charter.' This charter will be available at various locations throughout Old Sofia. Anyone will be able to sign it. Our goal is to call upon the authorities to preserve the area and to restore it to its original state."
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
One of the festival events takes us back to the early 20th century, when the first chocolate factory in the Balkans was established in Sofia. It was the work of industrialist Velizar Peev, and during the three days of the festival, its building at 12 George Washington Street will serve as one of the venues offering visitors engaging experiences:
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
"In the hall, across various floors and in the courtyard, we will showcase vintage furniture, as some pieces have already been restored, while others await restoration and a new owner. We are creating an exhibition that bridges the past and the future, featuring old furniture alongside works by contemporary artists, including modern art, sculpture, and installations. The event will also feature a vinyl music program and a lecture on vintage furniture, as well as the styles of furniture and architecture spanning the Art Nouveau, Secession, and later Modernist periods. It promises to be a fascinating three-day program, which you can also follow on our social media channels."
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
"The past in the future tense" – perhaps that is how we should define the essence of KvARTal Festival, believing that its mission to preserve and develop this part of the capital will unfold right before our eyes.

Chile is home to around 100 Bulgarians who cherish their homeland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:43:00 UTC
14:43:00 KST

Author
Hristina Taseva
News
Chile is home to around 100 Bulgarians who cherish their homeland
Bulgarians in Chile aim to establish their own association and maintain closer contact with the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad
Sunday 13 September 2026 08:00
Sunday, 13 September 2026, 08:00
PHOTO personal archive
Font size
Moving to Chile is like stepping into a new reality, where the distances, nature, and geographical features are completely different. This distant and little-known country is home to around one hundred compatriots, among them Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez, who has been living there for 30 years. She moved to Chile in 1997 with her Chilean husband and their two children, after they had lived in Bulgaria for 10 years. Today, she describes this step as a good decision, although there were also many uncertainties.
PHOTO Hristina Taseva
''I have a big, as they call it, corn family, like an ear of corn with many kernels on the cob. Families in Chile are always close-knit, like the kernels on a cob, and there is always someone who can help you. I became part of this family and felt like one of them. I spoke Spanish and very quickly found a job. This is extremely important because this is how social connections are established'', said Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
According to Miroslava, Chileans are not inclined to emigrate and prefer to build their lives at home. She attributes this characteristic to their islander mentality, as they live with a sense of being cut off from the world around them. Their country is vast in size. On one side, it borders the Pacific Ocean, while on the other are the Andes — a vast mountain range resembling a wall. To the north, the Atacama Desert stretches for 2,000 kilometers, while to the south lies Antarctica, which is also like a desert, but a cold one.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
It is therefore no surprise that over the past five years, Chile has increasingly attracted the interest of the most avid Bulgarian tourists. Miroslava works as a tour guide and says that her fellow Bulgarians are amazed by this distant country. “To go to Chile, you have to have a special taste for adventure, and anyone who goes there is amazed”, she says. From the desert, you find yourself in Polynesia and on Easter Island, which is Chilean territory.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
“They are very surprised because when they leave for Chile, they do not know what they are going to see. They set off for a country they do not know, but they are amazed by what they see. They usually spend more than 15 days in the country. This is because of the great distances: Chile has 4,000 kilometers of coastline along the Pacific Ocean. These distances cannot be covered by land; you have to fly. That is why you cannot get so quickly from the desert to Patagonia, or from Patagonia to Easter Island — it takes time. They are very surprised by the diversity of nature, by landscapes that look like those on the Moon or Mars. In the Atacama Desert, there is an area called the Mars Valley because the landscape is the same, and lunar rovers and Mars rovers have been tested there. It is a very dry place, with high levels of ultraviolet radiation, stunning landscapes and volcanoes.”
Miroslava is one of the active members of the Bulgarian community in Chile and takes part in organizing events to mark March 3, Baba Marta, and religious holidays. How will the community continue to develop?
Rayna Mandzhukova in Chile (April 2026)
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
''There are only a few of us Bulgarians in Chile, around 100, unlike in Argentina, where there are around 20,000. In Chile, Bulgarians have come either for work, like the musicians, or they are employees of shipping companies who were sent from Europe because Chile has large ports with links to North America, Japan and China. There are also people who came here with a Chilean husband or wife. There are not many of us, and so far we have not had a real organization, but I hope that we will have one now, thanks to the visit four months ago by Rayna Mandzhukova, Director of the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad. Following this meeting, the Bulgarians became enthusiastic about setting up an organization, and most likely, when I return, we will try to establish such a foundation. This would give us the opportunity to organize exhibitions and allow children to take part in the agency’s competitions — for songs, children’s drawings, camps, and so on. I hope that the next time I come, I will be able to tell you that we already have a foundation'', said Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
We say goodbye to Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez, agreeing to keep following the developments surrounding the future Bulgarian association and to share the most important aspects of its work.

Brics embraces AI but leaves job displacement largely unaddressed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:42:41 UTC
14:42:41 KST

Brics New Delhi Declaration backs AI-driven growth and worker re-skilling but leaves unanswered what happens to jobs lost to automation.
NEW DELHI: Brics has set out an ambitious plan to prepare people for an AI-driven economy, but its New Delhi Declaration leaves a key question largely unanswered — what happens to workers whose jobs are lost or sharply changed because of automation and AI?The declaration calls AI an “immense opportunity to stimulate economic growth and sustainable development for all” and backs wider access to AI, while stressing safety, security, inclusion and reliability. But on employment, its response is largely to prepare workers for changing skill needs rather than spell out what happens when technology replaces existing work.The declaration commits Brics countries to strengthen cooperation in “forecasting skills needs by analysing labour market trends in digital, green, care and other priority sectors”. It also welcomes Brics Connect, the “BRICS Cooperation Network for Capacity Building, Employability, and New Skills and Technologies”, focused on skills for changing labour markets.
The declaration addresses some changes already taking place. It calls for nationally tailored approaches to expand social protection for gig and platform workers and recognises the need to protect workers moving across borders, including through portability of benefits. It also notes an initiative to establish an “International Digital Platform for Remote Employment” for Brics countries.But there is no equivalent, specific commitment on workers whose existing jobs may disappear because of AI.
The declaration does not propose a Brics system to identify occupations exposed to automation, provide transition support to affected workers or measure AI-related job losses.That gap stands out because Brics is simultaneously encouraging wider use of AI across its economies. Its Centre for Industrial Competencies supports manufacturing companies, including SMEs, in adopting Industry 4.0 and advanced digital production technologies, including AI.
Brics does recognise some AI-related risks beyond employment. In the intellectual property section, it notes “risks relating to misappropriation and misrepresentation of knowledge, heritage, and cultural values” that are insufficiently represented in datasets and AI models.For workers the declaration promises labour markets that are “future-ready”, “ensuring that no worker is left behind”.

Drones struck one of Russia’s largest oil refineries in the Krasnodar Krai
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of September 13, drones attacked the Slavyansk Oil Refinery in the Krasnodar Krai. The plant supplies fuel to Russian military forces.
During the night of September 12–13, drones struck the Slavyansk Oil Refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. This was reported by the "Exilenova+" Telegram channel, according to UNN.
Details
Photos and videos showing the aftermath of the attack have appeared online.
Additionally
The Slavyansk Oil Refinery is one of Russia’s largest independent oil refineries, located in the city of Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Krasnodar Krai. It processes 5.2 million tonnes of feedstock (oil and gas condensate) per year.
The refinery’s main products are gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, aviation kerosene, and vacuum gas oil. The refinery is involved in supplying fuel to Russian military forces.
The facility has been attacked by drones repeatedly. This occurred in April and May 2024, December 2025, and January and June 2026.
Recall
Russian forces increased the number of their attacks on Ukraine using jet-powered drones. They are faster than comparable UAVs with piston engines, making them more difficult for Ukrainian air-defense units to intercept and destroy.

Live: Penrith pulls off shock switch for semifinal
Unknown

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
NRL finals: Nathan Cleary facing possible suspension after Panthers down Roosters in epic final
Nathan Cleary is at risk of being rubbed out of Penrith's preliminary final after booting the Panthers to a thrilling 19-12 finals win over the Sydney Roosters.
In a cracking Sunday afternoon qualifying final, Cleary was sin-binned for collecting Hugo Savala's leg before breaking a 12-12 deadlock with a late field goal at Parramatta Stadium.
Brian To'o then iced the win with a 77th minute try after pouncing on a spilled Roosters pass.
The result means the Roosters will host Cronulla in a do-or-die semi-final on Saturday night, while Penrith are one win away from their sixth grand final in seven years.
But all eyes will be on the NRL's charge sheet on Monday, with Cleary anxiously awaiting what sanction he will face for crashing into Savala's leg after the Roosters player kicked in the first half.
The Panthers star immediately gave a worried look, before referee Gerard Sutton told him his action had "force", was "very dangerous" and "carried a high risk of injury".
If Cleary was to receive a grade-two dangerous contact charge on Monday, the game's best player would be facing a ban from the preliminary final with an early plea.
If he elected to challenge the charge, he would then risk being rubbed out of the grand final if found guilty.
A grade-one charge would only attract a fine for Cleary, and prove a massive boost in Penrith's bid for a fifth premiership of their dynasty.
Panthers coach Ivan Cleary was adamant the challenge was not worthy of a suspension.
"God no, of course not," said Cleary.
"He was just trying to make a play and he was thinking the right thing but he got the angle wrong.
"I must say though, the same thing happened to him earlier in the game, but anyway.
"We just had to manage our way through that period and then it was a dogfight for most of the second half, like a real semi-final.
"You could tell he was disappointed. Hugo (Savala) is not injured, it's just a black and white thing we've brought into the game."
The Roosters failed to make use of Cleary's absence, with Savala missing the ensuing penalty goal and being denied a try for a double movement after the break.
That was one of the few chances during a scoreless opening 32 minutes of the second half, before Cleary stepped up as the game's ultimate ice man.
Sat in the attacking line after a searching Moses Leota run, Cleary was able to slot over the one-pointer with no pressure from Roosters defenders.
Daly Cherry-Evans then attempted to reciprocate moments later, but sprayed a shot from 20 metres out to the right before To'o's sealer under the posts.
"Execution of moments (cost us). It was a good contest, both teams were in there fighting," said Roosters coach Trent Robinson.
"You're looking for those little opportunities where can take advantage. Cleary took his with the one-point and we had some that we missed.
"We missed them and they got them. That's the tale of the tape really."
Cleary's boot had also wreaked havoc early on Sunday, with the Roosters unable to handle three of his bombs and Liam Martin leaping to score off one of his shallow cross-field kicks.
The Penrith halfback also changed the point of attack and went back inside to Dylan Edwards for the Panthers' second try, with the fullback swerving his way over to make it 12-12 after 38 minutes.
Mark Nawaqanitawase's freakish ability had kept the Roosters in the match in the first half, with two key intercepts.
The Roosters winger first helped deny a Penrith try when he reached out and held onto an Isaiah Papali'i ball in the third minute.
He then gave the Roosters a 12-6 lead when he stretched out to stop a Penrith break, juggled the ball three time as he fell, got up and ran 45 metres to score.

Indonesian rescue crews searching for 140 people after ferry hit bad weather
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:10:38 UTC
14:10:38 KST

Rescue workers in Indonesia said at least six people had died and 130 others were missing on Sunday after a ferry sailing between the islands of Java and Borneo capsized in bad weather.
Basarnas, Indonesia’s national search and rescue agency, said 107 people had been rescued from the Virgo Transport 8 vessel, which set sail on Saturday with 243 people onboard, including 30 crew members, from the East Java city of Surabaya.
The ferry’s last position before it lost contact at 2am on Sunday was in the Java Sea, about 150km (90 miles) from its destination, the city of Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province, said Heri Purwanto, the head of the Banjarmasin port authority.
Indonesia’s transport minister, Dudy Purwagandhi, said the vessel had capsized. “From the information we received, based on helicopter surveillance … the ship capsized but has not sunk. As of 3pm [local time] it had not sunk yet, but it was capsized,” he said at a news conference in Banjarmasin.
The local search and rescue chief, I Putu Sudayana, said rescuers were battling waves of up to 2.5 metres (8.2ft) to reach the ferry. “It is extremely risky for vessels. Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 metres long, is at great risk,” he said.
A Basarnas helicopter had joined the operation, he said, adding that evacuees had been transported using a number of different ships and some of them would be taken to an East Java port.
Paramedics and ambulances were on standby in Banjarmasin, where dozens of relatives and friends of passengers checked a whiteboard on which the names of the rescued were being updated.
Jenah, 26, told Agence France-Presse she had come to the command post for information about her older brother. “I am saddened and very shocked. Until now, I haven’t received any more information,” she said. “He was travelling alone. I hope he survives. I couldn’t contact him since last night.”
Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries, with sea routes more affordable and readily available than air travel. However, safety standards are not always rigorously enforced, resulting in a relatively high accident rate.
On Monday, a speedboat carrying eight people, including five journalists working for local and international news agencies, went missing near a volcano, Mount Anak Krakatau, in Lampung province.
Last month, a fire onboard a ferry killed one person and left five others missing, while 211 were rescued, in the Lombok strait off the island of Bali. The ferry had been heading from Bali to the island of Lombok when it ran into trouble in the early hours of 12 August.
In July, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small island south of Sulawesi.

New details on Iran-Oman Hormuz agreement released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:06:45 UTC
14:06:45 KST

Iran and Oman will soon announce a final agreement on new entry and exit routes for the Strait of Hormuz at a meeting with Persian Gulf foreign ministers, but the deal does not mean the strait will reopen, an informed source said.
The source said that intensive technical and diplomatic talks between Iran and Oman culminated in a final agreement in late August. The understanding is strictly between Iran and Oman, with other countries attending only to be informed of the details of the route and transit arrangements, so that their tacit non-objection is made clear to the international community.
Under the agreement, the entry route into the Persian Gulf will lie entirely in Iranian territorial waters, and part of the exit route from the Persian Gulf will also be in Iranian territorial waters. Transit along this route will be under Iranian arrangements. Once implemented, the southern route, which the United States insisted on opening and which was the main cause of the recent tension, will be closed.
In addition to Iran, Oman and other Persian Gulf coastal states, Iraq will also attend the meeting. These countries will only be informed of the outcome of the Iran-Oman talks, while decisions on the details were made in technical meetings between Iran and Oman.
Crucially, the source stressed that the understanding does not mean the Strait of Hormuz will open. Iran has conveyed seven conditions to the U.S. side through intermediaries for the strait to be reopened. Until those seven conditions, approved by Iran's highest military authorities, are implemented, the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed.
The understanding therefore means that if the strait is to open, it will open on the basis of this agreement, which represents a major step for Iran's exercise of sovereignty over the waterway. The opening of the strait depends entirely on American behaviour in implementing Iran's conditions.
MNA

One dead, 102 rescued from stricken ferry off Indonesia

Police officers ask information from Ela Nur Atika (L), a wife of a passenger of the Virgo Transport 8, as relatives seek their loved ones. (AFP Photo)
Rescuers in Indonesia said at least six people were killed and 130 others were missing on Sept. 13 after a ferry sailing between the islands of Java and Borneo was hit by bad weather and capsized.
The Virgo Transport 8, carrying 243 passengers and crew, had lost contact with its shipping company early on Sept. 13 after departing from Surabaya in East Java.
Basarnas, Indonesia’s national search and rescue agency, said in its latest update that six people were killed and 130 were missing. It said 107 people had been rescued.
There were 213 passengers and 30 crew members on board, the agency added.
Indonesian Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said the ship had capsized.
“From the information we received, based on helicopter surveillance, the ship capsized but has not sunk,” he said at a news conference in Banjarmasin.
Local search and rescue chief I Putu Sudayana earlier told AFP that the ship’s captain had reported to its owners before losing contact that the vessel was “tilting.”
Rescuers battled waves of up to 2.5 meters to reach the ferry, Sudayana told reporters.
“It is extremely risky for vessels. Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 meters long, is at great risk,” he said.
A Basarnas helicopter has joined the operation, he added.
The vessel’s last position had been detected in the Java Sea, around 150 kilometers from its destination.
Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat connections for daily transport and tourism.
Lax safety standards and unpredictable weather are the main reasons for the disasters.
On Sept. 7, a speedboat carrying eight people, including five journalists working for local and international news agencies, went missing near a volcano, Mount Anak Krakatau, in Banten province. That search is ongoing.
The journalists were sent to cover the volcano’s eruption that paralyzed Jakarta’s main airport and several others.
Last month, a fire on board a ferry killed one person and left five others missing while 211 were rescued in the Lombok Strait off Indonesia’s Bali island.
The ferry had been heading from Bali to Lombok when it ran into trouble in the early hours of August 12.
In July, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small island south of Sulawesi.

From tiny houses to skis: This Swedish company is finding creative uses for retired wind turbines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:05:19 UTC
14:05:19 KST

What happens to decommissioned wind turbines and blades? Some are finding new life as buildings.
Europe is on track for a record wind year, with 8.8 GW of new capacity installed in the first half of 2026 – a 30 per cent jump year on year.
That’s enough electricity to power around seven million European households and replace fossil fuel imports equivalent to 25 LNG tankers a year, according to industry nonprofit WindEurope.
But every turbine that goes up eventually means one coming down – and manufacturers are still working out how to make sure none of the materials go to waste.
Up to 90 per cent of a wind turbine’s mass is made of easily recyclable materials like steel, copper, aluminium and concrete. Composite materials, which make up the majority of blades, are more problematic.
“Separating the composite materials from the resin requires specialised processes, often involving high temperatures or other energy-intensive treatment methods,” Eva Julius-Philipp, Director of Environment and Sustainability of Business Area Wind at Vattenfall, tells Euronews Earth. “In some cases, these processes can affect the quality and value of the recovered materials, making large-scale recycling more challenging.”
Since introducing a landfill ban on blades, nacelle covers and nose cones in 2021, the Swedish company has come up with some creative alternatives.
From blades to buildings: Turbine components get a second wind
From the ground, it’s hard to appreciate just how large wind turbines are. Putting it into perspective, Vattenfall teamed up with design studio Superuse to turn a retired wind turbine nacelle cover – which houses the mechanical and electrical equipment – into a compact living space.
Four metres wide, 10 metres long and three metres high, the box once sat atop an Austrian wind tower. It’s now a tiny house fitted with a kitchen, bathroom and living space equipped with a heat pump, solar panels and a solar water heater.
It was showcased at Dutch Design Week in 2024 as part of an initiative exploring how materials could be reused with as little energy and emissions-intensive processing as possible.
Blades, too, have been re-envisioned as building materials. After being decommissioned in 2023, the 57 blades from Danish onshore wind farm Nørre Økse Sø found new life as a facade for a multistorey carpark in the city of Lund.
It’s opened the door to a multitude of inventive uses for retired blades, from frames for solar panels to alpine skis.
“Projects such as the Tiny House, blade-based building projects and recycled skis are not yet a large-scale solution, however they are intended to help us gain experience, develop new applications and stimulate the market for circular solutions,” says Julius-Philipp.
Provided it’s safe to do so, extending the operational lifetime of existing components through reuse and refurbishment is the preferred option, she adds.
Recycling wind turbine blades: A multilayered challenge
Wind turbine blades can be between 50 and 100 metres long and are designed to spin in harsh weather for up to 25 years. What makes them so durable is also what makes them difficult to recycle: materials such as glass fibre, carbon fibre, epoxy resin, balsa wood, metals and various fillers pressed tightly together in layers.
Aiming to achieve 100 per cent circularity for these composite materials by 2030, Vattenfall is working on new ways of reusing, repurposing, refurbishing and recycling blades.
“When composite materials cannot be recycled at a high value, they can be processed through energy recovery and/or cement co-processing,” says Julius-Philipp.
Currently, Vattenfall uses mechanical recycling processes to turn blade material into composite flakes or fillers for new products, while pyrolysis – a thermal recycling process – recovers fibres and other secondary materials.
But technology isn’t the only challenge: “Decommissioned blades do not become available in a steady and predictable flow, which makes it harder for recycling solutions to scale economically,” adds Julius-Philipp.
As the first generation of major European wind farms reaches the end of its operational lifespan in the coming years, more blades will enter retirement, increasing the need for solutions that are “scalable, cost-efficient and low in energy use,” she adds.
The EU has not yet enforced a ban on landfilling decommissioned blades. Only Austria, Finland, Germany and the Netherlands have their own binding national bans, and WindEurope is now pushing Brussels to make the commitment legally binding across all member states.
“What is needed now is a regulatory framework that enables circular value chains and secondary raw materials to scale,” says Julius-Philipp, who hopes the European Commission’s Circular Economy Act, expected to be proposed later this year, will help provide it.
Designed to recycle: The future of turbine blades?
Increasingly, manufacturers are taking end-of-life into consideration when designing turbine blades.
Siemens Gamesa’s RecyclableBlades, which are used at Vattenfall’s offshore windfarm Hollandse Kust Zuid (HKZ) in the Netherlands, are one example.
These blades use a resin type that dissolves in a low-temperature, mildly acidic solution. This separates the resin from the other materials in the blade: fiberglass, carbon fiber, plastic, wood and metal, without significantly impacting their properties – allowing for a broader use of the recycled materials in new high-quality products.
“While recyclable blades are not yet widely adopted, we see growing emphasis on developing technologies that enable more efficient blade recycling and help retain the value and quality of the recovered materials,” says Julius-Philipp.

US cannot claim Moon under its international obligations — Lunar Embassy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:04:24 UTC
14:04:24 KST

NEW YORK, September 13. /TASS/. The United States, like other countries, has no right to claim ownership of the Moon under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the press service of Lunar Embassy, an organization specializing in selling property rights to plots on extraterrestrial bodies, told TASS.
"The UN Outer Space Treaty of 1967 was ratified by nearly all the worlds' countries, including the United States, and which agreement states that no Governmental or Sovereign entity may own, have authority or any jurisdiction over any of the celestial bodies within our solar system," the organization said, adding, "So no, the United States or any other country by their own commitment and obligation, cannot take possession of, or own, the moon. They have all taken themselves out of that conversation by their own accord."
At the same time, the organization said the treaty does not prohibit private individuals from asserting claims, a loophole that Lunar Embassy founder Dennis Hope took advantage of. "This same treaty, makes no such statement or restriction to individuals, a glaring and likely intentional loophole within the document, and as such, the Lunar Embassy founder Dennis Hope, as individual, laid claim to the moon of earth, all other planets in our solar system, and their moons in entirety," the company said.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump called the Moon the property of the United States, posting a photograph of Earth's satellite on Truth Social with the caption "The Moon is ours" followed by a US flag.

Taiwan supporters march in New York for UN inclusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:03:41 UTC
14:03:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese lawmakers, NGOs, and overseas Taiwanese marched through Manhattan on Saturday in support of Taiwan's inclusion in the United Nations, chanting slogans including “UN for Taiwan” and “Keep Taiwan Free,” per CNA.
The annual march took place during the opening week of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, which began Sept. 8 at UN headquarters in New York. The General Assembly's 2026-27 session is being held under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All,” per a UN press release.
The march was organized by groups advocating Taiwan's participation in international organizations. Participants included Taiwanese lawmakers and overseas Taiwanese from New York, Boston, Washington, and other parts of the US. Marchers traveled along 42nd Street in Manhattan, passing the Chinese Consulate General, Times Square, and Bryant Park before reaching the New York Public Library, according to organizers.
Participants chanted “UN for Taiwan” and “Keep Taiwan Free,” while some passersby stopped to take photographs and show their support. DPP Legislator Wang Yi-chuan (王義川) led the march with Shih Shu-hua (史書華), chair of the Taiwan United Nations Alliance.
Wang said Taiwan is already an important member of the international community, particularly in semiconductors and technology, and called for the annual demonstration to continue so the voices of Taiwanese supporters can be heard by UN member states, per CNA.
He said he hoped Taiwan could eventually join the United Nations under the name “Taiwan.” Lee Chih-chiang (李志強), director of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in New York, addressed participants at the conclusion of the march and called on the UN to allow Taiwan to participate.
Shih said TAIUNA continues to support Taiwan's membership in the UN and World Health Organization, but the group has broadened its objectives to promote Taiwan's participation in international organizations more generally.
“Our goals are now broader,” Shih said, arguing that Taiwan should be able to engage in exchanges with international organizations and friendly countries, per CNA.
Marshall Islands Permanent Representative to the UN John Silk also attended the event in support of Taiwan. His government has previously voiced support for Taiwan's meaningful participation in the UN system.
The Taiwan government has also launched a promotional campaign in New York during the General Assembly session. The Foreign Ministry said it would use public diplomacy and other activities to highlight Taiwan's contributions to the international community and advocate for its participation in the UN system.

France apologises for criticising US’ human rights record after backlash
France’s permanent mission to the UN expressed regret over a social media post questioning Washington’s commitment to human rights
The French UN mission said it regretted an online post criticising how the United States voted during a UN General Assembly meeting, with US officials saying on Saturday that Washington appreciated the statement.
France’s permanent mission to the UN published the apology on Friday, saying it regretted a social media post criticising the US’ commitment to human rights.
“France and the United States recently took different positions on a vote at the United Nations General Assembly. This difference concerned one vote, and not the defence of human rights,” the mission said in an English statement on its website.
“Public differences of opinion on one vote do not stand in the way of close dialogue with the United States, and do not call into question our historical alliance, nor our ability to work together to advance peace, stability and prosperity, including within multilateral forums,” the statement said.
The mea culpa was well-received by Washington, which has been holding up the appointment of France’s next US ambassador as a result of the dispute.
“We note and appreciate France’s statement and look forward to working together to further shared values and interests,” a US State Department official said on condition of anonymity.

Brussels sets up ‘task force’ to tackle the rat infestation in the downtown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:01:00 UTC
14:01:00 KST

The City of Brussels has set up a pest control task force and tripled the budget for rat control efforts, Philippe Close, Mayor of the City of Brussels has announced after videos emerged showing a rat infestation in the pedestrian precinct in the city centre. “Since monitoring began in February, more than a thousand rats have been caught”, the mayor told reporters.
Large holes in the ground, half-uprooted saplings and patches of blue rat poison here and there: anyone walking through the pedestrian zone would find it hard to miss. The pedestrian zone seems to be in the grip of a rat infestation.
The City of Brussels has now made rat control efforts a priority, says Mayor Close. A task force has been set up, and the budget for rat control efforts has been increased from 35,000 to 100,000 euros.
A thousand rats already caught
“The results are here,” says the mayor. “Since measurements began in February this year, 1,073 rats have been caught in the course of 137 operations. Since 2025, there have been more than two thousand operations in total.”
According to Mayor Close, operations and measures were stepped up further during the hot summer months. He also emphasises that shopkeepers and hospitality businesses can call on the pest control service free of charge.
Nevertheless, criticism is being voiced from the opposition benches on Brussels city council. “I’m not hearing from shopkeepers in the pedestrian zone that the pest control effort is a success,” says Flemish ecologist councillor Stoops.
According to Stoops, more needs to be done quickly to make the pedestrian zone a liveable place once again. “Can you imagine it taking this long on the Champs-Élysées in Paris? It is also a shame that biodiversity wasn’t taken into account at an earlier stage as an option for deterring rats.”

UK government to offer clearer guidance on student loans after repayment row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:01:00 UTC
14:01:00 KST

University students taking out student loans are to be warned that the terms and conditions could change so they are better informed about what they are signing up to, the government has said.
In July, a report by MPs said slideshows that compared student loan repayments to the cost of a mobile phone contract, and YouTube videos that did not mention the fact that conditions could be altered amounted to mis-selling by the government.
The Treasury committee’s investigation followed a furore last November when the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, announced that the repayment threshold on plan 2 loans in England would be frozen at £29,385 for three years from April 2027. The threshold is currently £28,470 for this plan.
Some students had been led to believe that the thresholds would rise in line with inflation each year.
The committee’s report said the government had a “moral obligation” to reverse the freeze to maintain students’ trust and honour the terms under which the loans were sold to them.
In its response, published on Sunday, the government acknowledged the difficulties faced by graduates repaying loans, and said it kept “all aspects of the student finance system under review”, but did not commit to any change in policy.
It said it would redesign the guidance for new students to make it clear and unambiguous.
However it rejected the committee’s recommendation to issue new loans on a contractual basis so that terms could not be changed at a later date, saying it needed to be able to adapt the system to changing economic circumstances in order to keep taxpayers’ contributions stable.
In August, 121 MPs and peers from across party lines signed a letter to the new chancellor, John Healey, calling on him to urgently review the repayment system.
The letter said the frozen thresholds combined with inflation-linked interest rates meant young teachers, nurses, engineers, and entrepreneurs were facing “historically high” effective marginal tax rates.
“For many middle-income graduates, the combination of income tax, national insurance, and student loan repayments means they see less than half of any hard-earned pay rise,” it said.
Responding to the government’s commitment to offer clearer guidance, the chair of the Treasury committee, Meg Hillier, said: “The commitment to right a historical wrong by updating the information so that prospective students are properly informed before taking out a massive loan is an important step forward.
“Unfortunately, though, it doesn’t help graduates who are angry that they didn’t receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing.”
Hillier welcomed the fact that a reversal of the threshold freeze had not been ruled out.
“I recognise that finances are tight but I continue to urge the chancellor to look at this again. I sincerely hope he will use his upcoming budget to give graduates some much-needed breathing space.”
A government spokesperson said: “We are taking decisive action to improve the student finance system and break down barriers to accessing university, starting with improved and clearer guidance for those taking out loans.
“That includes increasing maximum maintenance loans, reintroducing targeted maintenance grants to expand opportunities for people from all backgrounds, and [we have] raised the repayment threshold for plan 2 loans for the first time since 2021.
“We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way.”

Europe dominates ranking of the world’s most beautiful cycling routes – these are rides to try
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

From the vineyards of Tuscany and lavender fields of Provence to the rugged Scottish coast and the peaks of the French Alps, Europe is home to some of the world’s most spectacular cycling routes, according to new research.
Tourism on two wheels is on the rise with a surge of 292% in Google searches for “cycling holiday”. There’s so much more to a cycling trip than just the bike, though, and new research has revealed the most beautiful routes worldwide.
It’s good news for European cycling fans, as a majority of the top 15 in the ranking are based on the continent.
A study by adventure booking platform Explore used eye-tracking software to assess the reactions of 200 participants to 52 renowned and attractive cycling routes from around the world.
The technology measured how quickly each route caught their attention and how long it held it for, and the metrics were combined into a weighted "eye-catching" score out of 100 to provide a definitive ranking.
“There's something about seeing a country from the saddle that no other kind of travel can match; you're moving fast enough to cover real ground, but slow enough to take it all in,” said Luke Judd, travel expert at Explore.
“What's interesting about this research is that it puts science behind what cyclists have always debated: which views genuinely stop us in our tracks.”
Canada’s Bow Valley Parkway, a scenic winding route between Banff and Lake Louise, was far and away the most popular option, with a score of 97 out of 100.
It was followed closely by Australia's Great Ocean Road, on the southwest coast of Victoria, which was awarded a score of 94.
Despite the top two being some distance from Europe, and the list spanning four continents, eight out of the 15 are actually in Europe itself.
Here’s where to head for a beautiful cycling experience closer to home.
European destinations dominate the rankings
In third place, with a score of 91, are the stunning Tuscany Gravel Routes in Italy. Most famous for the professional one-day race held there in the spring, the stunning route features cypress tree-lined climbs, working vineyards and centuries-old hilltop towns.
With a score of 90, the Elbe Cycle Route in Germany is in fourth place.
It follows the Elbe River for around 1,220 kilometres from Czechia towards the North Sea, and the route passes through Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, skirts several German states and travels right through Hamburg, offering a journey through historic cities, countryside and some of eastern and northern Germany’s most interesting landscapes.
In sixth place, Amsterdam Cycle Route 10 has a score of 86. The Netherlands goes hand in hand with cycling, and there’s arguably no better way to explore Amsterdam than by bike.
This circular route offers a brilliant introduction to the city and its surroundings, taking you past canals, parks and historic neighbourhoods before heading into quieter countryside.
In seventh and eighth places, with scores of 82 and 81 respectively, are Italy’s Stelvio Pass and the Provence Lavender Route in France.
While the Stelvio Pass is notorious as one of the most difficult cycling routes in the world – and the second-highest in the Alps – the Provence Lavender Route is, mercifully, significantly easier.
The scenic trip is best taken in the summertime when lavender plants are in full bloom. It winds through rolling countryside, hilltop villages and the Luberon and Valensole Plateau’s vast fields of purple blooms.
It’s back to challenging routes with Scotland’s North Coast 500, which is in 11th place with a score of 78.
Starting and finishing in Inverness, this route is more than 800km long and can take even the most competent cyclists up to five days to complete. Despite its trickiness, it’s well worth it for those who want to experience the rugged beauty of the Scottish coast.
The Route des Grandes Alpes is one of Europe’s great mountain road trips, stretching from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean through some of the French Alps’ most spectacular scenery.
It’s in 13th place, with a score of 78 – the same as the North Coast 500 in Scotland – and isn’t easy either. Expect towering peaks, deep valleys, mountain passes and picturesque villages along the way. It’s fairly challenging, with long, winding and sometimes steep sections, so it’s best suited to experienced cyclists.
The last European entry in the top 15 is the Lake Ohrid Circuit in 14th place, with a score of 76. The trip covers roughly 90 to 96 kilometres and crosses an international border between North Macedonia and Albania.
Those tackling it will take in the historic towns of Ohrid and Struga and the Monastery of Saint Naum near the southern border, as well as Pogradec on the Albanian lakeside. Just remember to bring your passport in order to experience the whole route.
The world’s top 15 most beautiful cycling routes
How each route is ranked according to an “eye-catching” score out of 100:
- 1. Bow Valley Parkway (Banff–Lake Louise), Canada - 97/100
- 2. Great Ocean Road, Australia - 94/100
- 3. Tuscany Gravel Routes, Italy - 91/100
- 4. Elbe Cycle Route, Germany - 90/100
- 5. Carretera Austral, Chile - 86/100
- 6. Amsterdam Cycle Route 10, Netherlands - 86/100
- 7. Pacific Coast Highway, USA - 82/100
- 8. Stelvio Pass, Italy - 82/100
- 9. Provence Lavender Route, France - 81/100
- 10. Road to Hana, USA - 78/100
- 11. NC500 (North Coast 500), Scotland (UK) - 78/100
- 12. Route des Grandes Alpes, France - 78/100
- 13. Slickrock Trail, USA - 76/100
- 14. Lake Ohrid Circuit, North Macedonia/Albania - 76/100
- 15. Vancouver Seawall, Canada - 75/100

India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:06 UTC
14:00:06 KST

India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
India spent decades casting Pakistan as the region’s rule-breaker. A tribunal ruling handed Islamabad the chance to return the favour
Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry.
On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that Delhi had no legal basis for suspending the water-sharing agreement, adding that India must also limit construction on the Ratle Hydroelectric Plant being built in Kashmir.
The court’s five-member panel was unanimous: none of the grounds India cited justified suspending or terminating the agreement.
It was a clean sweep for Islamabad, which brought the case after Delhi froze cooperation on the Indus and its tributaries – vital rivers that irrigate Pakistan’s agricultural heartland.

Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

Ukraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.
Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.
This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it?
The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022, then left them to sink or swim. Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors and paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’s nauseating Alaska summit, and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price.
Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About 60% oppose ceding Donbas land to Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians also want it to stop. And like Moscow, Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch, notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly a deal to be done. But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away.
Efforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has now extended to the Red Sea (Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modern forever war phenomenon. Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but to win a Nobel peace prize (plus lucrative Russian energy deals).
Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas. Trump’s “board of peace” and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fear fighting will drag on indefinitely. Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together.
Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led to war crime atrocities such as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedly killed more than 100 schoolgirls in February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy.
Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightly restricted international journalists’ access to Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost of successful Iranian strikes on US bases in the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict.
Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now.
Western democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly, urged here) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war.
- 
  Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Burnham must understand Wales is ‘not a region in England’, says first minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

Andy Burnham has to be serious about devolution and understand that Wales is a nation and “not a region in England”, according to the country’s first minister.
Rhun ap Iorwerth, who is the first non-Labour leader of the Senedd since devolution, told the Guardian that while he was encouraged by initial discussions with the new UK prime minister, he was wary about Burnham being captured by a consensus Westminster view against relinquishing further powers.
Separately in the interview, ap Iorwerth said his party, Plaid Cymru, would be willing to cooperate with Labour in the future to keep Reform UK out of power, as he would always want to block the “destructive politics” of Nigel Farage’s party.
Ap Iorwerth became Wales’s first minister in May, days after he led Plaid Cymru to victory in Senedd elections, breaking a 100-year period of Labour dominance, which included Labour being the biggest party in every vote to the Welsh parliament since it was created in 1999.
He has pushed for more powers to be given to his government, particularly over policing and the justice system, where Wales is the only UK nation not to have control.
Burnham’s background as Greater Manchester mayor was a positive, ap Iorwerth said: “He clearly understands the benefits of getting devolution right for Manchester. I’ve had really positive, constructive discussions with him.
“He now needs to know what devolution means for Wales, and it’s very, very different. We’re a nation. We’re not a region of England. There are different needs. We will work closely with the UK government on what empowering communities means. But it’s a totally different model, and it’s really important that Andy Burnham doesn’t confuse the two.”
Speaking in London after meetings with UK government officials, ap Iorwerth said, although Burnham had assured him he would “not bypass devolution”, he was concerned about institutional resistance to handing over police and justice powers.
In July, Burnham’s Welsh secretary, Stephen Kinnock, said he was not “entirely convinced” about the idea of devolving powers such as policing. Ap Iorwerth said: “The arguments for the devolution of policing and justice are very, very strong. Commission after commission and study after study have concluded this really needs to happen.
“Andy Burnham had more control over policing as the mayor of Manchester than I do as first minister of Wales, and it’s just not right. Burnham gives me the impression, and I believe him, that he’s ready to take a different approach.
“What I’m also acutely aware of is that those forces around him are probably equally as averse to devolving policing and justice as they have been under previous Labour leaders.”
With 43 Senedd seats, Plaid is the biggest party in the expanded 96-member chamber, with Reform forming the opposition. Reform enjoyed “a very significant result” in May in going from two members – both defectors from the Conservatives – to 34, ap Iorwerth said.
However, he pledged to stand against what he termed Reform’s “kind of politics that runs contrary to my core beliefs of cooperation and tolerance and supporting each other and looking after the weak”.
Asked if Plaid would potentially cooperate with Labour to block a potential Reform government, whether in Cardiff or Westminster, he said it would: “It’s not about keeping a political party out, it’s about keeping a kind of politics out, the negative influence that it has, and of course we do and will cooperate with Labour.”
At a press conference earlier this month to mark the start of the new Senedd session, ap Iorwerth took a somewhat downbeat approach, warning about a “very challenging” financial picture, with a real-terms decline in both day-to-day and capital spending this year.
Asked if he risked mimicking Keir Starmer’s sometimes gloomy approach in assessing the task of government, ap Iorwerth said that was not his intention: “I would certainly hope not, because I think a mistake Keir Starmer made was that the government almost gave up on its values, gave up on its beliefs under that administration, because things were difficult.
“We’ve taken a completely different approach, and if there was a sense of gloom, it was certainly not meant to be like that.”
On Monday, ap Iorwerth is due to hold a meeting in Cardiff with his equivalents in Scotland and Northern Ireland, John Swinney of the Scottish National party and Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, an event labelled by one Telegraph columnist as a “sinister cabal … plotting nothing less than the end of the United Kingdom”.
Asked about this description, ap Iorwerth smiles. “It’s just not the way that I see it,” he says. “I don’t come from the base of working, either ourselves or with any other partners, to break up the UK. I want to build up my nation. That’s all it’s about.”
Wales is, he says, on a “constitutional journey”, one in which he sees the ultimate destination as being independence – but without any set timetable or rush: “That’s in the hands of the people of Wales.”

Rosina, London SW17: ‘Bella Italia in Bolton this is not’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Rosina is a serene, heavenly-white neighbourhood Italian restaurant just off Wandsworth Common, on the same stretch as the much-celebrated Chez Bruce. It is Adam Byatt’s fifth place – he’s probably best known for Trinity, his Michelin-starred restaurant up the road in Clapham – and, lately, his very good, recipe-driven YouTube channel ran a Road to Rosina series in which he visits suppliers, eats pasta with nonnas and learns peak tiramisu skills from a woman called Pina (more of her tiramisu later). If any neighbourhood can stomach an achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced, candlelit trattoria where the cloakroom tags are actual Amalfi Coast pebbles engraved with numbers, it is Wandsworth Common, land of the hedge fund/interior design power couple who wouldn’t think twice about sipping a basil gimlet with a plate of melon with culatello di Zibello or gnocco fritto with mortadella. Bella Italia in Bolton this is not.
Rosina’s cocktail bar leans on art deco shapes, with a pale, marble-topped counter and walls covered in David Steen portraits. There’s a small second bar area for those bridging the gap between light dinner and semi-serious drinking, and a larger, linen-tableclothed area for the restaurant proper, with a back room for private dining. Rosina’s intimacy is an optical illusion: the place is as big as a tennis court, and the weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep.
The day-to-day cooking is in the hands of Will Bee, previously of Michelin-starred Lita in Marylebone and Paul Ainsworth at No 6 in Padstow, and the menu is hearty, as well as littered with little in-jokes; like all the most promising neighbourhood joints, however, it would take at least five visits before they began to grate. Small plates of fried taleggio, melanzane fritte and smoked sardines on toast give way to a list of pleasingly substantial pastas ranging from caviar linguine at £30 to a staggeringly pocket-friendly cavatelli cacio e pepe at just £8. There is also what’s dubbed as “post-service pasta” (spaghetti with anchovy, chilli and garlic) at £16, which is the first time I’ve seen a restaurant give a glimpse into what its owner eats after hours. More of this, I say. I want cocktail lists that offer “post-service fernet branca plus howling into the abyss about business rates”. Let the light in on the magic.
Hugh, my companion, ordered bruschetta of rabbit livers braised in chianti, and ate them with Lecter-ish lust. Two plump sardines, coated in breadcrumbs and with their little tails sticking out of one end, resembled something out of a cartoon. Carpaccio of wild sea bass came flecked with chilli and amalfi lemon, and doused in the kind of olive oil you hide from house guests: clean, sharp, precise. It was at this point that something shifted for me, from “this is perfectly pleasant” to “holy god, this is really quite special”. The arrival of the ’nduja strozzapreti only confirmed that: hugely simple, but wonderfully layered, with a rich tomato sauce enveloping a nourishing bowl of priest-stranglers.
Risotto bianco, made with Riso Buono carnaroli rice and topped with a bold, sunshine-yellow egg yolk, was rich, but it’s meant to be: risotto bianco is for people who laugh in the face of blood sugar spikes. There is nowhere to hide in a white risotto – it is a sensory bombardment of unctuous gloop – and Rosina’s is wonderful. Although, if I want to squander calories willy-nilly on genuine death row delicacies, it is to their fried potatoes that I might turn instead: tiny baby spuds no bigger than fingernails, roasted, crushed and tossed in herbs and oil. Absolutely remarkable. A hugely generous plate of roast summer vegetables came charred from the grill and drizzled with syrupy grape must saba from Modena. We ate those with perfectly cooked roast turbot.
Around us, Wandsworth Common conducted its typical Saturday business. The tyranny of school fees. The agony of basement excavations. The management of several homes at once, with only one housekeeper directing all the other housekeepers internationally. The true trials of life. These people deserve a good dessert menu, and Rosina offers an embarrassment of teeth-chattering riches. Dreamy, yesteryear-sounding things: orange riccarelli, marzipan fruits, iced cherries and a sharp, classic amalfi lemon tart with blackcurrant leaf ice-cream, which I demolished. And a bowl of Pina’s tiramisu, too, of course, of which we entertained a rather large amount. My congratulations to Pina: hers is a very good recipe: wet, light and stodgy in all the right places.
If this rather sumptuous spot needs anything quite as crass as my feedback, Rosina is a surefire hit. If you’re south of the river and on the lookout for an oasis of calm and fanciness at a range of prices, somewhere you can talk and be heard, Rosina is the perfect woman.
- 
  Rosina 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17, 020-8672 5888. Open all week, lunch noon-2.30pm, dinner 5.30-10pm. From about £50 a head à la carte, plus drinks and service

BRICS driving global economic growth – Putin: As it happened
Russian President Vladimir Putin has described BRICS as a key driver of global economic growth as the group’s 18th summit enters its second and final day in New Delhi.
Addressing the BRICS Outreach/BRICS+ session on Sunday, Putin said international interest in the group “continues to grow,” arguing that its commitment to an “independent and autonomous course” and international law appeals to countries around the world. He also said BRICS accounts for 49% of global GDP growth and that its potential for further development is “far from exhausted.”
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, speaking at the same session, said the trust of Global South nations in BRICS has grown because “their voices are heard, their experiences are respected and solutions are crafted not just for them, but with them.”
Modi also announced that members had reached a consensus on a BRICS Integrated Early Warning System for preventing and responding to infectious diseases, as well as guidelines for integrating early-warning data in disaster management.
The expanded session brings together the leaders of BRICS member and partner countries, as well as outreach invitees and representatives of international organizations, with discussions focused on resilience, innovation, cooperation and inclusive global growth. Further bilateral meetings are also possible on the sidelines.
On Saturday, BRICS leaders unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration, which calls for the reform of global institutions to give emerging markets and developing countries greater representation and condemns unilateral economic measures that violate international law. The document also calls for “maximum restraint” in the Middle East and stresses that dialogue and diplomacy are the only appropriate means of resolving international disputes.

Saudi oil delivery times to Asia could rise 2.5-fold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:49:37 UTC
13:49:37 KST

TOKYO, September 13. /TASS/. Voyage times for deliveries of Saudi oil to Asia would increase 2.5-fold to around 100 days round trip if the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is closed, according to data from the Japanese Shipowners' Association cited by the Asahi newspaper.
A voyage through the Strait of Hormuz, the traditional route for oil supplies from the Middle East to Asia, previously took 40 days round trip. A route through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which could serve as an alternative, takes roughly the same amount of time, between 40 and 50 days.
However, a route via the Suez Canal and the Cape of Good Hope, which would become necessary if the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is closed following the current blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, would take around 100 days round trip. This would inevitably lead to higher transportation costs, Asahi noted.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been blocked due to the US conflict with Iran, which has been ongoing since February 28.

OpenAI pushes IPO to 2027 amid fears of rogue AI, calls to slow down development, Altman confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:42:02 UTC
13:42:02 KST

OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Chief Executive Sam Altman said in remarks published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence that render "unacceptable" even a 10% risk that AI could cause human extinction by decade's end.
The comments come as more US lawmakers urge new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing AI could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
"I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don't feel pressure on that," Altman told business magazine Fortune.
Asked if there was a 10% chance of AI-driven extinction, Altman said he didn't know how to make such an estimate, but warned the risk was serious enough that AI companies and governments should act as though it could not be tolerated.
"Whether it's 10 or eight or six, the point is, we all have a tremendous amount of responsibility, and cannot let egos or incentives for profit or anything else get in the way," Altman added.
"We need to act such that we are not taking any of those numbers of risk, and I believe we can."
Instances of AI agents going rogue
Politicians, both Democrat and Republican, have responded with alarm and calls for more action after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies out of concern at the technology risks.
In June, the New York Times said San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off until next year on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO.
At the time, shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company's valuation to $1.8 trillion.
Asked by Fortune if an IPO date of 2026 was off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said, "I would say not 2026.
"We got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together."
Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI firms may be close to unveiling a pact to slow AI development and work together to tackle safety risks, Fortune said.
Call for deliberate approach
On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development.
"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote in an essay on X.
Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment.
"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," Altman wrote. "This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."
Safety concerns have not slowed Anthropic's own IPO plans. It is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.

US President Donald Trump criticized conservative commentator Tucker Carlson in a Friday interview with Jewish radio host Sid Rosenberg, saying he ended their relationship several months ago because he felt Carlson’s comments had crossed a line.
The discussion came after Vice President JD Vance said that despite political disagreements with Carlson, he still considers him a friend and would not “throw him under the bus” over political differences.
Rosenberg asked the US president about the contrast between Vance’s approach and Trump’s own decision to distance himself from Carlson.
“You were friends with Tucker Carlson for many years, and a few months ago, maybe even a year ago, you decided you were done with him,” Rosenberg told Trump. “JD comes out and says: I’m not going to do that, the guy is a good friend of mine, we’re best friends, and I’m not going to let politics dictate who my friends are.”
Rosenberg warned that the issue could become a challenge for Vance if he seeks to succeed Trump and run for president in 2028.
Rosenberg warns Vance over Carlson ties ahead of 2028
“If he really wants to win in 2028, beyond the issue of Jews with Tucker Carlson, Tucker Carlson also called you ‘the Antichrist.’ So if I’m a Trump supporter and I’m Jewish, JD Vance needs to be careful. That’s my advice to him, Mr. President,” Rosenberg said.
Trump did not criticize Vance or say that his vice president was wrong to maintain his friendship with Carlson. Instead, he reflected on his own complicated relationship with the former Fox News host.
“You know, I’ve known Tucker Carlson for a long time, and my relationship with him was on and off for years, very on and off,” Trump said. “He’s very inconsistent. And maybe I am too, but I’m telling you, he’s very inconsistent.”
Trump also described Carlson as “a fair weather guy,” referring to someone who is supportive mainly when circumstances are favorable.
He then confirmed that he had decided to cut ties with Carlson.
“Of course, I dumped him a few months ago, because I just felt it wasn’t appropriate,” Trump said. “He said bad things, very bad things.”
Trump said his decision was not primarily related to comments Carlson made about him personally.
“Not so much about me, but about a lot of other things that are going on. And you understand that,” Trump said.
Trump says Carlson’s attacks on Levin crossed a line
Trump pointed to Carlson’s criticism of conservative Jewish radio host and commentator Mark Levin as one example of remarks he objected to.
“He would attack somebody like Mark Levin, who in my opinion is fantastic, by the way,” Trump said.
Rosenberg responded that he was very close with Levin. Trump continued: “And others. And I just, personally, didn’t like it.”
Trump later described his relationship with Carlson as one that had gone through repeated periods of tension.
“I would say Tucker Carlson never really liked me,” Trump said. “I did a lot for him, in a sense, but I would say he never really… in other words, you know, with people you have chemistry, right?”
Trump then turned to Rosenberg and added: “Like I have chemistry with you. With people you have chemistry. Sometimes you don’t. And if you don’t have it, there’s nothing the hell you can do about it. And Tucker and I had a very bumpy relationship.”
Trump avoids criticizing Vance over Carlson friendship
Trump’s remarks were notable because he did not say that Vance was wrong for continuing to describe Carlson as a friend, nor did he directly address Rosenberg’s concerns about how the relationship could affect Vance’s potential 2028 presidential campaign.
Instead, Trump focused his criticism on Carlson, describing him as inconsistent, a “fair weather guy,” and someone he decided to distance himself from after Carlson “said some very bad things.”
The exchange highlighted a difference between Trump and Vance’s views on political relationships. While Vance has argued that friendships should not be abandoned because of political disagreements, Trump said that, in his own relationship with Carlson, he decided months ago that it was over.
