KINSHASA, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- The government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) said on Friday that its ongoing Ebola outbreak is "under control" and has passed its peak, although local flare-ups, continued transmission and the spread of the disease to a seventh province point to persistent risks.
"The 17th Ebola outbreak is under control, and the peak was reached at the beginning of the third week of August 2026," government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya said while reading a report from a cabinet meeting on Friday, citing Health Minister Roger Kamba.
According to the government, all major indicators point to a decline in cases, with 10 health zones affected before the latest expansion of the outbreak reporting no new cases for at least 21 days, while transmission has slowed in several regions in the eastern province of Ituri, the epicenter of the outbreak.
The authorities nevertheless called for continued vigilance and strict contact tracing, saying close surveillance remains necessary in regions where recent flare-ups have been reported.
Former Congolese Health Minister Jean-Jacques Mbungani Mbanda, now a member of parliament, urged caution over the assessment, saying on Saturday that the downward trend in some areas should not be taken to mean that transmission has been brought under control everywhere.
In an outbreak involving multiple transmission foci, different areas may reach their peaks at different times, he said, adding that the epidemic curve reflects detected cases and could be affected by infections that remain unidentified in communities.
In its latest weekly report on Tuesday, the World Health Organization said the outbreak "remains uncontrolled and increasingly heterogeneous," with transmission easing in some areas while intensifying or spreading geographically elsewhere.
"The outbreak is increasingly geographically heterogeneous rather than showing a uniform decline," it said.
The DRC government has also confirmed Thursday the first Ebola case in the northwestern province of Sud-Ubangi, making it the seventh province affected. Sud-Ubangi does not border any of the six provinces where confirmed Ebola cases had previously been reported.
According to Mbanda, the patient, a 23-year-old man who later died, had traveled extensively before arriving in Sud-Ubangi, with an itinerary spanning several provinces, neighboring Rwanda and Uganda, as well as both road and river routes.
As of Sept. 10, the DRC had recorded 7,022 confirmed Ebola cases, including 3,398 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 48.4 percent. The outbreak has now affected 62 health zones across seven provinces.
The current outbreak, declared in May, has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, behind the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

====================================================================================================

Europe expelled its Jews - now, it wants to decide where Jews may live in Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
21:22:10 UTC
06:22:10 KST

There comes a point when we have to stop trying to explain ourselves to people who have already decided that the problem is the Jew who refuses to leave.
Britain, France, and Canada have now moved to restrict trade in goods from Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria. They will call it policy. They will say it is about borders, settlements, and a two-state solution.
But for the Jewish people, there is a history here that cannot simply be brushed aside.
For centuries, European governments decided where Jews were allowed to live, what they were allowed to own, and when they had to leave. England expelled its Jews in 1290. France expelled Jews again and again.
Jewish property was confiscated, communities were uprooted, and Jews learned the hard way that acceptance could disappear the moment the political winds changed.
Then came the pogroms. Then came the Holocaust.
And after all of that, the Jewish people rebuilt sovereignty in our own land so that never again would another government have the final word on where a Jew may live or whether a Jew may defend his family.
That is why I find what is happening now so difficult to accept.
Jews told where they can and can't live
After generations of being told we could not live in their countries, Jews are now being told there are places in our own ancestral homeland where our homes and businesses make us unacceptable.
Britain, in particular, should understand why this strikes such a nerve.
In 1929, Britain was the governing power in the Land of Israel and responsible for security in Hebron. The Jewish community warned that danger was building. Violence had already begun. Jews asked the British authorities to protect them.
Then 67 Jews were murdered.
Families were slaughtered, yeshiva students were killed, synagogues were desecrated, and one of the oldest Jewish communities in the world was shattered.
Britain was not reading about it from London. Britain was governing the land. Britain controlled the security apparatus. Jews depended on it for protection, and that protection failed.
That history matters now, when Britain wants to use government power against Jewish life in the same part of the land. The method is different. It is not British police or a military order. It is trade restrictions, sanctions, and economic pressure.
But once again, London is deciding that Jewish presence in Hebron and the surrounding region is something to be acted against.
France should also look in the mirror. Jews in France are once again living with open antisemitism, threats, and fear. Britain has seen the same ugliness.
Since October 7, we have watched demonstrations across Western capitals where legitimate concern for Palestinian civilians too often crossed into glorification of Hamas, excuses for terrorism, and hatred directed at Israel simply because it is the Jewish state.
And then there is Canada, which is itself fighting over trade and tariffs with the United States and knows exactly what it means when economic access is used as political leverage.
Yet Ottawa has now decided to use that same weapon against Jewish communities thousands of miles away.
I am not saying every criticism of Israel is antisemitic. It is not. Israel is a democracy and its government can be criticized like any other government.
I am also not talking about Muslims as a group. Millions of Muslims reject terrorism and want nothing to do with Hamas.
Some of the most hopeful developments in the Middle East have come from Arabs and Jews choosing business, relationships, and opportunity over endless hatred.
But we should stop being afraid to say what we are seeing when extremists and Hamas sympathizers are allowed to set the terms of the conversation, and Western governments keep moving in their direction.
October 7 should have created one simple lesson: massacring Jews does not work.
Hamas terrorists entered Israeli communities, murdered families in their homes, burned houses, kidnapped civilians, and carried out the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust.
The answer from the free world should have been to make sure Hamas understood that terrorism brings only defeat, isolation, and consequences.
Instead, less than three years later, the pressure keeps finding its way back to the Jews.
Jews were massacred. Israel fought back. Now Jewish communities are being boycotted.
What exactly is Hamas supposed to learn from that? Commit atrocities, wait for the horror to fade, and eventually the international community will put the Jewish state back in the defendant’s chair.
That is not a path to peace. It teaches extremists that violence creates leverage.
There is also a hypocrisy here that is impossible to ignore. Western governments speak constantly about coexistence and improving Palestinian lives, yet these same policies threaten businesses where Palestinians earn their living.
Nobody in London, Paris, or Ottawa announced replacement jobs for those workers. Nobody offered to cover their salaries if factories lose business. The politicians get their statement. The worker still has to feed his family.
We have seen this movie before. When pressure helped push SodaStream out of its plant in Judea and Samaria, hundreds of Palestinians lost good jobs. The activists celebrated and moved on. The workers were the ones left asking what they had gained.
The Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce also fought Airbnb when it announced that it would remove listings from Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria.
We said then that discrimination by geography could not be allowed to become normal. Florida acted, lawsuits followed, and Airbnb reversed course.
The deeper issue, though, is not Airbnb, SodaStream, or even this latest boycott. It is whether Jews are going to keep measuring our legitimacy by the approval of people who move the goalposts every time we meet the last demand.
For too long we have explained, apologized, and tried to prove that if we just say things the right way, show enough restraint, or make one more concession, people who hate us will finally accept us.
Jewish history should have cured us of that illusion.
Hebron should have cured us of it.
The whole purpose of Jewish sovereignty is that our future is not dependent on finding favor in the eyes of rulers, mobs, or movements that may decide tomorrow that the Jew has become inconvenient again.
That does not mean we stop caring about peace. It means we understand that peace is not built by rewarding people who massacre Jews or by punishing Jews for refusing to disappear.
If Britain truly wants to talk about Hebron, then let Britain also answer for Hebron.
There should be a serious historical and legal examination of what British authorities knew before the 1929 massacre, what warnings they received, why the Jewish community was not protected, and what responsibility Britain carried as the governing power.
Britain regularly demands accountability from Israel. It should be prepared to face accountability itself.
France and Canada should also think carefully about what they are joining. The Jewish people were expelled from Europe often enough.
We are not going to accept a modern version of the same thinking in which Jews are told that there is always one more place where Jewish life is politically unacceptable.
We do not need to hate anyone. We do not need to stop reaching out to people who genuinely want to live with us in peace.
But we do need to stop chasing approval from those who excuse Jewish murderers, sympathize with Hamas, and then demand that the Jewish victim prove his morality for defending himself.
Sometimes people show you their true colors. We should believe them.
The answer to October 7 cannot be another boycott of Jews. The answer to Palestinian unemployment cannot be destroying Palestinian jobs.
And after a thousand years of expulsions, restrictions, and bloodshed, the answer from Europe cannot once again be to tell Jews where they are allowed to live.
Britain must answer for Hebron. And Britain, France, and Canada should think very carefully about the message they are sending now.
The writer is the founder and CEO of Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce.

====================================================================================================

France's trade ban on Israeli settlements is political theater dressed up as int'l law - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
21:21:39 UTC
06:21:39 KST

The worst French diplomacy since the occupation has delivered – by forceps – a declaration that is politically shameful and legally inapplicable.
On September 8, France’s foreign ministry issued a joint statement by 12 foreign ministers – France, the United Kingdom, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden – reinforced by a parallel declaration from three heads of government: French President Emmanuel Macron, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Its promise: to restrict, nationally or at EU level, trade in goods produced in Israeli settlements, “in accordance with national procedures.”
Read it twice, and the sleight of hand appears. The declaration borrows the vocabulary of international law while accepting none of its discipline. It is a communiqué, not a norm.
And the distance between the two is precisely where Israel’s case lives. It deserves to be argued with precision, because it is on precision – not slogans – that the text collapses.
A press release is not a statute
The text binds no one. It does not repeal the 1995 EU–Israel Association Agreement. It imposes no duty on a single importer. It does not bind a single parliament.
Its only immediate force is diplomatic: to align capitals, prepare opinion, and manufacture the impression of a legal consensus that the law itself has not delivered.
The signatories concede as much when they defer to “national procedures” – the procedures that have produced, to date, nothing.
Illegality and embargo are two claims, not one
The declaration asserts that the settlements are “illegal under international law” and that trade with them may therefore be restricted – as if the second followed automatically from the first. It does not.
The illegality thesis is the majority UN position: Article 49(6) of the Fourth Geneva Convention; the ICJ’s 2004 Wall opinion; Resolution 2334 (2016); and the ICJ’s July 19, 2024 advisory opinion holding Israel’s continued presence unlawful and calling on states not to “aid or assist” in maintaining it.
Grant all of it. Nothing in that corpus mandates an import ban – and three precedents prove it.
First, an advisory opinion is not a judgment. It carries no res judicata against Israel, which was not a party and did not consent to the Court’s jurisdiction. It weighs; it does not command.
Second – the objection to meet head-on – the 2024 opinion did go beyond “distinguish”: it spoke of a duty not to “aid or assist,” gesturing at economic dealings.
Yet three limits are decisive. The Court prescribed no import ban.
The duty of non-assistance is a doctrine built for how governments deal with governments – recognition, treaties, official cooperation – not for a shopper in Brussels buying Golan wine.
And if it reached the supermarket shelf, it would apply identically to Northern Cyprus, Western Sahara, Crimea, and Tibet. None of the 12 bans those goods.
An obligation that fires against one country alone is not law; it is policy wearing the law’s uniform.
Third, Israel’s case is not a nullity: Article 49(6) targets forcible transfers, not voluntary settlement; the West Bank had no recognized sovereign in 1967; the Oslo Accords, signed by the PLO, reserve the settlements to permanent-status talks; Resolution 242 speaks of “secure and recognized boundaries.”
A minority view – but one perfectly grounded in law and in fact; and a minority that will surprise no one, so thoroughly has the UN become a rubber-stamp chamber for the worst anti-Zionist ravings.
The real wall is Brussels, not Jerusalem
For eight of the 12, the fatal obstacle is European law. The common commercial policy is an exclusive EU competence (Articles 3(1) and 207 TFEU).
A member state cannot build its own import-ban regime without trespassing on a power surrendered to the Union.
As a trade measure, it needs a qualified majority; recharacterized as foreign-and-security policy, unanimity returns – and Berlin, Rome, or Budapest can veto.
A national ban under the Article 36 “public morality” exception must be necessary, proportionate, and non-discriminatory; an embargo on goods already circulating freely in the single market is none of those, and invites a losing day in Luxembourg.
Britain and Canada, outside the Union, escape this. France, Spain, Ireland, Denmark, Finland, Poland, Portugal, and Sweden are caught.
Then comes the WTO: an origin-based ban must clear GATT Articles XX or XXI (the security exception limited by the 2019 Russia – Traffic in Transit panel), and the “Israel vs occupied territory” origin question is a customs battlefield opened by Brita (C-386/08, 2010) and Psagot (C-363/18, 2019) – cases where the EU learned to distinguish without prohibiting.
A loud instrument that changes nothing
Even at its best, the measure moves no tank, disarms no cell, reopens no corridor. It falls on greenhouses and wine cellars – tens of millions in Jordan Valley dates, grapes, and cosmetics.
Call it precision; it is closer to theater, action taken where it costs European governments little at home and buys much with an electorate for whom the settlements are the conflict’s convenient moral shorthand.
And it is theater with a blind spot: it condemns October 7, then draws no conclusion from the fact that the enemy of Oslo wrote, rehearsed and filmed a plan to erase a state and slaughter its civilians.
France, of all countries, leads it
The initiative bears the fingerprints of the Quai d’Orsay, and that is its deepest irony.
Paris drives a coalition toward an instrument it cannot lawfully apply on its own – an import ban that collides head-on with the Union’s exclusive commercial competence, the very competence France helped make exclusive.
It spends real capital with Jerusalem to harvest applause at home; it hands Hamas the diplomatic dividend of watching Israel scolded while the movement that broke Oslo pays nothing; and it calls this statesmanship.
A diplomacy that picks a legal fight it cannot win, against a partner it needs, over a trade so small it barely registers, is not strategy – it is the worst French diplomacy in living memory: costly abroad, hollow at home, and legally inapplicable on the one day it would matter.
What it is worth
As a signal, a great deal: it isolates Israel in a circle of Western capitals that a decade ago went no further than labeling.
As binding law, very little – it collides with an exclusive EU competence, awaits parliaments that have voted nothing, must justify itself at the WTO, and is undone by its own selective logic.
It is a vast blow struck in water – futile in effect, deafening in noise – that history will nonetheless remember with a clang as the worst foreign policy modern France has produced: diplomacy debased to electoral ends, to court the votes of the far-left France Insoumise (LFI).
It is legitimate as the voice of executives that already distinguish Israel from the territories; far less so as a claim to pronounce, by press release, the last word on the law – and on the security of a state whose survival, across 15 kilometers of coastal plain, is not decided in the dates-and-wine aisle.
Until it produces a statute, a regulation, and judicial review, it remains a proclamation. In law, that is a great deal for an op-ed. It is very little for an embargo – and nothing at all for Israel’s security.
The writer is a Portugal- and Israel-based French entrepreneur, legal adviser, and expert in crypto assets, information security, and computer warfare. A former lecturer at the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale (IHEDN) on influence operations, he has participated in French parliamentary missions on economic intelligence and advised on digital threats facing France and European institutions. He regularly comments on French foreign policy and Middle East affairs.

AI generated
LOS ANGELES – OpenAI will not go public in 2026, chief executive officer Sam Altman said in remarks published on Sept 12, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence that render “unacceptable” even a 10 per cent risk that AI could cause human extinction by the end of the decade.
The comments come as more US lawmakers urge new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman told business magazine Fortune.
Asked if there was a 10 per cent chance of AI-driven extinction, Altman said he did not know how such an estimate could be made, but warned the risk was serious enough that AI companies and governments should act as though it could not be tolerated.
“Whether it’s 10 or eight or six, the point is, we all have a tremendous amount of responsibility, and cannot let egos or incentives for profit or anything else get in the way,” he added.
“We need to act such that we are not taking any of those numbers of risk, and I believe we can.”
Instances of AI agents going rogue
Politicians, both Democrat and Republican, have responded with alarm and calls for more action after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies out of concern at the technology risks.
In June, the New York Times said San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off until 2027 on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO.
At the time, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent the company’s valuation to US$1.8 trillion (S$2.3 trillion).
Asked by Fortune if an IPO date of 2026 was off the table in favour of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026. We got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”
He suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI firms may be close to unveiling a pact to slow AI development and work together to tackle safety risks, Fortune said.
Calls for more deliberate approach
On Sept 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he wrote in an essay shared on social media.
In response to Amodei’s post on the X platform, Altman wrote: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.”
Safety concerns have not slowed down Anthropic’s own IPO plans so far. It is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November, people familiar with the matter said. REUTERS

Bid to boost education, employability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
21:14:27 UTC
06:14:27 KST

NEW DELHI: Brics countries want to bring education and jobs closer together, with a new focus on STEM, vocational training, digital skills and AI, while also trying to identify what skills employers will need in the coming years.The New Delhi Declaration links the entire chain — from basic learning and digital literacy to higher education, technical training and jobs. It calls for cooperation in foundational literacy, digital literacy, and safe and human-centred use of emerging technologies, including AI. It also backs undergraduate and postgraduate scholarships in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), and stronger links between technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutions and industry to “expand job opportunities”.
A key part of the plan is to make training respond more closely to changes in the job market. Brics members have committed to studying labour-market trends in digital, green, care and other priority sectors to forecast the skills that will be needed. The declaration also welcomes Brics Connect, a network focused on capacity building, employability and new skills and technologies.The emphasis is not only on university education. The declaration recognises Brics TVET Cooperation Alliance as a platform for sharing information and resources and developing vocational training across member countries.
It calls for training programmes to be aligned with changing market needs by building stronger links between TVET institutions and industry.The industrial sector is being brought into this effort too. Brics Centre for Industrial Competencies, set up with UNIDO, is helping manufacturers and small businesses adopt Industry 4.0 and advanced digital production technologies, including AI. Brics Intelligent Manufacturing and Robotics Working Group is also working on talent development.
The declaration separately calls for greater cooperation in digital skills and capacity building, including proposed capacity-building centres aimed at creating a “future-ready workforce”.For Brics, therefore, the skills challenge is no longer confined to colleges and training centres. The declaration seeks to connect what students learn with what factories, businesses and other employers will need — while using labour-market trends to keep training relevant as technology changes.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

Trespasser stopped on former Vice President Kamala Harris’ Malibu property
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Security personnel at former Vice President Kamala Harris’ Malibu home stopped a woman who entered the property Friday night; Harris and husband Doug Emhoff were away.
- The incident renews scrutiny of Harris’ security after President Trump revoked extended Secret Service protection last year, leaving state and local agencies to coordinate coverage amid political backlash and resource concerns.
A trespasser tried to enter former Vice President Kamala Harris’ cliffside home in Malibu on Friday evening, according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department and a Harris spokesman.
Harris and her husband, Doug Emhoff, were not home at the time, according to Eduardo Negrón, a spokesperson for Harris. He did not respond to a question about the couple’s whereabouts.
“Last night, security personnel stopped an individual who illegally entered Vice President Harris and Second Gentleman Emhoff’s property before the individual reached the home,” he said in a statement. “They are grateful to the security and law enforcement personnel who responded swiftly.”
Harris’ on-site security contacted the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, which has jurisdiction over Malibu.
Lt. Jason Duron, a watch commander at the Malibu/Lost Hills sheriff’s station, said his department was contacted by Harris’ security detail when a woman attempted to enter the property. Sheriff’s deputies responded around 10:30 p.m., and the woman, who has not been identified, agreed to leave voluntarily. She was not arrested.
“We are stepping up patrols of the property to be safe,” Duron said.
Harris’ level of security has previously been scrutinized. Former vice presidents typically receive six months of Secret Service protection after leaving office, but former President Biden extended the coverage. President Trump, who beat Harris in the 2024 election, revoked the extension in August 2025.
That led Los Angeles and California law enforcement agencies to scramble to protect Harris. The Los Angeles Police Department quickly discontinued its involvement amid criticism that shifting manpower to protect the former vice president was hampering the agency’s ability to fight crime.
The California Highway Patrol continues to assist Harris’ security detail, but its officers were not on-site Friday night, according to CHP Sgt. Christian Stevens.

Text description provided by the architects. At the top of a hill, the city meets the forest. The site lies at the edge of Singapore's Central Nature Catchment Reserve, one of the island's most extensive natural landscapes. It seemed to offer an extraordinary opportunity: a family home immersed in nature, yet still within the city. The promise was clear. The difficulty was less apparent. At the levels where family life would ordinarily unfold, neighbouring houses surrounded the site and obscured much of the forest beyond. Opening the house indiscriminately towards its surroundings would expose the family to neighbouring views. Turning inward for privacy would risk losing the very landscape that made the site exceptional.

Saudi Arabia closes East-West pipeline as Houthis tighten grip on Red Sea

The 1,200-km pipeline has served as the main route out for global supplies of Middle East oil for the past six months while the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shut by war.
Saudi Arabia has shut down its East-West pipeline, after the vital oil conduit came under aerial attack in the widening Middle East war, threatening to send energy prices even higher.
The world’s largest crude oil exporter said it temporarily closed the pipeline as a precaution after a drone attack that both Baghdad and Riyadh said had originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday in response to the attack.
The 1,200-km (745-mile) pipeline running across the Arabian Peninsula has served as the main route out for global supplies of Middle East oil for the past six months while the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shut by war. It has been moving 4 million to 5 million barrels per day, amounting to 4% to 5% of global supply, sparing Saudi Arabia the brunt of the disruption that has crippled other Gulf oil and gas exporters.

‘We took only the clothes we wore’: Tens of thousands flee Houthi-held areas in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
20:45:10 UTC
05:45:10 KST

Tens of thousands of Yemenis have fled Taiz province and surrounding areas since Thursday following the Houthi capture of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha and their advance around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
“We couldn’t take anything with us, and even water is expensive,” Omar Abd al-Aziz al-Himyari, a resident of the province, told The New York Times. Al-Himyari said his family fled with virtually nothing. “We took only the clothes we were wearing, what we had on us. We couldn’t take anything with us because of the difficult terrain. We left all our property behind,” he said.
“I don’t know how we’re going to pay for food. The prices of flour and rice in the market have soared. Water is expensive too and can only be obtained from tanks.”
Al-Himyari moved into his brother-in-law’s home, leaving behind the fields he cultivated and his family’s livestock.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have portrayed their advance as the “liberation” of territory from Saudi control. Saudi Arabia supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in its conflict with the rebels.
“The presidential amnesty will apply to everyone who lays down their weapons and stops following the orders of the Saudi regime,” the Houthis said after entering the province.
“We call on residents of the ‘liberated areas’ to cooperate and report any suspicious movement to the security forces. We will restore conditions to normal and address the problems created by the actions of the Saudi regime’s mercenaries.”
The escalation has also spilled across Yemen’s border. Alerts were activated in Saudi Arabia Saturday evening after a Houthi projectile struck Jizan, the capital of Jazan province, injuring two people. Saudi civil defense authorities said a mosque was hit and several vehicles were damaged.
‘Thirty-four of us crammed into a truck’
The Houthis have sought to portray Saudi Arabia as an enemy of the Yemeni people and blame Riyadh for the blockade imposed on Yemen.
But areas described by the group as “liberated” are suffering from extreme poverty, disease, forced recruitment of children and adults, and arbitrary arrests. Remaining resources are being diverted toward Houthi fighters and leaders rather than residents displaced by the fighting.
A Yemeni security official told Ynet that conditions were extremely difficult. “There are many casualties. The rebels are acting against innocent people,” the official said.
Yemen’s Foreign Ministry called on the international community to act urgently over the humanitarian consequences of the Houthi escalation, warning that the expansion of the threat toward the strait was increasing the danger to civilians.
Abd al-Jabbar Ali Hadi, a resident of al-Wazi’iyah in Taiz province, is among more than 45,000 people who have fled their homes in recent days. “No one fully understood what was happening,” he told Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat. “Chaos and panic broke out. Everyone wanted to escape. Some tried to save their children, others had only their sheep and cattle. Women were crying. Everyone was looking for a way out.”
Al-Miqdad Hashem, who escaped with his family, described the desperate conditions of their flight after shells landed near their home and wounded his nephew. “It was difficult to take anything with us. We want the war to end so people can return to their homes,” he said. “The only way to the hospital was in a truck used to transport construction materials. Thirty-four of us crammed inside. We took one small bag.”
Asharq Al-Awsat reported long columns of displaced people traveling by cars and motorcycles, while thousands more fled on foot, some accompanied by livestock.
For many families, the displacement was not planned but a sudden flight driven by fear. Those unable to leave found themselves trapped under Houthi control and facing the threat of raids and arrests.
Reports from the area also described widespread looting and theft. According to the Saudi newspaper, Houthi forces took entire families hostage in some cases in an effort to pressure relatives who had fought alongside Saudi-backed forces to surrender.
Mohammed, a resident of the port city of Mokha who fled with his family in the middle of the night, described the scene to AFP. “The city was apocalyptic. Gangs looted us as we fled,” he said.
Another resident, Mohammed Khudairi, told The Guardian: “The attacks are continuing. It’s a disaster. We managed to get out, but others are trapped.”
No funding, no aid
The New York Times noted that the UN World Food Programme’s operations in Yemen have been suspended because of a lack of funding.
Carl Skau, the WFP’s acting executive director, told the newspaper that he had visited Yemen only a week earlier and toured several camps for displaced people. “Children are not going to school. People are selling family possessions for food,” he said.
Outside clinics, he said, mothers wait in long lines with malnourished children and struggle to afford even one meal a day.
Yemen’s crisis is being driven by more than fighting. Extreme weather has further damaged already limited domestic food production, while disruptions to shipping routes have pushed prices higher. Droughts and floods have also devastated agriculture.
Even before the latest escalation, around 4.5 million Yemenis had already been displaced by years of fighting with the Houthis.
Nearly half of the country’s health facilities are out of service, while repeated attacks on aid workers, including UN personnel, have forced humanitarian organizations to withdraw from some areas.

BRICS leaders adopt joint declaration at summit in New Delhi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:38:23 CST
05:38:23 KST

NEW DELHI, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Leaders of BRICS countries at the 18th BRICS Summit adopted a joint declaration in New Delhi, the capital of India, on Saturday, reiterating their commitment to inclusive global governance and strengthening multilateralism, calling for international and regional peace and security, and underscoring sustainable and inclusive global economic growth as well as strengthening cultural and people-to-people cooperation.
The New Delhi Declaration reiterated the leaders' commitment to reforming and improving global governance by promoting a more just, equitable, agile, effective, representative, and accountable international and multilateral system in the spirit of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits.
In the declaration, the leaders reiterated their commitment to strengthening multilateralism and multipolarity and to upholding international law, calling for greater and more meaningful participation and representation of emerging markets and developing countries as well as least developed countries in global decision-making processes and structures.
They also stated that they deplore attempts, including by deliberately withholding assessed contributions, to unilaterally undermine the work of global multilateral institutions and impair the implementation of their respective mandates.
The leaders also expressed concern about ongoing conflicts in many parts of the world and the current state of polarization and fragmentation in the international order, calling for the peaceful resolution of international disputes through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy.
They highlight, in the context of international disputes, the importance of preventive diplomacy and mediation, with the consent of relevant parties, as essential tools to avoid crises and prevent their escalation, in accordance with the Purposes and Principles of the UN Charter.
Noting that current global challenges are interlinked and impede economic growth while accentuating persistent development gaps across countries and regions, the leaders reiterated the particular importance of sustainable development and inclusive growth in the UN agenda.
The declaration said that the leaders recognize that artificial intelligence presents immense opportunities to stimulate economic growth and sustainable development for all.
Reaffirming the importance of BRICS people-to-people exchanges and initiatives in enhancing mutual understanding, friendship and cooperation, the leaders also called for more efforts to respect diversity of cultures, highly value inheritance, innovation and creativity, and to jointly advocate robust international people-to-people exchanges and cooperation.
The leaders also declared full support for China for its BRICS presidency in 2027 and the holding of the 19th BRICS Summit in China. ■

The EU has until Sept. 15 to renew its sanctions on more than 3,000 primarily Russian entities and individuals, but failed again on Sept. 11 to approve the extension. The measures were last extended on March 14.
Slovakia is holding up the agreement by repeating its call to lift sanctions against Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov — and for the first time, France has joined Bratislava in pushing for Usmanov to be delisted, four EU diplomats told the outlet Euronews.

"When the Ukrainian economy is simply a target for Russia, it is certainly not the time for Europe to view Russian oligarchs as friends," he said.
"When Russia uses every euro and dollar to prolong the war, it is immoral and self-destructive to give Russian businesses the opportunity to live in a way that allows them to avoid the consequences of the war. Usmanov and Fridman represent the very type of Russian business that needs to find the courage to take concrete steps against the war."

Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group and a member of Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle.

Usmanov is a Russian-Uzbek businessman who made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
Slovakia, arguably the most Kremlin-friendly government in the EU, has long called for the bloc to remove both Fridman and Usmanov from its sanctions list. France joining the demand is new, and has caused "huge frustration" among member states, diplomats told Euronews.
France reportedly is presenting the delisting of Usmanov as a political compromise, believing Slovakia is unlikely to give up both its demands in order to reach an agreement.
Extending the EU sanctions requires a unanimous vote, meaning one member state has veto power over the renewal.

However, there is little risk that the sanctions will lapse, an EU diplomat told the Kyiv Independent. The worst-case scenario would likely mean the measures would only be extended six months (instead of the desired 12), rather than expire altogether.
Ambassadors will convene again on Sept. 14, with the aim of reaching an agreement by the 15th.
Zelensky urged the EU to consider Russia's escalating assault against Ukraine's economy when finalizing its sanctions list. He emphasized that Russia continued to launch large-scale drone attacks, aiming to "destroy the Ukrainian economy in ordr to break our resistance."
"Russian businesses that pay taxes into the war budget, and Russian oligarchs ... must feel that there is no safe place for them in the world as long as this war continues," he said.

"Five hundred Shahed drones per day is certainly not the right time to even begin a discussion about easing sanctions," he said.

superstudio’s 12 ideal cities question the price of a perfectly designed life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
20:35:32 UTC
05:35:32 KST

Superstudio designed 12 impossible ways of living
In 1971, Superstudio imagined twelve cities designed to solve the problems of human existence and came up with solutions so complete that there was barely any life left to live. A person wakes up in a five-cubit cell. The temperature is permanently set at 25°C. The humidity never changes. Food and every other necessity arrive automatically. There is no work to do, no reason to leave, and no one else to meet.
The room knows what its inhabitant wants before they have to ask. It also knows when they are unhappy. This is the 2,000-Ton City, one of twelve imaginary settlements described by Gian Piero Frassinelli and Superstudio in Twelve Cautionary Tales for Christmas: Premonitions of the Mystical Rebirth of Urbanism, published in 1971. Better known as 12 Ideal Cities, the project is populated by disembodied brains, people who live through machines, citizens governed by books, and inhabitants carried through life by cities that operate like enormous industrial organisms.
They are strange, often funny, and increasingly cruel. More importantly, they are all built around the same trap: every city has found a solution.
In Superstudio’s cities there is no universal housing model, no master plan intended to work everywhere. Every story begins with a principle and follows it to its most extreme conclusion. What if every human need could be satisfied automatically? What if the body were no longer necessary? What if a city could organize its inhabitants according to perfect order? What if life could be made more efficient by treating the city as a machine? The questions may be simple, but the answers grow increasingly uncomfortable. This is what keeps Twelve Ideal Cities interesting. Superstudio takes familiar problems, gives them perfect solutions, then follows those solutions until they become something else entirely. In these cities, the system designed to make life easier gradually takes over life itself.
Twelve Ideal Cities – Twelve Cautionary Tales, 1971 | image via MAXXI
the city that gives you everything
The inhabitants of the 2,000-Ton City live alone, enclosed within individual cells. The city regulates the environment and responds to desire through an elaborate technological apparatus. A brain-impulse receiver communicates the wishes of the inhabitants to a central electronic system which organizes the response of the city.
Nothing needs to be searched for, made, or negotiated. It is difficult to imagine a more complete promise of convenience. Superstudio then introduces the detail that gives the city its name. If the system detects a citizen entertaining rebellious thoughts against their ‘perfect eternal life,’ a ceiling panel weighing two thousand tons drops. The problem has been removed and so has the person. It is an absurd image, but the joke is doing serious work. The 2,000-Ton City questions whether a life made entirely convenient is necessarily a life made freer. Its inhabitant has been relieved of almost every difficulty and, along with it, almost every opportunity to act. There is no need for other people because the system takes care of everything. There is no need to make decisions because the system anticipates them. The perfect home becomes a perfectly managed cell.
Superstudio, Terza città: New York of Brains, 1971 | image via Centre Pompidou, MNAM-CCI/Georges Meguerditchian/Dist. GrandPalaisRmn
no body, no house
The New York of Brains is exactly what its title suggests. Human brains are preserved in individual containers, sustained by technological systems and connected through electrodes. The traditional ingredients of habitation disappear with the body itself. No kitchens. No beds. No streets. No need to walk anywhere. In the City of the Hemispheres, bodies lie immobilized inside transparent containers while consciousness experiences the world through a separate apparatus.
In Spaceship City, inhabitants live through programmed experiences as the machinery around them controls the conditions of their existence. These stories make ordinary architecture suddenly seem very physical. A house is designed around bodies that need to sleep, eat, move, touch things, get sick, grow old, and share space with other bodies. Remove those conditions and the familiar architecture of daily life begins to disappear. Superstudio takes this idea to an almost grotesque conclusion. What is a home when there is no need to cook? What is privacy when the body itself has become a technical object? What is a city when its inhabitants no longer need streets? The answer is never presented as a technological triumph. The systems keep people alive, but Superstudio keeps asking, what kind of life is being preserved?
2,000-Ton City | image via Hidden Architecture
the city doesn’t need you. it needs you to work
Not every city isolates its inhabitants. Some absorb them. In the Temporal Cochlea-City, life happens inside an immense mechanical structure that continues according to its own physical logic. In other stories, cities become systems of continuous production, construction, and industrial activity. Here, the relationship between architecture and inhabitant begins to reverse. Usually, a city is understood as something built for people. Housing accommodates domestic life; streets allow people to move; infrastructure supplies what a population needs. Superstudio imagines a city that has its own rhythm. People must keep up. The inhabitant becomes a component within a much larger mechanism. It is a useful shift because it moves Twelve Ideal Cities away from the familiar image of radical architecture as a collection of spectacular drawings. The project is interested in what forms do to people. A spiral, a conveyor belt, or an enclosed machine is never just an image. Each produces a particular way of spending time, moving through space, relating to others, and reaching the end of a life. Architecture becomes a schedule, a social system, a biological system.
The strangest form of architecture in Twelve Ideal Cities may not look like architecture at all. In the City of the Book, the rules of life are carried by the inhabitants. The book contains the instructions by which existence is organized: norms, behaviors, and prescribed ways of acting.
The City of Order explores a similar idea. Control does not necessarily arrive in the form of walls, guards, or visibly oppressive buildings. It can appear as normality. Streets, houses, and everyday routines continue, while the system makes sure that deviation is corrected. Superstudio’s point is that control can be embedded in things that appear helpful, rational, or ordinary. A system can make life easier while deciding what kind of life it is designed to support. A housing plan can encourage one form of domesticity over another. An infrastructure network can determine who meets and who remains separated. A building can make certain activities effortless and others almost impossible. The City of the Book turns this invisible process into a literal instruction manual.
The Fourth City, Spaceship City- 1971 | image courtesy of Superstudio
the problem with an ideal city
It would be easy to call all twelve cities dystopias and leave it there. The project is more unsettling than a collection of bad futures. Each city begins with something recognizable: comfort, order, longevity, efficiency, pleasure, security or the elimination of unnecessary labor.
These are desires that remain among the reasons people build, design, plan, and invent. Superstudio’s trick is to ask what happens when one of them becomes the only thing that matters. A city devoted entirely to comfort eventually removes the need to do anything uncomfortable. A city devoted entirely to order has little use for disagreement. A system designed to eliminate uncertainty will eventually treat unpredictability as a malfunction. Superstudio takes each idea to its logical extreme. The cities offer clear answers to familiar questions about how we might live, but the further those answers are pushed, the stranger the resulting forms of habitation become.
Dodicesima città: città del libro (Twelfth City: City of Book), from Le dodici città ideali (Twelve Ideal Cities) | image via SFMOMA
leave some things unresolved
What makes Twelve Ideal Cities difficult to leave behind is that the absurdity is never really the point. Frassinelli takes ideas that already exist around him — the efficient city, the productive city, the perfectly controlled environment, the city organized around a single purpose — and refuses to stop at the point where they still sound reasonable. He keeps going until the consequences become impossible to ignore.
That method still works. We now live among many of the systems that were once easier to recognize as science fiction: automated environments, permanent connectivity, predictive technologies, and cities increasingly measured through data and performance. But the twelve cities are relevant because they ask a more basic question about what we are willing to give up in exchange for a life that is faster, easier, more efficient or more controlled.
The answer is different in each city, but the pattern is the same. Something is gained, and something else disappears. In one, the body becomes irrelevant; in another, production takes over the city; elsewhere, order becomes the organizing principle of everyday life, and the architecture follows. Eventually there is nowhere left for anything that does not belong. Frassinelli asks what happens when an idea about how we should live becomes the environment around us. Today, the question is still relevant: as technology becomes more involved in everyday life, how much of our lives do we want to let it shape?
Twelve Cautionary Tales for Christmas by Superstudio

‘Woman Unknown’ wins Gold Lion at Venice Film Festival

Unknown Publisher

20:05:28 UTC

‘Woman Unknown’ wins Gold Lion at Venice Film Festival
Danish filmmaker May el-Toukhy was the only woman directing a feature film in the main 21-strong film line-up
Danish filmmaker May el-Toukhy’s post-war drama Woman Unknown won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, with its star Mathilde Arcel also taking best actress honours in a rare double victory.
El-Toukhy was the only woman directing a feature film in the main, 21-strong film line-up, a disparity that drew criticism during the festival and prompted renewed scrutiny of the barriers facing women in cinema.
Set in the aftermath of World War II, Woman Unknown follows a housemaid played by Arcel whose past relationship with a German soldier threatens to destroy her future.
The film unfolds against the backdrop of a newly liberated Denmark, where women accused of fraternising with occupying German forces were often subjected to vigilante justice.
“To me personally, Woman Unknown is about the female body as a battleground and a public matter. And at the same time, the film tells the tale of women who are invisible, unseen, and voiceless,” el-Toukhy said in her acceptance speech.
South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong took the runner-up Silver Lion award for Possible Love, while Russian-born filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovsky won best director for DAU, a hugely ambitious project shot largely in Ukraine before the ongoing war that has attracted intense scrutiny and controversy.

Israeli filmmakers’ documentary ‘NAZA,’ that alleges IDF deliberately targeted Gazan civilians, wins special jury prize at Venice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
20:03:59 UTC
05:03:59 KST

Gaza documentary ‘NAZA’ wins special jury prize at Venice
Israeli co-director Yuval Abraham criticizes the film’s detractors during his acceptance speech; IDF rejects allegations about its conduct in Gaza
“NAZA,” a documentary about the Gaza war by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has won the special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival, with Abraham using his acceptance speech to criticize the film’s detractors in Israel.
“It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the Israeli politicians and journalists who are now attacking this film and denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said. “So much is being done not to look at reality.”
The documentary draws on interviews conducted over three years with 24 individuals presented as Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel; their identities are concealed. They describe surveillance, target selection and the approval of strikes expected to kill civilians, including allegations that the military knowingly authorized attacks causing extensive civilian deaths.
Filmed at night on Tel Aviv rooftops, the documentary takes its title from a Hebrew military acronym for “collateral damage.” It received a 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere.
The IDF rejected the film’s allegations, pointing out there were numerous issues with its credibility, including the question how could the anonymous interviewees access the information they discuss. It said claims about national and military strategy went beyond the knowledge of junior soldiers.
The military said it targets terrorist organizations, operates under the laws of armed conflict and takes measures to minimize civilian harm. Addressing allegations concerning artificial intelligence, it said decisions on selecting and approving strikes are made by human personnel.
Abraham and Szor previously co-directed “No Other Land” with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film, about Palestinian communities in the West Bank, won the Academy Award for best documentary feature in 2025.

Therapeutic gardening improves mental health for adults with chronic conditions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
20:00:54 UTC
05:00:54 KST

Getting your hands dirty in the garden might offer a moderate boost to mental health for adults managing chronic health conditions. A recent review of past research found that activities like planting and tending to community gardens help ease symptoms of depression and anxiety, though the benefits for physical ailments are less pronounced. The research was published in BMC Public Health.
Chronic health conditions encompass a wide range of long-lasting medical issues that persist over time. These include physical illnesses like cardiovascular disease, arthritis, and diabetes, alongside cognitive and mood disorders like dementia, anxiety, and depression. Managing these persistent health challenges places a heavy burden on individuals, families, and healthcare systems around the world. Because the aging global population is driving an increase in these long-term conditions, medical professionals are seeking new management strategies.
Nature-based treatments are frequently recommended to help people cope with these long-term health needs. Therapeutic gardening is one such approach, where patients actively engage with plants, soil, and outdoor environments. These programs treat horticulture as a structured leisure activity that encourages physical movement, social interaction, and a connection to the natural world. In places like the United Kingdom, healthcare providers even use a process called social prescribing to encourage patients to visit parks and community gardens.
Past research has documented various psychological and social benefits of spending time in green spaces. Public health researcher Feifei Wang of Fudan University and psychologist Szilvia Boros of Széchenyi István University wanted to quantify these benefits specifically for populations with existing medical diagnoses. They designed a study to evaluate exactly how gardening activities alter specific categories of health for adults living with chronic illnesses.
To understand the broader impact of these outdoor interventions, Wang and Boros conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis. A meta-analysis is a statistical technique that pools data from multiple independent studies to identify overall trends that a single experiment might miss. The researchers searched major scientific databases for peer-reviewed studies that tested gardening programs against a standard control group. They only included research focused on adults over the age of 18 who had at least one diagnosed chronic condition.
The team identified 23 relevant studies that included a total of 4,535 participants, representing a large combined sample size for this specific topic. The individuals involved in these trials lived with various chronic conditions, ranging from physical pain and obesity to high blood pressure, cognitive dysfunction, and cancer. The participants were primarily older adults with an average age of about 54 years, and roughly two-thirds of them were women. The included research featured a mix of randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental study designs.
Wang and Boros extracted the reported health outcomes from these studies and divided them into three primary categories to calculate an effect size. An effect size is a statistical measurement that tells researchers how much of a difference an intervention actually made. The mental health category included measurements of anxiety, stress, depression, overall mood, and loneliness. The physical health category tracked metrics like blood pressure and cognitive function. The general health category covered broader quality of life indicators, such as pain levels, sleep quality, and social connectedness.
When analyzing the combined data, the researchers found that gardening interventions offered a moderate improvement for mental health outcomes. Participants who spent time digging, watering, and harvesting reported fewer issues with depression and anxiety compared to those in the control groups who did not participate in the gardening programs. Many of these trials involved older adults experiencing cognitive decline, such as dementia, who seemed to benefit psychologically from the active lifestyle and socialization that community gardens provide.
The analysis revealed less encouraging results for the other two categories. Gardening activities produced relatively small effects on general health and almost negligible changes to physical health outcomes. The data did not show widespread physical improvements, such as lowered blood pressure or improved cognitive function, directly stemming from the gardening interventions. The researchers noted that while physical movement is involved in gardening, it might not be strenuous enough to dramatically alter physical disease progression in a short timeframe.
To ensure the reliability of their findings, Wang and Boros performed a sensitivity analysis using a standardized quality assessment tool. This process involves stripping away studies with a high risk of bias or low-quality methodology to see if the overall trends hold up. After removing the weaker studies, the positive effect of gardening on mental health became even stronger. At the same time, the evidence for physical and general health benefits remained weak and the results were not statistically significant.
The study comes with a few limitations related to the nature of the available research. The included trials exhibited high heterogeneity, meaning the methods, duration, and intensity of the gardening programs varied wildly from one study to the next. Some studies involved short sessions over a few weeks, while others spanned several months. This wide variation makes it difficult to recommend a specific type or amount of gardening for therapeutic purposes.
Many of the included trials also struggled with methodological challenges like selection bias and a lack of randomized participant placement. In medical research, it is difficult to design a trial where participants are blind to the treatment they are receiving if that treatment involves active physical tasks. Because participants knew they were engaging in an outdoor activity, their expectations might have influenced their reported improvements in mood, stress, and general life satisfaction.
High dropout rates in community-based interventions can also skew the results of a meta-analysis. If participants who do not enjoy gardening leave a study early, the final data will only reflect the experiences of those who liked the activity enough to stay. The researchers noted that achieving perfect experimental conditions is often unrealistic when testing lifestyle interventions in real-world community settings.
Future research will need to define standardized gardening activities to better measure their health impacts. While working with plants can support psychological well-being, the current evidence does not support using horticulture as a primary treatment for physical ailments. Medical providers looking to recommend nature-based therapies require more rigorous, uniform trials to understand exactly how different health conditions respond to specific outdoor environments.
The study, “Effect of gardening activities on domains of health: a systematic review and meta-analysis,” was authored by Feifei Wang and Szilvia Boros.

The moment I knew: I had planned to break up with him – then he snuck out of school to buy me hot chips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
20:00:43 UTC
05:00:43 KST

Dylan and I first started dating in high school when we were 16. He was a “bad boy” who got drunk at parties and occasionally spoke to other people with his fists.
One night, I was sitting at my computer, chatting with friends on MSN and Facebook and Dylan’s name popped up. I enjoyed playing online checkers with people from school, so I invited him to a game. During the game we chatted online, which led to flirting. The winner got to choose what they wanted. I lost and what did Dylan ask for? To date me. We agreed to one date at the movies and to declare to the school we were boyfriend and girlfriend. I thought this was hilarious, though I planned to break up with him after a few days.
The date went better than I thought – he offered to invite friends so that I wasn’t alone. He paid for my ticket, bought me Maltesers, and when I realised I’d left my glasses in the car, he ran back to the car park in skinny jeans and sandals to retrieve them.
At school, I remember the first time he tried to touch me, on my lower back. When his hand made contact with my shirt I immediately told him he was not allowed to touch me without my permission. And he didn’t. I liked this about him and felt more comfortable around him.
Days turned into weeks, and I still hadn’t broken up with Dylan. I liked that he had a strong relationship with his mother, worked two part-time jobs while at school, was eager to go to university and had great plans for his future. He also did a lot of pull-ups and had nice biceps.
On another date, we watched Toy Story 3 at the cinemas. Dylan pointed to the little girl character, Bonnie, and said, “That’s what our daughter would look like if we had one.” I was surprised that a teenage boy would think of this.
He said he wanted a long-term relationship, someone he could be with for ever, and said he would like that with me. I wasn’t too sure about that yet. I had a lot of plans of my own. I wanted to go to university and go into scriptwriting or become a novelist – both difficult career paths. Dylan wanted to be an engineer. His future was very assured, while mine felt unknown. I decided to end the relationship before we grew too attached.
Then one day at school, during lunchtime, I sat in a group with my friends and said I felt like some hot chips from KFC. Dylan overheard, and snuck out of the school grounds and walked all the way to the shops. I remember him jumping back over the school fence in his school uniform, clutching a brown paper KFC bag. I had no idea he was going to do it and was very surprised when he brought it to me – grinning, red-faced, hair a mess. He was put in detention. Dylan lost an afternoon, but he won my heart. And the chips were delicious.
From then on, this teenage boy would do anything for me. He drove me anywhere I wanted to go, stopped going to parties, never drank alcohol again and went to therapy to deal with his reckless spirit. I never asked him to do these things, but he said he did them for me. Although he did continue to ditch school and bring me KFC – which was traitorous, since he was doing weekend shifts at Red Rooster.
At 18, when we were at uni, Dylan and I moved in together. In our early 20s, we married. In 2020, our little girl was born – we named her Bonnie.
Dylan is so supportive of me. When I told him that I was going to work on becoming an author, the next day he renovated our spare room to become my office and surprised me with my dream computer. His way of saying “I love you” is by asking, “This weekend, should we buy some more books?” and “Do you want me to read what you’ve written today?”
And of course, on date nights, Dylan and I always go out for KFC.
- 
  Maleah Pearce writes under the pen name Penny Sunday. Kill To Love by Penny Sunday is available now through Hachette Australia (AU$24.99)

Xi, Modi conduct in-depth exchange of views, agree China, India should be partners
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
03:51:16 CST
04:51:16 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Ye)
NEW DELHI, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi conducted here on Saturday a candid and in-depth exchange of views, and reached important consensus that China and India should be partners.
The two leaders met on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi.
Xi said China has always viewed and developed its relations with India from a strategic height and with a long-term perspective.
Xi noted that he has met with Modi twice over the past two years, guiding bilateral relations from a new start to a further improvement.
Institutional exchanges between the two countries have gradually resumed, the list of areas of cooperation has continued to grow, and bilateral trade has reached a new record high, Xi added.
Xi said such hard-won progress should be cherished. Noting that China and India have different national conditions, Xi said they can draw on each other's strengths, support one another, help each other succeed and pursue common development.
Amid a turbulent international landscape, China and India, as the world's two most populous countries and important members of the Global South, shoulder important responsibilities, Xi said.
Xi called on the two sides to keep in mind the future of humanity and the well-being of peoples, work together to promote high-quality development of greater BRICS cooperation, and contribute more positive energy to world peace, stability, development and prosperity.
Underscoring objective and rational strategic perception in calibrating China-India relations, Xi said China and India are partners for cooperation, not rivals. The two countries provide development opportunities for each other rather than pose threats to each other, he added.
That is a strategic judgment based on the development stages of the two countries and the international environment, and serves the common interests of both countries and their peoples, Xi said.
Xi called on both sides to help each other succeed through win-win cooperation.
The two sides, Xi said, should focus on development as their greatest common denominator, while strengthening friendly exchanges and mutually beneficial cooperation.
He called on the two sides to expand cooperation in people-to-people exchanges, direct flights and other areas to effectively strengthen the public support for bilateral relations.
The two sides should also balance and address each other's economic and trade concerns, and promote a sound and stable development of bilateral economic and trade ties, Xi added.
Xi called on China and India to draw on political wisdom of mutual respect and understanding to overcome disruptions, urging both sides to pursue parallel progress in bilateral ties and border issues with the two tracks reinforcing each other, so as to maintain peace and tranquility in border areas.
He also urged China and India to promote multilateral cooperation with openness and inclusiveness to benefit the world.
Xi said the two countries should support each other as rotating chair of the BRICS, strengthen coordination within such multilateral frameworks as the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Group of 20, stand together in addressing global challenges, and unequivocally uphold international fairness and justice.
Modi said he has held several productive meetings with Xi, guiding India-China relations toward a positive direction, which serves the common interests of the more than 2.8 billion people of both countries.
The two major civilizations of India and China have, over thousands of years, learned from each other through exchanges and moved forward hand in hand, he said.
India always views India-China relations from a strategic height and a long-term perspective, and is willing to be a partner rather than a rival to China, and to regard each other's development as an opportunity rather than a challenge, he noted.
India adheres to an independent foreign policy, and the development of its relations with China is not subject to the influence of any third party, he said.
India's policy and position on the issues related to Taiwan and Xizang remain unchanged, and it does not allow any force to engage in anti-China activities in India, he said.
India is ready to maintain high-level exchanges with China on the basis of mutual respect and mutual trust, strengthen strategic communication, promote mutually beneficial cooperation, and enhance people-to-people exchanges, so as to advance bilateral relations to greater heights, Modi said.
The two sides should work together to safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas, he added.
India thanked China for its support for India's hosting of the BRICS summit and will fully support China in assuming the BRICS chairmanship next year, he said.
Modi said India is ready to closely coordinate and cooperate with China to jointly strengthen cooperation among Global South countries, promote a more multipolar world and global economic growth, and serve as a force for stability and progress in a turbulent world. ■

US court blocks Trump administration plan to cut disaster agency workforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:49:29 KST

US court blocks Trump administration plan to cut disaster agency workforce
US President Donald Trump has said he would like to abolish the agency.
A United States federal judge has ruled the Trump administration acted unlawfully by ordering job cuts at the federal agency in charge of responding to the country’s natural disasters.
On Friday, US District Judge Susan Illston in California said the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), exceeded its authority when it ordered personnel changes that effectively stripped the emergency agency of control over its own workforce.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Acting FEMA head David Richardson steps down after troubled tenure
- list 2 of 3Why did Trump fire Kristi Noem as DHS secretary; who is Markwayne Mullin?
- list 3 of 3US court rules Trump violated order by placing conditions on FEMA grants
The ruling centres on thousands of temporary FEMA reservists who are called upon to help communities after hurricanes, wildfires, floods and other disasters.
Labor groups representing federal workers sued to block the administration’s decision to stop renewing many of those contracts.
After Hurricane Katrina battered parts of the US Gulf Coast in 2005, the US Congress strengthened FEMA’s independence. US federal law says DHS cannot substantially or significantly reduce the agency’s authority, responsibilities or functions.
Illston, who was appointed by former US President Bill Clinton, said the Trump administration had failed to provide what she described as a “reasoned” explanation for its decision to restrict FEMA’s ability to renew contracts. She also noted FEMA was projecting a workforce of 11,383 employees for the coming fiscal year — about half of its previous level — without a clear justification for the figure.
The dispute comes amid a broader effort by US President Donald Trump’s administration to reduce the size of the federal workforce. Trump has previously questioned the need for FEMA and suggested that states, not the federal government, should assume greater responsibility for disaster preparedness.
The ruling did not immediately order the administration to reverse the cuts or impose penalties. Illston said those issues would be considered in a separate decision expected next month.
