Jimek: Polish hip-hop is one of the best in Europe, and I won't even apologize for saying that
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
15:03:37 UTC
00:03:37 KST

Two loves define Radzimir Dębski, aka Jimek - classical music and hip-hop. The Polish composer, conductor and producer has won praise from Beyoncé, Snoop Dogg and Nicki Minaj alike. Now he's talked to Euronews about his new album, featuring twelve Polish rappers and... a symphony orchestra.
Radzimir Dębski's creative life is crawling with the number twelve. On June 12, 2026, his album "Études for Piano, Sampler, Orchestra and Friends" came out, on which he invited twelve rappers, and on September 12 of that same year he'll be sharing the stage with them at a concert in Warsaw's Bemowo district.
And that's not all. It was back in 2012 that he won the remix contest for Beyoncé's single "End of Time," beating out more than three thousand creators from 25 countries. He happened to be in Berlin when Beyoncé herself called to tell him, "I wanna congratulate you because you are the winner." It was Queen B. herself who opened the door to a string of foreign gigs that have kept multiplying ever since. He's collaborated with, among others, Snoop Dogg at the BET Awards 2025 in Los Angeles and, in December of that same year, at "Snoop's Holiday Halftime Party" in Minneapolis.
The album "2015," which he made with Miłosz "MIUOSH" Borycki (a recording of a concert held at the headquarters of the National Symphony Orchestra of Polish Radio in Katowice), caught the attention of the legendary Deutsche Grammophon. Video clips from the concert were shared with admiration by stars including Ashton Kutcher, Mobb Deep, and Nicki Minaj. His artistic activity isn't confined to Poland and the United States, though. He's performed in Japan, Germany, and Kenya, among other places.
Jimek Chooses Poland Again
Despite these global opportunities — bolstered by the universalism of classical, symphonic music — Jimek is once again choosing Poland, and it's in Poland that he's preparing his next big musical project, one that completes his hip-hop-classical trilogy. In an interview with Euronews, he explains why:
"First of all, being at home, meaning going back to where you're from, is something that's become a need for me, and at the same time a way of searching for my own balance. If my own identity gets warped, that's something dangerous for me. But at the same time it's also an enormous pleasure and relief. Being yourself in Warsaw in the summer... There aren't many places in the world I like more. And I don't just mean Warsaw, but Poland in general," he says, adding that these are "down-to-earth" reasons.
There are also artistic reasons behind it. The album "Études (...)" (org. "Etiudy na pianino, orkiestrę, sampler i kolegów") is the result of a journey that, after many twists and turns, is coming full circle.
"First there was the story of American hip-hop, and because of how it spread, I understood right away that I'd have to do the story of Polish hip-hop too. At the same time, I dreamed from the start that all the artists I might want to include would be together on stage. Logistically, that was almost impossible."
Three Acts of One Story
The first concert at Bemowo (2022) was a test of whether it was even possible to get that many rappers in one place. The second — with the National Symphony Orchestra of Polish Radio at Silesian Stadium in 2023 — was a bigger risk, but it worked out. The third chapter is a concert with people he met while working on those earlier projects, with whom Jimek created songs from scratch.
"This concert will be different in that, having had all these opportunities, we also recorded a new album — new tracks came out of it, which might give this whole story its best possible punchline," Jimek explains to Euronews.
Just as in the previous two editions, both classic tracks and new material are featured.
An Album with Friends After 20 Years in the Basement
Classical music is clearly the glue holding the entire album "Études for Piano, Sampler, Orchestra and Friends" together, with the titular piano as the lead instrument — though it's clear that Jimek, as the host, approaches each of the twelve artists individually, trying to uncover what they need. In the case of Bedoes 2115's Étude No. 3, for instance, a guitar makes an appearance.
"When you've spent 20 years sitting alone in a basement with a computer, at some point you also want to meet another human being and see what different creative decisions get made in someone else's company," Jimek tells Euronews. "So I went looking for exactly that — a situation with another person that changes our decision-making process right from the start, just to see where it would take these tracks."
Polish Hip-Hop and the Power of Language
Jimek makes no secret of having two musical loves — classical and hip-hop. Especially the Polish kind, which, in his view, is among the best in Europe.
"This is completely biased, and I won't even apologize for it. Polish hip-hop is one of the best in Europe. It's very strong musically. That also comes from the samples — from the fact that it grew out of old Polish records, Polish jazz, Polish film scores, Polish popular and entertainment music, sometimes even electronic music," he lists.
"Maybe it's a coincidence, maybe it's the fact that our parents listened to good music. Under communism, jazz was the language of freedom. This Polish hip-hop never tried to be American, never tried to be different. It was Polish from the start, in that same genuine, honest way that a truly genuine and honest person doesn't even realize they're genuine and honest. And that's something you come to appreciate in hindsight — that introversion, the problems that came up in it, those lyrics," he adds, speaking with Euronews.
"I often translate Polish lyrics — from Polish tracks — for friends from abroad. And they're deeply surprised by how good it sounds, how much content is in there, philosophically too, all sorts of heavier things show up in it, and that it's something different. That's also the power of a language that has seven cases."
Études Against AI
The titular piano études are no accident.
"The piano was something I really missed while I was traveling so much. I managed to get hold of a piano for a longer stretch of time. And it was like going back to practice playing — while at the same time bringing back memories of walking to school, listening to hip-hop. Those two things didn't fit together at all, so in fact almost every track grew out of a little miniature like that, which I'll definitely write down — I think we might even put out a little notebook of these études. In case someone wants to practice something on the piano that's a bit different emotionally — hip-hop for piano."
The record is unpolished, unrefined. You can hear a lot of back-and-forth between the artists — comments, discussions, whistling, interaction.
"These times really are very polished right now. Absolutely. This is a protest against that. So in that sense it's some kind of reaction, a rebellion. Maybe a few years ago I wouldn't have gone this far with it."
Jimek explains that this "rawness" is also a nod to traditional hip-hop skits.
"Skits used to be those little interludes between tracks that, back before streaming and view-counting existed, made up the whole atmosphere of an album. You'd listen to the whole LP, and all those interludes were often conversations in a shop, conversations in a car, conversations in the studio — the whole backstage. For me, artistically, that backstage of the piano, of the process in the studio, is exactly that skit — and often it happens right within a track itself."
Manhood, Being a Guy, Sensitivity
There are no female rappers on the album. All twelve invited artists are men. Jimek explains to Euronews:
"It just happened on its own. At some point I noticed it and decided not to change it — quite the opposite, to turn it into an asset. Rap that's changing is also something we talk about a lot. It comes up in the lyrics. It used to be, maybe, kind of a men's sport, but today masculinity, being a guy, is a subject worth exploring. What does it even mean? We have different approaches to it. That sensitivity... how do you show it? That's a dilemma for a guy. Maybe in my generation there's this internal dialogue going on: what kind of man should I be, who should I become, what does the world need? Not long ago there was a mood in which traditional manhood was seen as passé. Now we're at a moment where maybe we're seeing again that it's needed."
The interview was conducted at the Hotel Polonia Palace in Warsaw.

Ukraine: Several killed in series of Russian strikes

Ukraine: Several killed in series of Russian strikes
September 12, 2026
Russia continued on Saturday its constant strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, killing at least four people and wounding dozens more.
According to Ukrainian officials, two people were killed in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, while steelmaker ArcelorMittal reported that two more people were killed at its plant in Kryvyi Rih, a city in the center of the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said that a Russian strike on an apartment building in Odesa wounded 37 people and that rescue teams are searching for two missing individuals.
He added that ten regions came under Russian attack last night and that Russian attack drones are still flying over many of them.
Ukraine retaliates by hitting chemical plants
In response to Russian attacks, Kyiv is fighting back. According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine has attacked "chemical enterprises" in the Perm region of the Urals and in the Samara region, which is located southwestern Russia.
The General Staff in Kyiv also reported a fire at a rubber factory in Togliatti, located in the Samara region. According to their statement, the company specializes in producing synthetic rubber important for tactical and ballistic missiles.
Togliatti Mayor, Ilya Sukhih, said that one person was hospitalized following a massive attack on the city. He added that several multi-story residential buildings were damaged.
Kremlin rebuffs Zelenskyy's meeting proposal
In an exclusive interview with DW, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he is willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit in Miami in December.
However, on Saturday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Moscow has yet to decide whether Putin will travel to the summit. "We don't know yet whether we'll be going to Miami," Peskov said, according to Russian media.
Commenting on Zelenskiy's proposal, Peskov reiterated Moscow's longstanding position that if the Ukrainian leader wants to meet with the Russian leader, he should come to Moscow.

Couple killed, two injured in mine blast on coast in Kobleve
According to Ukrinform, Heorhii Reshetilov, acting head of the Mykolaiv Regional Military Administration, reported this on Telegram.

Russian Attacks Kill 6, Injure Dozens in Ukraine as Moscow Says It Hit Ships, Plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Russian airstrikes in several Ukrainian regions on Saturday killed nine people, injured dozens and damaged residential buildings and infrastructure across the country, local officials said.
The civilian death toll has risen sharply in Ukraine over the past two months as Russia steps up attacks on power plants and other infrastructure. Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia, and both sides have targeted each other's shipping.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, writing on Telegram, said Russia had deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since early morning.
“Basically, the Russians have expanded the war away from the front, where they have no success, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war,” Zelensky wrote.
“Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance,” Zelensky added.
The city council in Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine's frontline “fortress cities” that Russia wants to capture, said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period. Four people were injured.
“These are not military targets,” the council said. “They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business.”
The governor of Ukraine's Zhytomyr Region west of Kyiv, Vitaliy Bunechko, said a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zvyahel. Bunechko said two gas stations also came under attack, as well as an unidentified “enterprise with foreign investment.”
Earlier, Zelensky reported attacks on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, his hometown.
The governor of Zaporizhzhia Region, Ivan Fedorov, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi Rih's military administration, said two people were killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles.
The Russian military said its forces hit Ukrainian steel maker Zaporizhstal in the city of Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro and several plants in Kryvyi Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex.
Reuters could not independently verify accounts from either side.
In the Black Sea port of Odesa, Regional Governor Oleh Kiper said nearly 40 people had been injured in attacks that extended from overnight well into Saturday evening.
The Russia-installed head of areas of eastern Donetsk Region under Moscow's control said three people had been killed in Ukrainian drone attacks.
In Moldova, on Ukraine's western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed.
Russian drones have regularly entered Moldovan airspace despite official protests. During one instance this week, the departure of Zelensky's aircraft to Norway was delayed.
Russian strikes on Ukrainian port
The Russian Defense Ministry said Russia's forces have maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, hitting a cargo ship in Odesa it said was carrying goods for military use.
Earlier in the day, the ministry said its forces struck two cargo vessels overnight in the port of Chornomorsk.
Ukraine's military said it hit one of Russia's largest synthetic rubber producers in Tolyatti in the Samara region, causing a fire. The Tolyattikauchuk plant specialized in the production of synthetic rubbers and fuel additives that are used in fuel for Russian missiles, it said.
Russian regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said industrial facilities in Samara region had been attacked by Ukrainian drones, without specifying which they were or whether they had been damaged, Interfax news agency reported.
Ilya Sukhikh, mayor of the city of Tolyatti in Samara region, said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured.

President Xi Jinping said India and China should "keep the future of humanity in mind" and work together to advance cooperation within the greater Brics framework.

Israel’s Tamar Steinberg wins windsurfing world title
The reigning European champion leads an Israeli one-two finish in England, with Sharon Kantor taking silver and Daniela Peleg placing fourth
Israeli windsurfer Tamar Steinberg won her first world title at the iQFOiL championships in Weymouth, England, with compatriot Sharon Kantor taking silver.
Steinberg, 20, won Saturday’s final after dominating the qualifying stage, winning seven of 16 races. Fellow Israeli Daniela Peleg finished fourth.
The victory adds to Steinberg’s European title earlier this year and follows her silver medal at last year’s world championships.
"I’ve been waiting for this title for a long time and am overjoyed that it’s finally happened. I came into this competition with a clear goal to win and gave it my all from the very first moment, but with the medal race format, anything can happen—so it’s amazing that everything worked out for the best," Steinberg said.
"It’s been an incredible week for the entire team; this time, the final race really felt like the Israeli National Championship, given that almost the whole squad was here. There are so many people supporting me and pouring their hearts and souls into making this happen, and it’s really important for me to say a huge thank you to everyone."
Israel also won two windsurfing medals at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where Kantor took silver in the women’s event and Tom Reuveny claimed gold in the men’s competition.

Analysis: The Saudis need a new strategy, fast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:56:16 UTC
23:56:16 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- The Saudis need a new strategy, fast
The Saudis need a new strategy, fast
With its key oil pipeline shut, the Houthis gaining ground in Yemen and Turkey and Pakistan standing idle, Riyadh’s diplomacy and defense pact offer little protection
It’s been just over a month since Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed “the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.” The agreement includes a collective security clause modeled on NATO's Article 5, stating that an armed attack on any one member is considered an attack on all three.
Since then, Saudi oil and energy sites have been hit in at least four major, distinct cross-border attacks, with the most recent attack on its key East-West pipeline in both Riyadh and Medina, forcing it to shut down. Turkey and Pakistan did not lift a finger. Add to that the Houthis driving out Saudi-backed forces from the Yemeni coast, and the militia’s takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, it’s been a rough month for the Saudis. More like a rough six months.
From the moment Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the war, essentially blocking the export of oil through the waterway, Saudi Arabia, like all other Gulf Arab countries, was left scrambling. Despite reaching a raproachment with Iran in 2023, the Islamic Republic attacked Saudi energy sites and infrastructure hundreds of times. There were singular reports of Saudi forces striking in Iran and Iraq during the war, but these strikes were insignificant to the course of the war.
Riyadh did have some alternatives. It was already exporting a smaller quantity of oil out of the kingdom’s west coast, mainly through Yanbu. It decided to increase capacity at its key East-West pipeline, which allowed it to bypass the Iranian blockade in Hormuz. It worked to a limited degree, until Iranian-backed militias in Iraq attacked it, taking it offline.
At the same time, Riyadh has continued to maintain open dialogue with Tehran, even as it was attacking the kingdom. There is even going to be a summit in Oman on Monday bringing together Iran, the six GCC countries, and Iraq. Tehran is coming to this meeting to make announcements, not consessions.
Additionally, while the quarrel between Saudi Arabia and the UAE requires a much deeper dive, looking for a second at its manifestation in Yemen, there are critics who link the departute of Emirati-backed forces from the scene, thus weakening the opposition, to the Houthis feeling emboldened, opening the door for a potential manuveure, which happened. In recent months, Iran has sent hundreds of IRGC advisors to Yemen to assist the Houthis in planning their attack, while still talking to the Saudis.
What is Riyadh saying? One newspaper in the kingdom explained that Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pulled out of the coastal area “as an elaborate trap to lure the Houthis out of their hideouts,” and that government forces will turn the territory into a graveyard for the Iranian-backed militia with their “kill zone” around the port city of Mocha. There aren’t too many buyers to this explanation. There are many more people scratching their heads, wondering “what the hell are the Saudis doing?” I’m one of them.
The Saudi strategy is incoherent. Its economy is shrinking. Iran has eclosed the Arabean Peninsula in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. And while the kingdom has some of the world’s most advanced U.S.-made fighting systems, it is unable to translate that into acheivements on the battlefield.
So, to recap: in the last six months, Iran takes control of the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis take control of Bab el-Mandeb, Aramco sites are attacked by IRGC, Iraqi militias and Houthis, the key East-West pipeline shuts down after attacks by Iraqi militias, and the Mecca Alliance is proven worthless.
Riyadh needs a new strategy, fast.

Australian Companies to Develop Interceptor Drone for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:54:50 UTC
23:54:50 KST

Two companies from South Australia have joined forces to develop and manufacture Arrow interceptor drones for delivery to Ukraine.
This was announced by Chris Picton, Minister for Defence and Space Industry for the State of South Australia.
The agreement calls for the integration of munitions manufactured by Zero Dawn into Praetorian Aeronautics’ Arrow counter-drone system. The system is designed to detect and intercept drones and other unmanned aerial systems in the face of enemy countermeasures.
Under the memorandum, the companies will collaborate on detailed integration, testing, certification, production preparation, and identifying market entry opportunities.
The signing of the memorandum was preceded by tests during which the companies successfully conducted a ground test of the warhead integrated into the interceptor.
The test was observed by Vasyl Myroshnychenko, Ukraine’s ambassador to Australia. Praetorian and Zero Dawn plan to export this system in 2027 to meet Ukraine’s urgent operational needs.
Praetorian Aeronautics is an Australian defense company founded in 2024 that specializes in autonomous aviation systems and software for countering drones.
Praetorian’s current product line consists of the Dagger autonomous interceptor drone, the Venator multi-purpose UAV, and the Hadrian command-and-control system, which uses artificial intelligence to assign targets to interceptors. Currently, there is no publicly available information about the Arrow interceptor or its specifications, so it is likely a new development.
Zero Dawn is an Adelaide-based Australian defense company specializing in the development of modular warheads. It claims to have in-house capabilities in research, design, prototyping, manufacturing, work with explosive materials, and ammunition testing.
The company also develops warheads in collaboration with a specialized partner and claims it can take a project from concept to a tested prototype in 30 days.
As a reminder, since mid-2026, the Australian Defence Force has joined the Norwegian-led multinational Operation Legio to train Ukrainian military personnel in Poland.
Since January 2023, Australian military personnel have been working alongside the multinational training mission Operation Interflex, led by the United Kingdom, as part of Operation Kudu. During this time, they have trained more than 3,650 Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel in basic infantry tactics, leadership, and military skills.

Will Lagarde bite the apple? ECB President leaves everyone guessing in Normandy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:50:36 UTC
23:50:36 KST

European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde addresses a press conference after a meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) in Berlin on September 10, 2026. | John Macdougall/ AFP via Getty Images
ÉPREVILLE–EN-LIEUVIN, France – As European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde shook hands and tasted oysters on the bucolic grounds of a Norman manor on Saturday, some might have seen a presidential candidate in waiting.
But, Lagarde swears, there is nothing to see here.
Speaking as a special guest at the Fête de la Pomme, an apple-themed political gathering organized by Normandy's regional president Hervé Morin, Lagarde dodged questions over her involvement in the French presidential race and her early departure from the ECB — despite mounting speculation on both matters.
Advertisement
On stage, she even encouraged reporters who made the trip to Normandy to cover her potential political comeback to pack up early, promising that they would be disappointed.
But there are signs suggesting that the ECB chief, who entered into politics during the presidency of France's apple-loving Jacques Chirac, is increasingly willing to weigh in on the campaign.
While she promised to stay at least until the end of the year, Lagarde previously refused to rule out leaving before the end of her term, which ends in October 2027.
Earlier this week, she announced that she would publish her first autobiography, Lady First, in January. She also waded into the French presidential debate by rejecting French far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s proposal to wipe out government debt.
Her presence at the apple festival in the 15th-century Manoir de la Fortière — an unconventional locale for a central banker's speech — might be yet another signal. Opening the event, Morin said that he tried to invite her for years but never managed to make it work. Until this year.
Christine Lagarde at the Fête de la Pomme, France, on September 12, 202. | Giorgio Leali/POLITICO
“Everyone is happy to have you here and I realized to what extent you have an exceptional reputation,” said Morin, who worked with Lagarde when they both served as ministers under conservative president Nicolas Sarkozy, including during the 2008 financial crisis.
Advertisement
While Lagarde declined to say whether she would become involved in the campaign, participants to Morin’s annual political rally didn’t rule that out.
“Several people mention Lagarde as a presidential candidate, but she is the only one who can answer that question,” said centrist senator Catherine Morin-Desailly.
“She is a Norman, French and European figure who must, of course, play an active role in helping to shape and develop future platforms for the presidential election. Good candidates will call on her expertise, and I hope they do.”
With centrist candidates Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe competing against each other and Bruno Retailleau, the leader of the conservative Les Républicains, also taking part in the race, the center-right side of the presidential spectrum is already crowded.
For Kristina Pluchet, a senator from Les Républicains who backs Retailleau, other candidates including Christine Lagarde could very well join the race, but they should compete in a primary election.
With French bond yields rising and the government led by Sébastien Lecornu struggling to cut the deficit, Lagarde’s financial résumé could prove to be an asset — although she complained to a local producer that the oysters she had during her time as the International Monetary Fund boss in Washington were washed with chlorine.
Advertisement
The ECB President didn’t give any hint on her political future in her speech. Instead, she used repeated references to calvados, Normandy's internationally famous apple brandy, to make the case for the benefits of EU membership.
She said that calvados, which could be found on the stands of the fête, can be better exported across the world thanks to the EU’s trade policy and is protected by the bloc’s geographical indications. And, unlike calvados which can flow freely between member states without tariffs, capital and services still face internal barriers imposed by member countries, she added.
“It is no surprise, then, that many of the people who want to build something new leave Europe altogether,” Lagarde said, calling for the emergence of a real capital markets union to rival the U.S..
As she walked back to a German-plated grey Mercedes S-Class, wearing a scarf with Normandy's two-leopards flag, Lagarde stopped for selfies, but kept sidestepping questions about her future.

U.S. consumer sentiment takes a hit in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
22:46:10 CST
23:46:10 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- U.S. consumer sentiment took a hit in September, according to preliminary data released Friday from the University of Michigan. Experts have warned of the weak economy ahead of the midterm elections.
Consumer sentiment receded less than 4 index points for the second consecutive month of decreases, according to the widely watched survey of consumers.
Democrats and Republicans alike posted sizable declines, while Independents were little changed from August. Year-ahead expectations for both personal finances and business conditions plunged, the report found.
With a resurgence in fuel prices and trade tensions, consumers anticipate greater pressures on their pocketbooks to come, according to the report.
Some experts said the report showed a significant decline in sentiment.
Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua: "This is a big hit to sentiment. Clearly people see a worse situation going forward. This is most likely due to people seeing little prospect of the Iran War ending soon. Sentiment is likely to remain weak until the war ends. It will get much worse if the AI (artificial intelligence) bubble crashes."
Overall, sentiment is now 16 percent below February, prior to the start of the Iran conflict, and 13 percent lower than a year ago.
Year-ahead inflation expectations jumped from 4.0 percent last month to 4.6 percent this month, the highest reading since June. The current reading substantially exceeds the 3.4 percent seen in February before the Iran conflict began. Long-run inflation expectations ticked up to 3.4 percent, ending three consecutive months at 3.3 percent.
This occurs just before the midterm elections, in which Republicans are expected to lose seats due to ongoing inflation in food, groceries, rent and home prices.
Some experts said the weak economy is the most crucial issue for many voters.
Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Darrell West told Xinhua: "The weak economy is the most important issue for many voters, and unless it improves, will drag down Republicans in November. The election is a referendum on (U.S. President Donald) Trump and it does not look like he will fare very well."
Other experts noted that the underlying inflation is also being fed by pressure on oil prices due to the Iran conflict.
Clay Ramsay, a researcher at the Center for International and Security Studies at the University of Maryland, told Xinhua: "Trump's midterm convention is an effort to rouse people who are less likely to vote and get them to the polls. However, inflation is what these occasional voters are most aware of."
"The underlying inflation left over from the post-Covid period is being fed by the Iran war's pressure on oil prices, plus the many tariffs. We are not in a business-friendly or a consumer-friendly environment right now. So urging people to vote who are focused on handling the day-to-day in their lives or small businesses may well backfire on Republicans," Ramsay said. ■

China Focus: Chinese solutions power global mining green transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
22:45:51 CST
23:45:51 KST

TIANJIN, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Autonomous mining trucks haul ore back and forth, intelligent systems crunch data in real time, and mineral processing equipment hums along efficiently.
At the 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition in north China's Tianjin Municipality, held from Thursday through Saturday, green technologies, intelligent equipment and smart mining solutions took center stage.
The products on display showed how Chinese solutions are increasingly woven into the global mining industry's green transition.
At the Xinhai Mining booth, a sand-table model shows a green mine in operation. On the central control screen, data such as ore hoisting volume, equipment load, tailings pond levels and personnel locations update in real time.
"Staff can monitor and control the mineral processing plant remotely from a computer screen," said Zhang Yunlong, chairman of Shandong Xinhai Mining Group Co., Ltd.
The company's whole-process smart mining solution has served more than 100 countries and regions. Zhang cited a gold mine project in Zimbabwe with a daily processing capacity of 500 tonnes, where an on-site clean energy supply system covering 100,000 square meters has been built, cutting costs by about 75 percent compared with diesel power generation.
A large magnetic separator on display also drew a crowd. With processing capacity and beneficiation requirements unchanged, the new technology shrinks equipment volume by about 50 percent and cuts operating energy consumption by about 30 percent, while boosting beneficiation indicators by about 20 percent.
Beneficiation in mining refers to the series of processes that transform raw ore into a concentrated product of higher economic value.
Li Chaopeng, deputy general manager of LONGi Magnet Co., Ltd., said the equipment has been deployed in more than 70 countries and regions, most recently at an iron ore project in Brazil.
"Our equipment uses less energy, recovers more resources from tailings and reduces iron ore waste, better meeting the mining industry's demand for automated and intelligent development," Li said.
These Chinese green practices caught the eye of Andrew Thake, an Australian mining industry practitioner and divisional director at Beacon Events & Exhibitions.
"When I speak to many of our Chinese clients, they take sustainability very seriously. They have very strong sustainability standards," Thake said, adding that China's green mining practices, built up over more than a decade, offer useful pointers for green development under different resource endowments and development conditions.
China has established complete institutional, standard and evaluation systems for green mining development, while vigorously promoting technologies, such as backfill mining, comprehensive utilization of solid waste and clean energy substitution in mining areas.
Chinese mining enterprises are also actively participating in overseas cooperation projects to advance green mining worldwide.
Zijin Mining, for instance, has built green mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo drawing on China's ecological civilization practices, while its green mine in Serbia has helped improve environmental governance in the mining area.
"I appreciate the efforts China has made in green development and environmental restoration," said Patricia, a Zimbabwean geospatial analyst. "I have followed some of the environmental restoration projects that have been carried out in China and I think they have been done quite well."
Dmitry Tetenkin, deputy minister of natural resources and environment of the Russian Federation, said green and intelligent industrial development is an urgent guideline for the mining industry.
"Digital technologies, innovations, rational use of resources and reduction of environmental burden are no longer issues of the distant future, but necessary conditions for the modern mining industry," he added. "Technological progress must work simultaneously for production efficiency and responsible attitude to the environment."
China's green development philosophy in mining is reaching further. Under the International Big Scientific Plan on Resources and Environmental Effects of Global Karst Dynamic Systems, China has carried out resource and environmental surveys, carbon cycle research and ecological protection studies in karst areas with multiple countries, gradually building a global karst monitoring network and exploring ways to balance resource development with ecological protection.
At the Ngorongoro Lengai geopark in Tanzania, a Chinese technical assistance project has helped upgrade the geopark's infrastructure and boosted the integrated development of geological research and tourism.
Orkotete Lesongoyo, from a village at the foot of Mount Lengai, became a local geological guide after training organized by the geopark, introducing the geological wonders of the Lengai volcano to visitors from around the world.
"This project has raised the international profile and influence of Tanzania's tourism resources and created new livelihoods for surrounding residents," said Ren Junping, director of the Southern Africa Geological Survey Cooperation Center, Tianjin Center, China Geological Survey.
From green mines to ecological protection and community development, Chinese solutions are offering richer practical examples for the global mining industry's green transformation, Ren added.
Green and low-carbon transition has become a key direction for the high-quality development of the global mining industry.
The Tianjin Declaration on Green Development of the Mining Industry, released at the conference, calls on more countries, international organizations and stakeholders to actively advance the global mining industry's transition towards green and low-carbon development and promote global sustainable development, to make positive contributions to building a better future of harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature.
Mohamed Noorain, CEO of Kossel Sudan mining enterprises, said China's technologies, standards and management experience in green mine construction are worth learning from. He looks forward to stronger exchanges and cooperation between China and more countries, including Sudan, in green mining to bring more green technologies and practices to the ground and achieve green development of the mining industry. ■

Chinese practices offer insights into sustainable fisheries development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
22:45:35 CST
23:45:35 KST

People attend a side event titled "Innovations in Aquaculture Production" during the 37th Session of the Committee on Fisheries of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), in Rome, Italy, Sept. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Jing)
ROME, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- China's experience in aquaculture innovation, fisheries governance and ecological conservation drew attention from experts attending the 37th Session of the Committee on Fisheries of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), which concluded in Rome on Friday.
The FAO Committee on Fisheries is a major intergovernmental forum for global fisheries and aquaculture. Participants said technological innovation, stronger governance and international cooperation are becoming increasingly important as demand for aquatic products grows amid mounting resource and environmental constraints.
Aquaculture was a major focus of the discussions. Zhang Wenbo, an associate professor at Shanghai Ocean University, said technologies including the Internet of Things, big data and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being applied to aquaculture production and regulation in China, helping make the sector greener and more efficient.
Eduardo M. Leano, director general of the Network of Aquaculture Centres in Asia-Pacific, said the Asia-Pacific region accounts for about 90 percent of global aquaculture production but faces growing constraints on land and water resources.
"What we need is not just further development, but a transformation of the aquaculture sector as a whole," he said.
Leano said China's experience in AI, smart aquaculture and deep-sea aquaculture can be useful to other countries, provided technologies are adapted to local conditions and supported by training and capacity building.
Digitalization was another major theme, particularly in efforts to combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing.
China became a Party to the FAO Agreement on Port State Measures in April 2025. The agreement is the first binding international accord specifically targeting illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing.
Matthew Camilleri, FAO Senior Fisheries Officer and PSMA Secretary, told Xinhua that digital tools are increasingly important in helping port states assess risks before vessels enter port and concentrate limited inspection resources on higher-risk targets.
"Digitalization is not an end in itself," Camilleri said, adding that its real value lies in providing reliable information, improving risk assessment and strengthening cooperation among countries.
China's ecological conservation experience was also highlighted through a themed display on the 10-year fishing ban in the Yangtze River. Since 2021, China has implemented the ban in key waters of the river basin as part of efforts to restore aquatic biodiversity and protect the river ecosystem.
Benjamin Bockarie of Sierra Leone, who studies fisheries and aquaculture management at University College Cork in Ireland, said China's experience in recirculating aquaculture systems and AI-based monitoring can be valuable for developing countries.
"Building the capacity of countries, helping them develop and localizing Chinese technologies so that they can adapt to local circumstances would solve many problems," he said. ■

Brics leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the Security Council to make it more democratic, representative, effective and efficient, with greater representation for developing countries.The declaration strongly condemned the April 2025 terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir and called for zero tolerance towards terrorism.
On trade, the bloc expressed serious concern over the growing use of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, saying they distort trade, threaten global supply chains and create uncertainty for international economic activity.Brics also reaffirmed support for reform of the World Trade Organisation and called for an open, equitable, transparent, fair, inclusive and rules-based multilateral trading system. It called for the immediate restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.In April 1955, representatives of 29 Asian and African governments gathered in Bandung, Indonesia, to discuss peace, economic development, decolonisation and the role of the developing world during the Cold War. The conference's core principles included political self-determination, respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs and equality.The Brics New Delhi Declaration was adopted at the 18th Brics Summit, being hosted by India. India's chairship is guided by the theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”

The boycott was meant to isolate Israeli settlements - it is doing the opposite - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:38:11 UTC
23:38:11 KST

For more than two decades, various organizations have sought to change Israeli policy through boycotts targeting products, companies, academic institutions, and Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria. Now, government sanctions are also being added to the equation, such as those announced by the United Kingdom.
One basic point must be made: no boycott can change history or undermine the connection between the Jewish people and the Land of Israel.
But after decades of boycotts, it is worth asking: Has the boycott achieved its goal?
The answer is no.
The settlement movement has not stopped. The policies of successive Israeli governments have not changed as a result of boycotts. And over the past 25 years, hundreds of companies and businesses have been established in Judea and Samaria, alongside new industrial zones and factories.
Take Airbnb, for example.
In 2018, the company announced that it would remove approximately 200 properties in Judea and Samaria from its platform. Ironically, however, the decision exposed tens of millions of tourists around the world to a simple fact: there are Airbnb properties in the biblical heartland, and people can visit.
Less than six months later, Airbnb reversed its decision. The boycott generated headlines, but it did not change reality.
The story of Ben & Jerry’s is also well known. In 2021, the company announced that it would not renew the sale of its products in what it called the “Occupied Palestinian Territory,” while emphasizing that it was not leaving Israel.
Following a prolonged campaign in which I was personally involved, the parent company, Unilever, sold its Israeli business to its Israeli licensee. As a result, Ben & Jerry’s products continued to be sold in Israel, including in Judea and Samaria.
Israeli policy unchanged by boycotts
Once again, the boycott created a media storm, but it did not change Israeli policy.
And that is the point: a boycott can cause harm and generate noise. But there is a significant distance between causing damage and changing policy. Boycotts fuel antisemitism. But they do not change Israel.
But here is where things get interesting: the boycott does have an impact. For better, too.
In the United States, it has generated a backlash. Thirty-seven states have already adopted laws or other measures against BDS, including restrictions on public contracts or investments involving companies that participate in boycotts against Israel.
And last week, on September 3, the US House of Representatives passed the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act by a vote of 237-169. The bill seeks to restrict certain federal funding to academic institutions participating in boycotts against Israel. The legislation still requires Senate approval.
A paradox has emerged: the boycott intended to isolate Israel has created an opposite movement in the United States, a movement seeking to protect Israel from boycotts through legislation.
And this impact is reaching Judea and Samaria as well. For example, American businesspeople have approached American Friends of Judea and Samaria seeking investment opportunities in Judea and Samaria, both as a response to British boycott efforts and because they believe that investing in the biblical heartland can bring prosperity to their businesses in America.
The boycott did not stop the settlement movement.
It did not change Israeli policy.
But it has encouraged more Americans to organize, take action, and deepen their connections with Israel and Judea and Samaria.
Therefore, instead of defending against each boycott separately, we should turn this challenge into an opportunity: strengthen the relationship between America and Israel, protect freedom of commerce, and encourage Americans to visit, do business, and invest in Judea and Samaria.
That is how we can turn the boycott into something that has an impact, for better.
The writer is the former CEO of the Yesha Council and CEO of American Friends of Judea and Samaria.

According to official statements, he went a kilometer into the sea in a kayak with his uncle and didn't manage to return to the surface during one of the free-diving attempts.
Contact was lost on Thursday at 5:30 p.m., when his uncle spotted him for the last time. The police didn't disclose the reason why he didn't manage to resurface.

In August 2023, he transferred to mandatory service in the Border Police and, after completing basic training, moved to the counter-terrorism undercover unit.
He was later assigned to the unit as an Observation and Drone Team member, and in 2025, after finishing his mandatory service, he enlisted for permanent service in the unit.
He grew up in a well-known family in the city of Haifa, the son of Judge Rona Persson and dentist Dr. Alex Persson. He is survived by his parents, two brothers, and two sisters.

Britain’s sanctions on Israeli settlements reveal hypocrisy of its ‘occupation’ policy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:38:05 UTC
23:38:05 KST

So the gloves are off.
The British government has banned trade with Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria, prohibited settlement goods, and restricted related services.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband went further, accusing “settler terrorists” of carrying out “ethnic cleansing.”
Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis called it “a dark day for British Jews.” He is right.
The announcement came three days before Rosh Hashanah. During the High Holy Days, synagogues across Britain will be packed. Their congregants will gather behind security guards, locked doors, and barriers, conscious that simply attending Jewish worship can make them a target.
For me, this is personal. We are approaching the first anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack at Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation on Yom Kippur. Two worshipers were killed and others seriously injured, including a friend of my son. The synagogue is less than a mile from my former home.
As another Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur approach, I fear for family and friends who will be especially vulnerable. God forbid that there should be another attack.
The British government will insist that its policy targets settlements, not Jews. But ministers cannot ignore the atmosphere in which their words are heard.
British Jews now feel less secure
At a moment of acute anxiety, branding Israelis as perpetrators of “ethnic cleansing” and turning Israel into a pariah makes British Jews feel less, not more, secure.
The timing is deplorable for another reason. Israel is weeks away from an election. President Isaac Herzog has called the move gross interference in Israel’s democratic process.
Whatever London intended, sanctions imposed during an election campaign will inevitably influence it and may strengthen precisely the politicians Britain opposes.
Israel’s response was swift. It announced the closure of the British Consulate in east Jerusalem and barred 12 British politicians and activists from entering, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott, John McDonnell, Zarah Sultana, and every Green Party MP.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich had demanded the expulsion of the British ambassador. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir suggested that Israel recognize Argentine sovereignty over the Malvinas, known in Britain as the Falkland Islands, and sanction Britain until its own “occupation” ends.
This sounds like political theater, but it raises a fair question: When is an occupation not an occupation? Apparently, when Britain is doing the occupying.
London calls Judea and Samaria “occupied Palestinian territory.” Jewish communities beyond the 1949 armistice lines are treated as inherently illegal. Yet the Falklands, controlled by Britain since 1833 and claimed by Argentina ever since, are called a “British Overseas Territory.”
There are important differences. Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain British, while Palestinians do not want Israeli rule. But the United Nations still recognizes a sovereignty dispute over the islands and calls for negotiations.
Britain says history, security, and the wishes of the present population matter. That is a reasonable argument. It is simply one Britain rarely permits Israel to make.
The Chagos Islands are even more uncomfortable.
Britain separated them from Mauritius, forcibly removed their inhabitants, and retained Diego Garcia for a vital British-American military base. In 2019, the International Court of Justice said Britain’s administration was wrongful and should end rapidly.
Britain did not leave. It eventually agreed to recognize Mauritian sovereignty while leasing Diego Garcia back for 99 years.
Then US President Donald Trump reversed his support, called the deal an “act of GREAT STUPIDITY,” and Britain put it on indefinite hold.
London therefore understands that international rulings do not make security needs and strategic geography disappear. When British interests are involved, there can be delay, compromise, and special arrangements. Israel is offered condemnation and sanctions.
Judea and Samaria were not the sovereign territory of a Palestinian state when Israel captured them from Jordan in 1967. The pre-1967 boundary was an armistice line, not a permanent border.
The Jewish connection to Hebron, Shiloh, and Beit El is thousands of years old.
None of that erases Palestinian rights or ends the legal argument over settlements. E1 is sensitive, and its consequences deserve serious discussion.
But this history cannot honestly be reduced to the single word “occupation,” and sanctions cannot substitute for negotiation.
Only last year, Britain recognized a Palestinian state whose final borders, capital, government, and security arrangements had not been agreed with Israel. Now it is using economic punishment to advance its preferred territorial outcome.
There is also a widespread suspicion that this is partly about British politics. The Labour party is losing support on its Left to the Green Party. The Greens immediately welcomed the sanctions and demanded more.
The measure looks less like peacemaking than political positioning designed to stem that flow of votes. The result is a policy announced before the Jewish New Year, during an Israeli election campaign, and against the warnings of British Jewish leaders. It has provoked retaliation, damaged diplomatic relations, and increased the anxiety of a community already living behind guarded doors.
Closing the British Consulate is a serious escalation, and expelling the ambassador would sacrifice a useful diplomatic channel. Israel should instead keep him in Jerusalem and ask him a simple question: Why are Britain’s territorial disputes historical, strategic, and complicated, while Israel’s can be reduced to one condemnatory word?
Britain is entitled to defend its interests. It is not entitled to deny that Israel has history, interests, and security needs of its own.
An occupation, it seems, is only not an occupation when Britain is doing the occupying.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

BRICS summit: Iran, UAE, others urge restraint over Middle East escalation

The BRICS group of nations unanimously adopted a joint declaration on Saturday, expressing "deep concern" over the war in the Middle East and urged maximum restraint, advocating for a "multilateral approach" that respects national viewpoints.
The declaration, adopted on the first day of the BRICS leaders' annual summit in New Delhi, comes at a time when US and Iran have resumed tit-for-tat strikes against each other, after a pause in fighting for much of August.
The BRICS bloc includes both Iran and Washington-ally United Arab Emirates, which was expected to make clinching a joint statement consensus a particularly challenging task for host New Delhi.
A call for exercising 'maximum restraint'
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in the Middle East...call for exercising maximum restraint...avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," the 'New Delhi Declaration' said.
The declaration also reiterated the commitment of member nations to a peaceful resolution of international disputes "through dialog, consultation, and diplomacy."
In addition, they voiced concerns about the rise of "unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures" that distort trade, against the backdrop of US sanctions against Tehran amid its war with the country, and against Russia over its conflict with Ukraine.
BRICS includes Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

No signed Hormuz deal expected yet from Oman, Gulf States meeting on Monday, Iranian official says

23:37:22 KST

A meeting between Iran and Gulf states planned for Monday in Oman will be a chance to discuss issues including the Strait of Hormuz, but is not expected to yield a signed agreement over the blockaded waterway, a senior Iranian official said on Saturday.
Iran has been negotiating for months with Oman, which controls the opposite bank of the strait, over a deal that would govern transport through it. Oman has long said other Arab countries in the Gulf support its negotiations.
Tehran announced on Friday that it was planning to attend a meeting with Gulf countries in Oman on Monday. Oman has not officially announced the meeting, and other regional states have so far remained silent. Bahrain said on Saturday it would not attend meetings with Iran.
The Kingdom of Bahrain said it will not attend the meeting to discuss the Strait of Hormuz until diplomatic ties between the two countries are restored, according to state media.
Oman called for meeting over Strait of Hormuz
The Iranian official, who discussed the plans on condition of anonymity, said Monday's meeting was called at Oman's initiative, and would provide a forum to discuss other regional issues as well as Hormuz.
According to the Iranian official, Iran still wants an agreement that would allow it to collect fees from ships that use the strait, which Oman rejects.
Around a fifth of global oil supplies transited the strait before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, launching the war.
Global oil prices have surged over the past week after the United States and Iran both fired on tankers in the strait, and Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen advanced near another crucial Middle East conduit for oil, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
Iran sees possible meeting as a path to open the Strait
Speaking to the semi-official Tasnim news agency on Saturday, an unnamed Iranian official source said any understanding between Iran and Oman does not provide for the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz but establishes the basis on which it could reopen.
The source said the arrangement would be a step toward Iran exercising sovereignty over the strait and that its reopening depended entirely on the United States meeting Tehran's conditions.
On Sunday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the regime's delegation at the BRICS summit in India had a "productive conversation" with the crown prince of Abu Dhabi, saying that they reached an agreement to "put the past behind us and build a promising future."
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

‘Why the hell are they laughing?’ Mamdani, AOC clip at 9/11 memorial sparks uproar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12

A four-second clip from New York’s ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks has ignited a political storm after Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were filmed smiling and speaking while the names of victims were being read aloud.
The footage, taken from a broadcast of Friday’s ceremony at Ground Zero, shows Mamdani standing beside Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive Democratic congresswoman widely known as AOC, as the two briefly talk and smile. Moments earlier, the broadcast had shown a young man crying beside the memorial, and the abrupt transition between the images quickly drew criticism from conservative politicians and commentators.
The ceremony lasted roughly four hours, and their conversation could not be heard. Michael Ragusa, who previously served as security chief for former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani, said the suggestion that the pair had been laughing during the ceremony was misleading. He said he had been standing near them and that Ocasio-Cortez was simply greeting Mamdani.
“The camera just caught her greeting him hello,” Ragusa wrote on X. “Multiple other politicians were laughing and joking behind me. Republicans and Democrats.”
Footage from other portions of the ceremony showed Mamdani standing silently with a serious expression.
CNN reported that it had contacted representatives for Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez for comment. The brief interaction nevertheless prompted a fierce online debate, with Republicans accusing the two New York Democrats of behaving inappropriately during the solemn ceremony and others arguing that the viral clip stripped the moment of its context.
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz shared the footage, writing: “How the hell do you laugh while the names of those murdered on 9/11 are being read aloud?”
Former New York State Assemblymember Yuh-Line Niou, who also attended the ceremony, dismissed the criticism as “ridiculous talking points.”
Niou noted that many politicians do not remain for the entire ceremony, while Mamdani “stayed for every name and even stayed after to talk to families for 45 minutes.” Ocasio-Cortez also remained until the end, she said, adding that the brief interaction occurred when the congresswoman approached Mamdani to say hello.
Niou, who said she has attended the Ground Zero ceremony every year for a decade, also pushed back on the suggestion that attendees remain visibly grief-stricken throughout the hourslong event.
“My friends and neighbors are not crying for 6 hours straight,” she wrote. “We are greeting each other, hugging each other, laughing at the memories and the jokes the families tell remembering their loved ones.”
Conservative television personality Meghan McCain, daughter of the late Republican Sen. John McCain, was among those criticizing the footage, asking on social media why the two were laughing.
The controversy came during an already politically charged anniversary for Mamdani, New York City’s first Muslim mayor.
Before the ceremony began, Mamdani approached Giuliani, who led New York during the September 11 attacks, and the two shook hands. The encounter drew attention because Giuliani had only days earlier said Mamdani’s presence at the memorial offended him and compared the mayor to the September 11 hijackers.
Aides said Mamdani and Giuliani “exchanged pleasantries,” with Giuliani telling the current mayor that running New York was a difficult job. A Giuliani representative later said the former mayor told Mamdani he was praying for him.
Asked afterward what the two had discussed, Mamdani declined to elaborate.
“He came over and we both extended our hands and exchanged pleasantries,” Mamdani said, according to remarks released by his office. “I think the focus for all of us is a focus on the families, a focus on first responders and to be here and hear the names of all those who were stolen from us 25 years ago and how the families have persevered through that time.”
Later Friday, Mamdani spoke at an interfaith memorial service at St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church and National Shrine, which was destroyed in the September 11 attacks and later rebuilt.
“Those who attacked our city, they did so because they thought they could break us at the fractures,” Mamdani said. “They thought they could frighten us, they could make us feel alone, they could leave us on our knees.”
“How wrong they were. How quick we were to stand back up.”

In Germany, one of the suspects in the sabotage at Leipzig Airport was linked to the GRU of the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
German investigators suspect Russian and Belarusian citizens of attempting to blow up a Ukrainian aircraft with a drone. One of them may be linked to the GRU
German investigators have identified two main suspects in an attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport. One of them, a Russian citizen, is believed to have links to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Welt am Sonntag reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the suspects are Russian citizen Oleg L. and Belarusian citizen Andrei K. Investigators believe the Russian may have been responsible for organizing and providing logistical support for the operation, including supplying the perpetrator with explosives. One of the key pieces of evidence in the case was DNA traces found on components of equipment that was likely used to control drones. The matches were found in law enforcement databases in Finland and Lithuania.
Investigators currently know that Oleg L. entered Germany via Turkey, then traveled around the country before flying from Berlin to Serbia. According to German intelligence services, he is currently in Russia.
Investigators consider the second suspect, Andrei K., a possible direct perpetrator. According to media reports, he entered the Schengen Area via Latvia approximately one week before the attack. The man also remains at large. Investigators are also examining a possible connection between Andrei K. and a fire at a home improvement store in the Polish city of Łódź in the summer of 2024. Polish law enforcement previously treated that incident as possible sabotage with a Russian link.
What happened at Leipzig Airport
The incident occurred on August 4. According to investigators, a drone carrying explosives deliberately flew toward a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft and struck its wing. At the time, the aircraft was carrying approximately 25,000 liters of aviation fuel. According to a journalistic investigation, the drone may have been carrying around 1.8 kg of Semtex explosives. An explosion was avoided, likely because the detonator became detached upon impact.
Investigators believe that at least several drones may have been used in the operation. According to law enforcement, one of them may also have been involved in damaging a DHL cargo aircraft.
Germany’s Federal Prosecutor General’s Office is investigating the case on suspicion of attempting to cause an explosion and dangerously interfering with the operation of air transport.
Germany’s Response
At the beginning of September, the German government officially stated that it considered Russia responsible for the attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the operation had allegedly been prepared in Russia over several months, and that a major disaster and loss of life had been avoided only by chance. In response, Berlin announced a number of diplomatic and political measures against the Russian Federation, including the closure of Russian institutions and increased pressure במסגרת its sanctions policy.
Moscow rejected the accusations.
Reminder
Earlier, we reported that Germany was expelling more than 150 Russian diplomats and their family members following the sabotage in Leipzig.

Drones Strike Russian Aviation Plant Servicing Tu-95 Bombers and Chemical Giant in Tolyatti

- Category

Drones Strike Russian Aviation Plant Servicing Tu-95 Bombers and Chemical Giant in Tolyatti
Drone attacks struck industrial and military facilities in the Russian cities of Taganrog and Tolyatti overnight on September 12, with fires reported near an aircraft complex that services A-50 surveillance planes and Tu-95 strategic bombers, as well as at one of Russia’s major chemical producers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Exilenova+ on September 12, satellite fire-detection data and footage shared by local residents showed several fires in Taganrog, including near the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex.
The facility specializes in maintenance and modernization of Russia’s A-50 airborne early warning and control aircraft, Be-series amphibious aircraft used by the Russian Navy, and Tu-95MS/MSM strategic bombers. Russia uses Tu-95 bombers to launch Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles against Ukraine.
NASA FIRMS satellite data showed fire hotspots in the area of the aviation enterprise. The nearby Taganrog-Yuzhny airfield serves as the Beriev complex’s main flight-testing base.
Separately, ASTRA reported that drones may also have targeted the Taganrog-Central military airfield, home to Russia’s 708th Military Transport Aviation Regiment. The 325th Aircraft Repair Plant, which repairs military transport aircraft, is located nearby.
Another fire was recorded near Taganrog’s automobile plant, according to satellite observations and reports from local residents.
In Tolyatti, Samara region, drones targeted the KuibyshevAzot chemical plant, according to monitoring group Exilenova+. A fire was reported on the plant’s premises following the attack.
KuibyshevAzot produces ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, ammonium sulfate, nitric acid, caprolactam, and polyamide products. The company is among Russia’s major producers of nitrogen fertilizers and caprolactam, a chemical used in the production of polyamide plastics and synthetic fibers.
Earlier, on September 11, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the sanctioned Volgogradpromproekt enterprise in Volgograd with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, triggering a fire at the facility. The company is involved in Russia’s military-industrial complex and produces ferrocene-based combustion catalysts and chemical production technologies.

Education centres opened with Estonia’s support give thousands of Ukrainian children and teachers the opportunity to build their future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:27:53 UTC
23:27:53 KST

In Malyn, an extracurricular education school damaged in a Russian bombing attack at the beginning of the full-scale war reopened its doors, enabling nearly 400 children to continue taking part in extracurricular activities. The EDUHUB opened in Zhytomyr, meanwhile, gives nearly 4,000 early childhood education teachers access to modern teaching practices. ESTDEV designed both projects so that their impact would extend beyond individual buildings and institutions and create models that could also be used in other regions of Ukraine.
“Alongside military, financial and political support for Ukraine, it is also important to invest in Ukraine’s future. Tanks help Ukraine defend its freedom today, but education helps build the country Ukrainians are fighting for. Both the EDUHUB education centre and the Malyn extracurricular education school are laying the foundations for educating the generations that will shape Ukraine’s future,” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
With an investment of nearly €2.4 million from ESTDEV, the war-damaged building of the Malyn extracurricular education school was restored, while the school’s curriculum, teachers’ skills and institutional management were also updated in cooperation with Estonian experts. Nearly 1,000 young people, teachers and parents were involved in the development of the Malyn school. Teachers also took part in training courses and study visits to Estonia to learn about modern teaching methods. Both teachers and parents were able to participate in trauma-awareness training to better support children and young people affected by the war.
The EDUHUB early childhood education competence centre opened in Zhytomyr gives more than 4,000 kindergarten teachers in the Zhytomyr region access to support in applying modern teaching practices. The centre was established with the support of ESTDEV, Liechtenstein and the City of Tallinn, in cooperation with Zhytomyr City Council and the Tallinn Teachers’ House.
“When rebuilding Ukraine, it is not enough simply to restore buildings damaged by the war. Alongside rebuilding the physical environment, we must also strengthen the people, institutions and systems that help society recover from the crisis, continue developing and prepare for accession to the European Union. Both the Malyn extracurricular education school and EDUHUB are good examples of how infrastructure reconstruction and substantive development can go hand in hand,” said Andrea Kivi, Executive Director of the Estonian Centre for International Development (ESTDEV).

BRICS New Delhi declaration rejects sanctions, nuclear threats and terrorism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:25:29 UTC
23:25:29 KST

BRICS New Delhi declaration rejects sanctions, nuclear threats and terrorism
The BRICS nations on Saturday called out “unilateral coercive measures,” condemned terrorism, and called for the peaceful resolution of global disputes through dialogue and diplomacy in their summit declaration.
The declaration adopted by the BRICS leaders at their 18th summit in New Delhi reaffirmed the bloc’s “opposition to unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law” and the UN charter, and called to eliminate them.
The leaders of emerging and developing countries pointed out that sanctions and secondary sanctions have “far-reaching negative implications” including for human rights and food security, and disproportionately affect the poor and vulnerable.
The BRICS leaders repeated their earlier calls to reform the UN and other global institutions to reflect the new global realities. The New Delhi declaration stressed that no single country or group of countries should have a monopoly over senior positions in the UN – which was formed in the aftermath of World War 2.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made the same point while addressing the leaders, saying a “rapidly changing world can no longer be governed by outdated institutions.”
⚡️ Seeds of Solidarity: BRICS Leaders Plant Saplings in Delhi#BRICS2026#BRICSIndia2026#IndiaBRICSChairshiphttps://t.co/jFFeLBM3e6pic.twitter.com/67iS09utSz
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) September 12, 2026
Importantly, China and Russia, the two BRICS members who are also permanent members of the Security Council, reiterated their support for “Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council.”
BRICS, which started as a five-member grouping two decades ago, has now expanded to 11 full members, raising its economic size and global influence.
The adoption of the 45-page declaration is itself seen as a success for Indian diplomacy, which was able to unite Iran and the United Arab Emirates – on different sides of the Middle East conflict – behind the document.
The presence of Chinese President Xi Jinping in New Delhi – after seven years – along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has added to the gathering’s gravitas amid rising global tensions and economic turbulence.
The BRICS leaders condemned all acts of terrorism as “criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation” – a point that host India has repeatedly made at various global fora. The declaration specifically condemned the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year, in which 26 civilians were killed. India clashed with nuclear-armed neighbor Pakistan with drones and missiles following that attack.
The BRICS countries also called out the unilateral blockade of Cuba, and expressed concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities in violation of resolutions by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
While the document does not mention the Ukraine conflict, it says ”nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm” – an obvious reference to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant, which has seen attacks by Ukrainian forces endangering its safety.
The BRICS nations opposed the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from “Occupied Palestinian Territory,” and any geographic or demographic changes in the Gaza Strip. They further called on Israel to withdraw its forces from all Lebanese territories.
The next BRICS summit will be held in China.

Farage’s Reform UK gets second record £36 million donation in 48 hours
The donation comes as the veteran Brexit campaigner’s party is confronting allegations about irregularities in its funding, which it denies
Cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne said on Saturday he had donated £36 million (US$49 million) to Britain’s anti-immigration Reform UK, matching an already record contribution to Nigel Farage’s party a day earlier as it prepares for the next election.
The donation gives the veteran Brexit campaigner’s party £72 million from two donors in less than 48 hours at a time when it is confronting allegations about irregularities in its funding, which it denies.
The figure exceeds what either the governing Labour Party or the opposition Conservatives spent during last year’s election campaign, according to Electoral Commission figures. The funds will help Reform, whose lead in opinion polls has slipped over the funding allegations, win over voters before the next election, which is due by 2029.
Harborne, already Reform’s biggest donor, disclosed the contribution in a Telegraph newspaper article, saying fellow crypto investor Ben Delo’s pledge a day earlier had inspired him to match it.
“What do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government,” Harborne wrote in the article.
Delo’s donation on Friday had already dwarfed the previous record of £10 million that British businessman John Sainsbury, who died in 2022, had left to the Conservatives, according to the Electoral Commission’s online database.
