‘I’ll never sleep soundly’: IAI chairman warns Israel will always need more interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:54:41 UTC
22:54:41 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries Chairman Boaz Levy says he will “never sleep soundly” over Israel’s interceptor stockpiles, warning that a prolonged war and sustained ballistic missile fire create a constant need to replenish the country’s missile-defense arsenal.
“There are Israeli constraints and there are American constraints,” Levy told Ynet on the sidelines of the MEAD conference when asked whether nearly three years of war had left Israel facing a genuine shortage of interceptors. “There will always be a shortage because the war is asymmetric,” he said, adding that IAI production lines are operating around the clock to meet demand from Israel’s defense establishment as well as overseas customers, including Germany.
Levy also used the interview to send a message amid disputes over additional defense spending. “If you want more interceptors, you need bigger budgets, and the blanket is too short,” he said.
He said Israeli decision-makers understand the need, while the Defense Ministry is responsible for defining requirements and the Finance Ministry ultimately determines the available budget.
Asked whether he sleeps soundly knowing the size of Israel’s interceptor inventories, Levy replied: “I will never sleep soundly when it comes to interceptor stockpiles, because there will always be a need for more. Our job at IAI is to provide them as quickly and efficiently as possible, but these are highly sophisticated systems, and their production time is not negligible.”
The comments came during a conference where, behind the scenes, meetings were also held with representatives from a number of countries, including some that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel.
Levy, who was appointed IAI chief executive in 2020 after previously leading the Arrow missile-defense project and the Barak 8 program, has attended the conference annually. He said he sees air defense not only as an operational capability but also as a potential foundation for deeper cooperation between Israel and countries across the region.
“This conference is a good platform,” Levy said. “IAI is both a defense and civilian company. It is a national company, and it has responsibilities that go beyond supplying systems to the security forces.”
IAI employs about 16,000 people, including some 8,000 engineers, and Levy said the company supports roughly 50,000 Israeli households. That scale, he argued, gives it a responsibility to help create technological bridges that can strengthen both security and the economy while opening doors to additional countries.
‘There is nothing like this anywhere else’
Levy said technology should serve as a bridge for both civilian and military cooperation, particularly as the distinction between the two becomes increasingly blurred.
“The boundary between civilian and military is becoming blurred,” he said, adding that the latest war had demonstrated that reality to Israelis directly. “In our worldview, we always imagined a war with a distant front, and then the war was in Tel Aviv.”
Artificial intelligence is changing that equation even further, Levy said. Continuous data collection, including through Earth-observation satellites, can be used not only to detect threats such as missile launches from Iran but also to analyze terrain, movement, agriculture and water resources in both hostile and friendly countries.
“If you can generate insights from that, you can sell them, share them and create alliances with countries. It’s a win-win,” he said.
Levy said regional cooperation could eventually include shared use of space-based assets to provide both civilian and military intelligence, combined with ground-based systems to build a regional defense network.
“When a missile is headed toward Israel, or toward any other country in such an alliance, it passes through other countries,” he said. “If you advance cooperation, you increase your ability to respond. That is what Israel should aspire to.”
Israel, he added, already has enough allies to pursue such cooperation, some through public relationships and others through ties that are less visible.
Levy said Israel’s particular advantage lies in its layered air-defense architecture, combining interception systems operating at different altitudes with early warning, command-and-control and cooperation between multiple systems.
“Today it is clear to every citizen in the world that Israel is the leading air-defense power in the world,” he said.
He pointed to advance warnings given to Israeli civilians before incoming missile barrages. “You sat at home and were told that a barrage would arrive in 10 minutes. There were no surprises,” Levy said, arguing that the combination of technology and civilian discipline helped limit casualties.
Defense cooperation as an engine for normalization
Levy said Israel’s air-defense capabilities could also become a diplomatic asset.
“Anyone who says, ‘I am entering an alliance with Israel and meet its criteria as an ally,’ can potentially share in your capabilities,” he said. “And this is already starting to happen. Requests are coming in from all over the world. They want to know.”
For national leaders, he argued, the ability to provide citizens with better protection offers an unusually strong justification for cooperation with Israel.
Levy said talks are underway with numerous countries in Europe and the Gulf, although in most cases they currently involve the sale of defense systems rather than formal alliances.
Many of those countries understand that such relationships take time to develop, he said, predicting that some of today’s commercial relationships could eventually evolve into broader strategic alliances.
He described defense cooperation as a potential “locomotive” for normalization with countries in the region.
“What are we talking about here? People’s lives,” Levy said. “That is the most legitimate basis on which a decision-maker can build cooperation. No one is going to condemn him for that. If a leader says, ‘Through cooperation with Israel, I am giving my citizens protection,’ what could be more legitimate than that?”
Levy said IAI’s broader strength comes from operating across space, air, sea and land, with systems that can connect detection, communications, command and control and interception into a single operational chain.

At the U.S. Open, Ben Shelton Has America Believing Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:53:47 UTC
22:53:47 KST

As we approach the U.S. Open final, which takes place Sunday in New York City, the optimism about American men’s tennis is clocking in at a level unseen since Andy Roddick won the tournament in 2003.
Ben Shelton, the big-serving southpaw who grew up in Gainesville, Florida, and won national team and singles championships at the University of Florida in 2021 and 2022, respectively, will face the event’s top seed—and the world’s No. 2-ranked player—Alexander Zverev of Germany.
Sure, topping Zverev—the reigning French Open champion and Wimbledon runner-up—is no simple task for Shelton, who’s trying to become the first American man to claim any Grand Slam tournament title since Roddick. The German is 5-0 all-time against Shelton, who has taken a lone set against Zverev on tour.
But let’s face it: The three American men who have reached a U.S. Open final since Roddick’s seminal victory had little chance of success against far superior opponents. Andre Agassi’s nostalgic run to the 2005 final, in his second-to-last U.S. Open, ran into a Roger Federer rally: Federer, 20-time Grand Slam singles champ and recent inductee into the International Tennis Hall of Fame, bested Agassi to win the second of his five straight U.S. Open crowns.
Roddick returned to the final in 2006. Like Agassi the year before, he managed to take a set off Federer before succumbing to his rival’s inevitable triumph.
Two years ago, Taylor Fritz won his semifinal over fellow American Frances Tiafoe to reach the final against Jannik Sinner, who was on the cusp of winning his second major championship and cementing his status, along with Carlos Alcaraz, as the alpha dogs of their game. Sinner beat Fritz in straight sets in 2024—and has since won three more Grand Slam championships.
I was there the night Fritz reached that final. I wrote all about it. And truth be told, until Friday, I pretty much forgot about it.
Bet I’m not alone.
Win or lose on Sunday, Shelton’s performance at this year’s tournament will be remembered. After all, he already outlasted Alcaraz, the defending U.S. Open champion and a seven-time Slam victor, in a five-set quarterfinal epic that ended at 3:33 a.m. Wednesday—the latest finish in tournament history. Shelton won in a 10-point, fifth-set tiebreaker.
By defeating Tiafoe, a close friend whom he called “a big brother,” in Friday’s semifinal 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5, Shelton became the first Black American man to reach a U.S. Open final since the event’s stadium namesake, Arthur Ashe, in 1972. Shelton’s the first Black American man to reach a Grand Slam singles final since MaliVai Washington, who lost to Richard Krajicek of the Netherlands at Wimbledon in 1996.
Against Tiafoe, Shelton showed the sort of mental fortitude he’ll need against Zverev. Shelton double-faulted late in the first set to give Tiafoe the first service break of the match. Tiafoe took advantage of Shelton’s error to take the set. Shelton, however, refused to let his mishap crush him. He broke Tiafoe right back to go up 2-0 in the second and eventually win that set. In the third, Shelton and Tiafoe dueled in a marathon game lasting more than 15 minutes: A Tiafoe unforced error, on Shelton’s third set point, gave Shelton the set and momentum he wouldn’t relinquish.
All match long, Shelton was able to extend rallies by chasing down Tiafoe’s best shots. At times he simply lobbed balls onto Tiafoe’s side of the net, almost daring his opponent to make a mistake. The match ended on a Tiafoe double-fault. Shelton delivered 20 aces, to Tiafoe’s three. Shelton’s energy reserves also gave him an advantage: In the fourth set, Shelton to his left and struck a full-court, diagonal winner that wowed the crowd.
On Sunday, Ashe will be Shelton’s home floor. American tennis fans have been thirsting for a winner on the men’s side, going on a quarter century.
“Let’s do this for the USA,” Shelton said on court after the match, drawing cheers from a crowd that had included Serena Williams, Shonda Rhimes, Nicole Kidman, Rami Malek, and NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson. Also in attendance was Shelton’s girlfriend, soccer star Trinity Rodman. Rodman has a 1 p.m. game in Washington on Sunday; Shelton-Zverev is slated to start at 2.
Zverev, for all his impressive play this year—he’ll be appearing in his third-straight Grand Slam final—remains a divisive figure in tennis, thanks to past allegations of domestic violence. Zverev has consistently denied the claims. One case was settled out of court in 2024, without a finding or admission of guilt. In another, an ATP investigation was unable to find sufficient evidence to support the allegations.
He’s a convenient foil for a united American audience.
After methodically picking apart Tiafoe, Shelton seems unbothered by past struggles against Zverev, pointing out that before the quarterfinal, he had also never beaten Alcaraz (in three tries). “I feel that I’m a different player,” says Shelton, who last faced Zverev last November, at the ATP Finals in Turin, Italy. “I feel like I have so many more tools. I feel like I know my identity, am comfortable in my own skin, and I know what it takes for me to be playing top-level tennis.
A reporter noted that a lot is riding on Sunday. “Is there?” Shelton responded, with a laugh.
The male American major title drought gets brought up ad nauseam. But Shelton knows he can’t dwell on the stakes.
“At the end of the day, I'm here in New York, I'm hanging out with my team, I'm with my homies playing a little bit of tennis,” he says. “Confidence and belief take over.”
He’ll need it. He has it. A chance at making history lies ahead.

Scientists find Ozempic may slow aging itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:52:50 UTC
22:52:50 KST

Scientists find Ozempic may slow aging itself
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, extended lifespan and reduced signs of aging in older healthy mice.
- Date:
- September 12, 2026
- Source:
- NIH/Office of the Director
- Summary:
- Semaglutide helped older healthy mice live longer while improving memory, muscle function, blood sugar control, and several biological signs of aging. Its effects went beyond those seen with calorie restriction, raising the possibility that GLP-1 drugs could tap into a separate biological pathway linked to longevity.
- Share:
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in popular GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy, may do more than suppress appetite and improve blood sugar. A National Institutes of Health (NIH) funded study found that the drug reduced several harmful effects of aging and extended lifespan in older, healthy mice.
Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley compared semaglutide directly with calorie restriction, one of the best-known interventions for extending lifespan in laboratory animals. The drug reproduced many of the anti-aging effects of eating less, but in several important areas, it appeared to go even further.
The findings raise an intriguing possibility: GLP-1 drugs may influence the aging process itself. Earlier animal studies have shown that these drugs can delay the onset of multiple age-related diseases. If semaglutide acts on biological mechanisms that drive aging, that could help explain why GLP-1 treatments have shown benefits across such a wide range of health conditions.
"Most chronic diseases are deeply rooted in the aging process. If GLP-1 agonists do indeed slow it down, then a wide range of clinical benefits is exactly what you'd expect to see," said Rafael de Cabo, Ph.D., a senior investigator at the NIH's National Institute on Aging (NIA), and author of a commentary on the new study.
Testing Semaglutide Late in Life
To see what semaglutide could do when aging was already well underway, a research team led by Danica Chen, Ph.D., gave the drug to 20-month-old female mice for three months.
Compared with untreated mice, the animals receiving semaglutide showed better muscle and cognitive function. Gene activity also revealed improvements in several biological features associated with aging, including reduced inflammation and less decline in the body's ability to repair and regenerate tissue.
The lifespan results were especially striking. In a separate group treated with semaglutide until death, median lifespan was nearly 100 days longer than in untreated mice.
Was Eating Less the Real Reason?
Because semaglutide reduces appetite, the researchers wanted to know whether the apparent anti-aging effects simply came from consuming fewer calories.
To test that idea, they directly compared semaglutide with calorie restriction. For five months, one group of 20-month-old female mice received semaglutide, while another was placed on a 24% calorie-restricted diet designed to match how much the treated mice were eating.
The two approaches produced many similar effects, and most physiological measurements remained stable. But semaglutide stood out in several areas.
Mice receiving the drug improved beyond their starting levels in exploratory behavior, spatial memory, and blood-sugar maintenance. Their metabolic rate also remained largely unchanged, while metabolism slowed in the calorie-restricted animals.
Those differences suggest that semaglutide may be doing more than simply recreating the effects of eating less.
"These differences point to the possibility that GLP-1 drugs tap into a biological pathway independent of calorie restriction. Uncovering this potential route and the benefits that may specifically stem from it is an important direction for future research into the development of longevity-enhancing interventions," said Chen, corresponding author of the study and professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley.
Could GLP-1 Drugs Affect Human Aging?
The findings could open new directions in longevity research, but they do not show that Ozempic, Wegovy, or other GLP-1 drugs can extend human lifespan.
Additional clinical research will be needed to determine whether the effects seen in mice translate to people. One example is the recent post-hoc analysis of the SLIM LIVER trial, but further studies will be necessary to establish whether GLP-1 drugs can meaningfully influence human aging or longevity.
Chen said future clinical studies may also investigate these drugs in healthy older adults. If researchers eventually find similar benefits in people without obesity or diabetes, the potential uses of GLP-1 treatments could broaden considerably.
NIH supported this research through NIA grants R01AG063404, R01AG063389, and R01AG082105.
Story Source:
Materials provided by NIH/Office of the Director. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yufan Feng, Marine Barthez, Yifei Wang, Yibing Chen, Huixian Qiu, Chih-Ling Wang, Kartoosh Heydari, Melaine Delcroix, Lene Juel Rasmussen, Vilhelm A. Bohr, Danica Chen. Late-life semaglutide treatment slows ageing and extends lifespan in female mice. Nature, 2026; 657 (8131): 469 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10940-7

The rapid advance of Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen has enabled them to strengthen their control over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and created a new problem for the United States amid its war with Iran. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The Houthis advanced southward along Yemen’s coast and on Friday reached Perim Island, located in the middle of the strait between Yemen and Africa. This strengthened their ability to block one of the key routes between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
The situation is particularly dangerous for Saudi Arabia, which, following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the war, redirected a significant portion of its oil exports through Red Sea ports. "The Houthis destroyed Trump’s plan"
According to Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, the Houthi advance has presented Washington with a difficult choice.
Just a few weeks ago, Trump chose a strategy of pressuring Iran’s economy while keeping the military conflict at a level too low to put pressure on the American economy. The Houthis destroyed Trump’s plan
The United States has no interest in the closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as this could further drive up energy prices and disrupt global trade. At the same time, direct intervention would mean opening another theater of hostilities for the U.S. military amid the war with Iran.
According to Reuters, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on Thursday and asked the United States for military assistance against the Houthis. Washington responded that it does not currently plan to intervene directly, but agreed to provide Saudi Arabia with intelligence.

Israel used AI to kill thousands of Palestinians in Gaza – documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:49:03 UTC

Israel used AI to kill thousands of Palestinians in Gaza – documentary
A new documentary alleging that Israel relied on powerful AI tools to kill thousands in Gaza has sent shockwaves through the Venice Film Festival, with one of the film’s insiders describing planning airstrikes as “insanely fun.” The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has categorically rejected the film’s portrayal, insisting that the whistleblowers cannot be verified.
The 80-minute-long film NAZA, which premiered on Thursday, is built around testimony from 24 anonymized Israeli military and intelligence insiders. Its title alludes to an Israeli military shorthand for expected “collateral casualties” in an attack.
The film, which was made by two Israeli Oscar-winning filmmakers, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, received a roughly 25-minute standing ovation – the longest on record at the event. The footage also showed a full audience, with some viewers holding Palestinian flags.
With 25 minutes of Applause, ‘NAZA’ broke the record for the Longest Ovation in the history of the Venice Festival #venicefilmfestival#NoOtherLand#PalestineSolidarity#StandingOvation#venicerecord#longestovation#HistoryMade#yuvalabraham#rachelszor#GazaDocumentarypic.twitter.com/Mr7FORlkt4
— The Cover Story (@Cover_Story63) September 11, 2026
In the film, Israeli insiders claim that the IDF used an AI system known as ‘Lavender’ to identify people for assassination. The filmmakers’ sources also alleged that the tool operated based on thousands of hacked phones, with even a single phrase, “daddy’s home,” picked up on a child’s phone being enough to launch an attack.
Other sources told the tale of brazen disregard for humanitarian laws, and a “general atmosphere” of “hatred” towards Palestinians. 
In one of the most chilling revelations, an insider claimed that at one point a strike on a single Hamas member was approved despite an expected toll of 500 civilians. 
“It was done on a mass scale, like a factory”, one source said, with others describing the profiling and targeting as “a video game” and “insanely fun.” 
“We are letting the soldiers and the officers speak about what they did,” Abraham told AFP, saying the filmmakers wanted to document in detail “how the systems of killing in Gaza looked” and operated.
On Friday, the IDF vehemently rejected the allegations, arguing that the identities of the whistleblowers “cannot be verified,” and that it is impossible to establish whether they served in the military at all.
It also stressed that allegations pertained to “national and military strategy that are clearly beyond the knowledge of junior-level soldiers.” The IDF added that targeting decisions are made “by human personnel only,” and that its operations are only directed at “terrorist organizations.”
The IDF has itself acknowledged using AI for military purposes, including a system known as ‘The Gospel’, to rapidly produce targeting recommendations.
In April 2024, several media outlets reported, citing Israeli intelligence sources, that Lavender had at one stage marked about 37,000 people as suspected terrorists, with the personnel sometimes spending only seconds reviewing machine-generated recommendations. Some sources quoted by The Guardian also alleged that “during the early weeks of the war they were permitted to kill 15 or 20 civilians during airstrikes on low-ranking militants.” The IDF has rejected the allegations.

Hungary PM Magyar says to scrap Orban-era restriction on gay adoption

Hungary PM Magyar says to scrap Orban-era restriction on gay adoption
BUDAPEST, Sept 12 - Hungary's government will change legislation passed in 2020 by Viktor Orban's former government that had effectively banned gay adoption, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Saturday.
Adoption in Hungary, a European Union member state, by gay and lesbian couples was possible until late 2020 if one partner applied as a single person.
Under the law passed by Orban's right-wing Fidesz party in 2020, single people had to have their adoption requests approved by the family affairs minister, which has amounted to an effective ban.
Magyar ousted Orban after 16 years in a landslide election win in April. Changing the system of adoption would be a significant measure to restore LGBTQ rights.
"We can state unequivocally that we will change this system: it should not be the minister, a politician ... who makes the decision in such cases, but rather professionals capable of determining the conditions under which a given young child can achieve ... a life that allows them to become a happy and harmonious member of society," Magyar told a briefing, in reply to a question.
Orban, who cast himself as a defender of what he called Christian values from Western liberalism, passed laws ending the change of gender in personal documents, effectively halting adoption by same-sex couples and banning materials in schools seen as promoting homosexuality or gender transition.
The erosion of LGBTQ+ rights had a traumatic effect on the community.
Orban's government violated European law with rules prohibiting or restricting access to LGBTQ content, which stigmatise and marginalise gay and trans people, the European Court of Justice ruled in April, just before the election.
Hungary has never allowed gay marriage but still recognises civil unions. REUTERS

No signed Hormuz deal expected yet from Oman meeting on Monday, Iranian official says
Sept 12 - A meeting between Iran and Gulf states planned for Monday in Oman will be a chance to discuss issues including the Strait of Hormuz, but is not expected to yield a signed agreement over the blockaded waterway, a senior Iranian official said on Saturday.
Iran has been negotiating for months with Oman, which controls the opposite bank of the strait, over a deal that would govern transport through it. Oman has long said its negotiations are supported by other Arab countries in the Gulf.
Tehran announced on Friday that it was planning to attend a meeting with Gulf countries in Oman on Monday. Oman has not officially announced the meeting and other regional states have so far remained silent. Bahrain said on Saturday it would not attend meetings with Iran.
The Iranian official, who discussed the plans on condition of anonymity, said Monday's meeting was called at Oman's initiative, and would provide a forum to discuss other regional issues as well as Hormuz.
According to the Iranian official, Iran still wants an agreement that would allow it to collect fees from ships that use the strait, which Oman rejects.
Around a fifth of global oil supplies transited the strait before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, launching the war.
Global oil prices have surged over the past week after the United States and Iran both fired on tankers in the strait, and Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen advanced near another crucial Middle East conduit for oil, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula. REUTERS

Israeli AI startup founder pleads guilty to $27 million fraud scheme in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:45:02 UTC
22:45:02 KST

Israeli citizen Ilit Raz pled guilty to securities fraud charges in the US after she was found to have defrauded investors of around $27 million by misleading them about the core aspects of a company she founded, according to the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York.
The company, Joonko Diversity, Inc., claimed to offer AI-based services designed to help employers identify and hire prospective job candidates.
Raz, the founder and former CEO of Joonko, made false claims about the company’s customers and revenue to raise around $27 million in funding from investors between 2021 and 2022.
To entice prospective and existing investors, Raz claimed that Joonko’s customers included large global companies, including fashion brands, a credit company, and a travel company.
According to a 2024 US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) complaint, Raz claimed that Joonko had more than 100 customers and had worked with over 100,000 job candidates.
The SEC complaint also detailed that she provided investors with fabricated positive testimonials of alleged customers praising Joonko’s effectiveness.
The US Attorney’s Office asserted that Raz knowingly misled investors and that the companies were never customers of her company.
Several victims of Raz’s fraud scheme were left with millions of dollars in losses when Joonko went bankrupt, according to US Attorney Jamie McDonald.
Joonko fraud scheme uncovered in 2023
The fraud scheme was uncovered around 2023 when one investor became suspicious about Raz’s claims and contacted her to request information about Joonko’s performance.
Raz then forged a bank statement showing that the company maintained an average balance of more than $5,000,000, when the company’s actual balance was millions of dollars less than that.
Raz also sent the investor fictitious purchase orders for alleged Joonko customers that contained forged signatures from entities that had no business relationship with the company.
Her scheme was uncovered, and after pleading guilty to the charges, Raz faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years.

Iran-backed Houthis seize strategic Mayun Island: Can they hold it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:45:00 UTC
22:45:00 KST

Iran-backed Houthis seize strategic Mayun Island: Can they hold it?
The takeover solidifies the group’s position in the Bab al-Mandeb, but holding it long-term could be difficult.
Houthi forces have taken control of the island of Mayun – also known as Perim – tightening their grip on the eastern coast of the Red Sea and giving the group a strategic foothold in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The takeover was confirmed on Friday by a senior military official of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and a Houthi official, according to The Associated Press news agency.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Houthi advance in Yemen is about more than just the Red Sea
- list 2 of 3Houthis celebrate seizing control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast
- list 3 of 3Yemen government forces say Houthi ‘members, vehicles’ targeted in Mocha
Analysts say the seizure represents a significant military advance that, if the Houthis can consolidate, could reshape their conflict with Saudi-backed forces in Yemen while benefiting their backer Iran in its broader regional struggle.
Here is what we know about the island’s seizure, whether the Houthis can consolidate control and what it means for Yemen and beyond.
Why is Mayun Island important?
Mayun Island is a 13sq km (five square mile) volcanic island in the heart of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow southern corridor at the entrance to the Red Sea.
In 2021, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had a presence on the island, after reports emerged of a UAE-linked airbase being built there. The UAE ended its involvement in the Yemen conflict at the end of last year and withdrew troops, but the status of the airbase on Mayun Island is unclear.
By controlling the island, which splits Bab al-Mandeb into two channels, the Houthis now have a physical outpost in the strait.
The Bab al-Mandeb Strait is crucial to global shipping as it is the southern entrance to the Red Sea with the Suez Canal at its northern end. The strait has become even more important to shipping since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula by the US-Israel war on Iran in March.
The Houthis also control the areas surrounding the strait, including the island of Hanish and the entire Red Sea coastline of Yemen, reported Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Yemen, Yousef Mawry, on Saturday. Houthi forces seized the port city of Mocha on Thursday.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security, policy and defence analyst, said the Houthis’ advance and seizure of the whole of Yemen’s Red Sea coast means the group now “has the real capability to shut down any maritime traffic through Bab al-Mandeb if they want to”.
That gives the rebel group a major advantage in its battle in Yemen against Saudi-backed government forces, their primary target. It also benefits the Houthis’ ally, Iran, in its conflict with the US by giving Tehran new leverage over another global chokepoint and making its own blockade of the Strait of Hormuz “even more efficient”, Pusztai told Al Jazeera.
Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said the development serves both the Houthis’ “domestic” aims as well as Iran’s negotiating position with the US and the world “on other files, not just Yemen”.
What does it mean for shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait?
The Houthis have said that general shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb is safe from attacks, except for vessels linked to Saudi Arabia, which they will blockade.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group would continue what his statement called a “siege for siege” and “escalation for escalation” strategy against Saudi Arabia, which has blockaded Houthi-held areas of Yemen.
However, the Houthis have previously targeted vessels with no links to Saudi Arabia in regional waters.
Between November 2023 and mid-2025, the Houthis attacked more than 100 commercial ships in the Red Sea. The Houthis said the attacks were against vessels linked to Israel or its allies, in a campaign of solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. However, some attacks targeted vessels that appeared to have no such links, according to shipping sources cited by Reuters and BBC Verify, the BBC’s fact-checking team.
If the Houthis again expand their targets beyond Saudi vessels, their new positions could make it easier for them to strike passing ships.
The Houthis would “be able to use shorter-range missiles rather than long-range artillery to attack the ships,” said Pusztai. “This makes it a very risky endeavour to pass through the strait if the Houthis don’t allow it.”
Any further disruption on Red Sea shipping would have immense repercussions on an already strained global energy market, said economist Javed Hassan.
“War-risk insurance and charter rates can rise before cargoes are formally interrupted, and the resulting pressure extends beyond oil into container shipping, dry bulk and the wider cost of traded goods,” Hassan told Al Jazeera. “The technical supply shock from Houthi attacks therefore becomes an inflationary shock through several commodities at once.”
Can the Houthis hold on to the island?
That will depend on how much effort Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, which reportedly quickly withdrew as the Houthis advanced on it, put into recapturing the island, said Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London.
The Houthis are in a strong position to hold the island in the short term due to their control of surrounding areas, Krieg told Al Jazeera. However, “the island itself is difficult to defend against an amphibious assault in the long run” though such an assault “would be a high-risk operation as well”.
“The key will be to hold the coastal areas of the mainland and its hinterland,” added Krieg.
Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House, said the Houthis’ rapid push across the Red Sea coast and onto Perim Island was not surprising.
He cited poor coordination and weak armament among government forces, despite a yearlong Saudi-backed effort to consolidate them into an effective fighting force and an effective years-long military build-up by the Houthis.
Speaking to reporters during his visit to Ireland, US President Donald Trump said the Houthis had asked the US not to intervene in the conflict against Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
He said the Houthis “called us”. “They don’t want to fight us, they let us know,” Trump said.
“They would much prefer not having us involved and they’re letting most ships go through. There’s just one country that they’re not too happy with and we’ll get that straightened out.”
Trump added that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is a “good friend” and “everything will work out fine”.

Iran used Chinese-sourced satellite images to target US bases, intelligence reveals - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:44:53 UTC
22:44:53 KST

Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery of a US base in Jordan from Chinese sources before launching the missile attack that killed three American soldiers in July, according to a Friday report by The Wall Street Journal, which cited US officials familiar with the matter.
The WSJ reported that Washington has drawn a direct line between the Chinese-sourced imagery and the July 17 strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, but did not confirm direct involvement from the Chinese government.
The officials told the WSJ that Iran acquired the images both ahead of and following the assault, though they would not name the Chinese firms involved and stopped short of accusing Beijing's government of direct involvement.
According to the WSJ report, Iranian ballistic missiles slammed into a housing area at the base in northeastern Jordan where US troops were sleeping, killing three soldiers and wounding four others who were evacuated for treatment.
The strike was one of three missile attacks on the base within a 24-hour span and represented the first American combat deaths since an April ceasefire.
The WSJ noted that within days of the attack, Iran published high-resolution images documenting damage across three sections of the base, visuals more detailed than the lower-resolution commercial satellite imagery WSJ's own analysis had reviewed, which showed harm to more than 20 structures.
Diplomatic tensions ahead of Trump-Xi summit
The disclosure comes weeks before a planned September 24 meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Citing officials, the paper said senior US figures had raised the imagery findings directly with Chinese counterparts, who demanded evidence and rejected the allegations.
US officials told the WSJ that Beijing has denied that Chinese companies supply such material to Iran.
A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, Liu Chang, did not directly address the specific claims but accused unnamed parties of "maliciously linking and smearing other countries," the WSJ reported.
A White House official, responding to the WSJ, said no outside assistance had improved Iran's ability to strike US targets, without directly addressing the imagery findings.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked days after the attack whether China was feeding Iran targeting data, declined to answer directly and said Beijing's actions had not altered the conflict's course.
Pattern of improving accuracy
The WSJ cited analysts and former officials as saying the satellite imagery was likely just one of several intelligence sources feeding Iranian targeting, alongside Tehran's own satellites, human intelligence and support from Russia.
Early in the war, US strikes on Iranian radar and satellite systems had degraded Iranian battlefield awareness, and Iranian strikes often missed militarily significant targets. But officials cited by the WSJ said that Iranian targeting accuracy appeared to improve over the summer.
A former CIA analyst specializing in Iran’s military, Jim Lamson, told the WSJ that updated high-resolution imagery could help Iran identify high-value targets more precisely and assess strike damage.
The Trump administration already sanctioned three Chinese companies in May, MizarVision, Earth Eye, and Chang Guang, over allegations that they provided or published satellite imagery usable by Iran against US forces.
The State Department had previously accused Chang Guang of supplying imagery that supported attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia.
The administration has briefed congressional intelligence committees in recent weeks on both Chinese and Russian support for Iran.

The oldest evidence of regular psychoactive substance use has been found on an island in Indonesia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12

The oldest evidence of regular psychoactive substance use has been found on an island in Indonesia
Kyiv • UNN
Sulawesi hunter-gatherers may have consumed betel nuts 25,000 years ago. Scientists found traces of them on severely damaged teeth.
Hunter-gatherers on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi may have regularly consumed betel nuts as early as 25,000 years ago. This is indicated by research conducted by scientists from Griffith University, Live Science reports, writes UNN.
Details
Researchers examined heavily damaged teeth belonging to two people who lived on Sulawesi during different periods. One man died approximately 25,000–16,000 years ago, while the other person died around 7,600–6,300 years ago. Both were approximately 40–50 years old at the time of death.
The teeth displayed characteristic grooves, and analysis of the samples confirmed the presence of traces of betel nuts. The seeds of the Areca catechu palm contain arecoline, a neuroactive substance that affects the nervous system.
They may have used it as a painkiller
According to one of the study's authors, Adam Brumm, ancient people may have sucked on whole betel nuts to numb their mouths and ease toothache. At the same time, this practice likely only worsened the condition of their teeth.
On one of the teeth, the groove was so deep that it exposed the inner pulp cavity.
It must have been incredibly painful
Approximately 4,000 years ago, the inhabitants of Sulawesi were already mixing betel nuts with slaked lime to produce a stimulant. A similar practice still exists in parts of South Asia and Oceania.
It now seems likely that betel chewing in the form in which we know it developed from a much simpler and more ancient practice — sucking on a whole nut
The study's findings were published in the scientific journal Science Advances.

====================================================================================================

Gujarat earthquake, Nepal floods &amp; more: What is it about the date 26?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:40:01 UTC
22:40:01 KST

Gujarat, the tsunami, 26/11, and now Nepal. Some of the disasters etched deepest into public memory have one oddly specific thing in common: they happened on the 26th.The coincidence surfaced again after the August 26 catastrophe in Nepal, where a glacier collapse unleashed a wall of mud, rock and water through the Himalayan valleys, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving thousands missing. As images of the destruction spread, so did an old question: what is it about the 26th?But is the date really unusually deadly, or are we simply very good at finding patterns once we know where to look?
When nature struck on the 26th
The natural disasters alone would be enough to build a legend around this date. The Gujarat earthquake of January 26, 2001, Republic Day, struck Kutch with such force that it killed close to 20,000 people and injured more than 160,000, flattening entire towns like Bhuj and Anjar. Three years later, on December 26, 2004, a magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off Sumatra sent a tsunami crashing into the coastlines of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, part of a disaster that killed or left missing roughly 228,000 people across the Indian Ocean rim. The following July, on July 26, 2005, Mumbai received close to 944 mm of rainfall in 24 hours, a deluge that killed more than a thousand people across Maharashtra and brought the city to a standstill for days.
Gujarat earthquake of 2001
The pattern isn't confined to Indian soil, or even to this century. Turkey's Erzincan earthquake killed an estimated 32,700 people on December 26, 1939. The Skopje earthquake of July 26, 1963 killed around 1,070 and left 200,000 homeless. Iran's Bam earthquake, which levelled a 2,000-year-old citadel city, struck on December 26, 2003, killing roughly 31,000 people. Indonesia's Yogyakarta earthquake killed more than 5,700 on May 26, 2006, and the Hindu Kush earthquake of October 26, 2015 shook Afghanistan, Pakistan and parts of northern India simultaneously.
When the 26th turned man-made
Where the 26th gets stranger is that it isn't only earthquakes and floods, events with no human author. It has also coincided with some of the worst disasters humans have caused deliberately or through negligence.The most seared into Indian memory is November 26, 2008, when ten Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai, laying siege to the city for nearly three days and killing 166 people. It is remembered simply as 26/11, a date that needs no year attached to be understood. It wasn't an isolated instance of terrorism landing on this date, either, the Ahmedabad serial blasts of July 26, 2008, one of the deadliest terror strikes on Indian soil that year, fell on the same date. Outside India, the Kabul airport bombing of August 26, 2021, carried out during the US-led evacuation from Afghanistan, killed at least 183 people, including 13 American service members.
Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai
Industrial and nuclear disasters share the date too, and this is where the list stops looking like a coincidence confined to any one country or cause. Reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded during a botched safety test on April 26, 1986, in what remains the worst nuclear accident in history. More than four decades earlier, on April 26, 1942, a gas and coal-dust explosion at China's Benxihu colliery killed 1,549 miners through carbon monoxide poisoning, one of the deadliest mining disasters ever recorded.
Crashes, collisions and the 26th
Then there is a third category that rarely makes it into casual conversations about the 26th, but rounds out just how wide its reach is: ordinary transport disasters, the kind that don't need an earthquake or a bomb, just a broken rail or a failed engine part.India's Khanna rail disaster, a derailment and collision caused by a broken rail near Punjab's Khanna town, killed 212 people on November 26, 1998. The Aurangabad air crash, when flight IC-491 went down while approaching the Maharashtra airport, killed 55 of 118 people aboard on April 26, 1993. Overseas, Lauda Air Flight 004 crashed in Thailand on May 26, 1991, after an uncommanded thrust-reverser deployment sent the Boeing 767 out of control, killing all 223 people aboard.
The date that refuses to be just a number
Laid end to end, the list stops looking like a curated coincidence and starts looking almost deliberately comprehensive — quakes, tsunamis, floods, terror attacks, a nuclear meltdown, a mine explosion, a rail crash, an air crash. Nearly every disaster category a newsroom covers has, at some point, chosen the 26th.
So, is the 26th actually cursed?
There's a statistical explanation for this, and it's less exciting than a curse. The British statistician David Hand has spent years studying coincidences like this, he calls it the law of truly large numbers. Basically, if disasters are happening somewhere in the world almost every day, and a month only has 28 to 31 possible dates, some date was bound to end up looking busier than the rest. It just happened to be the 26th. It could as easily have been the 9th.Then there's confirmation bias, which does a lot of the heavy lifting here. Once you start looking for disasters on the 26th, you notice every one that fits and forget the ones that don't. Bhopal's gas leak, India's worst industrial disaster, happened on the night of December 2-3, 1984. The Uttarakhand floods were in June 2013. The Balasore train collision that killed nearly 300 people was on June 2, 2023. None of these are anywhere near the 26th. Nobody brings them up when the "jinx" comes up, because once you believe a pattern, you stop counting the exceptions.
Uttarakhand floods of 2013
Numerology adds a third layer, and in India this one actually sticks with people. Add up 2 and 6 and you get 8, a number some numerology traditions link to upheaval and karmic reckoning. For anyone who already believes in that system, a disaster landing on the 26th isn't a coincidence: it's confirmation.
There's no actual link between a calendar date and earthquakes, floods or violence. But belief doesn't need a mechanism. It just needs enough stories that fit, and the 26th has no shortage of those by now.
What the 'jinx' really tells us
So what does the list really tell us? Not that the date is cursed; just that disasters don't check the calendar, and over a long enough stretch of history, every date ends up with its own body count. The 26th's list happens to include some of the most consequential disasters of the last century, ones big enough that they changed building codes, early-warning systems, even how countries think about security. That's really why the date sticks in memory. Not the number itself, but what it forced people to rebuild afterward.

====================================================================================================

When Statecraft Becomes Transaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Executive Order (EO) 14422, signed Aug. 27, 2026, counts icebreakers. The US Coast Guard supplies nine of the 11 icebreaking vessels on the Great Lakes and clears the commercial lanes without charge, the order observes; the United States has spent nearly four billion dollars on the freshwater ecosystem in a decade, and Canada far less. From that ledger the order draws its conclusion. Because the deepest water lies on the American side, “the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume.” Lake Ontario “becomes” Lake America.
Read the inference slowly, because it does not hide: contribution establishes ownership; ownership licenses the name.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The EO presents the inference as settled policy, restating a January 2025 EO on names as a commitment to recognize “the extraordinary contributions of the American people” by naming landmarks for shared achievements.
The earlier EO’s stated policy said nothing like that. Instead, it spoke of honoring “visionary and patriotic Americans” in the nation’s past. In the older document, contribution names what a patriot gave; in the newer one, what a nation has paid in.
Ten days after the lake order, President Trump began posting maps of New Mexico with “Mexico” struck through in red, an image the White House amplified and the state’s governor refused to entertain. No constitutional route exists for renaming a state, and none was attempted.
Russia’s War in Ukraine Has Cost Poland’s Economy More than €100 bln, Estimate Shows
                                                                                                                                                                         
But naming has never been only about names. It announces who holds the standing to say what a thing is.
None of this argues against bargaining: diplomacy bargains, as it must. European governments underinvested in their own defense for three decades, and an administration that forces allies to buy usable capacity rather than rent American cover is right about that. I grant that fully, and once, because what follows does not depend on denying it. What follows depends on a distinction between a method and a metaphysics.
An alliance, though, is not a subscription willy-nilly reducible to a method. Its worth lies partly in goods that never appear on an invoice: interoperability built over decades, intelligence relationships unavailable at market, and the deterrence produced when an adversary believes a commitment will hold under pressure.
The last item is the strange one. It exists only in the enemy’s mind, and it thins the moment the enemy suspects that the commitment itself is subject to continual repricing.
On assistance to Ukraine, at least, the ledger has shifted decisively. NATO’s Ankara Declaration of July 8, 2026 records that European allies and Canada now finance the vast majority of security assistance to Ukraine and pledges €70 billion ($81 billion) in equipment, assistance, and training for 2026, with at least equivalent levels promised for 2027. Burden-shifting has produced substantial results. The strategic question it was supposed to answer sits exactly where it sat.
Territory is one object of the war in Ukraine – it is not the war itself. The Charter of the United Nations treats the territorial integrity and political independence of states as constitutive of international order rather than as negotiable holdings, and the Secretary-General has called Russia’s full-scale invasion a clear violation of it.
Putin’s own account of his aims will not fit inside a real-estate frame. At the St. Petersburg forum on June 20, 2025, he grounded a claim on a premise about peoplehood: Russians and Ukrainians being one people, and so “all of Ukraine is ours.” Putin then supplied the operative rule: “wherever a Russian soldier sets foot, that’s ours.”
Set that beside the Lake Ontario EO… and something uncomfortable surfaces: because the largest constituent of the Russian Empire was Russia, because both Russia and Ukraine have a shared history, then “all of Ukraine is ours.”
Of course, one cannot justifiably claim that Trump’s EO and Putin’s nationalism are moral equivalents – that would be grotesque. However, the grammar of naming based on power and “possession” is the same. Each converts a prior claim (contribution in one case and kinship in the other) into title. In the Lake Ontario EO, title then licenses a name; in Putin’s historical argument, naming and genealogy serve as evidence of title.
What separates them is what each is prepared to do to make the title hold. Russia invaded a sovereign state, annexed its territory, and denies its separate political existence; nothing in an executive order about a lake belongs to that category, and an argument that blurred the distinction would deserve to fail. Yet the parallel is narrow. It is also instructive, because the same grammar deceives its user in both cases.
Putin’s longer argument, set out in his 2021 essay on the historical unity of Russians and Ukrainians, rests on genealogy – and carries its own refutation. The essay concedes that the medieval word behind Ukraine’s name appears in 12th-century sources “referring to various border territories.” Various: plural, relative to more than one center. Having granted that the word named several frontiers, the essay proceeds as though it had named one, and as though naming a frontier settled who owns it.
I decline to litigate whether Kyiv’s baptism under St. Volodymyr in 988 outranks Moscow’s first appearance in the chronicles in 1147. Why? To litigate is to concede the premise: that antiquity conveys title. Sovereignty is not an inheritance, and etymology is not a deed.
A negotiating framework of this kind fails here, and it fails on its own terms. If a rational actor accepts a sufficiently good offer, then everything turns on what counts as good, and instrumental rationality supplies no common scale. Putin need not be deranged to refuse terms Washington considers generous. A leadership may rank strategic depth, imperial standing, and the denial of a neighbor’s independent existence above sanctions relief and reconstruction contracts and rank them consistently for 20 years. A negotiator can handle the priceable dimensions of such a conflict with skill and still be working on the wrong problem. A scale calibrated for one quantity returns a number for anything you set on it. The number is not false; it is beside the point.
Early on Sept. 8, 2026, ending a three-day pause on strikes observed while American envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv, Russian ballistic and cruise missiles and drones struck Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing and injuring civilians and damaging more than 50 sites in the capital, among them residential buildings, dormitories, and schools.[12]Later that day, the Kremlin’s readout of an hour-long call described Trump pressing for a swift end to the war, which would open “impressive and far-reaching” prospects for restored relations, with particular benefit to trade.
Ukraine’s foreign minister answered in 10 words: “His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.” An offer denominated in trade normalization reached a party that had spent that same morning demonstrating what it values more.
Rhetorical domination compounds the difficulty, and its record can be checked. George C. Edwards III, surveying Trump’s public discourse, catalogs the branding and delegitimizing of opponents, the fueling of fear, and the stoking of division, and arrives at a finding easy to skip past: the rhetoric diminished the president’s capacity to govern.
Consider the clearest instance: on July 31, 2025, Dmitry Medvedev, answering a warning from Trump, invoked the “Dead Hand,” the Cold War-era system reputed to launch automatically should Russia’s leadership be destroyed – though he called it fabled even as he brandished it. The following day, Trump announced on Truth Social that he had ordered two nuclear submarines repositioned. That is, a social-media post moved strategic assets.
Whatever that is, it is not the pricing of interests; it is a contest over who is seen to yield, conducted with the instruments of nuclear deterrence. The same instinct shows in Vice President JD Vance’s assigned part, which Reuters described in 2025 as an attack-dog role, exercised in Munich and then in the Oval Office against President Zelensky.
Any comparison with Medvedev stops well short of equivalence: Vance has not invoked a doomsday system.
Moscow, meanwhile, has folded nuclear risk into the bargaining environment. The doctrine Putin approved on Nov. 19, 2024 reserves the right to answer with nuclear weapons a conventional attack creating a “critical threat” to Russian or Belarusian sovereignty or territorial integrity, where the 2020 formulation had spoken of a threat to the state’s very existence.
Analysts read the change differently: the Arms Control Association sees a lowered and blurred threshold, while the United States Institute of Peace argues the amendments codify guidance already operative and mark no real departure. Either reading serves the point, since ambiguity is the instrument.
A negotiator who prices deliverables cannot price this, because its worth to Moscow lies in its staying unresolved. Beijing repeats that nuclear weapons must not be used and nuclear war must not be fought. The statement matters and may constrain Moscow. It also remains a Chinese position serving Chinese interests, and expecting Beijing to enforce Western assumptions about tolerable Russian conduct would reproduce the original error at a higher level.
The danger begins not with bargaining but with the elevation of a partial truth into a master category. The objects of statecraft are not homogeneous: political communities have histories, identities, jurisdictions, and common goods; alliances embody commitments and serve strategic goods; sovereignty is a juridical status, not merely possession of territory. None is commensurable without remainder in a single metric.
Putin’s characteristic move is civilizational absorption: Ukraine’s independent political identity is subordinated to an alleged antecedent unity of peoplehood, history, and imperial space.
The Trump administration’s recurrent vocabulary is different (assets, leverage, contributions, burdens, and deals), but it raises an analogous question: does bargaining remain an instrument ordered toward political goods that exceed exchange value, or does the logic of the bargain become the measure of those goods themselves? Treat an alliance as a subscription, and its members learn to calculate cancellation.
Sovereignty includes territory and exceeds it, the way a marriage may include a shared address without being constituted by it. Each of these realities has a transactional dimension; none is exhausted by one. The error lies not in using a category that captures something real, but in allowing a partial category to become an exhaustive ontology. At that point, the category no longer merely guides policy; it governs what its user can see.
Which returns us to the issue of Lake Ontario. Federal maps will print the new name, since an executive order can compel that much, and the water will keep crossing a border that no order can move. There is the difficulty in miniature: a name can be assigned; the thing declines to be renamed.
Washington may yet win real concessions from Moscow, and nothing here forecloses it. But a settlement built on the assumption that Moscow must eventually want what Washington would want in its place is the same category mistake, now committed where the cost of error is counted in cities.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Russia Launches Large-Scale Missile and Drone Attack Across Ukraine, Killing at Least Four

Russia Launches Large-Scale Missile and Drone Attack Across Ukraine, Killing at Least Four
Russia launched a large-scale overnight missile and drone attack across Ukraine on September 12, killing at least four people and injuring civilians in Odesa, Kryvyi Rih, Zaporizhzhia, and the Kyiv region.
Odesa and the surrounding region were the primary target of the attack, the Ukrainian Air Force reported. At least 17 people were injured in Odesa, including a five-month-old baby, after a Russian strike significantly damaged a multi-story residential building, according to Odesa City Military Administration head Serhii Lysak.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Emergency and municipal crews were deployed to the damaged building, while an operational headquarters was established to assist residents.
In Kryvyi Rih, a Russian ballistic missile struck an industrial facility, killing one person and injuring two others, according to Dnipropetrovsk regional authorities. Another man was reported missing. The two injured men, aged 54 and 58, were hospitalized, with one reported in serious condition and the other in moderate condition.
Five apartment buildings, a primary healthcare center, three educational facilities, and several businesses were also damaged in Kryvyi Rih. The city was later targeted by attack drones.
Russia also struck a residential area of Zaporizhzhia with a drone, destroying at least one house and starting fires, regional defense officials reported. Rescue workers recovered the bodies of a 64-year-old woman and a 37-year-old man from the rubble. A 59-year-old woman was injured.
Authorities in the Kyiv region reported further damage from Russian attacks involving jet-powered drones. One person was killed and three others, including a child, were injured over the previous 24 hours.
Damage was recorded in the Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil, and Vyshhorod districts. At least 15 sites were affected, including seven private homes, vehicles, warehouses, hangars, and a power line.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force on September 12, Russia began the overnight attack at around 6 p.m. the previous evening and used ballistic missiles, eight sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles, and 129 drones.
The drones included Shahed-type attack UAVs, S8000 Banderol drones, and decoys. They were launched from areas around Kursk and Oryol in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk region and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
Russian ballistic missiles were launched from Russia’s Voronezh and Rostov regions and from temporarily occupied Crimea, while the Kalibr missiles were fired from the Black Sea.
As of 8:30 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 110 aerial targets, including six Kalibr cruise missiles, two Kh-59/69 missiles, one S8000 Banderol drone, and 101 Shahed-type and other drones, the Air Force said.
Russian missiles and attack drones were recorded hitting 20 locations across Ukraine, while debris from intercepted targets fell at four additional sites.
Ukraine used combat aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare systems, unmanned systems, and mobile fire groups to repel the attack. The Air Force said Russian drones remained in Ukrainian airspace after the initial interception figures were released.
Earlier, on September 11, Russian drones struck gas stations in Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts, injuring at least two people. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also reported a second strike on a gas station in the Obolonskyi district.

Leipzig Drone Attack Explosives Disguised in Food Can, Probe Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:37:00 UTC
22:37:00 KST

An attempted drone attack targeting a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 failed only because a detonator wire snapped, leaving approximately 1.8 kilograms of Semtex concealed in a vegetable tin can unexploded, German newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported.
According to investigators, the plot involved three unmanned aerial vehicles. Two drones crashed during launch due to unexplained technical failures, while the third successfully reached the Ukrainian cargo plane inside the airport’s security perimeter but did not detonate.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Investigators assessed that an explosion would have caused catastrophic structural damage to the transport hub, noting that the Antonov transport plane held roughly 25,000 liters of jet fuel at the time of the incident.
German security agencies have identified two primary suspects: Belarusian national Andrei K. and Russian citizen Oleg L. Investigators assessed that Oleg L. coordinated logistical operations on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence service, the Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU).
Logistics, entry route, and GRU connections
Investigation records show that Oleg L. entered Germany through Berlin-Brandenburg Airport via Turkey before traveling to Serbia and subsequently returning to Russia.
Although German security agencies possessed preliminary intelligence regarding his potential ties to the GRU at the time of his arrival, authorities did not establish physical surveillance on him during his stay in the country.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Command Posts and Supply Depots
Forensic investigators traced the suspects through DNA evidence recovered from work gloves abandoned near a radio antenna used to operate the drone. The DNA profile matched records held in Lithuania and Finland, where Andrei K. had prior documentation linked to petty criminal offenses.
Polish prosecutors have separately tied Andrei K. to a major summer 2024 arson attack on a home improvement hypermarket in Łódź, which Polish authorities formally classified as an act of state-sponsored sabotage directed by Russian intelligence services.
Investigators determined that the Semtex used in the Leipzig plot was smuggled across Europe through Bulgaria and Serbia hidden inside hollow vehicle compartments of commercial freight trucks.
Upon arrival in Germany, the explosive charges were buried in ground caches in areas surrounding Leipzig/Halle Airport. German federal police later located several hidden caches after analyzing telemetry and GPS data retrieved from a vehicle rented by the suspects.
Diplomatic expulsions and mutual facility closures
The investigative disclosures follow diplomatic fallout between Berlin and Moscow over the attempted airport sabotage.
On Sept. 1, the German federal government attributed the Leipzig/Halle incident directly to Russian intelligence agencies, accusing Moscow of deploying contract operatives to target critical logistics infrastructure utilized by NATO and Ukraine.
In response, Berlin ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate general in Bonn – mandating the departure of roughly 60 Russian diplomats and staff by Sept. 18 – and terminated its intergovernmental operating agreement for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
German intelligence officials assessed that approximately one-third of the personnel at the Bonn consulate were affiliated with Russian intelligence agencies.
On Sept. 7, the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched reciprocal measures, ordering the closure of the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg and terminating all branches of the Goethe-Institut cultural organization in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Yekaterinburg.
Russian authorities ordered German consular staff in St. Petersburg to vacate the country by Sept. 18 and gave the Goethe-Institut until Sept. 13 to shut down operations.
Western allies have characterized the airport incident as a major escalation in hybrid warfare against European aviation and critical infrastructure, with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warning that allied nations will respond to attacks on European territorial integrity and democratic stability.

Russian missile strikes hit two major Ukrainian metallurgical plants overnight on Sept. 12, killing two people and injuring six others, according to statements from Zaporizhstal operator Metinvest and ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih.
In Zaporizhzhia, four ballistic missiles struck the Zaporizhstal steel plant, injuring four employees and causing what Metinvest described as critical damage.
The attack was the third ballistic missile strike on the plant in a month, following earlier attacks on Aug. 11 and Aug. 27. Zaporizhstal had still not resumed production following the previous strikes, according to Metinvest.
"Zaporizhstal produced pig iron and steel for civilian needs. The plant did not manufacture products for military purposes and did not host anything on its territory that could make it a military target," Metinvest Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko said.
"Even this did not stop another attack," he added.
The strike damaged equipment in the plant's blast furnace and open-hearth shops, as well as its energy systems, internal networks, and logistics infrastructure, Metinvest said.
One of the four injured workers received treatment at the plant and declined hospitalization, while three others were taken to hospitals with moderate injuries.
"The scale of the destruction is increasing with every strike," Myronenko said. "It is not yet possible to fully assess it, but preliminarily we consider the damage critical."
Separately, a Russian missile strike hit the ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih steel plant, which is in the city of Kryvyi Rih in Dnipropetrovks Oblast, overnight — killing two employees of contractor companies and injuring two plant workers, the company said.
Production and auxiliary facilities were damaged, while search and rescue operations continued at the site. The company said specialists were assessing the extent of the damage and possible timelines for recovery.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih noted that the facility is a civilian mining and metallurgical enterprise.
The plant has been hit repeatedly during Russia's full-scale war. A December 2022 strike killed one employee and destroyed a rolling mill, while another attack in August 2026 killed two plant employees and one contractor and injured 18 others, damaging key energy and blast-furnace facilities and partially halting production.
The attacks on the two plants were part of a broader wave of Russian strikes across Ukraine overnight on Sept. 12 that killed at least 11 people and injured 96 others. Odesa Oblast was the main target of the overnight missile and drone attack, while deadly strikes were also reported in Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, and Kharkiv oblasts among others.

Researchers find a Wordle strategy that wins 99% of the time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:35:56 UTC
22:35:56 KST

Researchers find a Wordle strategy that wins 99% of the time
A mathematical strategy that prioritizes information over lucky guesses can solve Wordle 99% of the time.
- Date:
- September 12, 2026
- Source:
- Binghamton University
- Summary:
- Researchers at Binghamton University have developed a mathematical strategy that can solve Wordle with a 99% success rate. Instead of simply guessing words packed with common letters or choosing the most likely answer, the method uses Shannon entropy, a measure from information theory, to identify guesses that reveal the most useful information. Each guess is designed to rapidly shrink the pool of possible answers, even when the guessed word itself seems unlikely to be correct.
- Share:
Millions of people open Wordle each day hoping to solve its five-letter puzzle before their six guesses run out. Now, researchers at Binghamton University, State University of New York, say mathematics can dramatically improve the odds.
By applying information theory, the team developed a strategy that solved 99% of Wordle puzzles in simulations. The key is surprisingly counterintuitive. Instead of always trying to guess the answer as quickly as possible, the method favors words that reveal the greatest amount of useful information.
How Wordle Turns Every Guess Into a Clue
Wordle gives players six attempts to identify a hidden five-letter word. The game begins with no clues, so the first guess can be any valid word.
After each attempt, Wordle uses colors to show how close the player is:
- Grey means the guessed letter does not appear in the secret word.
- Yellow means the letter is in the secret word, but it is in the wrong position.
- Green means the letter is both correct and in the correct position.
Players use those clues to narrow the possibilities with each new guess. The game ends when all five squares turn green or when the player uses all six attempts without finding the answer.
That process of progressively reducing possible answers makes Wordle a natural problem for information theory, a branch of mathematics concerned with measuring and communicating information.
The Math Behind a 99% Wordle Strategy
The research team, led by Assistant Professor Congyu "Peter" Wu, focused on a concept known as Shannon entropy.
Shannon entropy is a mathematical way of measuring uncertainty. In simple terms, it can help determine how much useful information a particular choice is expected to reveal. The concept was developed as part of modern information theory and is widely used to study how efficiently information can be transmitted, stored, or processed.
In Wordle, that means asking a different question. Instead of simply choosing the word that seems most likely to be correct, the researchers looked for guesses that would eliminate the greatest number of possibilities.
"Let's say you're at a certain guess. The previous guesses will eliminate a whole bunch of options, and based on the remaining options, guessing some words will send you into a trajectory where information gain is speedier," said Wu, a faculty member at the Thomas J. Watson College of Engineering and Applied Science's School of Systems Science and Industrial Engineering.
A word that appears unlikely to be the final answer can therefore still be extremely valuable if its letters help divide the remaining possibilities into smaller groups.
"A subtle but important insight from the paper is that a guess doesn't have to be the most likely answer; it simply has to be informative," said Donald Stephens, a doctoral student at Binghamton University. "By applying Shannon entropy, the objective shifts to maximizing the expected reduction in uncertainty rather than the probability of being right. In practice, this approach can lead to solving the puzzle in fewer guesses."
Why the Best Guess Can Look Wrong
To a human player, some of the strategy's recommendations might initially seem strange or even random. But the goal is not necessarily to solve the puzzle immediately. It is to make each guess reveal enough information to make the next decision easier.
For example, when several possible answers remain, choosing a word that tests a useful combination of letters could eliminate many of them at once. Even if that word has little chance of being the actual solution, the feedback it produces may point much more clearly toward the correct answer.
Using the strategy during a real Wordle game would require running a separate script or program. After each guess, the player would enter Wordle's color-coded feedback into the program. The software would then calculate the next guess expected to provide the most information.
Information Beats Common Letter Guessing
The researchers compared their approach with a more conventional strategy centered on frequently used letters (e.g., "A," "E," "R").
The difference was substantial. In simulations, the information theory method successfully solved 99% of Wordle puzzles. The common letter strategy solved 90%.
That result highlights an important distinction between simply choosing letters that appear often and choosing guesses that provide the greatest amount of new information. Common letters can certainly be useful, but the mathematical approach continually adjusts its choices based on what has already been learned.
A Classroom Project Becomes Published Research
The work did not begin as a formal research project. Instead, it grew out of a class assignment in which Wu challenged students to demonstrate how information theory could be used to solve a real problem.
The students chose Wordle, turning a popular daily puzzle into a practical test of mathematical decision-making.
Co-author Talal Aladaileh said that the project's evolution from a classroom exercise into a published paper reflects the rigor, depth, and quality of the School of Systems Science and Industrial Engineering program at Binghamton.
"The courses here don't just teach concepts; they push you to apply them in ways that have real, lasting impact," Aladaileh said.
Wu said the project demonstrates how information theory can move beyond simply describing uncertainty and instead become a tool for making better decisions.
"What is especially creative and valuable about the team's intellectual contribution," Wu said, "is that it transformed a static measurement (Shannon entropy) in a scientific domain into a dynamic solution that helps accomplish a popular task better, which showcases the team's deep understanding of class material and their talent as engineers."
The paper, "Solving Wordle Using Information Theory," was published in the Northeast Journal of Complex Systems.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Talal Aladaileh, Donald Stephens, Mallak Alqaisi, Congyu Wu. Solving Wordle Using Information Theory. Northeast Journal of Complex Systems (NEJCS), 2026; 8 (1) DOI: 10.63562/2577-8439.1146
