Hong Kong teen battling rare disease creates AI avatar to ensure his story lives on
Chen Tsz-kin, 17, who suffers from muscular dystrophy, says that while life may come to an end, AI can allow his message of perseverance to continue
A Hong Kong teenager with a rare muscle-wasting disease has created an AI version of himself, hoping the digital twin can continue sharing his life story and message of perseverance even after he is gone.
Chen Tsz-kin, 17, unveiled “AI Tsz-kin” at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) on Sunday, weeks before his 18th birthday – an age the student said he had long feared reaching because he was once told it was the average life expectancy for people with his disease, Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
“Life may come to an end, but through different means, AI can allow [my message] to continue,” he said. “Even if one day I am no longer here, I just hope people remember the spirit behind it.”
Tsz-kin was diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy when he was just 1½ years old.
The progressive rare and deadly condition causes muscles to weaken over time, and he now uses a wheelchair, wears a back brace and relies on a breathing machine at night.
Even so, he has spent much of his childhood pursuing experiences that might have seemed impossible, including travelling to the Kyrgyz highlands, completing a 100km desert expedition with support from volunteers, paragliding and diving.

Israel steps up strikes on Gaza as elections approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:36:58 UTC
21:36:58 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel steps up strikes on Gaza as elections approach
Palestinians in the Gaza Strip continue to face deadly attacks by Israeli forces on an almost daily basis despite a theoretical "ceasefire", amid upcoming elections in Israel due to be held in October.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC for war crime, faces an increasingly competitive electoral battle in Israel and seeks to maintain a tough image on "security".
On Sunday, an Israeli drone strike hit a civilian vehicle in the Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, west of Gaza City, killing two Palestinians and injuring 13 others, according to local sources and eyewitnesses.
The strike set the vehicle ablaze as it travelled through the area. The Palestinian Red Crescent confirmed that two people were killed and 13 wounded, some critically, and said its teams transported the injured to hospital.
The Israeli army had not immediately commented on the attack.
The strike came as Israeli authorities also closed the Rafah and Kerem Shalom crossings to the movement of people and the entry of goods, tightening a de facto siege of the territory.
According to the Gaza Ministry of Health, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the ceasefire took effect in October, 2025.
The figures bring the overall Palestinian death toll since the start of Israel's war on Gaza on 7 October 2023 to 73,783, with 174,783 people wounded.
Netanyahu turns to 'security' as election race tightens
The continued Israeli attacks come as Israel moves towards elections for the 26th Knesset, with Netanyahu's Likud party facing growing competition from opposition parties.
Recent opinion polls suggest that Likud is losing ground to Yashar, a party led by former Israeli army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. Out of five recent polls, four show Eisenkot's party ahead, while Likud came first in an i24NEWS poll.
An average of the five surveys puts Yashar on 23.6 projected seats in the Knesset, compared with 21.4 for Likud. Naftali Bennett's Bennett 2026 party follows with an average of 12.4 seats.
The wider political picture remains divided. Netanyahu's bloc, including Ofer Winter's party, averages 53.4 seats, compared with 53.6 for the opposition, while Arab parties are projected to win around 12.2 seats, according to i24NEWS poll.
If Yoaz Hendel and Ron Zilcha join the opposition after it passes the electoral threshold, the opposition could reach approximately 54.4 seats.
The narrow margins have made security a central issue in the emerging campaign, with Netanyahu seeking to reinforce his credentials among right-wing voters by presenting himself as the leader best positioned to confront what he claims are threats facing Israel.
Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Hossam Al-Dajani told The New Arab that Netanyahu understands the importance of security issues in shaping Israeli voters' choices and is therefore seeking to keep the war and Gaza high on the political agenda.
"Netanyahu is attempting to present himself to the Israeli public as the man most capable of managing the war and protecting Israel," he said.
He argued that continued military operations reinforce Netanyahu's political narrative and allow him to portray himself as a leader capable of confronting security threats.
"The close polling makes it particularly difficult for Netanyahu to make major concessions over Gaza or significantly reduce military operations," he continued.
"Any significant scaling back of operations or concessions regarding the Gaza issue could be exploited by his opponents to accuse him of weakness," he explained.
Gaza remains central to Netanyahu's political calculations
Ramallah-based political analyst Esmat Mansour similarly linked the continuation of Israeli attacks during the ceasefire to Netanyahu's domestic political calculations.
He told TNA that Netanyahu was seeking to keep Gaza at the centre of Israeli political debate and prevent the war from being overshadowed by questions about domestic accountability and the failures surrounding the 7 October attacks.
"Netanyahu is facing a crisis linked to the failures of October 7," Mansour said, arguing that the prime minister is attempting to recast himself as a leader engaged in an "ongoing war" rather than one facing scrutiny over the political and security failures that preceded it.
With elections approaching, Mansour said, security is likely to remain one of the most important issues for Israeli voters.
"The electoral battle will not merely be about who ends the war, but about who can present themselves to Israelis as the most capable of ensuring security," he added.
For Netanyahu, maintaining pressure on Gaza could therefore serve a dual purpose: keeping the security issue at the heart of the campaign while strengthening his position among right-wing voters.
But Mansour cautioned that the strategy also carries political risks.
An escalation that results in further Israeli military casualties or generates stronger international criticism could ultimately damage Netanyahu rather than strengthen him, he said.
For Palestinians in Gaza, however, the political calculations in Israel continue to have deadly consequences.

South Africa's president calls for independent AI oversight mechanism under BRICS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:35:02 UTC
21:35:02 KST

Busra Nur Cakmak
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa on Sunday called for BRICS to establish an international mechanism for the independent scientific evaluation of artificial intelligence, warning that technological capabilities must not advance beyond humanity's ability to understand and control them.
Speaking at the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Ramaphosa said AI could usher in a new era of productivity and human progress, but warned of risks associated with increasingly powerful systems.
"The capabilities of artificial intelligence models are becoming increasingly more powerful and are rapidly reshaping almost every area of economic and social life," he said.
If used "effectively and responsibly," AI could help reduce inequality, poverty, and underdevelopment, and transform medicine, education, scientific discovery, and agricultural productivity, he added.
Ramaphosa, however, said governments should pay close attention to warnings coming from those developing the world's most powerful AI systems.
He cited risks, including advanced cyber operations, assistance in biological weapons development, autonomous action, manipulation, mass surveillance, and disruption of employment, as well as the possibility of systems whose capabilities become difficult for humans to control.
"We should therefore neither fear AI nor approach it recklessly," Ramaphosa said. "Our responsibility is to ensure that human governance advances as rapidly as artificial intelligence itself."
The South African president specifically backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for greater external oversight of AI developers.
"We agree with those in the industry, in the AI industry, that is, such as Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, who are arguing that AI companies should be subject to formal external checks, to audits and to government authority," he said.
Ramaphosa said such oversight is already standard practice in industries whose activities have significant implications for human safety and well-being, citing aviation, pharmaceuticals, nuclear power, and financial institutions.
"We must never reach a situation where technological capability has moved beyond our capacity to understand it, supervise it and control it," he said.
Ramaphosa proposed that BRICS establish an international mechanism for the independent scientific evaluation of AI, backed by "meaningful human control principles" and mandatory reporting of serious incidents.
He also called for progressively stronger safeguards as AI capabilities increase, alongside investment in sovereign AI capacity for developing economies.
Ramaphosa welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping's proposal to establish an AI ecosystem for BRICS, saying South Africa supports the initiative.

Surging inflation puts interest rates back in focus as policymakers meet in Japan, US and UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:33:16 UTC
21:33:16 KST

Central bankers in economies including the US, Japan and the UK will face a moment of truth this week, as surging inflation raises the prospect of higher interest rates.
Policymakers in all three countries will set rates in the next seven days against the backdrop of turbulent global bond markets.
In particular, investors will be watching closely to see if Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the US Federal Reserve, can face down Donald Trump’s demands for rate cuts and instead persuade Fed governors to raise them on Wednesday.
Warsh was handpicked by the US president, who has repeatedly demanded lower interest rates. In a Truth Social post this month, Trump claimed the US should have the “LOWEST RATE of any country in the World”.
He added: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.”
However, the central bank’s board of governors is having to contend with a renewed rise in oil prices after the US-Iran conflict intensified again.
The cost of a barrel of crude surged past $100 last week for the first time since July, as the strait of Hormuz remained all but closed to tanker traffic and Houthi rebels advanced along the Red Sea coast, threatening to choke off Saudi oil supplies.
Oil prices eased slightly on Friday amid hopes of fresh talks to reopen the waterway but remained well above levels in the summer, when Middle East hostilities temporarily abated.
Higher energy costs are expected to feed a fresh rise in US inflation, which has been above the Fed’s 2% target for more than five years. In a speech this month, Warsh said without continued progress towards the target, Fed policymakers would have “work to do”. Data published on Friday showed annual US inflation unchanged at 3.4%.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England governor, has struck a calm note about above-target inflation in the UK, saying rising mortgage rates have done some of the work of a rate rise without the Bank taking action. Markets and economists are predicting the Bank will hold rates at 3.75% on Thursday.
However, three of the nine members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for a rate rise in July, and data published on Friday showing stronger-than-expected economic growth could amplify fears about inflation.
Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at RSM, a consultancy firm, said the latest rise in energy prices had “materially increased the chance that the MPC will eventually follow other major central banks and raise rates”.
But he predicted a “hawkish hold” from the Bank when the MPC convenes on Thursday: a decision to leave rates unchanged, but with the published minutes pointing to potential future rises.
Financial markets are betting on four UK rate rises over the next 12 months – up from the three they were expecting before the latest surge in oil prices.
In Tokyo, Bank of Japan (BoJ) policymakers will announce their decision on Friday and are widely expected to raise interest rates, validating the recent recovery of the yen on foreign exchanges.
A quarter-point increase in the BoJ’s policy rate, to 1.25%, would take it to levels not seen for more than 30 years, since Japan first began fighting an extended battle against deflation, or falling prices.
The US Treasury joined Japanese authorities in intervening in foreign exchange markets to support the yen in July and Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, has made it clear that he expects rates to rise.
At an event at Southern Methodist University in Texas on Tuesday, Bessent said: “When we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do. I have asymmetric information. I am the house now. You can bet against me if you want.”
The European Central Bank raised interest rates on Thursday. Christine Lagarde, its president, said: “The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period.”

ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's government forces said Sunday that more than 500 soldiers were killed and about 1,500 wounded in month-long battles with the Houthis along the western coast, as the group mounted a sweeping advance toward the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
In a statement carried by Al-Joumhouriya TV, the government's National Resistance Forces said the casualties were recorded between Aug. 9 and Sept. 10, while claiming that more than 1,000 Houthi members were killed and thousands wounded. The figures could not be independently verified.
The statement said the fighting began with Houthi missile, drone and explosive-boat attacks before expanding from Hays in the southern part of the Red Sea province of Hodeidah to several fronts in neighboring southwestern Taiz province.
The casualties came amid a sweeping Houthi offensive launched on Sept. 3 that rapidly redrew front lines along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with the group capturing several government-held areas in Hodeidah province and neighboring Taiz province.
The Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday before pushing south on Friday into the Bab al-Mandab area and seizing Mayun Island at the heart of the strait, tightening their grip on the vital shipping chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Houthi forces subsequently advanced farther south toward neighboring Lahj province, where retreating government forces had regrouped, bringing the fighting closer to Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

Feature: Rooftop terraces lift Beijing urban renewal to new heights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:19:22 CST
21:19:22 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- "If you think you've seen Beijing, you haven't been here yet," Elizaveta, a Russian woman who has lived in China for seven years, wrote on her social media account.
The "here" she refers to is a rooftop terrace atop a commercial building on the site of the original Longfu Temple, a 15th-century Buddhist landmark. Now part of a vibrant cultural hub, the terrace offers one of Beijing's most compelling vantage points, where history and modernity meet beneath the skyline.
To the east, Beijing's glass-and-steel skyline rises against the horizon. To the west lies the older city, with the glazed roofs of the Palace Museum glistening, the forested slopes of Jingshan Hill stretching and the white pagoda of Beihai Park standing gracefully in the distance.
"For a moment," Elizaveta wrote, "I really feel like I'm standing at the edge of two eras."
The terrace reflects a broader citywide shift. Earlier this year, Beijing issued a plan for high-quality urban development, vowing to make better use of historic streets and industrial heritage, upgrade key commercial districts, and create new consumption scenarios. The initiative is part of a national drive to turn 1,500 old neighborhoods and industrial districts into new engines of consumption and culture by 2030.
Subject to building height limits, Beijing's central areas preserve a low skyline defined by iconic imperial red walls, yellow-tiled roofs and traditional alleys, where residents still live amid dense greenery. These open vistas offer visitors ample opportunities to appreciate the city's distinctive architectural heritage.
Amid urban renewal efforts, Beijing's Dongcheng district, home to many of the capital's most treasured historic sites and blocks of siheyuan, or quadrangle courtyards, launched in 2025 a "Breeze Terrace" initiative to turn idle rooftops into public gathering spaces.
Government, residents and merchants have worked together to bring in viewing decks, reading corners, dining spaces and craft workshops. According to planners, the idea is to let people see the city from a different angle without major demolition or construction.
Since its launch, the initiative has drawn more than 1 million visits. This summer, it added about 300 terraces across the district, linked by four themed routes covering Central Axis vistas, hutong discoveries, literary corners and night tours.
Chen Shiqi, an influencer who scouts shops and restaurants for his followers, called terraces "one of the surest ways to go viral" on Chinese social media. Comparing his own posts on Xiaohongshu, a popular Chinese lifestyle-sharing app, he found that using terrace photos as cover images consistently draws more readers.
Over the past year, about 30 to 40 percent of the spots Chen has reviewed have been rooftop venues. Sometimes when he doesn't name the location, followers message him privately to ask where it is.
Chen's observation points to a broader trend of the social media era. Visitors no longer simply experience a view. They photograph and share it, and rooftop terraces, with their sweeping backdrops and curated aesthetics, serve that purpose perfectly.
Yet all of this would be unthinkable without the blue skies above. Beijing's anti-pollution campaign, launched in 2013, has cut the annual average of PM2.5, the fine particles linked to respiratory disease, from 89.5 micrograms per cubic meter to 27 last year, a sharp drop of nearly 70 percent. "Beijing blue," once a novelty worth a social media post, has become the background of daily life.
In addition, Beijing's temperate climate and relatively low rainfall provide more clear-sky days for rooftop outings than many other major Chinese cities -- Shanghai included -- giving the city a natural edge for its growing terrace economy.
On a rooftop garden of the Jinbao Place shopping mall, visitors can join sunset yoga, pick herbs, attend moonlit cocktail parties, try on Hanfu, or even hold a wedding. The once-forgotten space has become a vibrant consumer destination.
"Rooftop terraces, as a key setting for urban renewal, hold great potential to nurture new consumption, improve public spaces and revitalize the old city's cultural heritage," said Xing Yan, deputy chief planner at the Beijing Tsinghua Tongheng urban planning and design institute.
The next step, Xing added, is to extend Beijing's urban renewal efforts across the ground level, building facades, and rooftops, unlocking greater value from the city's existing space.
The growing appeal of these rooftop spaces makes them a must-visit for Chen and his photography-obsessed friends.
"The only problem," Chen said with a laugh, "is that my friends are so obsessed with getting the perfect shot that they can easily spend an hour taking photos."
"Sometimes the food gets cold, and we have to ask the waiter to reheat it!" ■

Jilin University team develops deep Earth exploration system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:19:19 CST
21:19:19 KST

Professor Wang Yanzhang (C) discusses with doctoral students at a laboratory of Jilin University in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Sept. 8, 2026. Professor Wang Yanzhang, the executive deputy director of the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Exploration and Imaging at Jilin University, and his team have been deeply engaged in the field of deep Earth exploration for over a decade.
The team has developed an integrated exploration system combining airborne electromagnetic surveying with SERF magnetometry. Their self-developed helicopter-borne electromagnetic equipment acts like a "CT scanner for the Earth," revealing underground geological structures, while SERF magnetometers detect minute variations in the Earth's magnetic field. Together, the technologies make underground rock formations, mineral resources and geological hazards measurable and visible.
Since 2021, the team has conducted airborne exploration in various areas of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and Qinghai Province, acquiring subsurface geological information by penetrating ground surface to depths of over one kilometer. The technological advances have significantly enhanced the efficiency, depth and precision of deep resource exploration in China. (Xinhua/Zhang Nan)

Protests reported in Syria amid fuel price hikes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:19:12 CST
21:19:12 KST

DAMASCUS, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Protests and transport disruptions were reported in parts of Syria on Sunday following sharp increases in fuel prices, which authorities attributed to rising international costs, heavy dependence on imports and the shutdown of a major refinery for maintenance.
The Britain-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported protests, road blockages and a strike by some public transport drivers in several areas, particularly in the northeastern provinces of Hasakah and Deir al-Zour. Demonstrations and road disruptions were also reported in parts of Raqqa province.
The protests came hours after new temporary prices took effect at midnight, with diesel recording the steepest increase.
Under the new pricing bulletin, diesel rose 40 percent from 125 new Syrian pounds (about 1.03 U.S. dollars) to 175 pounds per liter. The price of 95-octane gasoline increased 28.3 percent to 195 pounds per liter, while 90-octane gasoline climbed 25.9 percent to 185 pounds.
Abdul Hamid Sallat, a media official with Syria's energy authorities, told the state-run Syrian Arab News Agency on Sunday that the authorities recognized that the increases would place an additional burden on Syrians already struggling with difficult living conditions and low incomes.
However, he said Syria's heavy reliance on imported energy products meant domestic prices could not be insulated from international market fluctuations. He said Syria currently produces around 100,000 barrels of crude oil per day, covering only about one-third of domestic demand. ■

At least 6 dead in Indonesia passenger vessel accident, with 130 missing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:18:56 CST
21:18:56 KST

JAKARTA, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- At least six people have died after a passenger vessel lost contact in Indonesia's Java Sea, while 130 remain missing and 107 others have been rescued, the country's National Search and Rescue Agency said Sunday.
Indonesian Minister of Transportation Dudy Purwagandhi said at a press conference later Sunday afternoon that, based on observations by a helicopter crew, the vessel had capsized but had not sunk. The cause of the accident remains under investigation.
The country's search and rescue agency had earlier said that the vessel had sunk.
The Chinese Consulate General in Surabaya confirmed to Xinhua that there were no Chinese nationals aboard the ship, citing information verified with relevant authorities of the Surabaya city government.
The passenger ship, Virgo Transport 8, was carrying 243 people when it lost contact at around 2:00 a.m. local time on Sunday after encountering bad weather, according to the search and rescue agency.
The vessel had departed from Surabaya in East Java province on Saturday and was heading to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province.
The cause of the accident remains unclear. Indonesian search and rescue authorities have deployed personnel, ships and a helicopter to waters near the vessel's last known position to conduct search and rescue operations.
Indonesia, an archipelagic country with around 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries and other forms of sea transportation to connect its islands and facilitate travel. Maritime accidents occur from time to time due to factors including weather conditions, sea conditions and vessel safety. ■

Le Pen in Hénin-Beaumont stronghold for damage control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:56:28 UTC
20:56:28 KST

It comes amid reported friction between Le Pen and Jordan Bardella, the president of the National Rally party.
Back in her political stronghold in northern France, Marine Le Pen is delivering her first major campaign speech this Sunday.
The far-right candidate for 2027 is relaunching her presidential election campaign in Hénin-Beaumont, following a gathering of her party’s MPs in Le Touquet (Pas-de-Calais) on Saturday.
Le Pen is leading in the polls, with 34% of voters signalling their intention to vote for her in the first round, regardless of the scenario, according to a survey carried out on 8 and 9 September by OpinionWay for Les Échos.
Despite this, recent weeks have been marked by a series of mishaps, amid alleged tension with the president of the National Rally (RN) party, Jordan Bardella, controversy over aid to Ukraine and the release of a video in which a police officer, a volunteer member of the RN’s security team, makes racist, sexist and conspiracy-theory-based remarks.
Meanwhile, Le Pen has still not reacted to the signing of an immigration pact between Bardella and Nigel Farage, the leader of the UK's hard-right, anti-immigration Reform UK party, which provides for migrants intercepted in British waters to be sent back to France if the two parties come to power.
What role will Bardella play?
Rumours are multiplying about alleged tensions between Le Pen and Bardella, the candidate for the post of prime minister.
According to the French daily Libération, the president of the National Rally is said to have declared "it’s her or me" on 31 August, while Le Pen is reported to have announced her intention to give a greater role in the campaign to her niece, Marion Maréchal, starting with a speech at the RN's parliamentary gathering in Le Touquet.
During the 2022 presidential campaign, Maréchal backed Éric Zemmour, the leader of the rival far-right party Reconquête, rather than her aunt.
Bardella has denied any tensions, telling the French broadcaster BFM-TV: "Everything is going very, very well, I assure you. I support her 2,000%."
He added that he had an "unbreakable political and personal affinity" with Le Pen while also denying that he wanted to "impose" his line on the party.
The fundamental differences between the two leading figures of the National Rally are mainly about economic policy, especially pensions.
According to Bardella, the current French pension system "is not economically sustainable."
He also seems hesitant to have his "boss" turn her proposed ban on the wearing of the veil in public spaces into a central campaign issue.
On 31 August, he insisted that the aim was not "to impose a dress code," stressing that a referendum on the issue would be held.
The president of the Patriots for Europe group in the European Parliament also appears more pro-market than Le Pen, who has traditionally been more supportive of protectionist measures.
Support for Ukraine
Beyond this, the RN is also facing disagreements over international issues.
Appearing on BFM-TV on 4 September, Louis Aliot, the party’s vice-president and mayor of Perpignan, was asked about aid to Ukraine.
"We turn off the tap. The health system, the education system, the whole economy, everything has been cut to the bone, and yet we still find money to fund more weapons (...) I’m willing to accept that, but who pays for all this? You also have to know how to stop a war," he said.
His comments quickly sparked a debate.
On X, Édouard Philippe, the centre-right Horizons party’s candidate for 2027, seized the opportunity to accuse the RN of "its support for Putin’s regime," arguing that "turning off the tap for Ukraine means serving Russia."
"Weakening Ukraine, as Marine Le Pen wants, means threatening the security of Europe and France. I will do everything to stop her," he added.
Le Pen hit back within the hour, reminding the former prime minister that he was in office when the Russian president was "received with great pomp at the Palace of Versailles and then at the Fort of Brégançon," and that he himself had welcomed Dmitry Medvedev, then Russian prime minister, to his home city of Le Havre in June 2019.
National Rally grapples with police scandal
On 8 September, French regional daily Midi Libre released a video from November 2025 showing several municipal police officers in Carcassonne making racist, sexist and conspiracy-related comments during a nighttime patrol.
The patrol leader, responsible for nearly 90% of the remarks made that evening, is a former paratrooper, but he had also volunteered for the RN's internal security service.
He notably escorted Bardella on several trips, including during the promotional tour for his book, as well as at the launch of the RN's municipal election campaign.
The officer in question was expelled from the National Rally on Wednesday. Bardella, for his part, has described his comments as "despicable."
The Carcassonne public prosecutor’s office also announced on Wednesday the suspension of the four municipal police officers who appear in the video.

Drugs marked with Gaddafi's face seized in Libya

Drugs marked with Gaddafi's face seized in Libya
CAIRO, Sept 13 - Libyan authorities have seized a shipment of tens of thousands of ecstasy pills, each marked with the face of ousted leader Muammar Gaddafi and smuggled in from Europe, security officials said.
Images released by a security agency in Tripoli showed sacks of brown pellets that were moulded into the shape of Gaddafi's head and shoulders, with the lines of his distinctive features and robes pressed into their surface.
Libya has become a major regional transit hub for synthetic drugs and other narcotics on their way to local users and other parts of North Africa and the wider continent, according to a U.N. report released in January.
Drug gangs were taking advantage of the tumultuous situation in the country since 2011, said the report by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. That year, Gaddafi was toppled in a NATO-backed uprising, plunging Libya into a prolonged period of internal conflict and division.
Security agents got a tip-off that a gang was planning to send the drugs by sea and tracked the shipment until it arrived, read the statement issued late on Saturday from Al Rada for Combating Terrorism and Organized Crime, a security agency under the Tripoli-based Presidential Council.
Officers intercepted the shipment after it arrived and found the pills hidden in a cargo van, the statement added.
"The operation yielded a total of approximately 100,000 'XTC' (Ecstasy) pills," and a number of suspects were referred to prosecutors, it said. The pills had come via a European country and arrived at a Libyan port, the agency added, without naming either.
Tripoli's Presidential Council has acted as head of state since a U.N.-facilitated dialogue with the U.N.-recognised Government of National Unity in 2021.
Libya remains divided between the GNU in the west and authorities under military commander Khalifa Haftar, who controls the east and much of its south. REUTERS

Are you smarter than a 15-year-old? Test your maths, science and reading with these PISA questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:56:10 UTC
20:56:10 KST

This week, the OECD's PISA report has revealed a global decline in 15-year-old's maths and reading skills — but how much better can the grown-up's fare?
Every three years, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD)'s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) evaluates 15-year-olds' reading, mathematics and science abilities through a standardised test.
The latest report, published on Tuesday, has revealed a concerning global decline in maths and reading skills in particular. Artificial intelligence (AI), smartphones and social media have been cited as contributing factors.
"The bottom line is quite simple: You don't get fit by watching sports. You get fit by doing sports," Andreas Schleicher, the founder of the OECD's renowned PISA tests, told Euronews.
"And the same is true with learning. Learning doesn't come through the consumption of content; learning comes by engaging with ideas to compare and contrast. And AI can hollow out that very process. That's what we observe."
But what about the adults? Are we any better? A 2024 study by Reading Agency found that half of the adults in the United Kingdom don't read for pleasure, while a Eurostat survey from the same year found that almost half of EU citizens have not read a single book in twelve months.
It begs the question: How much better than the 15-year-olds would we all fare?
Now's your chance to see — scroll to have a go at a sample of the OECD's questions. Answers can be found at the very bottom of the page (no cheating!)
Mathematics
Question 1: Alex drew the following pattern of red and blue triangles.
The first four rows of the pattern are shown below.
What percentage of the triangles in the first four rows of Alex’s pattern are blue?
A) 37.5%
B) 50.0%
C) 60.0%
D) 62.5%
Question 2: Are the statements below supported by the information shown in the graph pictured? Answer either Yes or No for each statement.
- The number of DVDs sold declined by about 50% from 2008 through 2014
- The number of DVDs sold declined by the same amount each year from 2008 through 2014
- The slope of the line is the average yearly decline in DVDs sold from 2008 to 2014
Science
Question 1: Many people are concerned about the global environmental impacts of the manufacture and disposal of clothing.
Cotton fibres come from the outer layer of the cotton plant’s seeds. Compared to synthetic fibres, cotton fibres need less processing and biodegrade more easily.
The production of cotton textiles requires a lot of water, fertilisers, pesticides and other harmful chemicals. To try to solve these issues, sustainable cotton production methods are being developed.
Which of the following actions can be taken to reduce the negative environmental impacts of producing cotton textiles? Highlight all correct answers.
- Use water more efficiently
- Reduce the quality of the cotton textiles produced
- Increase the number of staff that cotton farms employ
- Use pesticides that are harmful only to the pest species being targeted
- Dispose of chemical waste in areas far away from the sites involved in cotton production
Question 2: When lightning strikes, an observer immediately sees a flash of light. Thunder occurs at the same time, but the observer hears it a little later.
The time taken before an observer hears thunder depends on factors including the distance between the observer and the location of the lightning strike.
Which one of the following statements best explains why lightning is seen before thunder is heard?
- The speed of light through air is faster than the speed of sound through air.
- Light does not need to travel through the air to be seen, but sound does need to travel through the air to be heard.
- Particles of light are not as heavy as particles of sound, so they are easier to detect
- Eyes detect light faster than ears detect sound
Reading
Question 1: In this test, you will read some sentences and decide if they make sense or not. Answer YES if the sentence makes sense and NO if the sentence does not make sense.
- The red car had a flat tire
- Airplanes are made of dogs
- The student read the book last night
Question 2: You are visiting your relatives, who recently moved to a farm to raise chickens. You ask your aunt, “How did you learn how to raise chickens?”
She says, “We talked to a lot of people who raise chickens. And, there are lots of resources on the Internet. For example, there is a Chicken Health forum that I like to visit. It was very helpful to me recently when one of my hens hurt her leg. I’ll show you the conversation I had.”
What does Ivana_88 want to know?
- If she can give aspirin to an injured hen
- How often she can give aspirin to an injured hen
- How to contact a veterinarian about an injured hen
- If she can determine the pain level of an injured hen
Financial literacy
Greg buys a bike.He takes out a loan with the bike shop's in-store finance company.How much is Greg likely to pay?
- Less than 600 zeds
- More than 600 zeds
- Exactly 600 zeds
Answers:
Mathematics 1. A, 2. Yes, No, Yes.
Science 1. ’Use water more efficiently’ and ‘Use pesticides that are harmful only to the pest species being targeted'. 2. ‘The speed of light through air is faster than the speed of sound through air.’
Reading 1. Yes, No, Yes. 2. “If she can give aspirin to my hen”.
Financial literacy 1. The second response or third response with explanation that Greg will pay additional charges.

Scholar says Abe reshaped Japan’s Taiwan policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:51:31 UTC
20:51:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Japanese Prime Minister Abe Shinzo left one of the most important strategic legacies in Taiwan-Japan relations, Lai I-chung (賴怡忠), president of the Prospect Foundation, said Sunday.
Abe’s statement that a contingency for Taiwan is a contingency for Japan and for the US-Japan alliance changed the way Japan views Taiwan, Lai said, per CNA. This shift in thinking has gradually become a key foundation for Japan’s political discussions on the Taiwan Strait, he added.
Lai said that in the past, Japan often viewed Taiwan “through the lens of China.” Japanese government officials handling Taiwan affairs were mostly from the so-called “China School,” with expertise in China.
Taiwan also tended to position itself within the Japan-China-Taiwan framework, seeking to compete with China for Japan’s support, according to Lai. He said that after the DPP first came to power in 2000, Taiwan elevated its framework to “US-Japan-Taiwan.”
Lai also cited TSMC’s investment in Kumamoto as an example of structural changes in Taiwan-Japan economic ties. “It is no longer just Japan supporting us; we are also able to help Japan,” he said.
While the two peoples share goodwill and maintain close exchanges in disaster relief, tourism, and culture, security and strategic cooperation between their governments remain limited, Lai said.
He suggested that Taiwan and Japan should set clear, measurable shared goals. For example, the two countries could set targets for bilateral investment and define the level of cooperation in scientific research and advanced technology following TSMC’s investment in Japan.

Israeli troops call for 'conquest of Damascus' amid continued attacks on Syrian territory
Israeli reservists have called for the military to expand its illegal operations deeper into Syrian territory, with a senior officer saying many troops would favour advancing as far as Damascus, according to Israeli media.
Reserve officers serving with the Israeli army's 210th Division have criticised limits on the scope of its operations in southern Syria and called for increased activity inside Syrian villages and surrounding areas, Israeli news site Walla reported.
The officers reportedly argued that deeper incursions would help push what Israel considers potential threats further away from its border.
A senior Israeli officer defended the military's current approach but acknowledged the appetite among reservists for a more wide-scale invasion of Syria.
"Would the reservists like to conquer Damascus? Many of them would," Walla quoted the officer as saying.
The issue was also raised during a visit by Israeli military chief of staff Eyal Zamir around two weeks ago, according to the report.
The officer said reservists deployed to Syria often arrived after serving in Gaza and Lebanon, where the operational environment was significantly different.
"What is happening today in Syria is beyond anything we imagined and any activity we thought of - the activity is non-stop," he said.
Israel currently operates from 10 military positions inside Syrian territory, according to Walla, conducting operations around the clock based on intelligence and military assessments.
The report said Israeli forces have conducted raids well beyond the immediate border area, singling out Beit Jinn in the western Damascus countryside, around 11 kilometres from the occupied Golan Heights.
The senior officer said some reservists wanted to reach Beit Jinn "every day", saying that 14 militants had been killed in three separate Israeli raids in the area.
The comments come amid continuing Israeli military operations around Beit Jinn and elsewhere in southern Syria.
Israeli forces carried out a series of incursions in the Damascus and Quneitra countrysides on Saturday, sources told The New Arab.
An Israeli force comprising two tanks, a bulldozer and more than 10 other vehicles entered agricultural land surrounding the Beit Jinn farm area in the western Damascus countryside, according to the sources.
Another force of three military vehicles entered an area west of Saida al-Hanout in the Quneitra countryside, while four Israeli military vehicles entered the town of al-Rafid, where soldiers searched several homes.
Israeli forces also fired an artillery shell at agricultural land in the Ain al-Shaara area near Beit Jinn following similar shelling overnight.
Israeli military operations have become increasingly frequent in southern Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime in December 2024.
Israel moved troops into the UN-patrolled buffer zone separating the two countries following Assad's fall and has since established military positions and carried out raids, arrests and strikes deeper inside Syrian territory.
Syria and the United Nations have said Israel's deployment violates Syrian sovereignty and the 1974 Disengagement Agreement governing the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces.
France on Friday called for Israeli troops to withdraw from Syrian territory, while reiterating its support for efforts to reach a security agreement between Damascus and Israel.
The French foreign ministry told Syria's official SANA news agency that any military deployment within the separation zone constitutes a violation of the 1974 agreement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has condemned Israel's violations of Syrian sovereignty, saying Damascus had received support from more than 40 countries at the UN Security Council.
He reaffirmed Syria's territorial integrity and said it would continue defending its rights through "all legitimate political and diplomatic means".
A UN commission investigating Syria said earlier this week that Israeli military activity in the country's south had become "increasingly sustained and entrenched", warning that some Israeli actions could amount to war crimes.

Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

Russians on the Goethe-Institut: 'Hostage to politics'
September 13, 2026
Germany's Goethe-Institut is set toclose all Russian branches by Sunday, amid one of the worst spats in the history of relations between Russia and Germany.
The Russian Foreign Ministry ordered the closure of the German cultural centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Novosibirsk in response to Berlin's reaction to the attempteddrone attackat Leipzig airport in early August. The German authorities blamed Moscow for organizing the attack and announced sanctions. They include closing the Russian culture and education center in Berlin, known as the Russian House, and the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, as well tightening visa restrictions for Russian citizens.
"All employees must cease their work in Russia as of September 13, 2026," Goethe-Institut Secretary General Gitte Zschoch said in a statement. "No more books can be borrowed from our libraries, and no further training can be offered. German language teachers are losing an important source of professional training and support. For people in Russia, this further restricts access to the German language, culture and reliable information from and about Germany."
DW asked its users in Russia to share how the closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect them personally. The responses received do not constitute a representative survey. All users shared their stories on conditions of anonymity. Russian authorities labeled DW an "undesirable organization" making every cooperation with the media company a criminal offense.
'We'll have to travel to another country' for German exams
Many DW readers fear that, after the closure of the Goethe-Institut branches, they or their relatives will no longer be able to take exams in Russia for internationally recognized German language certificates.
Some readers pointed out that closing the Goethe-Institut in Russia will hit ethnic Germans willing to relocate back to Germany, or late repatriates, especially hard.
"I no longer live in Russia, having emigrated as a late repatriate, but my parents are still in Russia and were planning to take exams at the Goethe-Institut this fall or winter before submitting their resettlement documents. It looks like they'll have to take the exams in another country, which means additional stress and expenses for them," one reader said.
DW also received responses from parents whose children are learning German and plan to continue their education in Germany.
"My son attends a German school, and now we won't be able to take the exam in Russia. We'll have to travel to another country," one message said.
It remains unclear whether exams, language courses and educational programs will continue in Russia in another format or through partner organizations. Several readers expressed hope that at least some services will remain available online.
Goethe-Institute closures hit teachers hard
The closure of the institute will affect not only those planning to move to Germany or enroll at a German university. A German language teacher from the Moscow region told DW that her school had cooperated with the Goethe-Institut for more than 15 years.
"This partnership was one of the most important pillars of our work. The institute supported us with high-quality teaching materials and provided modern books and publications about life in Germany, helping us make lessons engaging and relevant. Our students attended additional courses, and many successfully passed the Goethe certificate exams," she wrote.
"I teach German and can't find a job in Russia," another teacher told DW.
"It's terrible. I'm a German teacher, and I feel professionally stranded and lost," a third wrote.
Despite the restrictions imposed since the beginning of Russia's war in Ukraine in 2022, demand for the institute's services remained high. According to the Goethe-Institut, around 10,000 people studied German through its programs and partnerships in 2025. Before 2023, that number used to stand at around 16,000 people. The institute administered roughly 22,000 exams, and its libraries were visited by 6,700 people in 2025.
'Culture has become a hostage to political decisions'
Many readers perceive what is happening as another stage in the destruction of ties between Russia and Germany.
"We would like cultural relations between the Russian Federation and Germany not to be destroyed," one DW user responded. "It is sad to realize that culture has become a hostage to political decisions. The closure of the Goethe-Institut will affect people who have no way of influencing politicians."
Some DW readers from Russia specifically draw attention to the responsibility of politicians. One reader called the decision to close the institutes another step toward isolating the country and wondered why its consequences affect ordinary citizens rather than the Russian politicians who make such decisions.
"Why can the people making decisions to isolate Russia from Europe simultaneously provide their own children and close relatives with a European education and a European way of life?" a DW user asked, proposing a ban on the education of the children and close relatives of members of Russia's top leadership at universities in Germany and other EU countries.
Part of the audience considers Moscow's decision expected.
"The closure of the branches looks like a logical response to the closure of the Russian House in Germany. Could it have been otherwise? It is a pity that cultural and humanitarian ties between the countries are becoming hostages to politics," one reader wrote.
Some Russians hold Germany responsible for deteriorating relationship
Some Russians however believe that closing the Goethe-Institut branches in Russia was the right step and blame Germany for the recent escalation of the conflict with Russia.
"German authorities have buried cultural cooperation with Russia by shutting down the Russian House. The responsibility lies entirely with the German side, " said one of the survey participants.
A bilateral intergovernmental agreement between Russia and Germany from 2011 regulates the work of the Russian House in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut's branches in Russia. It obliges both countries, on the basis of reciprocity, to ensure conditions necessary for the operation of their cultural centers. However, it does not in any way provide for the automatic closure of one country's cultural centers in response to the other country doing so.
President of the Goethe-Institut Gesche Joost called the closure of its branches in Russia "the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations."
According to its website, the Goethe-Institut has 154 branches in 100 countries. This number includes the three branches in Russia that are now being closed.

Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:49:26 UTC
20:49:26 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
A Russian-linked hacking operation used Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence models to automate cyberespionage targeting Ukrainian government officials, military personnel, diplomats, defense companies, and drone technology suppliers, with more than 20 organizations identified as targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a threat intelligence report published by Anthropic on September 10, the company tracked the group as GTG-20006 and said its attribution was consistent with public reporting linking the activity to Midnight Blizzard, a Russian state-linked hacking group.
Anthropic said the hackers used customized AI-driven workflows to automate much of the attack process, including reconnaissance, acquiring infrastructure, phishing, maintaining access to compromised systems, and extracting stolen information.
The company identified more than 20 organizations targeted during planning, reconnaissance, or active operations. They included government ministries, intelligence and defense agencies, diplomatic missions, think tanks, and defense companies, primarily in Ukraine and Europe.
Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic personnel were among the most frequent targets. The group scanned email and remote-access systems belonging to more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations, according to Anthropic.
Drone technology was another major focus. The hackers exported mailboxes belonging to at least two drone component manufacturers, targeted a military drone producer, and stole a proprietary software development kit used for a drone vision system.
Anthropic said the attackers spent several days reverse-engineering the stolen software, reconstructing the system’s architecture, hardware components, supplier dependencies, and details of an unreleased product. Firmware related to military drone control and AI-based vision systems appeared to be of particular interest.
Claude was also incorporated into malware development and evasion. Anthropic found that AI agents monitored whether security software detected the group’s malicious programs. When a tool was flagged, the system could identify the affected component, modify it, rebuild the malware, and repeat the process until existing security products no longer detected it.
The hackers also used AI to research and register domains, configure phishing infrastructure, send malicious emails, monitor successful compromises, harvest credentials, and move through victims’ networks.
According to Anthropic, Claude assisted with processing and organizing hundreds of gigabytes of stolen information, including bulk exports from compromised email accounts. The AI was also used to help preserve access to infiltrated systems and automatically register attacker-controlled devices inside compromised organizations.
The operation sometimes targeted organizations connected to intended victims rather than attacking them directly. Anthropic said the hackers compromised at least three companies providing hotel guest Wi-Fi services and changed DNS records to redirect connected devices toward infrastructure controlled by the attackers.
The technique allowed the group to collect information about hotel guests and deliver malware to Windows, Android, and iOS devices. Individuals connected to Ukraine, including government officials and drone manufacturers, were among the targets.
The hackers also targeted WhatsApp accounts by linking attacker-controlled devices to victims’ profiles. Using automation tools, they suppressed read receipts while exporting conversations in Ukrainian and Russian. Anthropic said at least two former senior Ukrainian officials were targeted through the method.
In another part of the operation, the group exploited authorization weaknesses in video surveillance services to obtain tokens providing access to victims’ live camera feeds.
The same actor was linked by Anthropic to an intrusion into a North African government technology agency, where hackers stole a database containing more than 300,000 national identity records and commercial registry information covering more than half a million companies.
Russian-linked hackers have also been tied to major cyberattacks against Western companies. In June, The New York Times reported that Russian hackers were behind the 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover, which halted production for five weeks and caused an estimated $2.5 billion in damage to the UK economy.

France climbs down in social media row with U.S. after ambassador’s appointment blocked
The appointment of French diplomat Aurélien Lechevallier as France’s envoy to Washington stalled following a diplomatic dispute between France and the U.S.
BRUSSELS — France has defused a social media row with the U.S. after an online spat over voting in the U.N. General Assembly reportedly led to the delay in the confirmation of Paris’ envoy to Washington.
In a statement on Friday reported by AFP, France’s mission to the U.N. in Geneva made amends for an online remark it posted in July questioning Washington’s commitment to human rights. “France and the United States recently adopted divergent positions during a vote at the United Nations General Assembly. This divergence concerned a single vote and did not relate to the defense of human rights,” the statement read.
“Differences in public opinion on a vote do not impede close dialogue with the United States and do not call into question our historic alliance, nor our ability to work together to promote peace, stability and prosperity, including within multilateral forums.”
Advertisement
AFP reported that the U.S. State Department responded positively to the apology. “We take note of France’s statement and appreciate it; we look forward to collaborating with them to promote our common values and interests,” a State Department official told AFP on condition of anonymity.
The appointment of French diplomat Aurélien Lechevallier as ambassador to the U.S. was blocked by Washington as a result of the spat, France24 reports.
The dispute began in July when the French mission to the U.N. in Geneva posted on X that “The U.S. used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore.” This comment came after the U.S. voted against renewing the term of the UN Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk.
Two days later after the French mission’s social media post, the U.S. walked out of a U.N. security council meeting when France’s representative began to speak.
The apology from France and acceptance from the U.S. paves the way for Lechevallier to be confirmed for the Washington role. Currently chief of staff to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, Lechevallier is set to replace Laurent Bili as France’s U.S. envoy.
It’s not the first time the two countries have had a diplomatic spat. Last year, France summoned U.S. Ambassador Charles Kushner after he published an open letter accusing President Emmanuel Macron’s government of not doing enough to combat rising antisemitism in his country.

Only slim chance government will meet target of building 1.5m homes, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:23:10 UTC
20:23:10 KST

The government is unlikely to meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England, Angela Rayner has acknowledged, saying there was only a “slim chance” enough houses would be built before the next election.
The manifesto pledge to build 1.5m houses by the next election was a “stretch target”, the communities secretary added, but said it was not being ditched and she was “definitely not giving up”.
The government’s target has been significantly hampered by inflation owing to the US war with Iran. Housebuilders have cut back the number of developments despite Labour’s planning reforms which were hoped to increase the numbers of new homes.
Rayner, who returned to the role after Andy Burnham became prime minister, acknowledged for the first time on Sunday that she could miss the target.
She told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “It’s a slim chance, but I’m definitely not giving it up. I think it’s really important that we keep a target that it was always a stretch target.”
Rayner said Burnham’s main focus was now on building council houses, suggesting that was taking priority over efforts to increase the overall target.
“The prime minister wants us to make sure we’re building council houses. He’s made that absolutely, fundamentally clear,” she said. “We’ve just announced £10bn into a social and affordable homes programme. We’re seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference.
“But the headwinds that are coming our way internationally and through those construction costs are having a negative effect on that target.”
Burnham recently backtracked on plans for cash from the 10-year affordable homes programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which he had suggested he was minded to do. Instead the £10bn will be spent on the mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.
The funds will build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing. London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.
Ministers are keen to find other ways to relax regulations for private sector builders, including instructing councils to give a “default yes” approach to housing developments that are within a reasonable walking distance of well-connected train and tram stations.

Voting under way in Sweden with far right eyeing first role in government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:17:15 UTC
20:17:15 KST

Voting is under way in Sweden in a high-stakes election that could lead to the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) entering government for the first time.
It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Polls suggest an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs.
Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (7am UK time). A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting.
Early indications of results will come at 8pm when the first exit polls are released, followed by a forecast from the broadcaster SVT an hour later. The first preliminary vote count is expected between 10.30 and 11pm. Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months.
The right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.
The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.
The rightwing coalition broke a longstanding taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.
SD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.
After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it has shifted much of the Swedish establishment to the right, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition wins, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.
SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Its controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them.
The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader, Magdalena Andersson, why she was so angry during a TV debate.
Another leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave.
Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.
“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”
Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for the Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.
The prime minister and leader of the Moderates, Ulf Kristersson, has put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused Andersson of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.
Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. The attack reportedly took place in Ukraine's Volyn region. There are not believed to have been any casualties from the incident.
"For the second day in a row, the enemy has been attacking the railways. Today in the Volyn region, two km from the border with Poland, the enemy struck the locomotive of a passenger train," Ukrzaliznytsia said on Telegram.
A tragedy was apparently averted thanks in part to an early warning. The team responsible for monitoring threats to the rail service detected the danger and alerted the train crew in good time, allowing them time to take measures to protect passengers and staff, per the company.
"We are continuing to monitor aerial threats, ensure the smooth running of trains and take every possible measure to ensure the safety of passengers and railway staff," it added.
The strike near the Polish border came as part of a broader Russian air offensive.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched more than 450 drones at Ukraine overnight, including jet-propelled drones and Banderol missile drones.
At least three people were killed and 36 people were injured in the overnight strikes.
Russian attacks also hit regions of western Ukraine bordering Poland.
The scale of the attacks meant that traffic at Polish–Ukrainian border crossings had to be temporarily restricted. Border Guard spokesperson Major Dariusz Sienicki told the PAP news agency that checks had been suspended overnight for safety reasons.
Border traffic has now returned to normal at Dorohusk, Zosin and Dołhobyczów. Processing at Hrebenne was also expected to resume.
The Border Guard did not record any direct threat at Polish crossings.
"We only received information from the Ukrainian side that a drone struck and destroyed a lorry at a distance of about 800 metres from the Jagodzin crossing," Major Sienicki said.
Russia 'knocking at the doors of the EU and NATO'
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric Russian strikes" were "not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders."
"This is Putin’s terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," he wrote on X, while also calling for further sanctions against Moscow.

Poland scrambled military aircraft
In response to the Russian attacks on western Ukraine, the Polish armed forces took steps to secure the country's airspace, with the deployment of Polish aircraft and other preventive measures.
Residents of the Lublin and Podkarpackie regions received a morning alert from the Government Centre for Security warning of a Russian air attack on Ukrainian territory and informing them about the activity of Polish military aircraft. The alert was cancelled at around 9 am, after roughly five hours.
Shortly before 10 am, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces announced that military aircraft were no longer operating in Polish airspace. It stressed at the same time that Poland's airspace had not been violated.
Poland's defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Polish defence systems had detected an early-morning attack using Geran-5 drones in western Ukraine.
"One of them struck 1 km from the border with Poland, another 5 km. The Polish airspace was guarded by F16 aircraft, helicopters, and the SAAB airborne reconnaissance aircraft. There was no breach of our border," he said.

Clad in a pale blue suit, the 59-year-old who in 2021-2022 became the first woman to serve as Sweden’s prime minister voted with her husband at a school in her home municipality of Nacka, south of Stockholm.
Opinion polls have long credited the four parties in her left-wing bloc with a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats.
But the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days of the campaign.
“It is now up to the Swedish people to decide which direction our country should take. Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats? Something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of cooperation?” Andersson told reporters after voting.
Her party, which governed the Scandinavian country for the better part of the 20th century and remains Sweden’s largest, has pledged to bolster the welfare state and help struggling households cope with rising costs.
Turnout Surges in Saxony-Anhalt State Election
‘Make Sweden great again’
Outgoing Prime Minister Kristersson has meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes’ everyday lives now that his government’s clampdown on organised crime and immigration has begun to show results.
Deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks have decreased significantly in recent years, and asylum applications are at a record low.
“We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people... to make Sweden great again,” Kristersson told AFP before the vote, borrowing US President Donald Trump’s famous catchphrase.
His three-party minority coalition cut a deal in 2022 with the Sweden Democrats giving them influence over government policy, in particular on immigration and crime, in exchange for their support in parliament.
Over the past two decades, far-right leader Jimmie Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream.
It is now hoping to enter government. Kristersson has promised the far right key cabinet posts if the right-wing wins the election.
“I think it’s a very important election this year, and hopefully a lot of people will realise that we have to change course... so that everyone will feel included in society,” store manager Linda Eriksson, 48, told AFP as she voted at a polling station.
Ingrid Rudien, a 64-year-old assistant secretary, said she hoped the country “can unite together as a nation even though we may have a close result”.
‘We’ve already won!’
Akesson was confident of victory at a final election rally on Saturday in the Swedish capital.
“We’ve already won!” the 47-year-old said to thunderous applause in Stockholm’s Kungstradgarden Park.
“Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish,” he said, surrounded by blue and yellow campaign posters blaring “Make Sweden Sweden Again”.
Agneta Andersson, a 78-year-old pensioner attending the rally, told AFP she was voting for the far right.
“Like Jimmie, I want it to be like it was when I was young, in the old Sweden. I can’t cope with all this violence in society.”
Voting stations close at 8:00 p.m. when exit polls were to be published, with the first reliable results expected several hours later.
Some eight million people are eligible to vote in the election, in a country of 10.6 million where voter turnout regularly tops 80 percent.
Around half of voters have cast their ballots in advance.
If the right wing were to win the election, the formation of a new government would be fairly straightforward.
But as the four left-wing parties are splintered ideologically, tough negotiations would be needed to form a government even if they hold a majority.

Some Dutch people are about to be more equal than others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:56:53 UTC
19:56:53 KST

Some Dutch people are about to be more equal than others
Robin Pascoe
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Earlier this month the SNBN, a foundation which lobbies for better rights for Dutch nationals who live abroad, held its annual campaign day in The Hague. The event included a panel discussion about legislation which would allow Dutch expats to retain their Dutch nationality if they adopted a second one – and which would also clear the way for more foreigners who become Dutch to keep their original passports as well.
The legislation, drawn up by D66 and the former Labour party, PvdA, has been around for almost 10 years but was dusted off again last year. It should have been debated in parliament in June but that was postponed to October. Now the debate has again been delayed – this time to December 7.
Should all the foreign nationals in the Netherlands who pay tax, contribute to society and would like to become Dutch but can’t because of practical considerations be cheering? Is the country really about to align with most of the rest of Europe and allow dual citizenship? Not at all. If the SNBN panel discussion made anything clear, it is that the VVD – part of the current coalition administration – is not in favour of allowing foreigners dual nationality at all.
Security risk
After all, as MP Bente Becker told the panel, they could be foreign agents, using their diaspora to do the work of foreign governments and posing a security risk. “If you come to the Netherlands, you have to really opt for the Netherlands,” she said. “Being a Dutch citizen,” she added, “is something very special.”
Becker made it clear that without change, her party will not support the legislation – which means, once again, it will either go on the back burner, or the part about extending dual nationality rights to foreigners will be cut out. The CDA, she said, thinks the same way.
D66 MP Jan Schoonis was extremely coy when pressed several times about whether he would be prepared to butcher his party’s bill. “We are here to talk about Dutch people abroad and that is what we are going to organise,” he told the audience. “Everything else we will talk about later.” Not exactly a promising answer.
Exceptions to the rule
I was able to get a Dutch passport while keeping my British one in the wake of Brexit because I am married to a Dutchman and have lived here for over 15 years. I am one of the lucky ones, along with the over-65s who have lived here for a long period, and children who were born here and stayed until the age of 18.
In fact, around 50% of the people becoming Dutch do so by using one of these escape clauses – known as the optieregeling. You opt in to become Dutch. The rest, however, have no choice but to go for naturalisatie and give up their original nationality – with all the problems that can entail.
Discrimination
Legal experts argue that it would be discriminatory to allow people who are originally Dutch to have more than one passport but not new Dutch nationals, and the Council of State, the government’s highest legal authority, has also said that treating people differently would conflict with the constitution.
But the debate about dual citizenship in the Netherlands is not about the legal situation. It is about the loyalty of immigrant groups. Research from 2017 by Maastricht University indicates that the Dutch themselves are more tolerant of Dutch emigrants taking on a second nationality than of immigrants to the Netherlands becoming Dutch and retaining their original one.
The situation is unlikely to have improved since then, given the further rise of the far right.
Anti-foreigner feelings
What the VVD are saying is that Dutch people who are born in the Netherlands and have Dutch parents can have two nationalities without any problem if they move abroad, but those people wishing to become Dutch need to be regarded with suspicion – they must have an ulterior, and possibly sinister, motive if they want to keep their original passports as well.
It’s indicative of the current anti-foreigner sentiment running through large chunks of Dutch society. And it’s a sad reflection on the Netherlands and its “very special” passports.
Do you want to become Dutch and are you faced with giving up your original nationality, or have you already done so? Or have you decided against such a step? We’d like to hear your stories for an article. Please have your say on our social media channels or email, in complete confidence, editor@dutchnews.nl

Croatia: 'Monster' fire triggers evacuation on Brac island
September 13, 2026
Nearly 700 people were evacuated amid a wildfire on the Adriatic island of Brac, Croatian media outlets reported on Sunday, following a tense night which saw hundreds of firefighters defending homes and tourist accommodations from the approaching blaze.
The situation was especially dramatic near the small town of Milna on the island's western coast.
"Last night was a disaster. It was simply impossible," Milna Mayor Frane Lozic told Net.hr news outlet. "I would have not believed that [the fire] can wipe out everything in its path so quickly."
The fire was first reported on Thursday, but firefighting efforts were complicated by inaccessible terrain.
Even so, Lozic said that the authorities believed they had the situation in hand by Saturday.
"We thought we got it reined in yesterday, that it is all over, and then it happened: Sea wind starts blowing at 9 p.m. and out of nowhere, there is a monster," he said.
No deaths reported in blaze
Tourist ships joined the rescue efforts overnight, with many tourists spending the night at the beach, waiting to be evacuated.
No deaths were reported due to the blaze. However, one 76-year-old Croatian woman was hospitalized in critical condition, according to Index.hr news portal. The woman is believed to have fallen off a ship during the evacuation process. A 27-year-old man required medical aid for smoke inhalation and was then released.
Authorities estimated some 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) were affected by the fire, according to a report by the AFP news agency.
Officials confirmed some buildings were damaged, but said it was too early for a full damage assessment.
Firefighting planes active on the scene
As of Sunday morning, Croatian authorities said there were no more "open fires" but added teams were still in the field to prevent reignition. Four specialized firefighting planes are also operating in the area.
Two government ministers and the head of Croatia's national firefighting service are set to attend a high-level meeting on Brac this afternoon with local officials and leaders of the local firefighting teams, after which they are expected to provide more information about the blaze.
