Cycling in Switzerland twice as dangerous as in Netherlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

Cycling in Switzerland twice as dangerous as in Netherlands
The accident rate in Switzerland is twice as high as in the Netherlands when measured in terms of kilometres cycled, according to a new study.
Between 2019 and 2022, an average of 0.19 cycling accidents were recorded per 100,000 kilometres cycled in Switzerland – compared with 0.09 in the Netherlands, as shown by the analysis published in the specialist journal Journal of Safety Research.
For the study, researchers from the University of Twente in the Netherlands and the federal technology institute ETH Zurich analysed more than 86,000 police-recorded cycling accidents from 2019 to 2022 in Switzerland and the Netherlands.
The findings revealed that locations in Switzerland where cyclists encounter other road users are particularly problematic. For instance, the risk of accidents for cyclists at public transport stops in Switzerland is significantly higher than in the Netherlands, and tram tracks also prove to be accident blackspots. The risk is also significantly higher at junctions in Switzerland.
More
Cycling accidents in Switzerland rise by 50% in ten years
More cycling infrastructure, less risk
The researchers cite differences in infrastructure as a possible explanation for the higher risk of accidents in Switzerland.
According to lead author Georgios Kapousizis, bus and tram stops are a clear example of this. While in Swiss cities bicycles often ride directly past waiting buses or pedestrians, in the Netherlands cycle paths usually run behind the stops, Kapousizis explained to the Swiss News Agency Keystone-SDA. This means they do not get in the way of cars on the road or passengers getting on and off, and vice versa.
To improve road safety for cyclists, Kapousizis suggests that Switzerland could focus on the three problem areas identified in the study: public transport stops, tram tracks and junctions.
“Switzerland and many other countries do not need to reinvent the wheel,” he said. At stops, it could adopt the Dutch model; at junctions, protected cycle lanes and dedicated cycle traffic lights could help. Where tram tracks are concerned, structural solutions are needed to prevent bicycle wheels from getting caught in the rails.
Where physical separation is not possible, Kapousizis recommends lower speed limits. The study shows that on roads with a 50km/h speed limit, the probability of an accident was almost three times higher than on those with a 30km/h limit.

Chinese researchers extend future memory endurance 100-fold in semiconductor advance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:52:17 UTC
19:52:17 KST

Chinese researchers extend future memory endurance 100-fold in semiconductor advance
Restricting nitrogen-vacancy movement in wurtzite ferroelectrics looks to improve the reliability of next-generation storage, scientists find
Chinese researchers have developed a way to make an emerging type of memory chip much more durable, potentially overcoming a critical reliability barrier to its use in high-performance computing and future artificial intelligence systems as the AI boom drives demand for more advanced semiconductors.
The team demonstrated more than 10 billion writing cycles in wurtzite ferroelectrics, a class of materials that can switch between two electric states to store data. The result was roughly 100 times the endurance previously achieved with the same material and could help advance a potential next-generation memory technology, according to an online report published on Saturday by local media outlet Xian Daily.
The breakthrough looks to bring ferroelectric memory closer to practical use in future computing hardware.
The research, led by scientists at Xian-based Xidian University in collaboration with City University of Hong Kong and Fudan University, was published on Thursday in the journal Science.
In recent years, wurtzite ferroelectrics such as aluminium scandium nitride, or AlScN, have gained attention as promising next-generation memory materials because they offer rapid switching speeds and potentially low energy consumption.
Crucially, AlScN is also compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes, potentially streamlining its integration into future memory devices.
However, the material has faced a significant hurdle: deterioration after repeated electrical switching. Existing AlScN devices have typically failed after roughly 100 million writing cycles – far shy of the billions required for commercial application.

Rajasthan SET 2026: Students boycott exam in Jaipur over delayed papers, alleged irregularities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:51:35 UTC
19:51:35 KST

(Representative image): The candidates also alleged that they were asked to either enter the examination hall and remain quiet or leave when they questioned officials about the delay.
Students walked out of a Rajasthan State Eligibility Test (SET-2026) centre in Jaipur on Sunday after alleging that question papers were distributed nearly 30 minutes after the scheduled start, triggering protests and a boycott over what they described as serious exam irregularities.The disruption took place at Pink City Senior Secondary School on Bainar Road, where candidates said the exam was due to begin at 11am. They alleged that the question papers did not reach the centre until around 11.30am. Several candidates then left the centre and protested outside.The candidates also alleged that they were asked to either enter the examination hall and remain quiet or leave when they questioned officials about the delay.Anita Lamba, one of the candidates, questioned whether the same leniency would be extended to students who reached an examination centre even a minute after the gate-closing time."When we questioned the institution, they threatened us, saying that if we wanted to give the exam, we should go inside and sit quietly, or we could leave...This has been happening with children in the past, continues to happen, and will happen in the future," she told reporters.
Candidates claim exam was cancelled
The situation escalated after candidates approached the police and raised their concerns with authorities present at the centre.Lamba said that after discussions with the police, the principal showed the candidates a notice stating that "the exam is being cancelled"."We have accepted the fact that the exam is cancelled," she said.However, there was no official notification confirming cancellation of the examination at the time of reporting.Another candidate, Sania Kaval, alleged that students were repeatedly asked to wait for five or 10 minutes as they waited for the question papers to arrive. When the papers eventually came, candidates were reportedly told that they would be given additional time to compensate for the delay."The invigilator at my centre was an 11th-grade student; she was signing papers as clumsily as a toddler might scribble. We asked why the paper hadn't arrived by 11:00 AM, and they told us it was on the way, asking us to wait for five minutes, then another ten minutes. The paper still didn't arrive, and when it came ten minutes late, they said we would get extra time...we want the cancelled exam to be held again, and second, we want this centre to be cancelled," she told ANI.Candidates said they ultimately agreed to appear for the examination after raising their concerns with the authorities. However, the delay and the manner in which the situation was handled led to a boycott by students at the centre.
Exam irregularities have repeatedly triggered protests
The Jaipur episode comes against a wider backdrop of repeated complaints over the conduct of competitive and government recruitment examinations in India. Delayed papers, question-paper leaks, impersonation, technical failures and allegations of administrative lapses have repeatedly led to cancellations, re-examinations and protests by aspirants.
The Rajasthan Eligibility Examination for Teachers (REET) has previously been hit by question-paper leak allegations and other irregularities, while the state has also seen recruitment examinations disrupted by paper leaks and cheating allegations. The Rajasthan Police constable recruitment examination, for instance, had a paper leak controversy in 2022, leading authorities to cancel the affected paper and order a re-examination.For the SET candidates in Jaipur, the immediate demand is for clarity on whether Sunday's examination will stand or be cancelled. They have also demanded that the Bainar Road centre be removed from future examinations and that the test be conducted again if it is formally cancelled.

Trump’s 51st state threat backfires as Canada turns to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:34:11 UTC
19:34:11 KST

After decades in which the United States was its main economic and strategic partner, Canada is beginning to reconsider the direction it wants to take. According to The Wall Street Journal, amid the trade war, President Donald Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state and strained relations with Washington, Prime Minister Mark Carney is pursuing a significant rapprochement with Europe — including exploring a model that would allow Canada to integrate more deeply with the European Union.
According to the American newspaper, shortly after Canada and the U.S. became embroiled in a bilateral trade war, Carney began calling European leaders and asking to take Canada’s relationship with the European Union to the next level. For months, he spoke with leaders across the continent and even with members of some of Europe’s lesser-known royal families in an effort to explore how his country could become more closely integrated with the 27-member bloc.
In fact, the Journal reported, the threat to turn Canada into the 51st U.S. state pushed America’s northern neighbor so close to Europe that leaders began half-jokingly referring to it as the European Union’s newest member. According to people familiar with the matter who spoke with the American newspaper, Carney instructed his special envoy to Europe to explore the most ambitious options available, short of full EU membership.
Working groups are still hammering out the details, but Carney has even floated a new designation for Canada to European leaders: “associate member of the European Union.” Officials on both sides told the Journal that the EU, which is not known for flexibility in enforcing its membership rules, is open to the idea.
European and Canadian officials are exploring ways Canada could informally integrate into Europe’s market in areas such as energy, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and, with greater urgency, defense. In practical terms, that could eventually allow goods and workers in those sectors to move freely between Europe and Canada. According to two people familiar with discussions between Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron, they even discussed the possibility of allowing Canadians to live and work in Europe without a visa.
In the energy sector, Carney is promoting the construction of pipelines that would allow Canada to redirect to Europe gas that currently flows through the United States. Officials are also considering expanding the transportation of goods via Arctic shipping routes. The initiative comes after decades in which the Canadian economy became increasingly integrated with the U.S. economy.
The White House is betting that the two countries’ mutual dependence will draw Canada back to the negotiating table more willing to make concessions. Carney, however, believes he can fundamentally change that dynamic.
But such a new alliance would also have consequences: Canada may be reluctant to surrender any degree of sovereignty in order to integrate with the European Union. Countries that trade freely with the EU, for example, generally contribute money to its budget, accept its workers and comply with its regulations.
In private discussions, according to the Journal, some of Europe’s most senior officials have expressed concern about the challenge of reconciling Carney’s ambitions with reality. During their meetings, EU officials have tried to determine whether the Canadians are merely using Europe as leverage in their negotiations with Washington. On Thursday, Carney is expected to address the European Parliament and lay out his vision for strengthening ties with Europe.
Trade war and 'annexation' in a social media post
About two-thirds of Canadian exports currently cross the U.S. border, but two and a half weeks ago, in a sharp response to the sweeping tariffs Trump imposed on Canada, the country announced that it would impose tariffs of up to 50% on imports from the United States. The measures cover about $20 billion worth of goods and some 700 products. Tariffs of 50% will be imposed on steel, dairy products, electrical appliances and agricultural equipment, among other goods.
The previous weekend, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian goods following the collapse of talks on a trade agreement between the two countries. The Canadian tariffs took effect Sept. 8 and are expected to drive up prices for American consumers. Canada is the United States’ second-largest trading partner after Mexico. In the first half of 2026, about 14% of all U.S. exports went to Canada.
Three days after Canada’s announcement, Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America,” marking a further escalation in relations between the two countries.
“The lake change, 'Lake of America', was something I've been thinking about for a long time,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both.”
Asked why he was so intent on antagonizing Washington’s allies, Trump replied: “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They're nasty people.”
"People oftentimes they'll ask me who's the worst to deal with on trade, and I said that's easy, Canada. They are the worst to trade, and they feel entitled, and just we can't have that," he added
Over the past month, Trump has published a series of posts attacking Canada after declaring his desire to “annex Canada and make it the 51st state” and even depicting the country as part of the United States.

China, Russia, India push for inclusive global growth at BRICS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:32:41 UTC
19:32:41 KST

BRICS leaders have concluded two days of talks in New Delhi focused on inclusive global growth, after reaching a rare agreement calling for calm in the Middle East.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged cooperation within the bloc on Sunday, addressing leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The power of BRICS lies in our diversity and cooperation,” Modi said. “We have tried to push inclusive global growth.”
Putin said the bloc was working to create a “new, more just, multipolar world order”.
Xi warned that a “world without rules is like an intersection without traffic lights; chaos and disorder are inevitable”.
Modi has said the bloc represents 50 percent of the world’s population, 40 percent of global GDP and more than 25 percent of global trade.
“We may be rooted in different realities, but together we rise through cooperation and blossom for humanity,” he said.
Created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers, BRICS is seeking to expand its global role while addressing conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
'Maximum restraint'
The Middle East conflict dominated Saturday’s opening talks, with leaders, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, issuing a joint statement after intense diplomatic efforts by host India.
“We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in the Middle East/West Asia,” the statement said, calling for “maximum restraint”.
The agreement followed a failure by BRICS foreign ministers to reach a joint statement in New Delhi in May, when Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
Modi maintains relations with both Iran and US ally Israel, while carefully managing India’s ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war partly by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s full-scale war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
'Advancing together'
Xi's participation in BRICS was also important because it was his first visit to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
His visit came six years after a deadly military clash along the disputed Tibetan border between China and India, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
"Although our two countries are different in many respects, they are fully capable of complementing each other's strengths, supporting one another, achieving mutual success and advancing together," Xi said as he met Modi, according to a video released by New Delhi.
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border.
In a statement released after the meeting, India's foreign ministry said that the two leaders had expressed their commitment to finding a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution to the boundary dispute.
Deep mistrust remains, with a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry complicating ties.
"Both sides should... work hand-in-hand to promote high-quality major financial cooperation, advocate an equal and sustainable global order, and foster an economic globalisation that is open and inclusive," Xi said.
Xi's visit was the target of protests by dozens of Tibetans in New Delhi, exiles like their Buddhist leader, the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959.

2026-09-13

Reform UK’s record £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires could be caught in a new bill which will apply retrospectively, a cabinet minister has suggested.
Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week to restrict domestic donations in the elections bill after two donors – Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend.
Several MPs said they believed the government should have adopted an amendment by the Labour MP Stella Creasy to the representation of the people bill. Creasy’s amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it had the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote after the government said it would ask a taskforce to look at the proposal.
The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, said the bill would have restrictions on foreign donors and that the government was examining rules on domestic donations. The bill will go to the House of Lords this week.
The two donors who gave Reform UK £36m each have both previously been based outside the UK. Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. It is unclear when Delo returned to live in the UK and whether Harborne remains a resident of Thailand.
As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March. Reform UK has said it is confident the donations have been made within the law.
“All donations to Reform UK comply strictly with Electoral Commission rules and UK law,” a spokesperson said. “Both men are British citizens who are fully entitled to support political change in their own country, despite the establishment’s desperate attempts to silence opposition.”
The restrictions came after recommendations in a review of overseas donations by the former permanent secretary Philip Rycroft.
The government has said the rules will apply from the date the Rycroft review was published – 25 March – if donors were registered as overseas electors, or if they were not registered then it would date back to 6 July which is the date the government announced its response to the review.
Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme that the government had been clear in its intentions since the review was published and had always said the changes would be retrospective.
“We’re really clear on that. And that legislation is going through parliament at the moment. And we’ve also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy,” she said.
Rayner – the minister responsible for the bill – said it was not targeted at individual donors or parties. “I’m not going to get into individual donors and their money … People can see the 17 recommendations which the government has accepted.
“This was before these donations came through, to be fair. We didn’t know that donors were going to be putting that money in, and this isn’t about individual donors to a political party. This is an issue that has been raised about protecting our democracy from foreign interference, and the government is taking action on that.”
Reform’s economy spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the two donors were well aware of the law. He said: “[Ben Delo] has actually returned to the UK in part so that he can comply with the changes to law.
“Now, look, it might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform. Nothing would surprise me, but as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law.
“And I just say it’s a huge vote of confidence in Reform. It’s a breakthrough moment, really, for the party. It means that we will be battle ready if Andy Burnham calls an election, and we can compete now finally on a fair, even playing field with the two old parties.”

Try These 3 iOS 27 Safari Settings to Get More Out of Apple’s Browser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

At Apple’s recent hardware event, the software powering its foldable iPhone Duo stood out, with translucent Liquid Glass effects and vertically stacked icons. But you don’t need to snatch a folding smartphone to reap the benefits of Apple’s iOS 27 updates.
When iOS 27 leaves beta on Monday, Siri AI’s standalone app and smartphone search integration will likely be the most immediately obvious change for many iPhone users. But it’s worth digging even deeper to uncover helpful additions to key apps, like Apple’s Safari browser, as well as revamps to underutilized apps, like Shortcuts.
The version of Safari available in iOS 27 looks fairly similar to the last iteration, with a few key updates tucked away in the settings. These Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer (they're also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27).
Notify Me
If you’re shopping online and want a quick price-drop notification, you can use the “Notify Me” feature to scan a webpage on a certain cadence and look for changes. First, head to the page you want to track and tap the three-lined hamburger menu icon in the top right corner of Safari. About halfway down, you’ll see this option listed.
“Safari can let you know when a website updates the content you’re interested in,” reads the feature’s description. Here you’ll find an open text box where you can describe what change in content you want Safari to scan for, as well as how often you want it to check.
For example, my couch is broken, so I’ve been eyeing a few different replacement options. I have two final contenders from CB2, but both are out of my price range. So, I set up a “Notify Me” for Safari to scan the pages each day for a significant discount. Whichever one goes on sale first will likely be what I decide to get, and now I don’t have to refresh the pages manually every day.
While many other browsers have similar shopping features, like the price-tracking bell in Google Chrome, I appreciate how this feature stretches beyond just buying stuff. You can also use Safari to scan for ticket drops, privacy policy changes, and other content updates.
Describe an Extension
If you’ve experimented already with the “Describe a Shortcut” feature for iPhone automation, then “Describe an Extension” for Safari will seem familiar. It's located under the same settings menu as the “Notify Me” tool, just a little further down.
The feature asks you to type what you want the extension to do, then generates a custom option. Some of the suggested prompts in Safari revolve around boosting productivity, like “display a reading time estimate as a badge on the extension,” maintaining better focus, like “make the web page grayscale,” and more random ideas, like “show a colorful and explosive firework every time I tap.”
It took only a few seconds for each of those three examples to generate. Safari also suggests pre-made extensions during the process that could fit what you’re looking to do. As I scrolled through the internet with all three of the new extensions activated, everything worked as expected. While I’ll likely only keep the grayscale one to help me focus while reading online articles, the fireworks felt whimsical in small doses.
Organize Tabs
I am a glutton for mobile tabs, especially on Safari. I’m rarely ever exiting out of anything and always just pop open something new, which leaves me with hundreds upon hundreds of loosely connected, completely unorganized tabs—until now.
This feature is in the wider browser tab view accessible by tapping the two overlapping squares at the bottom-right corner of your screen. Swipe to a tab group brimming with websites and look for the three-lined button in the top-left. Here’s where you can choose to allow Safari to “automatically create topics” based on those tabs.
It takes a few seconds to organize everything after you activate this feature, but it did a great job of finding helpful trends in those 500+ tabs. For example, it grouped all the WIRED articles I had open and created a tab topic for upcoming San Francisco event pages and comedy clubs I was considering checking out.

Carer’s allowance scandal victims could wait until 2054 for justice, charities warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:12:47 UTC
19:12:47 KST

Unpaid carers who were pursued for bills for thousands of pounds after welfare officials unlawfully changed benefit rules could wait years before learning whether they will get the money back, campaigners have warned.
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is working through 200,000 cases where carer’s allowance benefit recipients were incorrectly given overpayments. An estimated 25,000 carers could receive full or partial refunds.
However, several months into the two-year reassessment exercise just a tiny fraction of the caseload has been processed – and at current rates charities say the project will not be completed until 2054.
Campaigners are concerned by the slow pace of progress and worry that unless it speeds up some unpaid carers may die, or become untraceable after stopping their claim for carer’s allowance, before they are repaid.
The reassessment followed an official review, which concluded systemic DWP failures caused hundreds of thousands of carer’s allowance recipients unknowingly to run up debts as high as £20,000 through no fault of their own.
The review was triggered by an award-winning Guardian investigation, which revealed how years of government neglect and mismanagement forced unpaid carers into severe financial hardship and emotional despair and resulted in hundreds of millions of pounds being misspent.
Ministers promised in December 2024 to end a scandal they consider to be an inheritance from the previous government, but nearly two years on MPs and campaigners have repeatedly expressed doubts about the speed of the response, the DWP’s appetite for change and its handling of the process.
Although the DWP has hired more staff and taken steps to try to stop overpayments, more than 30,000 more overpayments were made in 2025-26, including 78 for over £20,000. Last year official figures revealed 144,000 carers were still paying off carer’s allowance overpayment debts accrued over several years.
There was fury early this year when it emerged the DWP had slapped overpayments on 1,400 carers for allegedly breaking carer’s allowance rules, even though officials knew the decisions to issue penalties were based on faulty and discredited guidance.
The reassessment process, which started in April, is looking specifically at cases where the DWP breached the law by failing to allow carers with irregular wages from part-time work to average their incomes over a year, unfairly exposing them to being penalised for breaching earnings limits.
Last week Stephen Timms, the welfare minister, told MPs so far 3,000 cases had been reviewed as part of the £75m reassessment programme, and the DWP was on track to complete the process in the planned timescale.
Carers UK said it was concerned that, so far, just 1.5% of the total projected caseload had been processed, and at current rates the reassessment would take 27 years to complete. It is unclear whether any carers have been repaid.
“We are seriously concerned by the pace of progress of the reassessment exercise and would like to see a clear and realistic plan for speeding it up, to ensure that carers who have been wrongly given overpayments over the last decade get a swift resolution,” said Emily Holzhausen, the director of policy and public affairs at Carers UK
She added: “Many carers who are owed a refund or the writing off of their overpayment debt to DWP have already been waiting for years – some for over a decade – to get justice and fair treatment from the department.
“For those who still don’t know whether their case will be reassessed and when, a lengthy reassessment process will only compound the worry and uncertainty they are facing. We cannot risk carers being left to wait for years for a resolution to an injustice which was not their fault.”
A DWP spokesperson said: “We are on track to complete the carer’s allowance reassessment exercise within the three years previously announced.
“To support the exercise, we have been recruiting and training new Decision Makers in a rolling programme, ensuring we take the time to get things right.
“We have plans in place to increase resource at a steady pace over the course of the exercise.”

A kingdom within a republic: Inside Uganda’s Buganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:12:15 UTC
19:12:15 KST

A kingdom within a republic: Inside Uganda’s Buganda
The kingdom’s traditions and institutions have endured through colonial rule, independence and decades of upheaval
Kampala, Uganda – Uganda became independent from British colonial rule in 1962, but independence did not mean the end of its traditional kingdoms. The new republic inherited a political landscape in which old monarchies and the modern state had to find a way to exist alongside each other.
More than six decades later, that history is still visible in Buganda, where a centuries-old monarchy exists within the modern Ugandan state.
The Buganda Kingdom is headed by a king, known as the Kabaka, and has its own traditional institutions, including the Great Lukiiko, which the kingdom describes as its parliament, and an administration headed by the Katikkiro, or prime minister.
These are institutions of the kingdom, rather than of Uganda’s national government. Under Uganda’s constitution, traditional and cultural leaders cannot exercise the administrative, legislative or executive powers of the state.
Buganda says its traditional territory covers about 61,000 square kilometres (24 square miles) and is home to roughly 12 million people.
The kingdom’s own history dates its establishment to the late 14th century, while oral traditions trace its origins further back to the 13th century and the figure of Katu Kintu.
The beginnings
As written records from that era do not exist, the precise timeline of how the early chiefdoms were unified into one of East Africa’s most powerful kingdoms remains a matter of historical interpretation.
According to Ugandan historian Semakula Kiwanuka, the kingdom emerged as local clan structures gradually moved from fragile entities towards a centralised authority.
“This consolidation was not necessarily driven by economic motives,” Kiwanuka said. “Oral traditions suggest that the strongest chiefdom brought its neighbours under its authority, establishing the foundation of the kingdom.”
Buganda’s oral traditions attribute the earliest unification efforts to Kabaka [King] Katu Kintu. But Kiwanuka said Kintu’s historical existence remains unverified, as the name is also shared by a figure in Buganda folklore.
Official kingdom accounts offer another version of the kingdom’s early history.
Owek Israel Kazibwe Kitooke, Buganda’s minister of information and official spokesperson, said from the kingdom’s administrative headquarters in Kampala that Kabaka Chwa I formed an alliance of five clans in the early 14th century: The Ffumbe, Lugave, Nnonge, Njaza and Nnyonyi.
As the kingdom expanded, six additional clans joined. According to Kitooke, Kabaka Chwa brought the constituent groups together through a council of clan leaders who served as royal advisers. He said the principles established through that system later evolved into the kingdom’s constitution.
Pillars of governance
Buganda’s system of governance rests on three primary pillars, according to Kitooke.
The first is the royal lineage. According to Kitooke, the reigning Kabaka selects an heir from the royal family, who is then tutored by senior clan elders in diplomacy, statecraft and traditional customs.
The second pillar is the clan system.
Clans are identified by traditional totems drawn from the local environment, including the civet, squirrel, goat and raven. Kitooke said respect for nature and the surrounding ecosystem remains central to Buganda’s cultural identity.
The third pillar is the people.
Citizens are not excluded from the kingdom’s institutions. The Kabaka appoints ministers, leaders and officials from among the wider population, allowing subjects to serve the monarchy in leadership roles, according to Kitooke.
Islam and the colonial era
During the 19th century, Islam reached Buganda under Kabaka Muteesa I, who welcomed Arab traders from the north. According to Buganda’s historical accounts, the Kabaka regularly hosted traders at his palace and observed Ramadan in 1877 after adopting the faith.
His successor, Kabaka Mwanga II, who also embraced Islam, ruled from 1884 to 1888 and again from 1889 to 1897. Mwanga II resisted British colonial expansion and fought against imperial forces.
“The name Buganda signifies a bundle of bound sticks,” Kiwanuka said, explaining the kingdom’s endurance. “Our people hold diverse religious beliefs, Christianity, Islam and traditional religions, but they share the view that their unity is the source of their strength.”
The kingdom was placed under a British protectorate in 1894. British officials used the name “Uganda” for the wider territory, a name derived from the Swahili rendering of Buganda.
Defeated by the British, Mwanga II was captured and exiled to Seychelles, where he died in captivity. Buganda’s historical records commemorate him as a martyr king.
According to the kingdom’s oral history, the traditional men’s attire, which resembles the Arab thobe, was inspired by clothing worn by Arab merchants who visited the kingdom and developed trade relations with it.
Independence
Uganda’s self-government arrangements took effect in March 1962, before the country gained independence from Britain on October 9 that year.
Under the 1962 Independence Constitution, Buganda retained a special federal position within the new state, with certain legislative powers assigned to its government. The central government retained most legislative powers.
But the relationship between the kingdom and the central government soon became turbulent.
In 1966, Prime Minister Milton Obote ordered a military assault on the Buganda royal palace, suspended the constitution and abolished the traditional kingdoms.
“We never forgave him,” Kiwanuka said.
“We lived through the regime of Idi Amin and witnessed the dismantling of cultural institutions, yet the kingdom remained resilient, rallying around the king,” he added.
The monarchy was restored in 1993, when Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II was enthroned as the 36th Kabaka.
Today, Uganda’s Constitution recognises traditional and cultural leaders and allows their institutions to exist according to the customs and traditions of the communities they represent. But it separates those institutions from the powers of the state. Traditional leaders cannot exercise the government’s administrative, legislative or executive powers, and they cannot participate in partisan politics.
The culture of the kingdom
For Buganda, the monarchy is about more than the Kabaka and the institutions around him.
The kingdom has insisted on preserving its political identity at times and its cultural identity always, Kitooke said.
“Our traditions are summarised in key matters, including the way of life at home, where we learn the etiquette of speaking to people, receiving guests, and the rules of hospitality, what to say, what to refrain from saying, and so forth,” he said.
He added that traditions also help maintain social cohesion, including visiting family and extended family, maintaining kinship ties, reaching adulthood, marriage and the payment of a bride’s dowry.
“The council of elders oversee family matters, promote unity and help resolve disputes between spouses,” he said. “These are very important; they are all part of our way of life.”
The kingdom and the republic
The Kingdom of Buganda celebrates its national day one day before Uganda’s national day. Neither the historian nor the minister offered an explanation beyond the fact that the kingdom itself is older than the Ugandan state.
On the coexistence between the kingdom and the state, Kitooke said the restoration of cultural rights was accompanied by an effort to preserve them within the laws of the central government.
“When our cultural rights were restored, we were keen to preserve them within the laws of the central state,” he said. “And the authority granted to the kingdom is a traditional cultural authority, and we do not play direct political roles. However, on the ground, we are actively engaged in political work through our institutions.”
For Kiwanuka, the Kabaka’s influence extends well beyond the palace.
“The Kabaka is the most popular figure in the kingdom, and even on the national level,” he said. “When he steps out of his palace, which is located one mile from the seat of the government, you can see tens of thousands of people lining up to welcome him.
“And if he were to say now that ‘we shall fight,’ then we will fight,” Kiwanuka said.

Lithuania’s authorities have issued an all-clear (code white) following an earlier air alert warning over a potential drone sighting, which later turned out to be a flock of birds.
“The Lithuanian Armed Forces inform: AIR ALERT IS OVER (WHITE). You may leave safe places or shelters,” the authorities said in an emergency message on Sunday afternoon.
The yellow air alert over a potential drone sighting was issued on Sunday at around 13:00 local time in Vilnius and the surrounding region, as well as the Trakai and Elektrėnai regions. Flights at Vilnius Airport were temporarily suspended.
The yellow alert meant there was no danger yet, but people were advised to locate their nearest shelter in case the threat level was elevated to code red.
The authorities later clarified that NATO jets confirmed the radar sighting was a flock of birds.

US approves $140 million Black Hawk helicopter sale to Argentina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:09:53 UTC
19:09:53 KST

- The U.S. approved a possible $140 million sale of four UH-60L Black Hawk helicopters to Argentina's Army, notified to Congress on September 10, 2026.
- The helicopters would be the Argentine Army's first Black Hawks, replacing an aging fleet of roughly 50 Bell UH-1H Hueys.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible $140 million sale of four UH-60L Black Hawk helicopters to Argentina, a deal that would give the Argentine Army its first Black Hawks. The approval, notified to Congress on September 10, 2026, follows through on a purchase Argentine officials confirmed earlier this year.
The package includes the four helicopters, two spare T700-GE-701D engines, and a long list of supporting gear: identification and navigation systems, a rescue hoist, a fast-rope insertion and extraction system, an internal auxiliary fuel tank, training equipment and spare parts. Sikorsky, the Lockheed Martin subsidiary that builds the Black Hawk in Stratford, Connecticut, would serve as the main contractor. The approval covers a potential sale rather than a signed contract, and the final price could come in lower depending on exactly what Argentina orders.
The helicopters are meant to replace Argentina’s aging fleet of Bell UH-1H Hueys, roughly 50 of which remain the Army’s primary helicopter type. The Army first tried to buy three secondhand Black Hawks through a tender launched in December 2024, but canceled that process in January 2025 after budget cuts. In June 2026, Lt. Gen. Oscar Santiago Zarich, the Argentine Army’s chief of staff, said the service would move ahead with an initial order of four Black Hawks still in U.S. service, with officials describing plans to grow the fleet further over time.
Argentina isn’t entirely new to the aircraft. A single VIP-configured Black Hawk has served the country’s presidential fleet since 1994, though it was transferred to the Argentine Air Force in 2024. The Army itself has never operated the type.
The UH-60L is an earlier version of the Black Hawk than the UH-60M now built for the U.S. Army and most export customers. Sikorsky runs a separate modernization program that fits older UH-60Ls with a digital cockpit and updated avionics closer to UH-60M standards while keeping the original airframe, an option Argentina could pursue later if it wants to extend the helicopters’ service life.
The purchase fits a pattern of incremental, budget-constrained modernization across Argentina’s armed forces, which have also recently picked up secondhand F-16 fighters from Denmark and P-3 Orion maritime patrol aircraft from Norway.
The State Department said the sale would not require additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Argentina and that no offset agreement has been proposed so far. Argentina has not set a delivery timeline, and the sale still needs to move from this approval into a finalized contract.

Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:09:00 UTC
19:09:00 KST

Vanuatu ferry capsize leaves one dead, 30 missing
September 13, 2026
At least one person has died and another 30 remain missing after an inter-island ferry in Vanuatu sank in poor weather on Friday.
The South Pacific archipelagic island nation with a population of just under 350,000 is located about 1,750 kilometers (1,090 miles) east of Australia.
The vessel went down in very heavy seas somewhere between the islands of Santo and Ambae, according to authorities.
The MV Matui, operated by the Tui Shipping Agency, set sail Friday from Santo with more than 40 passengers and crew but never arrived in Ambae.
Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday morning said that one body had been recovered, 15 passengers had been "accounted for alive" and "over 30 people are missing at sea."
Napat's office took charge of the search and rescue effort on Sunday afternoon after the prime minister expressed frustration over being unable to reach senior officials.
In a statement, Napat's office said, "Search and rescue operations are continuing," adding that the search "in open waters is being eased off whilst efforts move toward a search along the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors."
"To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of those missing and those we have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief," the statement continued.
Napat's office also announced that an investigation into the incident had already been launched amid suspicion of negligence on the part of operator Tui.
"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded," it said, "and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel."
Local frustration at lack of urgency from authorities
Reports of how the rescue effort began are hazy, with Vanuatu parliamentary representative Matai Seremaiah — who took part in the search — telling New Zealand public broadcaster RNZ that a crew member had swam ashore and "alerted us that the ship had capsized."
French news agency AFP cited a hotel owner on Santo who told reporters an employee of his had pulled a survivor in a life vest to shore on Saturday afternoon and authorities were immediately alerted.
It is unclear if these accounts refer to the same survivor.
"He looked like he had been in the bathtub for 25 hours — he was wrinkled up and white. He was cold," said hotel owner Ashley Beveridge.
"There was no rescue started until this guy got washed up on our beach — lucky he got washed up in an inhabited area," he added.
Beveridge told AFP that locals had expressed great frustration at the lack of urgency shown by authorities, with private citizens mobilizing cargo ships and a plane on Saturday afternoon to search for survivors on their own.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Center (MRCC) in Noumea, New Caledonia, has said it is now assisting in the search effort.
A French Armed Forces aircraft from New Caledonia was also deployed on Sunday morning.
The MRCC said that 12 people had been located Sunday morning.
Local media reported that survivors were being treated at Northern Provincial hospital on Santo Island.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) lauded Taiwan’s efforts in cancer research and treatment in a video address marking the 20th anniversary of the Taiwan Society for Molecular Medicine on Sunday.
Lai said the government is actively implementing various strategies, including boosting funding for cancer screening from NT$2.8 billion (US$88.48 million) to NT$6.8 billion and expanding screening items, target groups, and age ranges, according to the Presidential Office. The measures are expected to benefit nearly 6 million people, the president said.
Lai said Taiwan also began including next-generation sequencing (NGS) in National Health Insurance coverage in May 2024, covering 19 types of cancer. This September, applicable cancer types were broadened, allowing more cancer patients to benefit, the president said.
“Through NGS, we aim to more comprehensively map the genetic profile of cancer cells, helping doctors identify appropriate treatments for patients and turning relevant medical data into the basis for new drug evaluation and improved therapies,” Lai said.
At the same time, the Cancer New Drug Fund has been allocated NT$10 billion over the past two years to help economically disadvantaged cancer patients access innovative treatments and reduce their financial burden, Lai said. Taiwan possesses strong biomedical R&D capabilities and a comprehensive healthcare system, he added, and the government will continue to invest resources and improve policies in the field.
Molecular medicine will continue to transform approaches to disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, he said.

Ukraine Reportedly Opens New Drone Front Against Russia in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:06:01 UTC
19:06:01 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Reportedly Opens New Drone Front Against Russia in Africa
Ukraine is expanding its use of drone warfare beyond Europe, deploying specialists to Africa to support forces confronting Russian troops and Moscow-linked military structures.
Around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are currently operating in Mali, helping local forces counter Russia’s Africa Corps through training, technical support, and operational planning, CNN reported on September 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian team works closely with the Azawad Liberation Front, a predominantly Tuareg rebel group active in northern Mali. Rather than taking part in frontline combat directly, the Ukrainian specialists assist local fighters with planning and conducting drone operations.
One Ukrainian drone operator told CNN that he coordinates local fighters remotely. “I coordinate their operations remotely. The signal from their drone comes to me via the internet, and I immediately tell them by radio what to do and where to fly,” he said.
According to CNN, the operator receives live drone footage over the internet and relays instructions to local pilots by radio. He said Ukrainian personnel have been ordered not to deploy directly to frontline positions.
Ukraine expands drone operations across Africa
CNN reported that Ukrainian specialists have also operated in Sudan, while personnel from Chad, Niger, and Burkina Faso have traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian instructors.
The missions are part of a broader effort by Kyiv to apply expertise developed during Russia’s full-scale invasion in other regions where Moscow is expanding its military presence.
Ukrainian teams have also traveled to at least five countries in the Middle East, according to CNN, where they trained local forces to counter Iranian-made Shahed attack drones, which Russia has repeatedly used against Ukraine.
In exchange for Ukrainian technical expertise, Kyiv has received security cooperation agreements and commitments involving ammunition supplies, CNN reported. The deployments also allow Ukrainian specialists to test equipment and tactics in environments significantly different from the Ukrainian battlefield.
In Mali, daytime temperatures regularly exceed 43 degrees Celsius, while dust and sand accelerate wear on drones, electronics, cooling systems, filters, and batteries. A Ukrainian intelligence representative told CNN that the tactical environment is also markedly different.
“In Ukraine, it is high intensity, massed strikes, constant pressure. Here, it is more maneuver warfare across large areas, ambushes, control of routes, work by small groups and dependence on knowledge of the terrain,” the source said.
According to CNN, Ukrainian personnel teach local fighters how to use drones while learning desert survival and combat techniques from forces familiar with the Sahel.
Ukraine targets Russia’s position in Mali
Ukrainian personnel also described operations around Kidal, a strategically important city in northern Mali.
Earlier in 2026, Tuareg rebels and militants launched attacks against Russian forces in the area. Moscow later accused Kyiv of involvement and claimed Ukrainian and European instructors had helped prepare local forces for the operation.
CNN cited a Ukrainian intelligence source as saying that Kyiv views such missions as a way to increase pressure on Moscow and weaken Russia’s image as a reliable security partner in Africa. “We are turning our experience in drones into a foreign policy tool,” the source said.
Russia has significantly expanded its military presence across the Sahel following the withdrawal of French and other Western forces from several countries in the region.
After the Wagner Group was dismantled, Moscow transferred parts of its African operations into the Defense Ministry-controlled Africa Corps, which supports governments aligned with the Kremlin and helps protect Russian strategic and economic interests.
Ukrainian naval drone teams reportedly operate in Libya
Ukraine’s activities in Africa also extend to Libya, CNN reported. According to the outlet, Ukrainian naval drone operators are active in northwestern Libya and have used a base in Misrata to support operations against vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
The fleet consists of tankers used to transport Russian oil and reduce the impact of international sanctions, providing Moscow with continued export revenues.
CNN reported that one explosive-laden Ukrainian naval drone involved in such an operation later moved beyond the control of its operators and appeared near the Greek island of Lefkada. Greece issued a diplomatic protest, after which Kyiv formally apologized, according to the report.
The reported missions in Mali and Libya show how Ukraine is increasingly using drone expertise developed during the war against Russia to contest Moscow’s military and economic activity outside Europe.
“It puts pressure on them. This whole story has both psychological and real consequences,” a Ukrainian operator told CNN.
Russia, meanwhile, continues expanding its military footprint in Africa as it seeks political influence, access to natural resources, and strategic positions in countries where Western involvement has declined.
The reported missions come months after Ukraine unveiled its first comprehensive strategy to expand its presence and influence across Africa. In March, Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov said Kyiv aimed to strengthen its political, economic, and security role on the continent and more actively defend Ukrainian interests there.

Israeli regime besieged by self-made crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:56:23 UTC
18:56:23 KST

In recent years, the Zionist regime has faced a fundamental contradiction more than ever before; on the one hand, it possesses one of the most powerful armies in the region and extensive American support, and on the other hand, it has faced serious difficulty in converting this military power into a lasting political and strategic achievement. Tel Aviv has entered extensive operations on several fronts, but the end of none of these conflicts has been able to create the security and stability that Israeli leaders promised.
This situation became more evident especially after October 7. The Hamas attack was not only a major security and intelligence failure for Israel, but also called into question the image that Tel Aviv had built of its ability to control the security environment around it. Israel subsequently launched extensive operations in Gaza, and despite the high volume of military operations, it has still not been able to turn the Gaza issue into a sustainable political solution. The persistence of the resistance issue and the inability to create a political order desired by Tel Aviv show that military power alone is not sufficient to resolve a complex crisis.
On the northern front, the conditions are not much different. Israel has tried for years to limit the Hezbollah threat and reduce the group's military capability, but developments in Lebanon have shown that such a threat cannot be permanently eliminated simply through military operations. Even if heavy blows are dealt to a group's infrastructure and command, political, social, and regional factors can still provide the ground for rebuilding its capability. For this reason, Israel has once again faced the same issue it faces in Gaza: the ability to inflict a blow is different from the ability to end a crisis.
The confrontation with Iran has also highlighted this same gap. In recent years, Israel has repeatedly tried to limit Iran's strategic capacities through military and security operations, but these measures have not been able to remove the Iran issue from the region's security equations. Even in circumstances where Tel Aviv can achieve part of its military objectives, changing the regional balance and creating a stable situation is a far more complex matter. In fact, the more the scope of the conflict expands, the clearer it becomes that there is a considerable gap between "striking" and "winning."
Israel's problem, of course, is not limited to the military battlefield. Prolonged wars, economic pressure, political disputes, and social divisions have also placed the Zionist society under pressure. Since the beginning of the recent crises, the Netanyahu cabinet has faced extensive political disputes, and the controversy over the government's performance, the conduct of the war, and responsibility for the October 7 security failure continues. This situation has weakened the image that Israel presented for years of a cohesive, stable society enjoying intelligence and security superiority.
On the international stage, too, the costs of Tel Aviv's policies have increased. Although Israel still enjoys considerable American support, the continuation of the conflicts and the rise in international criticism have raised the political cost of the regime's actions. The important point is that Israel needs not only military power to maintain its superiority; it also needs political legitimacy, foreign support, and the ability to manage its relations with allies. The prolongation of the wars has ultimately placed all three of these areas under pressure.
Under such circumstances, the remarks of Yuval Noah Harari, a Zionist author and historian, take on greater importance. In an article in the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, Harari held Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet responsible for part of the recent failures and described the past four years as one of the most dangerous periods in the history of the Zionist regime. He stressed that the security institutions' warnings before October 7 about existing threats were ignored, and that the Netanyahu cabinet was preoccupied with its own domestic political priorities.
Harari went on to not only refer to the failure before October 7 but also criticized the way the war was managed afterward. From his perspective, Israel achieved successes in some military operations, but was unable to convert these successes into a lasting political and strategic achievement. He ultimately, using a very harsh expression, likened Israel's leadership situation to "lions led by donkeys."
The importance of these remarks lies in the fact that such criticism is no longer raised only by Israel's foreign opponents, but voices of criticism have also grown louder from within the regime's society and intellectual circles. In fact, the issue Harari refers to is not an individual weakness or merely a problem related to Netanyahu; rather, it is a larger question about the quality of strategic decision-making in Israel.
Israel today faces a serious contradiction: the regime's military capability remains high, but its ability to convert this power into a desired political order has declined. Tel Aviv can target facilities, infrastructure, and military objectives, but it cannot eliminate the roots of a political or security crisis simply through military operations. The experiences of Gaza, Lebanon, and the confrontation with Iran have each, in a different way, demonstrated this same reality.
From this perspective, Israel's failure should not be measured only by the number of operations or the amount of damage inflicted on the opposing side. The more important criterion is the extent to which Israel, after expending this volume of military and political resources, has moved closer to its strategic objectives. If the goal is to create lasting security, eliminate the main threats, prevent the expansion of regional rivals' influence, and preserve internal cohesion, the performance of recent years at least shows that Tel Aviv has still not achieved an important part of these objectives.
For this reason, Israel's current crisis is less a crisis of military power than a crisis of converting power into results. A regime that enjoys military superiority but cannot turn war into peace, operations into strategy, and temporary victories into lasting security will face a problem beyond a defeat on the battlefield. Perhaps the most important part of Harari's remarks is this; that Israel's problem is not only the enemies surrounding it, but part of the crisis goes back to the way decisions are made and managed by those who are supposed to contain these enemies.

Ukraine’s finances face a “very difficult winter” as Russia hammers economic targets and the costs of war soar, the Ukrainian economy minister and other senior finance officials have warned.
Taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of interceptors, Moscow is now launching daily strikes on the country’s logistics and business infrastructure.

The port of Odesa, which plays a vital role in exporting grain, has come under constant attack, reducing its ability to operate. At the same time warehouses, factories, logistics facilities and even filling stations have been targeted.
The strikes not only disrupt business activity and deprive the state of sorely needed tax revenue but also force the government to provide financial support for businesses, putting more pressure on the beleaguered budget.

“So what we estimate in the Ministry of Economy is that basically the total destruction of infrastructure and fixed assets is close to around $10 billion per year.”
Russian Strikes Hit Gas Station, Kyiv-Warsaw Train, Near Polish Border
He added that the financial instruments the government now has at its disposal will fail to cover the needs of businesses suffering from the attacks.
Cost of war
Roksana Pidlasa, a Ukrainian member of parliament and chair of the parliament’s budget committee, told the same conference that the war is now costing Ukraine around $190 million a day, compared to $140 million a day just two years ago, in a sober assessment of the state of Ukraine’s finances.
She added that preliminary reports on the “budget implementation” for the first eight months of the year show that national security and defense cost the government almost $42 billion in that period.
“We have raised only $39 billion from our own resources, which includes budget revenues and domestic borrowing. So unfortunately, this year the war has gotten so expensive that we can’t even cover our share of the costs... in the previous year our own resources were covering the basic military needs such as soldier salaries. We’re now using international money to pay soldiers’ salaries.”
As an example of how revenue has declined, Pidlasa cited VAT, which, she said, had “underperformed by $1.35 billion over eight months”. A quarter of this sum, she added, was lost in August alone—a month of intensive Russian attacks.
Hunting for cash
To mitigate the problem the government has said that it is preparing resilience strategies for the energy and logistics systems that will help them absorb Russian attacks.
Also speaking at the YES conference, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Saturday that the government can also draw upon the Special Program for Ukraine Recovery (Spur 2), a specialized financing initiative organized by the World Bank in which it matches funding for Kyiv provided by other international donors.
This money will be channeled into providing some support and relief for businesses affected by Russian strikes.
“We are in the process of negotiating with our European partners [on additional funding] and using the frozen assets of the Russian Federation, trying to identify sources outside the European Union and rationalizing all the spendings inside Ukraine,” he added.
Ukraine also intends to utilize military force, or the threat of it, to relieve the pressure on the budget.
“Russia knows that if they strike – and they are preparing to strike our energy system in the winter – Russia will receive the exact same,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday in a threat made, possibly, in the hope of deterring Moscow from attacking and thus saving Ukraine from associated financial costs.
“If they cause us blackouts, we will try to respond to them in kind,” he added.

U.S. Army finished dismantling Cold War nuclear plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:54:40 UTC
18:54:40 KST

- The Army Corps of Engineers has completed dismantling SM-1, the Army's first nuclear reactor, at Fort Belvoir, Virginia.
- SM-1 was the first U.S. facility to supply nuclear-generated electricity to the commercial grid, operating from 1957 until its 1973 shutdown.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has finished dismantling the SM-1 nuclear power plant at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, the Army’s first nuclear reactor and the first facility in the country to send nuclear-generated electricity into the commercial power grid. The Corps’ Baltimore District completed the last field work this year, closing out a project that began mobilizing crews in 2021.
The job involved clearing non-radioactive hazards, safely removing and disposing of radioactive materials and equipment, tearing down the plant’s structures, hauling away debris, and restoring the site. What was once a working reactor is now a graded, seeded plot of land. Planning for the teardown dates back to 2014, and the Corps received its formal decommissioning permit in 2020 before field crews arrived the following year.
“This team set out to execute a complex mission methodically, protect the installation and the National Capital Region through every phase, and deliver a lasting result worthy of the Army’s trust,” said Col. Francis B. Pera, Baltimore District commander and district engineer. “It’s a credit to the health physicists, engineers, project managers, field personnel, and contractor workforce who executed this mission day after day.”
SM-1 traces back to 1954, when the Army launched its Nuclear Power Program and tasked the American Locomotive Company with building a small reactor at its Corps of Engineers headquarters in Fort Belvoir. The reactor reached criticality, the point where a nuclear chain reaction becomes self-sustaining, on April 8, 1957, and began feeding power into the commercial grid months before Pennsylvania’s much larger Shippingport reactor came online that December. SM-1 produced only a modest 1.5 megawatts of electricity from roughly 10 megawatts of reactor heat, but it also doubled as a training site, teaching reactor operations to personnel from the Army, Navy and Air Force. The plant ran until 1973, when it was shut down and placed in long-term storage rather than torn down right away.
The Corps awarded a roughly $68 million contract in August 2020 to a joint venture of APTIM and AECOM to carry out the decommissioning work. Baltimore District leaned on expertise it had already built up dismantling a related Army reactor, the MH-1A, which sat aboard a converted cargo ship called the STURGIS. That floating power plant was tested at Fort Belvoir before it was sent to the Panama Canal Zone in the 1960s to supply electricity there, and the Corps completed its own decommissioning in 2019.
The timing lands on a symbolic bookend for Army nuclear power. As the Corps closes the book on SM-1, the reactor that opened the Army’s nuclear era nearly 70 years ago, the service has separately launched a new push to put small nuclear reactors back on its bases. Under a program called Janus, launched in October 2025 through the Defense Innovation Unit, the Army has paired commercial reactor companies with five host installations, including Fort Benning, Georgia, where a company called Radiant Industries is set to install three one-megawatt microreactors. The Army has said it is targeting 2028 for the first Janus reactors to come online.
The Army says the completed SM-1 project now gives it a full picture of a nuclear plant’s life span, from construction through decades of operation to final teardown, a body of experience it says will help inform this next generation of reactors as they move from installation through years of service and eventual retirement of their own.

Israel’s PISA collapse exposes a failing education system threatening its future - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:52:10 UTC
18:52:10 KST

On the eve of 5787, and as the election campaign gets underway, Israel has posted shocking results in this year’s PISA tests – the global benchmark for comparing education systems.
You might think this is because of the haredim (ultra-Orthodox) – after all, a growing share of Israel’s children belong to an education system that does not provide enough instruction in mathematics, science, and English.
But the problem revealed by results released this week is general – and disastrous.
Haredi schools are indeed included in the PISA sampling framework, but haredi boys are very poorly represented.
A Knesset Research and Information Center report on PISA 2022 found that haredi boys made up only 3% of the actual sample before weighting, whereas haredim are a sixth of the population and even more of the youth – mainly because most haredi boys’ schools refused to participate. Moreover, haredi girls performed rather well.
The figure that should truly alarm Israel is that the 2025 collapse is occurring not at the margins of the education system, but at its core.
Israel’s reading score fell by 38 points in just three years, from 474 in 2022 to 436 in 2025. Mathematics fell by 25 points, to 433, and science by 23 points, to 442.
In all three subjects, these are Israel’s lowest-ever PISA results, and they are significantly below the results recorded in 2012, 2015, and 2018. Israel is now below the average of the OECD – the club of developed economies – in all three subjects.
In mathematics, 46% of Israeli students fail to reach even the baseline level of proficiency, compared with an OECD average of 35%.
Similar gaps were recorded in all subjects, and the share of top performers is also below the average for developed countries.
The attitudes of students themselves toward learning and the education system should also set off alarm bells.
According to the organization’s report, “only 68% of students in Israel agreed or strongly agreed with the statement ‘I am curious about many different things,’ compared with 73% on average across OECD countries (and) 37% of students in Israel agreed or strongly agreed with the statement ‘School has been a waste of time,’ compared with just 24% on average across OECD countries.”
More children attend schools where principals say there are insufficient resources. More students report skipping school.
What about the Israeli Arab sector? There is actually a narrowing gap between students there and the Hebrew-speaking education system because the latter deteriorated faster. That is the sort of equality no country should aspire to.
Similarly, Israel’s educational gaps have narrowed somewhat – but again, not because weaker students improved, but because the share of top performers significantly declined.
Yet Israel remains among the countries with some of the largest gaps in the world between its strongest and weakest students – also bad.
The wars of recent years may be part of the explanation (COVID is not, because everyone went through it) – but the downward trend predates that.
What should be done?
First, obviously, a modern country cannot continue funding schools that fail to provide their students with meaningful core instruction in mathematics, English, and science.
As the haredi share of the population grows, the economic and social cost of this arrangement grows with it. Genuine core studies should be a condition for receiving public funding, and the matter is far too urgent to remain a bargaining chip in coalition negotiations.
But the 2025 PISA results make clear that this is not the main problem.
The emergency begins with the people the system manages to put in its classrooms.
Israel expects teachers to perform one of the most important and difficult jobs in society, yet for years it has failed to make teaching a profession in which enough talented people can build attractive professional and economic lives.
Add to this the workload, burnout, and a professional status that does not match the responsibility.
According to the OECD, Israel invests 22% less per student in education than the average, and far less than top performers.
Removing politics and placing education at the forefront
Above all of this lies the chronic politicization of Israeli education.
Education ministers come and go, each arriving with a worldview, flagship programs, and priorities of their own, while an education system requires planning measured in decades.
Education repeatedly becomes a battleground over identity, religion, nationalism, and politics, instead of having fundamental goals stable enough to survive the next minister and the next government.
The same applies to the place occupied by Jewish and traditional studies.
These are important and legitimate components of education in a Jewish state, and Israeli children should know the culture, history, and tradition from which the country emerged.
But classroom hours are a finite resource, which means this is also a question of proportion and effectiveness.
When the ability to read, write, calculate, and understand science is deteriorating rapidly, the curriculum cannot be managed as though these choices carry no cost.
Israel therefore needs a long-term education policy whose central elements are insulated as much as possible from changes of governments and ministers.
There must be broad national agreement on what an Israeli student must know, how much the country is willing to invest to bring excellent people into the classroom, and how to measure whether any of this is actually happening.
The education system cannot reinvent itself every time the person sitting in the education minister’s office changes.
Israel’s qualitative edge derives first and foremost from the quality of the people it produces and their ability to think, invent, research, and build.
That qualitative edge has been a major source of Israel’s economic and technological advantage, and from it has also grown a central part of its military advantage.
A small country with a small population cannot compete over the long term through mass; it competes through quality. If the education system stops producing that quality, there is no reason to assume the economic advantage will endure.
And if the economic and technological advantage erodes, the military advantage is not some permanent asset promised to Israel forever.
This connects to an even larger and more disturbing picture. Israel also depends on allies, foreign investment, scientific and technological cooperation, international legitimacy, and its standing as part of the developed democratic world.
As the country undergoes a process of nationalist radicalization, increasing religiosity, and damage to its liberal institutions, it places those assets at risk as well.
A society that allows sectoral politics to determine what children learn, that struggles to pay enough to attract excellent people into teaching, that changes its educational priorities with every minister, and that devotes ever more energy to culture wars and battles over identity is damaging the foundation from which the Israeli miracle arose in the first place.
The current right-wing religious coalition is not the source of every failure in Israel’s education system, some of which have been building for decades.
But it is deepening precisely the trends Israel now needs to reverse: politicization, sector preference, religious encroachment, and the prioritization of coalition demands over the construction of a modern education system with a uniform set of fundamental skills required of every child.
These are not separate crises.
Israel is accustomed to thinking of education as a demographic problem.
If only we take the haredim out of the equation, many secular and middle-class Israelis tell themselves, and if we also separate the Arab education system, what will emerge behind them is the “real Israel”: an educated, Western, technological country whose education system may be mediocre but is certainly not collapsing.
The 2025 PISA results should put an end to that illusion.
Add this to the long list of reasons why change is urgently needed in 5787.
The writer is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

STOCKHOLM, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Polling stations opened across Sweden on Sunday morning in a closely watched parliamentary election that could see the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) enter government for the first time or the center-left return to power after four years in opposition.
Opinion polls had generally put the center-left opposition ahead of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's governing right-wing camp. Still, the gap narrowed sharply in the final days of the campaign, making the race tighter as voting began.
The SD, long excluded from government by established parties because of its far-right roots, has supported Kristersson's government from outside the cabinet since 2022 and is now seeking ministerial posts if the right-wing bloc retains power.
On the eve of the election, SD leader Magdalena Andersson, leader of the opposition Social Democratic Party, said that she would "never allow herself to be controlled by extremist forces" if she became prime minister. She accused Kristersson of being unable to make the same promise.
Kristersson defended his cooperation with the SD, saying it helped address crime and immigration and make decisions needed to revive the economy.
More than 8 million people are eligible to vote, with healthcare, education, law and order, immigration and integration among the key issues. Polling stations are open from 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) to 8 p.m., with preliminary results expected later Sunday. Regional and municipal elections are also being held.
"I cannot see which side would make my life any better. It all sounds like political rhetoric to me," a Stockholm restaurant waiter who declined to give his name told Xinhua.
Sweden's parliament, the Riksdag, has 349 seats, with parliamentary elections held every four years. ■
