Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sunday that trade among BRICS countries has reached $1.2 trillion.
Speaking at a meeting of the BRICS Outreach format in New Delhi, Putin said that the population growth rates in the BRICS countries are increasing from year to year, domestic markets are strengthening, and infrastructure of all kinds has been built.
“Domestic trade within our association has already reached $1.2 trillion. The participating countries account for almost a quarter of global exports, and it is the BRICS that provides the main dynamics of global GDP – 49%,” he said.
Putin emphasized that the potential for further development of BRICS is “far from exhausted.”
“One of the main reserves that has not yet been fully utilized is the complementarity of the economies of the participating countries. Differences in their structure and specialization provide ample opportunities for practical cooperation, for the creation of new production chains, technologies, services and markets,” he said.
"In fact, we are talking about forming a common BRICS growth platform that organically combines the competitive advantages of our economies," Putin noted.
The Russian president added that attention to BRICS activities in the world continues to grow.
He said the group's values and ideals were becoming increasingly attractive, adding that BRICS advocates equal and unrestricted opportunities for all countries to achieve social and economic growth.
Putin also said the group was actively contributing to the formation of a more just multipolar world order.

“When I called Apple customer service, they hung up on me immediately. What should I do?” she asked.
It took her half an hour to reach an HSBC customer service officer to suspend her credit card, and she subsequently filed a police report.

On Sept 12th, 'everyone was compassionate': The world needs 'to be together again' - Richard Roeill

Unknown Publisher

On Sept 12th, 'everyone was compassionate': The world needs 'to be together again' - Richard Roeill
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Richard Roeill, former New York Firefighter and 9/11 First Responder. His testimony reframes the legacy of September 11th not as a historical event confined to a single day, but as living history. The former New York City firefighter describes an anniversary that reactivates trauma, while the illnesses suffered by first responders make the consequences of Ground Zero ever present decades later. Yet Roeill’s testimony is not simply a narrative of sacrifice. He says that responders were misled about the dangers they faced, demanding accountability and long-term healthcare for those exposed to the very toxic air.
At the same time, Roeill resists ending with anger. His memory of September 12 - when, in his telling, distinctions of race, religion and gender temporarily receded before a sense of common humanity - becomes both an ideal and an implicit critique of the present. What he ultimately asks viewers to remember, therefore, is not only what was lost on September 11, but what solidarity looked like immediately afterward, and what we owe those still living with its consequences.
His account moves between vulnerability and duty: declining lung capacity, the deaths of colleagues and the emotional burden of repeated funerals coexist with his striking insistence that, knowing what he knows now, he would still have responded exactly as he had done. "Absolutely. There's a lot of legacy firemen now, meaning that the ones that have passed from 9/11, that their kids are following in their footsteps, and it's a really wonderful thing. I got to witness about six months ago at Rescue 4. There were a few legacy children and firemen there, and it was great to see that they had great camaraderie, and they all stuck together because they had another bond that other people didn't. And it was really — it was beautiful to see, actually. It really was, knowing that they were there for each other and keeping their parents' legacies alive."

Russian Nuclear Head Says Ukraine Attacked Fuel Trucks, Endangered Zaporizhzhia Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
07:17:03 UTC
16:17:03 KST

The head of Russia's state nuclear energy corporation accused Ukraine on Sunday of attacking diesel fuel trucks, killing two Russian servicemen and deliberately jeopardizing safety at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Ukraine.
Alexei Likhachev said the attack took place on Friday and also resulted in injuries to other Russian soldiers.
The Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe's largest with six reactors, was seized by Russian forces in the early weeks of the Ukraine war that broke out in February 2022. Each side has regularly accused the other of actions that endanger safety at the plant and increase the risk of a nuclear accident.
Likhachev issued a statement saying Ukrainian forces had launched “a series of combined strikes” on Friday on fuel trucks which deliver diesel to the station.
“The strikes hit very close to the perimeter of the station's site,” he said.
“Two servicemen were killed, and a large number of Russian soldiers were injured, some seriously. They were all involved in supporting this purely civilian mission.”
Fuel is critically important for the plant as diesel generators provide power to keep nuclear fuel in the reactors cool when the plant's two external power links are down. Both were down for nearly three weeks in August and September.
Ukraine has demanded that Russia abandon the station and hand its operation back to Kyiv, a demand rejected by Moscow. The fuel currently generates no electricity.
The UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, has stationed an observer team permanently at the station, along with Ukraine's three other working plants.
The agency has repeatedly acted as an intermediary when disputes arise and last month helped arrange a local ceasefire in order to carry out repairs and restore external power links.
Russia Hits Truck Near Polish Border in Latest Strike Near NATO
Russia attacked a truck near Ukraine's border with Poland, Polish and Ukrainian officials said on Sunday, the latest strike to hit areas near NATO as Moscow and Kyiv intensify their long-distance strikes to try to shift momentum in the war.
Polish border guards told Reuters that the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack around 800 meters (half a mile) from Poland, but that the crossing has since resumed operations.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in Western Ukraine. Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.
Russia has begun targeting Ukraine's border crossings with its Western allies in recent weeks, part of a growing campaign by both sides to erode the other's economic infrastructure more than four years into Russia's invasion.
India and China Offer to Help Broker Peace
In India, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had been attending the BRICS summit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping had offered help brokering a peace settlement, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Last month, at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Modi told Putin that the war must end, one of several calls for peace by leaders of nations that have traditionally strong relations with Russia.
Last month, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly told Putin that he should halt the conflict along the front line, which has remained largely static this year.
Russia has ruled that out, saying Ukraine should pull back to leave the industrialized eastern Donbas region in Moscow's hands, something Kyiv has said it will never do.
Both Brazil and China, themselves founding BRICS members, have called for a resumption of peace talks.
TASS cited Peskov as saying that Putin had informed Modi of the situation “on the ground” in Ukraine, and that Russia had not ruled out resuming three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States in October.

Tallinn strengthens cooperation with South Korea in innovation and entrepreneurship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:42:54 UTC
15:42:54 KST

This week, a Tallinn delegation visited South Korea on a business mission aimed at expanding cooperation in innovation and entrepreneurship. The visit focused on creating new opportunities for Tallinn-based companies in the Korean market and promoting Tallinn among Korean businesses as a gateway to Europe.
“South Korea’s experience shows that a complex geopolitical situation does not necessarily prevent a country from attracting foreign investment and developing its economy. On the contrary, a strong innovation ecosystem, international partnerships and support for entrepreneurship can provide an important competitive advantage. I am pleased that Tallinn has established meaningful cooperation with the Seoul Business Agency, enabling us to help Tallinn companies enter the Korean market while supporting Korean start-ups in finding opportunities for growth in Tallinn and the wider European market,” said Tallinn Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan.
A central part of the visit was Try Everything, a major start-up and innovation event in Seoul, where Tallinn hosted its own programme and exhibition stand. The programme was opened by Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan and Estonian Ambassador to South Korea Tanel Sepp. Tallinn presented its business and innovation ecosystem and the opportunities it offers international companies to test and validate solutions, find partners and enter the European market.
Five Tallinn-based companies participated in the business mission: 5.0Robotics, SafePAS, Digiotouch, UP Catalyst and Creatomus Solutions. At Try Everything, the companies presented their solutions and met potential partners, customers, investors and representatives of innovation organisations.
One concrete outcome of the mission was the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Digiotouch and the Korean company ZEP Co at the Estonian Embassy in Seoul. Digiotouch develops an AI-powered meeting automation solution, while ZEP Co creates interactive digital environments and metaverse solutions. ZEP Co was also selected for Tallinn’s Test in Tallinn innovation programme, through which the company’s solution will be piloted in Estonian schools.
The Tallinn delegation also met representatives of the Seoul Metropolitan Government’s Digital City Bureau. Discussions focused on exchanging experience in smart-city development and digital innovation, using digital-twin technology, and improving urban safety, resilience and crisis preparedness.
During the visit, the delegation toured Pangyo Techno Valley, one of South Korea’s leading technology and innovation clusters, the MARU360 start-up and entrepreneurship centre, and the internationally recognised robotics company ROBOTIS. The company is best known for its DYNAMIXEL intelligent robotic actuators and its humanoid and service robots. ROBOTIS presented its latest robotics developments, including a humanoid robot currently under development, while the parties discussed rapid advances in robotics and artificial intelligence. Although ROBOTIS technologies are already available in Europe, Tallinn could potentially become the location of the company’s future European headquarters.
The visit took place within the framework of Tallinn’s cooperation and delegation exchange with the Seoul Business Agency. The partnership aims to give Tallinn companies more opportunities to explore Korea’s innovation ecosystem, establish contacts with local partners and enter the Korean market. At the same time, Tallinn is introducing Korean companies to opportunities to test and develop new solutions in the city and use it as a launchpad for entering the European market.

It had sailed from Surabaya on the Indonesian island of Java on Saturday and was heading for Banjarmasin, a port city on Borneo.
Basarnas said in its latest update that six people were killed and 130 were missing. It said 107 people had been rescued.
There were 213 passengers and 30 crew members on board, the agency added.
Indonesia’s Ministry of Transportation said in a statement that the ship had capsized.
The ship encountered rough weather, said I Putu Sudayana, head of the local search-and-rescue office in Banjarmasin.
The ferry’s last known position was in the Java Sea, about 81 nautical miles (equivalent to about 150km) from Banjarmasin, the AFP news agency reported.
Rescue ships and a helicopter have been searching the area, where Sudayana said waves as high as 2.5 metres (8.2ft) have hampered the operation.
“It is extremely risky for vessels. Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 metres (131ft) long, is at great risk,” Sudayana told reporters, referring to the country’s search-and-rescue agency.
Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington, reporting from Indonesia’s capital, Jakarta, said authorities have yet to determine the cause of the sinking.
An investigation is under way, Washington added, with authorities examining factors including the weather and possible technical failures.
People in Indonesia, an archipelago of 17,000 islands, rely on ferries as a key mode of transport, with sea routes more affordable and readily available than air travel.
Last month, a fire on a ferry sailing between Bali and Lombok killed one person and left five missing. In July, a ferry carrying more than 70 people sank near Selayar Island, south of Sulawesi.

Indian premier says confidence in BRICS has increased amid rising global tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:25:28 UTC
15:25:28 KST

Ahmad Adil
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
- BRICS agrees on a bloc-integrated early warning system for response to infectious diseases, says Indian premier
 
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said Global South countries' confidence in BRICS has increased amid rising tensions across the world.
 
Delivering an opening statement at the expanded session on the second day of the BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi, Modi said: “We have tried to promote inclusive global growth through the BRICS.”
 
“We believe that the benefits of developed solutions in the BRICS should not only be limited to the BRICS. They should be made adaptable and accessible according to the needs of the Global South,” he said.
 
Noting that the “number of tensions in the world is constantly increasing,” Modi said the pandemic, climate disaster, and supply chain disruption have “shown that in today’s interconnected world, no crisis is limited to one area. That is why we have focused on increasing resilience in all areas.”
 
Addressing the BRICS leaders, Modi said: “The confidence of the countries of the Global South has increased in the BRICS.”
 
“Their voice is heard in the BRICS. Their experience is respected. And solutions are not only made for them, but are made together with them,” he added.
 
The BRICS bloc has been holding the annual summit of its leaders, including those of its partner nations, in the Indian capital since Saturday.
 
Modi was addressing the session on “resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability.”
 
Stating that the power of BRICS “is in our diversity and cooperation,” Modi said: “We may be rooted in different realities, but together we rise through cooperation and blossom for humanity.”
 
“Our diversity, our identity, our cooperation, our inspiration, and our progress should be useful to the entire humanity,” he said.
 
Regarding the number of countries participating in the BRICS summit, Modi said: “This is proof of the increasing power, attraction, and unparalleled faith of BRICS.”
 
 BRICS agrees to establish early warning system
 
Modi said the bloc has “focused on increasing resilience in all areas.”
 
“We have agreed on a BRICS-integrated early warning system for the prevention and response of infectious diseases. Early warning data integration guidelines have been prepared for disaster management,” he said, adding that the BRICS logistic supply chain cooperation framework will help our supply chains become more reliable and resilient.
 
He also said the BRICS Incubator Network “will connect our startups and incubators to each other through innovation,” and the network on digital agriculture will create new opportunities for farmers.
 
Noting that the "weaponization of technology and critical minerals can be a barrier to our sustainable development," Modi said, adding: "We have focused on inclusivity in the adoption of technology."
 
The weekend summit in New Delhi is attended by the Chinese, Russian, and Iranian presidents, among others, and comes at a time when the US-Iran war has been ongoing for around seven months, while the Russia-Ukraine war has continued for more than four years.

France expresses regret over UN diplomatic spat with Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:23:05 UTC
15:23:05 KST

France’s permanent mission to the UN has expressed regret over an online post criticising the United States’ commitment to human rights, following a dispute that has held up approval of France’s next ambassador to Washington.
A US State Department official told AFP on Saturday that Washington welcomed the statement, which the French mission published on Friday.
“We note and appreciate France’s statement and look forward to working together to further shared values and interests,” the official said on condition of anonymity.
The French mission published its statement on Friday, saying it regretted the post on X.
“France and the United States recently took different positions on a vote at the United Nations General Assembly. This difference concerned one vote, and not the defense of human rights,” it said.
“Public differences of opinion on one vote do not stand in the way of close dialogue with the United States, and do not call into question our historical alliance, nor our ability to work together to advance peace, stability and prosperity, including within multilateral forums.”
“US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore”
The dispute began after the United States voted against extending Volker Turk’s term as UN human rights chief at the UN General Assembly on July 24. It was one of 10 countries to oppose the extension, alongside North Korea, Russia and Nicaragua, among others.
“The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore,” the French mission wrote on X after the vote.
The post prompted an immediate backlash from Washington. Days later, the US representative walked out of a UN Security Council meeting when France’s ambassador took the floor, in protest at the comments.
Washington has also held up approval of Aurelien Lechevallier, President Emmanuel Macron’s choice to replace Laurent Bili as France’s ambassador to the United States.
Lechevallier is currently French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot’s chief of staff.

Ukraine Is Better Prepared for Winter Strikes, Koretskyi Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
06:21:00 UTC
15:21:00 KST

Ukraine is better prepared for potential Russian strikes on its energy grid than it was last winter, though fully shielding every facility remains impossible, Prime Minister Serhi Koretskyi stated during the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) annual conference in Kyiv.
Speaking at the forum, Koretskyi said the government has drafted a comprehensive resilience plan and is preparing response mechanisms ranging from baseline contingencies to severe crisis scenarios.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The winter will be hard – I have nothing new to add to that. But we have no other plan than to get through this winter with dignity,” Koretskyi said.
Koretskyi noted that Russian forces continue to subject Ukrainian power infrastructure to sustained aerial attacks, making total physical defense unfeasible. However, he emphasized that structural lessons drawn from the previous heating season have significantly bolstered state readiness.
“Russia may view the current period and the winter season as an opportunity to exert rapid pressure on Ukraine,” Koretskyi explained, adding that the government intends to navigate the coming months through internal coordination and continued assistance from international partners.
Decentralization and multi-tier response plans
According to the prime minister, the core of Ukraine’s winter energy strategy centers on the decentralization of critical utility and life-support networks across regions, cities, and oblasts to prevent localized damage from triggering systemic grid collapses.
Russian Attack Halts US-Owned Oleina Sunflower Oil Plant in Dnipro
Koretskyi stated that the scale and destruction of Russian strikes have multiplied over the past two months, creating additional strain on the national economy. Despite the escalation, he maintained that the government possesses the resources, reserves, and operational readiness necessary to address winter disruptions.
Koretskyi referenced his administrative experience managing energy operations during previous wartime campaigns when he served as head of national oil and gas company NJSC Naftogaz of Ukraine.
Fuel stockpiles and municipal heating preparations
Koretskyi’s assessment follows official confirmations that Ukraine reached its natural gas storage targets for the 2026–2027 heating season approximately one month ahead of schedule.
On Aug. 28, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal announced that Ukrainian underground gas storage facilities had accumulated 14.6 billion cubic meters of natural gas, fulfilling baseline requirements for the autumn-winter season.
The milestone was achieved through coordinated extraction and storage by domestic producers, the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine (GTSOU), and Naftogaz.
Concurrently, the Ministry of Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport reported in late August that roughly 100,000 residential buildings – representing approximately 70% of the government’s seasonal target – had completed winterization procedures, alongside preparations for 12,400 boiler houses and 11,700 kilometers of municipal heating networks.
The government previously allocated nearly Hr 6.8 billion ($152 million) for energy infrastructure repairs, backup generation, and physical barriers, prioritizing autonomous backup power for municipal water and heating services during potential grid outages.

Swedes vote in close general election that could usher far right into government
Swedes are heading to the polls Sunday for a general election that will either bring a far right party into government for the first time or shift the country back towards the liberalism it has long been known for. The centre-left opposition holds a narrow lead over the ruling right-wing bloc but Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's four-party alliance – which includes the far right Sweden Democrats – has been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning.

Polling stations opened across Sweden on Sunday in a close general election that will see either the far right enter government for the first time or the left-wing opposition reclaim power.
Opinion polls have long credited the four parties in the left-wing bloc with a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's four-party alliance, which includes the far right Sweden Democrats.
Read more'Swedish society has changed': The rise of the far-right Sweden Democrats
But the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days of the campaign.
"We all knew it was going to be a very close election, I've said that all along," Magdalena Andersson, the 59-year-old opposition leader and head of the centre-left Social Democrats, said at a campaign rally in Stockholm on the eve of the vote.
"Now it's up to voters: do they want a government that will be totally dominated by the Sweden Democrats, or do they want a government led by me?" said Andersson, the first woman to serve as prime minister in 2021-2022.
Her party, which governed the Scandinavian country for the better part of the 20th century and remains the biggest party, has pledged to bolster the welfare state and help struggling households cope with rising costs.
Outgoing Prime Minister Kristersson has meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes' everyday lives now that his government's clampdown on organised crime and immigration had achieved its intended results.
An otherwise tranquil country, Sweden has endured over a decade of deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks.
The violence has decreased significantly in recent years, and asylum applications are at a record low.
Read moreThousands rally for climate action in Sweden ahead of general election
"We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people ... to make Sweden great again," Kristersson told AFP, borrowing US President Donald Trump's famous catchphrase.
His three-party minority coalition cut a deal in 2022 with the Sweden Democrats giving them influence over government policy, in particular on immigration and crime, in exchange for their support in parliament.
Far-right leader Jimmie Akesson, who has headed the party for over two decades, is now hoping to enter government, culminating the party's meteoric rise since entering parliament in 2010.
Kristersson has promised the far-right key cabinet posts if the right-wing wins the election, with Akesson widely expected to be given the migration portfolio.
'We've already won!'
Akesson was confident of victory at a final election rally on Saturday in the Swedish capital.
"We've already won!" the 47-year-old said to thunderous applause in the Kungstradgarden Park.
"Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish," he said, surrounded by blue and yellow campaign posters blaring "Make Sweden Sweden Again".
Agneta Andersson, a 78-year-old pensioner, told AFP she was voting for the far-right.

Forget low-calorie food, Chinese youth turn to tasteless, chewy snacks to lose weight
One individual even admits to chewing on dog chew sticks to help alleviate severe exam anxiety
Young dieters in China are increasingly turning away from low-calorie foods in favour of a new trend: chewy snacks.
On social media, they are sharing their new-found favourites, including beef jerky, frozen buns, and even baby teething biscuits – each characterised by their toughness and chewiness.
Many prefer chewy foods as a way to keep their mouths busy and trick their brains into feeling satisfied, reducing the urge to eat more.
For these dieters, taste is not the top priority; instead, the focus is on the toughness of the snacks. The harder to chew, the more effective they believe it is.
One 37-year-old netizen from Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, using the handle @yigexiangmujingli, has taken to munching on dangshena root thought to bolster the spleen and lung in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) – as her chewy snack of choice.
She shared with the SCMP that while she maintains a workout routine, she struggles with self-control around food. Hence, she seeks chewy snacks that keep her focused at work without adding weight to her body.

The cause of the incident remains unclear. Search and rescue vessels and personnel have been deployed to the area, with maritime authorities, the navy and the water police also involved in the ongoing operation. ■

The Energy Ministry said the increases were temporary and reflected an exceptional rise in the cost of procuring petroleum products from international markets, alongside the major overhaul of the Banias refinery, a key supplier of fuel to the domestic market.
The latest increases came just over a week after another adjustment took effect on Sept. 4, when gasoline and diesel prices were each raised by five pounds per liter, while household and industrial gas prices remained unchanged. ■

Preservation and development of Old Sofia – focus of KvARTal Festival

Font size
In 2016, a new festival was born in the center of Sofia in the small streets surrounding the mosque, the Central Market Hall, and the Central Mineral Baths, an area that surprises visitors with its remarkable buildings and an atmosphere preserved from the last century. "KvARTal Fest" was one of the first attempts to answer the question, "Why haven't we noticed them until now?" while aiming to showcase the district's cultural and historical potential.
Today, in 2026, KvARTal Festival is a beloved and eagerly awaited event held around the Day of Sofia on September 17th.
This year’s program - running from September 18 to 20, features over 60 locations: galleries, studios, cultural spaces, spots for dining and tasting the flavours of Old Sofia, pedestrian festival zones, music stages, installations, exhibitions, tours, a children’s architecture zone, workshops, and other initiatives dedicated to history, architecture, and cultural heritage. We spoke with the festival’s initiator, Martina Stefanova, about the eleventh edition.
Martina Stefanova
PHOTO Yoan Kolev
“The festival aims to invite visitors to the capital and Sofia residents to the old historic city, in order to experience it through flavours, history, and various educational programs. It is a festival where we get to feel the city and come to love our history, because without history, there is no future.”
This year, the festival’s main theme focuses on the future of Sofia’s historic center and the preservation of its cultural heritage. Prior to the festival's opening, the "Future of the Old City" forum will take place on September 16. Architects, experts, and professionals in the sphere of cultural heritage will participate in the event. Representatives from all relevant institutions have been invited to discuss topics such as 20th-century architecture, archaeology, the city's mineral water heritage, including its baths, as well as the future of museums.
PHOTO Martina Stefanova
"It is important that we are announcing two new initiatives this year," Martina Stefanova says. "The first is 'Adopt a Building,' which we will present to companies and citizens wishing to donate for the restoration of a historic building. The other key initiative is the 'Neighborhood Charter.' This charter will be available at various locations throughout Old Sofia. Anyone will be able to sign it. Our goal is to call upon the authorities to preserve the area and to restore it to its original state."
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
One of the festival events takes us back to the early 20th century, when the first chocolate factory in the Balkans was established in Sofia. It was the work of industrialist Velizar Peev, and during the three days of the festival, its building at 12 George Washington Street will serve as one of the venues offering visitors engaging experiences:
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
"In the hall, across various floors and in the courtyard, we will showcase vintage furniture, as some pieces have already been restored, while others await restoration and a new owner. We are creating an exhibition that bridges the past and the future, featuring old furniture alongside works by contemporary artists, including modern art, sculpture, and installations. The event will also feature a vinyl music program and a lecture on vintage furniture, as well as the styles of furniture and architecture spanning the Art Nouveau, Secession, and later Modernist periods. It promises to be a fascinating three-day program, which you can also follow on our social media channels."
PHOTO Kvartal Festival
"The past in the future tense" – perhaps that is how we should define the essence of KvARTal Festival, believing that its mission to preserve and develop this part of the capital will unfold right before our eyes.

Chile is home to around 100 Bulgarians who cherish their homeland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

News
Chile is home to around 100 Bulgarians who cherish their homeland
Bulgarians in Chile aim to establish their own association and maintain closer contact with the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad
Sunday 13 September 2026 08:00
Sunday, 13 September 2026, 08:00
PHOTO personal archive
Font size
Moving to Chile is like stepping into a new reality, where the distances, nature, and geographical features are completely different. This distant and little-known country is home to around one hundred compatriots, among them Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez, who has been living there for 30 years. She moved to Chile in 1997 with her Chilean husband and their two children, after they had lived in Bulgaria for 10 years. Today, she describes this step as a good decision, although there were also many uncertainties.
PHOTO Hristina Taseva
''I have a big, as they call it, corn family, like an ear of corn with many kernels on the cob. Families in Chile are always close-knit, like the kernels on a cob, and there is always someone who can help you. I became part of this family and felt like one of them. I spoke Spanish and very quickly found a job. This is extremely important because this is how social connections are established'', said Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
According to Miroslava, Chileans are not inclined to emigrate and prefer to build their lives at home. She attributes this characteristic to their islander mentality, as they live with a sense of being cut off from the world around them. Their country is vast in size. On one side, it borders the Pacific Ocean, while on the other are the Andes — a vast mountain range resembling a wall. To the north, the Atacama Desert stretches for 2,000 kilometers, while to the south lies Antarctica, which is also like a desert, but a cold one.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
It is therefore no surprise that over the past five years, Chile has increasingly attracted the interest of the most avid Bulgarian tourists. Miroslava works as a tour guide and says that her fellow Bulgarians are amazed by this distant country. “To go to Chile, you have to have a special taste for adventure, and anyone who goes there is amazed”, she says. From the desert, you find yourself in Polynesia and on Easter Island, which is Chilean territory.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
“They are very surprised because when they leave for Chile, they do not know what they are going to see. They set off for a country they do not know, but they are amazed by what they see. They usually spend more than 15 days in the country. This is because of the great distances: Chile has 4,000 kilometers of coastline along the Pacific Ocean. These distances cannot be covered by land; you have to fly. That is why you cannot get so quickly from the desert to Patagonia, or from Patagonia to Easter Island — it takes time. They are very surprised by the diversity of nature, by landscapes that look like those on the Moon or Mars. In the Atacama Desert, there is an area called the Mars Valley because the landscape is the same, and lunar rovers and Mars rovers have been tested there. It is a very dry place, with high levels of ultraviolet radiation, stunning landscapes and volcanoes.”
Miroslava is one of the active members of the Bulgarian community in Chile and takes part in organizing events to mark March 3, Baba Marta, and religious holidays. How will the community continue to develop?
Rayna Mandzhukova in Chile (April 2026)
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
''There are only a few of us Bulgarians in Chile, around 100, unlike in Argentina, where there are around 20,000. In Chile, Bulgarians have come either for work, like the musicians, or they are employees of shipping companies who were sent from Europe because Chile has large ports with links to North America, Japan and China. There are also people who came here with a Chilean husband or wife. There are not many of us, and so far we have not had a real organization, but I hope that we will have one now, thanks to the visit four months ago by Rayna Mandzhukova, Director of the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad. Following this meeting, the Bulgarians became enthusiastic about setting up an organization, and most likely, when I return, we will try to establish such a foundation. This would give us the opportunity to organize exhibitions and allow children to take part in the agency’s competitions — for songs, children’s drawings, camps, and so on. I hope that the next time I come, I will be able to tell you that we already have a foundation'', said Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez.
PHOTO Facebook /Miroslava Petrova
We say goodbye to Miroslava Petrova-Gutiérrez, agreeing to keep following the developments surrounding the future Bulgarian association and to share the most important aspects of its work.

Brics embraces AI but leaves job displacement largely unaddressed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:42:41 UTC
14:42:41 KST

Brics New Delhi Declaration backs AI-driven growth and worker re-skilling but leaves unanswered what happens to jobs lost to automation.
NEW DELHI: Brics has set out an ambitious plan to prepare people for an AI-driven economy, but its New Delhi Declaration leaves a key question largely unanswered — what happens to workers whose jobs are lost or sharply changed because of automation and AI?The declaration calls AI an “immense opportunity to stimulate economic growth and sustainable development for all” and backs wider access to AI, while stressing safety, security, inclusion and reliability. But on employment, its response is largely to prepare workers for changing skill needs rather than spell out what happens when technology replaces existing work.The declaration commits Brics countries to strengthen cooperation in “forecasting skills needs by analysing labour market trends in digital, green, care and other priority sectors”. It also welcomes Brics Connect, the “BRICS Cooperation Network for Capacity Building, Employability, and New Skills and Technologies”, focused on skills for changing labour markets.
The declaration addresses some changes already taking place. It calls for nationally tailored approaches to expand social protection for gig and platform workers and recognises the need to protect workers moving across borders, including through portability of benefits. It also notes an initiative to establish an “International Digital Platform for Remote Employment” for Brics countries.But there is no equivalent, specific commitment on workers whose existing jobs may disappear because of AI.
The declaration does not propose a Brics system to identify occupations exposed to automation, provide transition support to affected workers or measure AI-related job losses.That gap stands out because Brics is simultaneously encouraging wider use of AI across its economies. Its Centre for Industrial Competencies supports manufacturing companies, including SMEs, in adopting Industry 4.0 and advanced digital production technologies, including AI.
Brics does recognise some AI-related risks beyond employment. In the intellectual property section, it notes “risks relating to misappropriation and misrepresentation of knowledge, heritage, and cultural values” that are insufficiently represented in datasets and AI models.For workers the declaration promises labour markets that are “future-ready”, “ensuring that no worker is left behind”.

Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese lawmakers, NGOs, and overseas Taiwanese marched through Manhattan on Saturday in support of Taiwan's inclusion in the United Nations, chanting slogans including “UN for Taiwan” and “Keep Taiwan Free,” per CNA.
The annual march took place during the opening week of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, which began Sept. 8 at UN headquarters in New York. The General Assembly's 2026-27 session is being held under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All,” per a UN press release.
The march was organized by groups advocating Taiwan's participation in international organizations. Participants included Taiwanese lawmakers and overseas Taiwanese from New York, Boston, Washington, and other parts of the US. Marchers traveled along 42nd Street in Manhattan, passing the Chinese Consulate General, Times Square, and Bryant Park before reaching the New York Public Library, according to organizers.
Participants chanted “UN for Taiwan” and “Keep Taiwan Free,” while some passersby stopped to take photographs and show their support. DPP Legislator Wang Yi-chuan (王義川) led the march with Shih Shu-hua (史書華), chair of the Taiwan United Nations Alliance.
Wang said Taiwan is already an important member of the international community, particularly in semiconductors and technology, and called for the annual demonstration to continue so the voices of Taiwanese supporters can be heard by UN member states, per CNA.
He said he hoped Taiwan could eventually join the United Nations under the name “Taiwan.” Lee Chih-chiang (李志強), director of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in New York, addressed participants at the conclusion of the march and called on the UN to allow Taiwan to participate.
Shih said TAIUNA continues to support Taiwan's membership in the UN and World Health Organization, but the group has broadened its objectives to promote Taiwan's participation in international organizations more generally.
“Our goals are now broader,” Shih said, arguing that Taiwan should be able to engage in exchanges with international organizations and friendly countries, per CNA.
Marshall Islands Permanent Representative to the UN John Silk also attended the event in support of Taiwan. His government has previously voiced support for Taiwan's meaningful participation in the UN system.
The Taiwan government has also launched a promotional campaign in New York during the General Assembly session. The Foreign Ministry said it would use public diplomacy and other activities to highlight Taiwan's contributions to the international community and advocate for its participation in the UN system.

UK government to offer clearer guidance on student loans after repayment row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:01:00 UTC
14:01:00 KST

University students taking out student loans are to be warned that the terms and conditions could change so they are better informed about what they are signing up to, the government has said.
In July, a report by MPs said slideshows that compared student loan repayments to the cost of a mobile phone contract, and YouTube videos that did not mention the fact that conditions could be altered amounted to mis-selling by the government.
The Treasury committee’s investigation followed a furore last November when the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, announced that the repayment threshold on plan 2 loans in England would be frozen at £29,385 for three years from April 2027. The threshold is currently £28,470 for this plan.
Some students had been led to believe that the thresholds would rise in line with inflation each year.
The committee’s report said the government had a “moral obligation” to reverse the freeze to maintain students’ trust and honour the terms under which the loans were sold to them.
In its response, published on Sunday, the government acknowledged the difficulties faced by graduates repaying loans, and said it kept “all aspects of the student finance system under review”, but did not commit to any change in policy.
It said it would redesign the guidance for new students to make it clear and unambiguous.
However it rejected the committee’s recommendation to issue new loans on a contractual basis so that terms could not be changed at a later date, saying it needed to be able to adapt the system to changing economic circumstances in order to keep taxpayers’ contributions stable.
In August, 121 MPs and peers from across party lines signed a letter to the new chancellor, John Healey, calling on him to urgently review the repayment system.
The letter said the frozen thresholds combined with inflation-linked interest rates meant young teachers, nurses, engineers, and entrepreneurs were facing “historically high” effective marginal tax rates.
“For many middle-income graduates, the combination of income tax, national insurance, and student loan repayments means they see less than half of any hard-earned pay rise,” it said.
Responding to the government’s commitment to offer clearer guidance, the chair of the Treasury committee, Meg Hillier, said: “The commitment to right a historical wrong by updating the information so that prospective students are properly informed before taking out a massive loan is an important step forward.
“Unfortunately, though, it doesn’t help graduates who are angry that they didn’t receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing.”
Hillier welcomed the fact that a reversal of the threshold freeze had not been ruled out.
“I recognise that finances are tight but I continue to urge the chancellor to look at this again. I sincerely hope he will use his upcoming budget to give graduates some much-needed breathing space.”
A government spokesperson said: “We are taking decisive action to improve the student finance system and break down barriers to accessing university, starting with improved and clearer guidance for those taking out loans.
“That includes increasing maximum maintenance loans, reintroducing targeted maintenance grants to expand opportunities for people from all backgrounds, and [we have] raised the repayment threshold for plan 2 loans for the first time since 2021.
“We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way.”

Europe dominates ranking of the world’s most beautiful cycling routes – these are rides to try
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

From the vineyards of Tuscany and lavender fields of Provence to the rugged Scottish coast and the peaks of the French Alps, Europe is home to some of the world’s most spectacular cycling routes, according to new research.
Tourism on two wheels is on the rise with a surge of 292% in Google searches for “cycling holiday”. There’s so much more to a cycling trip than just the bike, though, and new research has revealed the most beautiful routes worldwide.
It’s good news for European cycling fans, as a majority of the top 15 in the ranking are based on the continent.
A study by adventure booking platform Explore used eye-tracking software to assess the reactions of 200 participants to 52 renowned and attractive cycling routes from around the world.
The technology measured how quickly each route caught their attention and how long it held it for, and the metrics were combined into a weighted "eye-catching" score out of 100 to provide a definitive ranking.
“There's something about seeing a country from the saddle that no other kind of travel can match; you're moving fast enough to cover real ground, but slow enough to take it all in,” said Luke Judd, travel expert at Explore.
“What's interesting about this research is that it puts science behind what cyclists have always debated: which views genuinely stop us in our tracks.”
Canada’s Bow Valley Parkway, a scenic winding route between Banff and Lake Louise, was far and away the most popular option, with a score of 97 out of 100.
It was followed closely by Australia's Great Ocean Road, on the southwest coast of Victoria, which was awarded a score of 94.
Despite the top two being some distance from Europe, and the list spanning four continents, eight out of the 15 are actually in Europe itself.
Here’s where to head for a beautiful cycling experience closer to home.
European destinations dominate the rankings
In third place, with a score of 91, are the stunning Tuscany Gravel Routes in Italy. Most famous for the professional one-day race held there in the spring, the stunning route features cypress tree-lined climbs, working vineyards and centuries-old hilltop towns.
With a score of 90, the Elbe Cycle Route in Germany is in fourth place.
It follows the Elbe River for around 1,220 kilometres from Czechia towards the North Sea, and the route passes through Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, skirts several German states and travels right through Hamburg, offering a journey through historic cities, countryside and some of eastern and northern Germany’s most interesting landscapes.
In sixth place, Amsterdam Cycle Route 10 has a score of 86. The Netherlands goes hand in hand with cycling, and there’s arguably no better way to explore Amsterdam than by bike.
This circular route offers a brilliant introduction to the city and its surroundings, taking you past canals, parks and historic neighbourhoods before heading into quieter countryside.
In seventh and eighth places, with scores of 82 and 81 respectively, are Italy’s Stelvio Pass and the Provence Lavender Route in France.
While the Stelvio Pass is notorious as one of the most difficult cycling routes in the world – and the second-highest in the Alps – the Provence Lavender Route is, mercifully, significantly easier.
The scenic trip is best taken in the summertime when lavender plants are in full bloom. It winds through rolling countryside, hilltop villages and the Luberon and Valensole Plateau’s vast fields of purple blooms.
It’s back to challenging routes with Scotland’s North Coast 500, which is in 11th place with a score of 78.
Starting and finishing in Inverness, this route is more than 800km long and can take even the most competent cyclists up to five days to complete. Despite its trickiness, it’s well worth it for those who want to experience the rugged beauty of the Scottish coast.
The Route des Grandes Alpes is one of Europe’s great mountain road trips, stretching from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean through some of the French Alps’ most spectacular scenery.
It’s in 13th place, with a score of 78 – the same as the North Coast 500 in Scotland – and isn’t easy either. Expect towering peaks, deep valleys, mountain passes and picturesque villages along the way. It’s fairly challenging, with long, winding and sometimes steep sections, so it’s best suited to experienced cyclists.
The last European entry in the top 15 is the Lake Ohrid Circuit in 14th place, with a score of 76. The trip covers roughly 90 to 96 kilometres and crosses an international border between North Macedonia and Albania.
Those tackling it will take in the historic towns of Ohrid and Struga and the Monastery of Saint Naum near the southern border, as well as Pogradec on the Albanian lakeside. Just remember to bring your passport in order to experience the whole route.
The world’s top 15 most beautiful cycling routes
How each route is ranked according to an “eye-catching” score out of 100:
- 1. Bow Valley Parkway (Banff–Lake Louise), Canada - 97/100
- 2. Great Ocean Road, Australia - 94/100
- 3. Tuscany Gravel Routes, Italy - 91/100
- 4. Elbe Cycle Route, Germany - 90/100
- 5. Carretera Austral, Chile - 86/100
- 6. Amsterdam Cycle Route 10, Netherlands - 86/100
- 7. Pacific Coast Highway, USA - 82/100
- 8. Stelvio Pass, Italy - 82/100
- 9. Provence Lavender Route, France - 81/100
- 10. Road to Hana, USA - 78/100
- 11. NC500 (North Coast 500), Scotland (UK) - 78/100
- 12. Route des Grandes Alpes, France - 78/100
- 13. Slickrock Trail, USA - 76/100
- 14. Lake Ohrid Circuit, North Macedonia/Albania - 76/100
- 15. Vancouver Seawall, Canada - 75/100

India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:06 UTC
14:00:06 KST

India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
India spent decades casting Pakistan as the region’s rule-breaker. A tribunal ruling handed Islamabad the chance to return the favour
Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry.
On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that Delhi had no legal basis for suspending the water-sharing agreement, adding that India must also limit construction on the Ratle Hydroelectric Plant being built in Kashmir.
The court’s five-member panel was unanimous: none of the grounds India cited justified suspending or terminating the agreement.
It was a clean sweep for Islamabad, which brought the case after Delhi froze cooperation on the Indus and its tributaries – vital rivers that irrigate Pakistan’s agricultural heartland.

Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

Ukraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.
Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.
This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it?
The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022, then left them to sink or swim. Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors and paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’s nauseating Alaska summit, and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price.
Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About 60% oppose ceding Donbas land to Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians also want it to stop. And like Moscow, Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch, notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly a deal to be done. But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away.
Efforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has now extended to the Red Sea (Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modern forever war phenomenon. Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but to win a Nobel peace prize (plus lucrative Russian energy deals).
Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas. Trump’s “board of peace” and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fear fighting will drag on indefinitely. Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together.
Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led to war crime atrocities such as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedly killed more than 100 schoolgirls in February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy.
Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightly restricted international journalists’ access to Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost of successful Iranian strikes on US bases in the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict.
Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now.
Western democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly, urged here) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war.
- 
  Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Burnham must understand Wales is ‘not a region in England’, says first minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

Andy Burnham has to be serious about devolution and understand that Wales is a nation and “not a region in England”, according to the country’s first minister.
Rhun ap Iorwerth, who is the first non-Labour leader of the Senedd since devolution, told the Guardian that while he was encouraged by initial discussions with the new UK prime minister, he was wary about Burnham being captured by a consensus Westminster view against relinquishing further powers.
Separately in the interview, ap Iorwerth said his party, Plaid Cymru, would be willing to cooperate with Labour in the future to keep Reform UK out of power, as he would always want to block the “destructive politics” of Nigel Farage’s party.
Ap Iorwerth became Wales’s first minister in May, days after he led Plaid Cymru to victory in Senedd elections, breaking a 100-year period of Labour dominance, which included Labour being the biggest party in every vote to the Welsh parliament since it was created in 1999.
He has pushed for more powers to be given to his government, particularly over policing and the justice system, where Wales is the only UK nation not to have control.
Burnham’s background as Greater Manchester mayor was a positive, ap Iorwerth said: “He clearly understands the benefits of getting devolution right for Manchester. I’ve had really positive, constructive discussions with him.
“He now needs to know what devolution means for Wales, and it’s very, very different. We’re a nation. We’re not a region of England. There are different needs. We will work closely with the UK government on what empowering communities means. But it’s a totally different model, and it’s really important that Andy Burnham doesn’t confuse the two.”
Speaking in London after meetings with UK government officials, ap Iorwerth said, although Burnham had assured him he would “not bypass devolution”, he was concerned about institutional resistance to handing over police and justice powers.
In July, Burnham’s Welsh secretary, Stephen Kinnock, said he was not “entirely convinced” about the idea of devolving powers such as policing. Ap Iorwerth said: “The arguments for the devolution of policing and justice are very, very strong. Commission after commission and study after study have concluded this really needs to happen.
“Andy Burnham had more control over policing as the mayor of Manchester than I do as first minister of Wales, and it’s just not right. Burnham gives me the impression, and I believe him, that he’s ready to take a different approach.
“What I’m also acutely aware of is that those forces around him are probably equally as averse to devolving policing and justice as they have been under previous Labour leaders.”
With 43 Senedd seats, Plaid is the biggest party in the expanded 96-member chamber, with Reform forming the opposition. Reform enjoyed “a very significant result” in May in going from two members – both defectors from the Conservatives – to 34, ap Iorwerth said.
However, he pledged to stand against what he termed Reform’s “kind of politics that runs contrary to my core beliefs of cooperation and tolerance and supporting each other and looking after the weak”.
Asked if Plaid would potentially cooperate with Labour to block a potential Reform government, whether in Cardiff or Westminster, he said it would: “It’s not about keeping a political party out, it’s about keeping a kind of politics out, the negative influence that it has, and of course we do and will cooperate with Labour.”
At a press conference earlier this month to mark the start of the new Senedd session, ap Iorwerth took a somewhat downbeat approach, warning about a “very challenging” financial picture, with a real-terms decline in both day-to-day and capital spending this year.
Asked if he risked mimicking Keir Starmer’s sometimes gloomy approach in assessing the task of government, ap Iorwerth said that was not his intention: “I would certainly hope not, because I think a mistake Keir Starmer made was that the government almost gave up on its values, gave up on its beliefs under that administration, because things were difficult.
“We’ve taken a completely different approach, and if there was a sense of gloom, it was certainly not meant to be like that.”
On Monday, ap Iorwerth is due to hold a meeting in Cardiff with his equivalents in Scotland and Northern Ireland, John Swinney of the Scottish National party and Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, an event labelled by one Telegraph columnist as a “sinister cabal … plotting nothing less than the end of the United Kingdom”.
Asked about this description, ap Iorwerth smiles. “It’s just not the way that I see it,” he says. “I don’t come from the base of working, either ourselves or with any other partners, to break up the UK. I want to build up my nation. That’s all it’s about.”
Wales is, he says, on a “constitutional journey”, one in which he sees the ultimate destination as being independence – but without any set timetable or rush: “That’s in the hands of the people of Wales.”

At least 1 dead, more than 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:33:03 UTC
13:33:03 KST

Saadet Gokce
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
At least one body was recovered while more than 30 people are missing after an inter-island ferry sank off the South Pacific island nation of Vanuatu, the prime minister's office said Sunday.
Of the more than 40 crew members and passengers on board, 15 people have been accounted for alive, according to a statement on US social media platform Facebook.
The statement, citing Luganville MP Matai Seremiah, said the search in open waters is being scaled back as efforts shifted to the southeast coast, where currents may have carried survivors.
"The loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel," said the prime minister's office.
It urged ship owners to prioritize safety, ensure vessels are seaworthy and properly equipped, and maintain reliable communication systems.
"Ignoring strong marine warnings puts lives at risk," it said, adding that a full investigation would be done to establish the facts and prevent a recurrence.
The vessel, the MV Matui, was carrying 47 people, including crew members, from Santo to Ambae on Saturday, according to the Vanuatu Broadcasting & Television Corporation.

'Proud to be a houso': Anthony Albanese condemns Hanson's remarks on late mother
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:31:22 UTC
13:31:22 KST

IN BRIEF
- One Nation leader Pauline Hanson criticised the time Albanese's mother spent in public housing.
- Albanese told reporters on Sunday that his mother was "way out of Pauline Hanson's league".
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has criticised Pauline Hanson's comments about his late mother living in public housing for decades, saying he was proud of his upbringing and defending his mother as "way out of Pauline Hanson's league".
"She made comments about me being complaining about being growing up in public housing — nothing could be further from the truth," Albanese told reporters in Sydney on Sunday.
"I'm proud to be a houso and I'm proud of the community in which I grew up."
The comments follow resurfaced footage from Hanson's February appearance on a podcast, in which she mimicked Albanese crying while mocking his account of growing up in social housing in Sydney's inner west.
She argued Albanese's mother should not have remained in the same public housing property all her life.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
What did Pauline Hanson say?
Appearing on The Karl Stefanovic Show in February, the One Nation leader was asked about Albanese. In response, she feigned tears while delivering a joke impression of the prime minister.
"Oh, I've actually grew up in a housing commission house. You have no idea how hard it is to grow up in a housing commission house. Oh, my God... talk about a Prime Minister," Hanson said on the podcast.
Hanson added that she had grown up on a street with housing commission homes and that the people who lived in them "had jobs, they worked".
"He said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years. Sorry, that's not on, to me," she continued.
"It should be a limited time — you've been given a hand up, move it on to the next ones coming through."
On Friday, she doubled down on those comments, telling The Australian the prime minister "complains about his housing commission upbringing".
She also questioned Albanese's account compared to Australians "being forced to live in cars and tents" because of what she called "his government's high immigration numbers".
'Way out of Pauline Hanson's league'
Albanese's mother, Maryanne, was a single mother and disability pensioner who lived with chronic rheumatoid arthritis for most of her adult life.
She died in 2002, aged 65, having spent decades in the same public housing property where Albanese also grew up.
Albanese gave an extended account of her life on Sunday morning, describing a woman who worked cleaning offices overnight to support him and who was left barely able to hold a knife and fork as her arthritis worsened.
"She was compassionate, not uncaring. She was generous, not mean. And she was kind, not nasty," Albanese said.
"She was a person of great character. She had a tough life … [but] she never complained. She never denigrated anyone.
"I grew up in a community that looked after each other. It was the opposite of being elite."
Albanese said he hadn't seen the comments when they first aired, but was "stunned" to see them when they resurfaced.
"She was a battler, and for Pauline Hanson to attack someone and their character — who died in 2002, some 24 years ago, at age just 65 — because she did have such a tough life with her health from an early age," he said.
"I am stunned at these comments, but I'll make this point: if Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that's fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league."
Condemnation across the board
Hanson's remarks drew criticism from both sides of politics.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie — who is currently locked in a separate, escalating dispute with Hanson after she posted a cartoon labelling him a "traitor" over his testimony in the Ben Roberts-Smith defamation case — said the comments were another sign she was unfit for office.
"Let's leave mums out of it," he told News24 on Sunday. "This is another indicator to the Australian people that she's not fit to be prime minister."
Trade Minister Don Farrell called the remarks "appalling".
"Anthony loves his mother … to have them attacked publicly in this way is just appalling," Farrell told News24 on Sunday.
"There's a certain bitterness in One Nation’s approach to the world that I find quite un-Australian actually."
He said that if she wanted "dignity and respect" from those in politics, an apology was necessary.
"Attacking the prime minister's mother like this is not a way to get respect and dignity from your colleagues," he said.
On Saturday, Energy Minister Chris Bowen said: "attacking a woman who has been dead for more than 20 years for living in public housing is off-limits".
"We can have a debate between politicians – leave families alone, particularly a family member who's deceased. For God's sake, there's a line — and Pauline Hanson regularly crosses the line."

Russia's losses in the war against Ukraine have reached 1.506 million military personnel — General Staff
Kyiv • UNN
Over the past day, the Russian army lost 1,520 military personnel and equipment. Russia's total losses since the beginning of the invasion have reached approximately 1,506,900 personnel.
The total combat losses of Russian troops since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine have reached approximately 1,506,900 military personnel. In the past day alone, Russia lost another 1,520 personnel, reports the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, writes UNN.
Details
As of September 13, the enemy's total losses also amount to 12,344 tanks, 25,330 armored combat vehicles, 49,678 artillery systems, 2,120 MLRS, and 1,635 air defense systems.
Over the past day, the Defense Forces destroyed 8 armored combat vehicles, 2,142 UAVs, and 17 enemy NKKs.
Russian troops also lost 410 vehicles and fuel trucks, as well as 5 pieces of special equipment.
Since the beginning of the full-scale war, Russia's losses amount to 442 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 5,111 cruise missiles, 35 warships and boats, and 2 submarines. The General Staff noted that the data is being уточнено.
As a reminder
According to the General Staff, Russia's losses in the war against Ukraine have exceeded its combined losses in all wars over the past 80 years.

 Authorities determined the drones were launched from the province.
 Two Iraqi security sources reported finding drone launchers near the al-Shib border crossing in Missan on Sept. 12.
 The government initially closed three crossings to reorganize operations and boost intelligence efforts to stop violations.
 The crossings will gradually reopen for passengers and trade on a timeline from Sept. 13 until Sept. 17, the security media cell said.
 These crossings include Shalamsheh in Basra, al-Shib in Missan, and al-Mandali in Diyala.
 Shalamsheh and al-Shib reopened to passengers on Sept. 13 but not to trade, the government media cell noted.
 No group claimed responsibility for the attack.
 An alliance of Iran-backed Iraqi armed factions denied striking the pipeline.
 Riyadh previously accused Iraqi groups of targeting its oil infrastructure.
 The United States and Saudi Arabia struck Iran-backed militants in Iraq in July.
 The strikes came in response to attacks on U.S. forces and Saudi oil facilities.
 Pro-Iran armed groups have supported Tehran during the Middle East war, claiming hundreds of attacks on U.S. bases in Iraq and across the region.
