superstudio’s 12 ideal cities question the price of a perfectly designed life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
20:35:32 UTC
05:35:32 KST

Superstudio designed 12 impossible ways of living
In 1971, Superstudio imagined twelve cities designed to solve the problems of human existence and came up with solutions so complete that there was barely any life left to live. A person wakes up in a five-cubit cell. The temperature is permanently set at 25°C. The humidity never changes. Food and every other necessity arrive automatically. There is no work to do, no reason to leave, and no one else to meet.
The room knows what its inhabitant wants before they have to ask. It also knows when they are unhappy. This is the 2,000-Ton City, one of twelve imaginary settlements described by Gian Piero Frassinelli and Superstudio in Twelve Cautionary Tales for Christmas: Premonitions of the Mystical Rebirth of Urbanism, published in 1971. Better known as 12 Ideal Cities, the project is populated by disembodied brains, people who live through machines, citizens governed by books, and inhabitants carried through life by cities that operate like enormous industrial organisms.
They are strange, often funny, and increasingly cruel. More importantly, they are all built around the same trap: every city has found a solution.
In Superstudio’s cities there is no universal housing model, no master plan intended to work everywhere. Every story begins with a principle and follows it to its most extreme conclusion. What if every human need could be satisfied automatically? What if the body were no longer necessary? What if a city could organize its inhabitants according to perfect order? What if life could be made more efficient by treating the city as a machine? The questions may be simple, but the answers grow increasingly uncomfortable. This is what keeps Twelve Ideal Cities interesting. Superstudio takes familiar problems, gives them perfect solutions, then follows those solutions until they become something else entirely. In these cities, the system designed to make life easier gradually takes over life itself.
Twelve Ideal Cities – Twelve Cautionary Tales, 1971 | image via MAXXI
the city that gives you everything
The inhabitants of the 2,000-Ton City live alone, enclosed within individual cells. The city regulates the environment and responds to desire through an elaborate technological apparatus. A brain-impulse receiver communicates the wishes of the inhabitants to a central electronic system which organizes the response of the city.
Nothing needs to be searched for, made, or negotiated. It is difficult to imagine a more complete promise of convenience. Superstudio then introduces the detail that gives the city its name. If the system detects a citizen entertaining rebellious thoughts against their ‘perfect eternal life,’ a ceiling panel weighing two thousand tons drops. The problem has been removed and so has the person. It is an absurd image, but the joke is doing serious work. The 2,000-Ton City questions whether a life made entirely convenient is necessarily a life made freer. Its inhabitant has been relieved of almost every difficulty and, along with it, almost every opportunity to act. There is no need for other people because the system takes care of everything. There is no need to make decisions because the system anticipates them. The perfect home becomes a perfectly managed cell.
Superstudio, Terza città: New York of Brains, 1971 | image via Centre Pompidou, MNAM-CCI/Georges Meguerditchian/Dist. GrandPalaisRmn
no body, no house
The New York of Brains is exactly what its title suggests. Human brains are preserved in individual containers, sustained by technological systems and connected through electrodes. The traditional ingredients of habitation disappear with the body itself. No kitchens. No beds. No streets. No need to walk anywhere. In the City of the Hemispheres, bodies lie immobilized inside transparent containers while consciousness experiences the world through a separate apparatus.
In Spaceship City, inhabitants live through programmed experiences as the machinery around them controls the conditions of their existence. These stories make ordinary architecture suddenly seem very physical. A house is designed around bodies that need to sleep, eat, move, touch things, get sick, grow old, and share space with other bodies. Remove those conditions and the familiar architecture of daily life begins to disappear. Superstudio takes this idea to an almost grotesque conclusion. What is a home when there is no need to cook? What is privacy when the body itself has become a technical object? What is a city when its inhabitants no longer need streets? The answer is never presented as a technological triumph. The systems keep people alive, but Superstudio keeps asking, what kind of life is being preserved?
2,000-Ton City | image via Hidden Architecture
the city doesn’t need you. it needs you to work
Not every city isolates its inhabitants. Some absorb them. In the Temporal Cochlea-City, life happens inside an immense mechanical structure that continues according to its own physical logic. In other stories, cities become systems of continuous production, construction, and industrial activity. Here, the relationship between architecture and inhabitant begins to reverse. Usually, a city is understood as something built for people. Housing accommodates domestic life; streets allow people to move; infrastructure supplies what a population needs. Superstudio imagines a city that has its own rhythm. People must keep up. The inhabitant becomes a component within a much larger mechanism. It is a useful shift because it moves Twelve Ideal Cities away from the familiar image of radical architecture as a collection of spectacular drawings. The project is interested in what forms do to people. A spiral, a conveyor belt, or an enclosed machine is never just an image. Each produces a particular way of spending time, moving through space, relating to others, and reaching the end of a life. Architecture becomes a schedule, a social system, a biological system.
The strangest form of architecture in Twelve Ideal Cities may not look like architecture at all. In the City of the Book, the rules of life are carried by the inhabitants. The book contains the instructions by which existence is organized: norms, behaviors, and prescribed ways of acting.
The City of Order explores a similar idea. Control does not necessarily arrive in the form of walls, guards, or visibly oppressive buildings. It can appear as normality. Streets, houses, and everyday routines continue, while the system makes sure that deviation is corrected. Superstudio’s point is that control can be embedded in things that appear helpful, rational, or ordinary. A system can make life easier while deciding what kind of life it is designed to support. A housing plan can encourage one form of domesticity over another. An infrastructure network can determine who meets and who remains separated. A building can make certain activities effortless and others almost impossible. The City of the Book turns this invisible process into a literal instruction manual.
The Fourth City, Spaceship City- 1971 | image courtesy of Superstudio
the problem with an ideal city
It would be easy to call all twelve cities dystopias and leave it there. The project is more unsettling than a collection of bad futures. Each city begins with something recognizable: comfort, order, longevity, efficiency, pleasure, security or the elimination of unnecessary labor.
These are desires that remain among the reasons people build, design, plan, and invent. Superstudio’s trick is to ask what happens when one of them becomes the only thing that matters. A city devoted entirely to comfort eventually removes the need to do anything uncomfortable. A city devoted entirely to order has little use for disagreement. A system designed to eliminate uncertainty will eventually treat unpredictability as a malfunction. Superstudio takes each idea to its logical extreme. The cities offer clear answers to familiar questions about how we might live, but the further those answers are pushed, the stranger the resulting forms of habitation become.
Dodicesima città: città del libro (Twelfth City: City of Book), from Le dodici città ideali (Twelve Ideal Cities) | image via SFMOMA
leave some things unresolved
What makes Twelve Ideal Cities difficult to leave behind is that the absurdity is never really the point. Frassinelli takes ideas that already exist around him — the efficient city, the productive city, the perfectly controlled environment, the city organized around a single purpose — and refuses to stop at the point where they still sound reasonable. He keeps going until the consequences become impossible to ignore.
That method still works. We now live among many of the systems that were once easier to recognize as science fiction: automated environments, permanent connectivity, predictive technologies, and cities increasingly measured through data and performance. But the twelve cities are relevant because they ask a more basic question about what we are willing to give up in exchange for a life that is faster, easier, more efficient or more controlled.
The answer is different in each city, but the pattern is the same. Something is gained, and something else disappears. In one, the body becomes irrelevant; in another, production takes over the city; elsewhere, order becomes the organizing principle of everyday life, and the architecture follows. Eventually there is nowhere left for anything that does not belong. Frassinelli asks what happens when an idea about how we should live becomes the environment around us. Today, the question is still relevant: as technology becomes more involved in everyday life, how much of our lives do we want to let it shape?
Twelve Cautionary Tales for Christmas by Superstudio

Xi, Modi conduct in-depth exchange of views, agree China, India should be partners
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
03:51:16 CST
04:51:16 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Ye)
NEW DELHI, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi conducted here on Saturday a candid and in-depth exchange of views, and reached important consensus that China and India should be partners.
The two leaders met on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi.
Xi said China has always viewed and developed its relations with India from a strategic height and with a long-term perspective.
Xi noted that he has met with Modi twice over the past two years, guiding bilateral relations from a new start to a further improvement.
Institutional exchanges between the two countries have gradually resumed, the list of areas of cooperation has continued to grow, and bilateral trade has reached a new record high, Xi added.
Xi said such hard-won progress should be cherished. Noting that China and India have different national conditions, Xi said they can draw on each other's strengths, support one another, help each other succeed and pursue common development.
Amid a turbulent international landscape, China and India, as the world's two most populous countries and important members of the Global South, shoulder important responsibilities, Xi said.
Xi called on the two sides to keep in mind the future of humanity and the well-being of peoples, work together to promote high-quality development of greater BRICS cooperation, and contribute more positive energy to world peace, stability, development and prosperity.
Underscoring objective and rational strategic perception in calibrating China-India relations, Xi said China and India are partners for cooperation, not rivals. The two countries provide development opportunities for each other rather than pose threats to each other, he added.
That is a strategic judgment based on the development stages of the two countries and the international environment, and serves the common interests of both countries and their peoples, Xi said.
Xi called on both sides to help each other succeed through win-win cooperation.
The two sides, Xi said, should focus on development as their greatest common denominator, while strengthening friendly exchanges and mutually beneficial cooperation.
He called on the two sides to expand cooperation in people-to-people exchanges, direct flights and other areas to effectively strengthen the public support for bilateral relations.
The two sides should also balance and address each other's economic and trade concerns, and promote a sound and stable development of bilateral economic and trade ties, Xi added.
Xi called on China and India to draw on political wisdom of mutual respect and understanding to overcome disruptions, urging both sides to pursue parallel progress in bilateral ties and border issues with the two tracks reinforcing each other, so as to maintain peace and tranquility in border areas.
He also urged China and India to promote multilateral cooperation with openness and inclusiveness to benefit the world.
Xi said the two countries should support each other as rotating chair of the BRICS, strengthen coordination within such multilateral frameworks as the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Group of 20, stand together in addressing global challenges, and unequivocally uphold international fairness and justice.
Modi said he has held several productive meetings with Xi, guiding India-China relations toward a positive direction, which serves the common interests of the more than 2.8 billion people of both countries.
The two major civilizations of India and China have, over thousands of years, learned from each other through exchanges and moved forward hand in hand, he said.
India always views India-China relations from a strategic height and a long-term perspective, and is willing to be a partner rather than a rival to China, and to regard each other's development as an opportunity rather than a challenge, he noted.
India adheres to an independent foreign policy, and the development of its relations with China is not subject to the influence of any third party, he said.
India's policy and position on the issues related to Taiwan and Xizang remain unchanged, and it does not allow any force to engage in anti-China activities in India, he said.
India is ready to maintain high-level exchanges with China on the basis of mutual respect and mutual trust, strengthen strategic communication, promote mutually beneficial cooperation, and enhance people-to-people exchanges, so as to advance bilateral relations to greater heights, Modi said.
The two sides should work together to safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas, he added.
India thanked China for its support for India's hosting of the BRICS summit and will fully support China in assuming the BRICS chairmanship next year, he said.
Modi said India is ready to closely coordinate and cooperate with China to jointly strengthen cooperation among Global South countries, promote a more multipolar world and global economic growth, and serve as a force for stability and progress in a turbulent world. ■
Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Sept. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Yan Yan)

US court blocks Trump administration plan to cut disaster agency workforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:49:29 UTC
04:49:29 KST

US court blocks Trump administration plan to cut disaster agency workforce
US President Donald Trump has said he would like to abolish the agency.
A United States federal judge has ruled the Trump administration acted unlawfully by ordering job cuts at the federal agency in charge of responding to the country’s natural disasters.
On Friday, US District Judge Susan Illston in California said the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), exceeded its authority when it ordered personnel changes that effectively stripped the emergency agency of control over its own workforce.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Acting FEMA head David Richardson steps down after troubled tenure
- list 2 of 3Why did Trump fire Kristi Noem as DHS secretary; who is Markwayne Mullin?
- list 3 of 3US court rules Trump violated order by placing conditions on FEMA grants
The ruling centres on thousands of temporary FEMA reservists who are called upon to help communities after hurricanes, wildfires, floods and other disasters.
Labor groups representing federal workers sued to block the administration’s decision to stop renewing many of those contracts.
After Hurricane Katrina battered parts of the US Gulf Coast in 2005, the US Congress strengthened FEMA’s independence. US federal law says DHS cannot substantially or significantly reduce the agency’s authority, responsibilities or functions.
Illston, who was appointed by former US President Bill Clinton, said the Trump administration had failed to provide what she described as a “reasoned” explanation for its decision to restrict FEMA’s ability to renew contracts. She also noted FEMA was projecting a workforce of 11,383 employees for the coming fiscal year — about half of its previous level — without a clear justification for the figure.
The dispute comes amid a broader effort by US President Donald Trump’s administration to reduce the size of the federal workforce. Trump has previously questioned the need for FEMA and suggested that states, not the federal government, should assume greater responsibility for disaster preparedness.
The ruling did not immediately order the administration to reverse the cuts or impose penalties. Illston said those issues would be considered in a separate decision expected next month.

====================================================================================================

Not your average Jewish mother: Lisa Edelstein on Hollywood, identity, and ‘Long Story Short'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:49:19 UTC
04:49:19 KST

When actress and artist Lisa Edelstein met her now-husband, artist Robert Russell, he came with a deep desire to rediscover his Jewish identity and pass it on to his sons from a former marriage, then three and five. He found the perfect partner for the job in Lisa.
In addition to being Jewish, Lisa has played numerous Jewish women, including Dr. Cuddy on House, the lead (and a producer) of Bravo’s Girlfriends’ Guide to Divorce, and the adult daughter of Alan Arkin’s character on Netflix’s The Kominsky Method.
Now she’s playing the matriarch anchoring Long Story Short, Netflix’s time-shifting adult animated series about three generations of a Jewish family.
The following is a blend of a written and a Zoom interview. She was warm, funny, and thoughtful.
Lisa grew up Conservative and kosher, building sukkahs and sitting through four-hour Seders, attending synagogue on Saturdays and Hebrew school until she was sixteen. Shabbat dinner was non-negotiable.
“My father would usually give a very simple Parsha,” she told me. “I didn’t know that’s what he was doing at the time. I just knew that every week he talked about the Torah portion. And that continued for my whole childhood.”
Edelstein's Jewish roots
HER GRANDPARENTS were immigrants, their first language Yiddish. Pogroms and war had scattered the family. Some cousins went to America, but many more ended up in Argentina and Israel.
Her father’s Aunt Leah founded Kibbutz Daliya in the early 1900s. “They turned the rocky, dry land into a forest and farm and hosted dance festivals once a year. That part of the family is still there, although some of their descendants have left the kibbutz.”
Other family members live in Tel Aviv, Herzliya, Nir Zvi, Haifa, and by the border of Lebanon. Her last visit was a few days after the last living Oct. 7 hostages came home.
“Israel is a beautiful, messy, complicated, diverse, loud, funny, tragic, amazing, gorgeous, powerful country, and I’m grateful for its existence.”
She drifted away from Jewish traditions in her young adulthood, but meeting her husband – and his own Jewish journey – pulled her back in.
“When we met, it was pretty apparent to both of us that we were going to stay together forever, and so we created a home. The boys were going back and forth 50/50 between our household and their mom’s, and we wanted to find a way to give them a joyous Jewish experience in this house.”
Their solution was a “hip-hop Shabbat” with dance lessons from an instructor followed by a big Shabbat dinner. When the boys outgrew hip-hop, it became Shabbat Dungeons & Dragons: friends over for dinner, then up half the night immersed in the fantasy tabletop game.
The boys have since graduated high school, but the joyous Shabbat dinner tradition continues at the Edelstein-Russell household, now with dozens of friends and family members.
ALTHOUGH SHE grew up in a Jewish neighborhood, Lisa got a taste of antisemitism and “otherism” at an early age. Her family moved to Wayne, a Jewish enclave in New Jersey, in 1967 – the same year the Civil Rights Act finally forced the town to take down the “No Negroes, no Jews, no dogs allowed” signs in shop and restaurant windows.
During a re-election campaign, the head of the school board claimed that the Jew running against him was going to cancel Christmas. In response to this outlandish charge, The New York Times dubbed the town “The Home of Antisemitism in the United States of America.”
“He won the election, by the way, and then he became mayor for 12 years. So that guy was running my town in one way or another during my entire childhood there,” Lisa said.
Her feelings of otherism, however, “weren’t because someone pointed at me and yelled JEW,” she explained. “It was our culture, in general, that somehow accepted the idea that Jewish women were spoiled princesses that only cared about Bloomingdale’s … that they had big noses and frizzy hair and were grating.”
I remember the jokes and the moniker Jewish American Princess, with its derisive acronym JAP. Jokes like, “What does a Jewish American Princess make for dinner? A reservation.” And, “How do you tickle a Jewish American Princess? Gucci, Gucci, goo.”
“I didn’t want to own that stereotype,” she continued. “And I guess on some level, I believed that that was true because that was what I was being told, and so I felt shame around my Jewish identity.”
When Lisa left home to study drama at New York University, she made a concerted effort to separate herself from that unpleasant association. “I felt like it was a part of myself I had to grow out of or away from, or somehow bury or erase.”
Edelstein's reinvention and journey of self-exploration
THAT REINVENTION, and an explosion of self-exploration, led her into the New York City club scene and a walk on the wild side. She became so well known in the clubs that famed journalist Maureen Dowd wrote a feature about her in The New York Times titled “Lisa in Wonderland.”
Dowd painted a colorful picture of the full-time drama student and celebutante: “She talks fast, walks fast, laughs often. Her stride is a fast-motion version of Marilyn Monroe’s bouncy gait. Everything about her, from her vivid alto to her mane of brown curls, seems to vibrate.”
Lisa immersed herself in a world of experimental theater and experimental human beings. “It was the most exciting and diverse group of creative people I’d ever seen,” she said of the club life.
“I couldn’t get enough of how weird and wonderful and psychedelic the city could be. I learned an enormous amount, met incredible people, and was immersed in a community bursting with imagination and juice. So it was more than just fun for me; it was me finding out what excited me, what surprised me, even what terrified me.”
In the club scene, she went by Lisa E, unsure how to “own a name like Edelstein out in the world without having to constantly battle with the preconceived idea of what that meant.” In time, she realized the stereotype had nothing to do with her.
Writing an AIDS-related musical, Positive Me, forced a decision: Lisa E, or Lisa Edelstein, on the poster? “Am I moving forward as myself, or am I moving forward as this creation?”
She decided she couldn’t leave herself behind. Changing her name felt like “Hitler would win. Like I was abandoning my people and my heritage and my ancestors. I started to realize, you have to find a way to carry yourself with you, despite what people might think.”
For decades, Jewish actors anglicized their names. Woody Allen was born Allan Stewart Konigsberg. Peter Coyote was Robert Peter Cohon. Winona Ryder changed her name from Winona Horowitz. And Albert Brooks was born Albert Einstein. Okay, you can’t blame him for that one.
JOINING THE Screen Actors Guild, Lisa said, marked another milestone. Was she worried about typecasting?
“The answer is yes, and for sure it got in my way. I had several experiences where producers would call me crying or tell me years later that they were not allowed to cast me because I was too Jewish. If I had changed my name, maybe that wouldn’t have happened. Who knows? I got jobs anyway, and a lot of those characters became Jewish without my trying, because people saw me that way, so that’s fine.”
That’s more than fine with me. The casting of non-Jewish actors in Jewish roles, a rare practice today for other marginalized groups, remains ubiquitous in Hollywood. I don’t love the idea of artificially restricting actors who can convincingly play other ethnicities, but if we are calling for authenticity for other minorities, we should do the same for Jews.
Lisa has also portrayed many Jewish mothers, so I asked her to describe her mother. “HA!” she playfully responded, “describe YOUR mother.” I didn’t, but Lisa did.
Bonnie Edelstein graduated high school at 16 and married at 19. She’s tough, critical, deeply opinionated, “confused by technology but offended by that confusion,” and loves playing solitaire on her phone.
Bonnie’s mother, Grandma Gertie, was one of Lisa’s favorite people – an unstoppable force of hilarity and attitude. “She smoked two packs of cigarettes for 70 years and then gave it up in a day. She was the president of the sisterhoods of five different synagogues in Coney Island and Brighton Beach.”
Both women fed directly into Lisa’s performance as the matriarch of Long Story Short, Naomi – a feisty, witty woman unafraid to pick a fight over something that matters to her. She loves her family the best way she knows how, but she still gets under the skin of her three kids.
Lisa admitted Naomi leans toward the stereotypical “cloying Jewish mom,” but believes it’s those very expectations that trick the audience into falling in love with her.
In a second-season twist, we learn, right alongside her children, that she’s beloved by the wider community and a heroine to many. It strikes me that in families, we’re all playing roles. Whether you’re the provider, the nurturer, the rebel, or the complainer, we get locked into those parts, and it keeps the people closest to us from ever fully knowing who we are.
Edelstein explores hidden histories in Little Bird
THAT THEME of hidden histories carries into another project of Lisa’s: Little Bird, a six-episode Canadian miniseries about the “Sixties Scoop,” when government policy tore Indigenous children from their families to be raised in foster care or adopted into non-Indigenous homes, cut off from their culture.
Adoptive parents believed they were rescuing abandoned children, not participating in a kidnapping scheme.
Lisa plays Golda Rosenbaum, a Holocaust survivor who immigrated from Poland to Montreal and adopted a young Saskatchewan girl, raising her as a Jew and renaming her Esther.
“Golda thinks she’s raising somebody who she shares the experience with of having lost their families,” Lisa explained. “She adopts her when she’s 5, and by the time her daughter is 25 and ready to get married, her daughter cannot move forward without finding out what actually happened to her.” So Esther sets off in search of her Indigenous family.
When a member of her Indigenous family dies, Esther processes her grief through both traditions. Lisa and I talked about how ritual and tradition help us process events and regulate our emotions.
“No one does mourning better than Jews,” Lisa opined. “We’ve got a guidebook like no other guidebook. There’s a written plan about how you walk through this tragedy in your life, and it’s beautiful.”
Jewish characters are rare in film and television outside stories with intrinsically Jewish storylines. Yet, Lisa made her Abby in Girlfriends’ Guide to Divorce, a show about a recent divorcee going through a common modern experience, a member of the tribe.
“That was a dream job. One that I’m so glad I got to experience while I could still wear really, really high heels for any length of time. To get to be funny and sexy, smart, and emotional all in one job was deeply fulfilling,” she said.
Edelstein's impulse to create
LISA STARTED PAINTING as an extension of a lifelong impulse to create, transforming what she once viewed as a private coping mechanism into an applauded second career.
“My husband gave me a painting on our second date, and asked me for a drawing in return,” she shared. Exchanging handmade gifts gradually became central to their relationship, helping her recognize that “that part of myself was valuable.”
The turning point came when COVID slowed the world. Looking for a subject for her artwork, Edelstein immersed herself in family photographs she inherited after helping her parents downsize. She discovered “so many stories, so many memories, so many things I didn’t remember,” and decided “to make myself a coloring book out of these images.”
What began with magic markers evolved into increasingly intricate works. When friends urged her to abandon markers for paint, she switched to watercolor, opening new creative possibilities.
She worked obsessively – sometimes “6 hours, 10 hours” – and found the experience exhilarating. Since then, she has moved into oils and mounted four exhibitions, with two works entering museum collections.
“It’s been a really magical journey,” she told me.
I was struck by the paintings’ vivid colors and dense patterns, which evoked their eras without overshadowing the people. Edelstein explained that her early reliance on markers naturally led her to seek photographs rich with pattern, making the 1970s of her youth “just a gift.”
Although her source material now spans about 100 years, she unifies work with a consistent palette.
“Mostly what I’m looking for in these images is narrative,” Edelstein said. She is drawn to photographs that “accidentally tell a story,” revealing something unexpected about a person’s character or life. Carefully posed family portraits rarely interest her.
One of my favorite paintings is Vampirella, a portrait of Lisa at eleven, in glasses and a nightgown, surrounded by the intimate clutter of her bedroom. Another painting that stays with me is Celebration, which bursts with affection and movement. Lisa believes the original photo was one of her grandparents’ wedding anniversaries.
What captivates her is not the event but the exuberant humanity within it: “There’s just so much momentum, there’s so many stories in that image.”
I am struck by the family dynamics – fathers and daughters, husbands and wives – and by the many yarmulkes. Edelstein explained that the visible Jewish identity in her work became an intentional artistic choice even before the Oct. 7, 2023 massacre of innocent Israelis and visitors by Hamas.
The impact of Oct. 7 on Edelstein's Jewish identity
When preparing for her first gallery show, she remembered being asked, “Are you sure you want to go this Jew-forward?”
“Well, yeah, it’s my family. We are also a minority,” she said, “and we have a rich culture in this country [USA].” After Oct. 7, that commitment deepened, and since then, she has made sure every exhibition includes work reflecting Jewish life and culture.
LIKE MOST JEWS, Lisa and Robert were devastated by the attack, but the reactions from friends were mixed.
“We have a few friends who cried with us, who checked in frequently, who never stopped wanting to talk about what happened and what we have all been going through,” she said.
On the other hand, “We had to end a few friendships completely because they were total dead ends. It has been painful and sad and also made us furious.”
While the hostages were still being held captive, Lisa wore a Star of David she bought during a visit to Israel in the 70s along with a yellow ribbon hostage pin. At work, a colleague referenced the star and pin, saying, “It seems like you’re making a very political statement. Are you sure you want to do that?”
“A Jewish person said this to me!” an exasperated Lisa told me.
“It doesn’t matter what statement people think I’m making by wearing this,” she told her colleague. “It matters that they know who they’re talking to, and edit accordingly.”
And then there was the silence.
“I confronted one of our friends post-Oct. 7. I felt she’d let her politics get in the way of her empathy when she didn’t even bother to check in with us after such a traumatizing event. Her excuse surprised me: she had no idea we would care about what was happening there. She had no idea that Jewish people feel connected to each other,” Lisa shared.
“She was shocked to be confronted, and I was shocked to realize that this was something completely unique to us. We are a people. We feel each other’s successes and failures, triumphs, and tragedies. Some of us are annoyed by ‘others of us,’ but we are still, somehow, an ‘Us.’ And that isn’t something most people experience or comprehend. It makes us incredibly special.” ■

From Australian judge to Israeli tour guide: David Parry's aliyah journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:48:51 UTC
04:48:51 KST

"I felt the mission of my life was to get here,” says David Parry from his home in Zichron Ya’acov.
To fulfill that mission, the Sydney native took early retirement from his law career. He had worked his way up from specialist magistrate in administrative law to Australian District Court judge and deputy president of the State Administrative Tribunal in Perth, on Australia’s west coast.
“It was a tremendous privilege to uphold the rule of law and to resolve disputes between citizens and governmental authorities.
“I had a tenured position for another 15 years, but I resigned in favor of a lifelong dream to come to Israel. I always felt it was part of my life destiny,” David says. “My career enabled me to retire at the age of 55 with a pension that puts us in a position that we are truly blessed.”
To his baffled colleagues in Australia, he explained that he felt obligated to grab an opportunity that past generations had been denied “to make a contribution to the reestablishment of Jewish sovereignty and society in the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people.”
David, Sharon Parry join four kids, one grandchildren in Israel
Why Zichron Ya’acov? This bucolic Haifa district town is where David and Sharon Parry’s oldest daughter, Gabriella, who works in public relations for Israeli start-ups, lives with her husband, Joe, and their daughter – the Parrys’ only grandchild, with another on the way.
All four Parry kids made the move from Australia to Israel. Natalie and her husband, Yehuda, live in Jaffa; she is a senior data analyst. Mia is a Middle Eastern studies student at Shalem College in Jerusalem. Jacob, soon finishing his IDF service, has built up a 40k-strong social media presence (as @jakey_parry on Instagram) and is an actor in Michael Aloni’s new theater company, HaMakor.
“Sharon and I are incredibly proud that they all made the decision on their own to make aliyah and found their lives and communities and passions here,” says David, who’d happily spent his morning having breakfast with his granddaughter and then taking her to preschool.
“We were incredibly happy in Perth, and it was a great place to raise our children. But we always knew it was temporary.”
David and Sharon carve new path after arriving in Israel
BOTH DAVID and Sharon embarked on new careers after arriving.
David completed a tour-guiding course in English at the University of Haifa School of Tourism, received his license, and opened a website, TourWiseIsrael.com.
He is partnering with Israel Maven Tours in Jerusalem to offer three-day guided tour packages for English-speaking immigrants who want to explore their adopted land with peers: one to the Galilee and Golan in October and March (israelmaven.com/tzafonatour) and one to the Negev in January and February (israelmaven.com/negbatour).
David says he was always “an avid student of the extraordinary history, geography, and geopolitics of Israel and had visited many times. But after making aliyah, I finally had the time and space to tour and study this incredible land in depth.
“What a privilege it is to guide people in the country that has contributed to the world like no other and to help explain what is, perhaps, the most misunderstood place on the planet.”
He has discovered that the professional skills he developed as a judge are equally valuable as a tour guide: “mastery of facts, weighing different perspectives, clarity of expression, the ability to communicate complex issues to people from all backgrounds, and treating every person with respect.”
Sharon’s transition was more complicated. She has a doctorate in physiotherapy, with a specific interest in the deleterious health effects of desk-based work and how to mitigate them.
For the 18 years prior to aliyah, she was a university lecturer and researcher, and ultimately an adjunct professor of physiotherapy.
“The only negative aspect of our aliyah story is that the bureaucracy defeated her in converting her degree,” David says. “The Health Ministry decided that, although she was registered as a physiotherapist in Australia, because she was employed as a ‘lecturer’ and not a ‘physiotherapist’ for 18 years, she would have had to prove the number of hours she did in clinical training for her bachelor’s degree, which was 40 years ago. That was impossible.”
Therefore, Sharon decided to apply her expertise to a related endeavor: running workshops for companies, particularly hi-tech companies, on how to improve the workplace to prevent health problems of sedentary workers. Through her website, MoveWiseActive.com, she’s also offering workshops on fall prevention for seniors.
“She found something based on her experience that’s even more meaningful,” says David. “We’re hoping to do a bit of collaboration, combining her workshop with my tour.”
Though the couple has studied spoken Hebrew at ulpan, they work exclusively in English and have gained a close circle of friends in Zichron from English-speaking countries. Together, they take trips around Israel, play pickleball, and spend time at the beach.
David hopes for uptick in tourism
Of course, like all tour guides here, David is hoping for an uptick in foreign tourism.
“I’d ideally like to guide delegations and missions; I’m in touch with organizations from Australia and North America about that,” he says.
“There’s an incredible pent-up demand to come to Israel. There is a thirst to see the country. The second [that] flights open, tourists flock in.
“There’s simply no other place like Israel, no other place that was the crossroads of the world from the beginning. I would love to show not just its beauty and history, but the depth and meaning that lie beneath the surface.”
Married 35 years, the Parrys are happily starting over in Israel.
“It’s such an incredible blessing to be here. I really feel it was the mission of my life to facilitate my family’s return to Israel,” David emphasizes.
“Coming from the outside, we appreciate so much that we live here according to Jewish time; that the Jewish holidays and the rhythm of Jewish life are part of the culture of the country. I will never take that for granted.” ■

Type 31 schedule challenges being monitored
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
20:40:22 BST
04:40:22 KST

The Type 31 frigate programme continues to face schedule challenges linked to its ambitious build timeline and the integration, testing and assurance of ship systems, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard set out the position in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what challenges remained following references in the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s Major Projects Annual Report 2025 to 2026.
Pollard said the MOD was continuing to work with Babcock, the prime contractor for the five-ship Type 31 programme, to keep the build aligned with Royal Navy requirements and the planned delivery timetable.
He said: “The Ministry of Defence (MOD) continues to work closely with Babcock, the prime contractor, to ensure the Type 31 programme meets all user requirements to deliver a maritime security capability at a value for money price, in a timescale that is competitive with other international warship procurement programmes.”
The programme is based around an intentionally fast build schedule, with Babcock constructing the frigates at Rosyth using a repeatable production approach intended to support a steady flow of ships through assembly, integration and completion.
Pollard added: “Challenges can be expected when delivering a complex warship against an ambitious build timeline. Working closely with Babcock enables us to resolve any issues that may arise, alongside maturing the design and progressing construction, ensuring the build programme is stable and repeatable going forward.”
The minister also pointed to the complexity of bringing together the ship’s combat, communications, navigation, propulsion and other onboard systems while keeping testing and assurance aligned with the wider programme schedule. He added: “The complex nature of this work can present challenges, however all activities are subject to ongoing oversight by the MOD to ensure successful delivery to the RN.”
Readers should note that this answer does not identify a specific new delay or single integration issue affecting the programme, but confirms that schedule pressure remains tied to an ambitious construction plan and the need to complete ship-system integration, testing and assurance without disrupting the pathway into Royal Navy service.
Type 31 is intended to provide the Royal Navy with five general-purpose frigates, replacing part of the Type 23 fleet and increasing the number of modern surface combatants available for maritime security, presence and other tasks. The ships are being built by Babcock at Rosyth, with the programme also intended to demonstrate a more repeatable approach to warship production that can support future export opportunities and maintain shipbuilding activity across the yard.

Watch first naval battle in history fought entirely by drones: Ukrainian uncrewed boat spots, fires on, and sinks Russian one in Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:04:57 UTC
04:04:57 KST

For the first time, two unmanned boats have fought a battle at sea, and the Ukrainian one sank its Russian rival. The Ukrainian Defense Intelligence has spotted a Russian drone in the Black Sea, and a Sargan-3000 naval drone armed with a remote-controlled machine-gun turret opened fire and destroyed it, the Ukrainian Navy said on Telegram, calling it "the first-ever naval battle between unmanned boats."
Drone-versus-drone combat has moved from the sky to the sea. Ukraine has already rewritten naval warfare with uncrewed boats, sinking warships and pushing much of Russia's Black Sea Fleet back to port without a navy of its own to speak of.
Now it has fought and won the first duel between two robot vessels, a glimpse of automated sea combat. The claim is the Navy's. It released a video of the encounter but did not provide a date, an exact location, or the type of Russian craft, and it has not been independently verified.
A gun turret decides the duel
The Russian vessel was detected by units of the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence, the Navy said, before the Sargan-3000 closed in.
The Ukrainian drone carried an automated 12.7mm Protector remote weapon station, a turret of the same type mounted on some NATO warships, and used it to sink the Russian boat.
The published footage shows the two drones engaging and the Russian craft going under.
The Sargan-3000 reaches far
The Sargan-3000 is a Ukrainian multi-purpose strike drone that passed combat testing in April. It has a combat radius of up to 1,600 kilometers, runs at 40 to 55 knots, and carries up to 450 kilograms of payload, according to Militarnyi.
It is the same class of boat that sank the Russian border patrol ship Izumrud near Novorossiysk in July.
Ukraine keeps rewriting naval war
The battle fits a campaign that has reshaped the Black Sea. Ukrainian sea drones have sunk the corvette Ivanovets (link) and the landing ship Caesar Kunikov (link), in 2025, even shot down a Russian Su-30 fighter jet (link), and in the last ten weeks alone struck 285 vessels of Russia's shadow fleet (link).
Russia is now racing to build its own uncrewed fleet, and satellite imagery suggests it is constructing a dedicated naval-drone port in occupied Crimea, a sign that the sea, like the sky, is filling with machines that fight each other (link).

Right-wing US think tank tracked thousands of Muslim Americans for 2 decades: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:04:54 UTC
04:04:54 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
A US right-wing think tank has maintained a database of thousands of Muslim Americans and Muslim organizations for about two decades, according to a report by the HuffPost news site on Friday.
The Middle East Forum (MEF), a controversial organization founded in 1994, compiled more than 4 million data points, including individuals' names, social media accounts and tax information, as well as details on mosques, schools, businesses and other organizations, the report said.
The database also includes people and groups considered allies of the Muslim community.
MEF disclosed the existence of the archive after HuffPost questioned the organization about the database and indicated that it planned to publish a report. The group said it would allow scholars, journalists and other researchers to apply for access to the material.
Gregg Roman, MEF's executive director, said the organization had planned to announce the initiative later this year, but welcomed the earlier disclosure.
MEF says its mission is to defend Western values and highlight what it describes as the dangers of "lawful Islamism." Civil rights organizations, however, accuse the group of contributing to Islamophobia and spreading misinformation about Muslims.
The database consists of information obtained from public records, but its scale has raised concerns among civil rights advocates.
Caleb Kieffer of the Southern Poverty Law Center described the archive as "very concerning," pointing to what he called growing anti-Muslim rhetoric in the US.
Mobashra Tazamal of Georgetown University's Bridge Initiative characterized the database as a potential "target list," warning that such information could be used to monitor or intimidate Muslim individuals and organizations.
The revelations come amid heightened concerns among Muslim Americans over Islamophobia, as well as political tensions surrounding President Donald Trump's policies, the crackdown on pro-Palestinian protesters and rhetoric from some Republican lawmakers.
MEF defended its practices, saying that mapping ideological networks is common among US civil society organizations and arguing that other groups maintain similar databases.

Venice Film Festival 2026, «Woman Unknown» of May el-Toukhy wins the Golden Lion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:02:40 UTC
04:02:40 KST

El-Toukhy's drama depicts the life of a young nanny and housekeeper who marries her wealthy and older widower employer, but harbours a shameful secret that threatens to unravel her new life and status in the post-World War II anarchy.
“Woman Unknown,” a drama about Denmark in the aftermath of the Nazi occupation directed by May el-Toukhy, won the prestigious Golden Lion at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Saturday.
El-Toukhy was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year.
Her film centres on a young Marie, played by Mathilde Arcel, whose Best Actress win makes it a rare double victory. Marie is a nanny and housemaid who is about to marry her wealthy employer in the immediate aftermath of the war. But she harbours a secret past intimate relationship with a German soldier that threatens to upend her reputation.
South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s poetic portrait of class and labour, “Possible Love,” won the Silver Lion grand jury prize, the runner-up award. “Possible Love” is Lee’s first film in eight years, following his acclaimed 2018 title “Burning.”
“NAZA,” a harrowing documentary about military strategies employed in the war in Gaza from Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was awarded a special jury prize.
“It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film,” Abraham said.
The film was added to the main competition late — at the request of the filmmakers — and debuted late in the schedule as well, but its impact was felt: It received a record-breaking standing ovation, lasting some 25 minutes, after its premiere.
Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years, “NAZA” features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders including intelligence officers and soldiers give who insight into the war in Gaza and what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians.
The jury gave the Silver Lion for directing to Ilya Krzhanovsky for his film “Dau,” a project about the Soviet physicists who built the atomic bomb that has taken over 20 years to make.
Krzhanovsky, who renounced his Russian citizenship in protest of the war in Ukraine, dedicated the prize to Ukrainians, including his mother who was born there.
The Maggie Gyllenhaal-led jury announced the winners in a ceremony on Saturday night, which included a best actor prize for John Malkovich for his performance in the dark CIA comedy “Wild Horse Nine”.
Malkovich was not in attendance at the ceremony, but he sent a video message, explaining that he is shooting in Montreal.
“I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” Malkovich said.
Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine was also met with a standing ovation, lasting well past 10 minutes. The dark comedy follows two CIA agents travelling to Easter Island shortly before Chile's 1973 military coup.
The film's stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell's performances were among the elements that drew attention at the premiere.
McDonagh has previously premiered two films at the festival, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin.
He has previously won screenplay prizes for both films, while Colin Farrell received an acting award for the latter.
“Unknown Woman” star Mathilde Arcel was visibly emotional accepting the best actress award, which she said was very heavy and decided to place on the floor while she spoke.
“This is my first lead role in a movie and my first time at a film festival,” she said. “I’m extremely honoured.”
French director Stéphane Brizé’s won the screenplay prize for his corporate drama “A Good Little Soldier.”
Malou Khebizi was given the Marcello Mastroianni award for emerging actor for her role in Cédric Kahn’s “15/18 (A Place to Heal)” which is set in an adolescent psychiatric ward in a public hospital.

Afghan woman deported in first use of US Alien Terrorist Removal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:02:39 UTC
04:02:39 KST

Afghan woman deported in first use of US Alien Terrorist Removal Court
The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created in 1996, but had never been used before Nazira Haji Zada’s case.
An Afghan woman accused of supporting the ISIL (ISIS) armed group has been deported from the United States in the first case brought before an obscure and long-dormant court created 30 years ago to remove people classified by the government as “alien terrorists”.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) announced on Friday that Nazira Haji Zada was deported to Afghanistan after being brought before the Alien Terrorist Removal Court.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US immigration agents arrested more than 49,500 people in July
- list 2 of 3Cuban and Afghan immigrants deported from US under Trump arrive in Guyana
- list 3 of 3‘Handcuffed and blindfolded’: Is the US targeting Ecuadorian fishermen?
The 47-year-old lawful permanent resident, who had been living in Fort Worth, Texas, was arrested in 2024. US Attorney General Todd Blanche filed the papers for her removal on July 15 this year. She waived her rights to challenge her detention and was subsequently deported to Afghanistan.
The DOJ accused Haji Zada of helping conceal an ISIL-inspired plot for a mass shooting in the US state of Oklahoma on election day in 2024. She was never charged with a crime, but her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, pleaded guilty to related charges.
The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created by Congress in 1996 as part of a broader effort to combat international terrorism. It is a specialised US federal court made up of five judges serving staggered five-year terms. It allows the US government to submit classified information in cases where disclosure could threaten national security, while requiring an unclassified summary that the court determines is sufficient for the accused to prepare a defence. The government must prove with strong evidence that the person is an “alien terrorist”.
The defence said that bringing lawful permanent residents before a court while withholding the evidence against them violated due process and predicted the court would eventually be found unconstitutional.
DOJ officials described the deportation as a national security victory.
“Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said, adding that the case showed the department would use “every tool at its disposal” to protect the country.
Haji Zada’s attorneys said her decision to consent to removal “should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy.”
“Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process,” the defence lawyers said in a statement. “We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue.”
It is unclear whether the DOJ would pursue additional cases through the previously unused court.

The Coalition finds voice in One Nation battle and starts new free speech fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Labor will drag Coalition's free speech fight onto harder ground
The dividing line in Australia's next big fight over the internet is not whether online harm exists, but who gets to define it.
As fresh battle lines were drawn up over Labor's proposed digital duty of care this week, another ongoing war entered a new phase.
The escalating stoush between Andrew Hastie and Pauline Hanson got personal after a One Nation video branded the Liberal frontbencher and former SAS officer a traitor.
Hastie viewed it as a slight on all veterans and challenged the One Nation leader to take responsibility for material her party endorsed and authorised.
Angus Taylor has agreed the video should come down.
But the opposition leader has been eager to stress it was a question of "morality" more than "legality".
That distinction was central to Taylor's reasoning for why he could call for the video to be removed in the same breath as criticising Labor's duty of care proposal as a "blank cheque for political censorship".
Wells takes aim at Taylor
Many inside Labor believe the opposition's outcry is instead driven by a desire to "out One Nation, One Nation" and woo conservative voters.
Communications Minister Anika Wells has been at pains to stress the laws are about shifting more responsibility onto tech companies to anticipate and reduce foreseeable harms created by their services.
The Coalition has agreed children need protection but, scarred by the mis- and disinformation laws killed off last term, are convinced the duty of care will become a "backdoor" to censorship.
Their main concern is the ministerial discretion embedded in the proposed laws to add more categories of harm to the duty of care.
Labor may ultimately have to clarify these powers, but senior figures believe the Coalition would simply find some other reason to remain opposed.
The government was disgusted on Thursday when word got around that Taylor had told his partyroom colleagues to be careful with their criticism lest Wells hold a press conference with parents who blame social media for the deaths of their children.
Wells herself took aim at Taylor later that day, accusing the opposition leader of heckling her in Question Time about "hiding behind grieving parents".
"He's wrong on that, this government proudly stands with grieving parents," she thundered back.
It is unedifying for anyone to diminish the agency of those families in order to score a political point.
Tech companies already choose what we see
These parents who have lost children to suicide after bouts of eating disorders, bullying or other harmful content are clear-eyed about the role tech played in their grief.
The problem is that leaving governments out of decisions about what constitutes harm does not leave an internet where nobody is making choices about what Australians see.
Tech companies already do.
Their algorithms decide which posts and videos are recommended, amplified and repeatedly pushed to millions of people.
This opaque system also chooses what content to deprioritise and largely disappear from view.
Even the Coalition acknowledges that problem, with Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson agreeing algorithms are "driving harm".
The Coalition may want a fight about who decides what Australians are allowed to see, but the average parent is far more concerned with what responsibility a tech company has for the harms its systems actively deliver or amplify.
PM heads to the US
That will be front of mind for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the end of this week when he travels to the US where he will tour the Apple headquarters in San Francisco before attending the UN General Assembly in New York.
Albanese's Apple adventure was instigated by chief executive Tim Cook, who invited the prime minister to come and learn about the company's new child safety features "inspired" by Australia.
Apple claims it is making it easier for parents to control what their kids see and do online, including setting screen time allowance and limiting the range of apps they can access.
They're precisely the type of changes Australia had hoped would indirectly flow from the social media age ban.
Piecemeal improvements are no replacement for the effective enforcement of that law, but in the David and Goliath battle of regulator versus big tech the small wins still count for something.
But getting a demonstration of the new folding iPhone is far from the main agenda item on Albanese's US itinerary.
Once at the UN, he will be meeting with a raft of world leaders eager to learn more about Australia's tech regulation efforts.
Albanese understands for things like AI data centres or digital safety laws to succeed, the laws must work beyond borders.
Loading
Coalition and Labor try to fight on different grounds
Back home, the Coalition has at best a few months to secure concessions from Labor and orchestrate a climb down from their current position on duty of care.
After years of consultation, the government is not interested in dragging out the issue and would work with the Greens to pass the laws if necessary.
One Nation will remain opposed on free speech grounds.
Even as critics lined up to condemn the "traitor" video, Hanson continued to bait Hastie with a post on Friday thanking him for drawing attention to her cartoons.
Hastie for his part has not blinked.
With each return serve he appears to have galvanised his fellow Liberals into a rare position of strength against the conservative insurgents. It's almost as if that was his plan all along.
Standing up to One Nation over its treatment of Hastie has allowed Liberals to defend the boundaries of political debate, without retreating from free speech.
The duty of care is harder terrain.
One Liberal MP this week privately complained about Albanese "always" going for the "wedge" on free speech issues.
"They want to trap us," the MP said.
The Coalition has chosen censorship as the ground on which it wants to fight it, but Labor will keep dragging the argument back to children and systemic failures.
Taylor can argue against giving politicians broad discretion to define harm, but outright opposition would mean defending a status quo where all that power remains in the hands of big tech.

‘It’s time to go home’: After 57 years in America, a Holocaust survivor comes home to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
18:54:10 UTC
03:54:10 KST

Morton Pancer, 86, and his wife, Carole, 82, spent 57 years of marriage building a life together in Maryland. This week, after decades in the United States, they decided it was finally time to move home to Israel.
On August 25, the couple arrived on an El Al flight and officially made aliyah with Nefesh B’Nefesh, moving to Israel to be closer to their family and begin a new chapter of their lives.
One of their daughters, Jessica Gertel, made aliyah with her family in the early 2000s, while another, Shoshana Lerner, made aliyah this year with her family, giving them even more incentive to join them in the Jewish state.
For Morton, a Holocaust survivor born in Poland in 1939, whose immediate family survived the war after fleeing to Siberia, the decision to come to Israel is deeply rooted in Judaism.
“We’re Jewish,” he told The Jerusalem Post. “Aliyah – this is the place for the Jews, our own country that we didn’t have for many centuries. It seems like a good thing to do is to come home.”
The Pancers’ move comes as North American immigration reached record levels in August. The Post reported that more than 1,100 North Americans made aliyah through Nefesh B’Nefesh last month, marking a new monthly record for the organization.
The idea of making aliyah had been on their minds for years. Looking back, Morton wonders why they waited so long.
“I don’t understand why we didn’t come right away,” he said.
Carole said she believes Israel is the natural home of the Jewish people – and that Jews who have the opportunity to come should do so.
“I think every Jew should be here. It’s our own homeland,” she said.
Just one week into their new life, Carole said she already knows they made the right choice.
“We’d like to help Israel and contribute in any way we can to the country,” she said. “I think we made the right decision. I can say that even after a week.”
The move also brings the Pancers closer to most of their family. Eight of their 12 grandchildren and seven of their great-grandchildren already live in Israel, while four grandchildren remain in the United States; Carole believes the other four will eventually join them here in Israel.
A life built in America
Carole grew up in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in a family with several generations of roots in the United States. Her parents were born in the US, while her grandparents came from Lithuania and Russia in the early 20th century.
After graduating from the Art Institute of Pittsburgh, she moved to Baltimore after being offered a job as a fashion illustrator.
She worked for a department store, drawing clothing that was featured in newspaper advertisements, and later as a freelance artist producing illustrations for ads.
In Baltimore, she met Morton on a blind date arranged by a mutual friend. The two married and spent the next 57 years together in Maryland, including 29 years in Silver Spring.
Now Carole hopes to bring her artistic talents to her new home. “I’m an artist, so I’d like to capture Israel on my canvas,” she said.
Carole enjoys painting portraits and nature. She also wants to attend an ulpan to learn Hebrew, volunteer, spend time with her family, make new friends, and have fun in her new surroundings.
Morton spent most of his professional life working for the US government, including at the IRS. Then spent about 25 years working on financial management systems for various branches of the US armed forces. He retired in 1998.
America became the country where the couple built their life. But Morton said that Israel remained the homeland of the Jewish people.
“It’s the land that we all belong to,” he said.
A Holocaust survivor’s journey
Morton was born in Tomaszów Lubelski, Poland, in 1939, shortly before the outbreak of World War II. He was only seven months old when his family fled the town. His parents and older brother escaped toward the Russian side of Poland, while Morton was initially left with his grandmother.
An uncle eventually reunited the family and helped smuggle the infant through the woods along the German-Soviet border.
Soon afterward, the family was transported to Ukraine and then deep into Siberia, where they remained for about five years.
“The Russians saved us,” Morton said.
During their grueling time in Siberia, his father was sent to a slave-labor camp, while his mother struggled to keep the family alive under terrible conditions. Food was scarce, and Morton remembers that at times only one loaf of bread fed the entire family.
His mother sold items on the black market to obtain food.
“If it weren’t for my mother, we would have never survived,” Morton said. “She was one tough lady.”
The decision to flee Tomaszów Lubelski would ultimately save Morton’s life, he and his family believe.
German forces heavily bombed the town in September 1939. Records indicate its Jewish population numbered more than 5,600 at the beginning of the war. The Nazis later established a ghetto there before deporting the town’s Jews to the Belzec extermination camp, where they were murdered.
Had Morton remained in the town, his family believes he would have been killed either in the bombing or during the subsequent destruction of the Jewish community.
When the war ended, Morton was about six years old. The Russians allowed the family to return to Poland, where they hoped to discover who had survived.
Instead, they encountered devastation and found no survivors.
Morton remembers the journey back on wooden cattle cars. Jewish partisans would greet the trains and tell the Jews they would protect them, but the journey remained dangerous, with attacks against Jews returning to Poland. Amid the fear and uncertainty, he distinctly remembers huddling around a stove inside the cattle car for warmth.
“It took several months to get back to Poland,” he said. “I don’t know how we survived. I was scared.”
After the war, Zionist groups sought to send Morton and his older brother to what was then British-mandated Palestine. However, his mother refused to send the children away on their own.
The family remained in Poland for about a year before moving to Austria and then Germany, where they lived in a displaced persons camp under the care of the US Army.
Eventually, a relative in the United States, Rabbi Moshe Boehm, sponsored the family’s immigration.
In 1951, they boarded the USS Hershey for the journey to America.
For Morton, America represented safety and opportunity.
“Everyone wanted to go to the US,” he recalled. “They claimed the streets were paved out of gold.”
The US ultimately became the country where Morton built his career, and where he and Carole raised their family.
From protecting Germany to protecting Israel
After graduating from high school in Baltimore, Morton joined the US Army at age 18. He was sent to Germany for two years with the 3rd Armored Division’s 15th Infantry Battalion.
The assignment struck him as deeply ironic.
“They sent me to Germany for two years, protecting the Germans against the Russians who saved us,” he said. “If that’s not irony, I don’t know what is.”
Morton said he wasn’t happy about the assignment but had no choice.
Decades later, after building a life in Maryland, Morton and Carole made another journey.
This time, they were not fleeing. They were coming home.
Morton said he had always wanted to live in Israel and had returned over the years to support Sar-El, an organization that enables volunteers to support the IDF. During his visits, he worked on army tanks.
The couple currently lives with one of their daughters in Gush Etzion while they search for a more permanent place to live, potentially in an apartment or an independent-living community.
For Morton, his new life in Israel comes with a sense of responsibility.
He said he has always tried to help Israel from the United States, but now wants to contribute from within the country. “It’s the land that we all belong to,” he said. “We have to make sure it grows and prospers.”
He also believes Jews have a responsibility to ensure that Israel remains strong and secure.
“We’ve gone through a lot,” he said. “The Jewish people, for thousands of years, we didn’t have a country. Now that we have a country, we have to make sure we do the right thing and make sure it’s strong and secure.”
His own history gives that belief a deeply personal meaning.
“What happened in the past should never happen again,” Morton said. “We have to make sure this never happens again – the Holocaust.”
Carole, meanwhile, is looking forward to her new life as an artist, wife, mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother in Israel.
For now, she is taking in the experience of finally being here.
And she has a message for other American Jews who may be considering the same journey.
“Now is the chance to come home to Israel before things get worse,” she said. “Every Jew should be here.”

Yemen government forces say they hit Houthis in Red Sea city
Yemen's Riyadh-backed government forces said on Saturday that they had struck Houthi fighters in the strategic Red Sea city of Mocha.
Following a week-long offensive, the Houthis on Friday captured Yemen's Red Sea coast, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the US-Iran war.
They had seized Mocha the day before after heavy fighting.
"The armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime" near Mocha's port, the government news agency Saba reported on Saturday.
The spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they had also struck Houthi vehicles and fighters on the Mocha-Dhubab road, just outside the city, according to Saba.
Nazili said on Friday that government forces had begun shelling areas in Mocha, and called on citizens not to use the Taiz-Mocha and Mocha-Dhubab roads.
The fall of the city to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
On Friday, Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha's airport, while a local official said the city's seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
News site Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had twice called US President Donald Trump to request American strikes on the Houthis last week.
But on Saturday, Trump told reporters that "the Houthis called us and they don't want to fight with us".
He didn't say if Washington would take action, but added "everything's gonna work out fine and dandy" in the region.
The United States previously conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis, starting in March 2025, in response to the group's repeated attacks on international shipping in support of Hamas in the war on Gaza.
That effort ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel.
More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis' ground offensive, launched last week, has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 76,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Saturday, a figure that had quadrupled since last week.
Yemen's civil war began with the group's takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014, and was paused by a 2022 truce that fell apart in July.

'First-ever battle' — Ukrainian naval drone destroys Russian unmanned boat in Black Sea, Navy says
A Ukrainian unmanned surface vessel destroyed a Russian naval drone in the Black Sea in what Ukraine's Navy described as the "first-ever naval battle" between unmanned boats.
The operation was carried out jointly with Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR), whose units detected the unmanned Russian vessel, the Navy said on Sept. 12.
The Russian drone was destroyed by a Ukrainian Sargan-3000 unmanned boat, equipped with a 12.7-mm Protector remote weapons station, according to the Navy. The drone-on-drone encounter marked a historic first.
"This is the first-ever battle between unmanned naval boats," the Navy said.
The military also published video footage of the operation on its official Telegram account.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the Navy's report at the time of publication.
The joint operation represents a shift from naval drones attacking conventional ships to drone-on-drone maritime combat. Both Ukraine and Russia are increasingly moving toward unmanned warfare at sea.
Ukraine has dramatically expanded maritime-drone operations in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, hitting dozens of Russian vessels and maritime logistics targets this summer, striking 105 Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov campaign alone.
Russia is also developing and deploying more unmanned surface systems. Recent satellite imagery indicated Moscow was building what appeared to be its first dedicated naval-drone port in occupied Crimea.
Ukraine's Sargan-3000 is a naval unmanned system that passed combat testing in April 2026. The multi-purpose platform is "highly maneuverable" and capable of executing strike missions, according to the Navy.

BERLIN – Tens of thousands of protesters took part in demonstrations across Germany on Sept 12 against the far-right AfD, after the party scored a crushing victory in a state election on Sept 6.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) topped the vote in the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt, and is now seeking to form the first extreme-right state government in Germany since World War II.
About 150,000 demonstrators took to the streets in around 20 cities nationwide, including Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, in protests that were called by Pruef, which advocates for a ban on the AfD, organisers said.

The rise of the AfD has unnerved many who feel Germany has a special responsibility to atone for its Nazi past, and calls have grown for mainstream parties to seek to ban the group.
But hurdles for a formal ban are high in Germany, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz, of the centre-right CDU party, remains sceptical about taking such an approach.
In Berlin, police said several thousand protesters took part in several demonstrations.
The AfD held a counter-demonstration in the capital, attended by Kristin Brinker, its lead candidate in next weekend’s regional elections in Berlin.
Campact said there were around 25,000 demonstrators in Hamburg and 12,000 in Munich.
The anti-immigration, Russia-friendly party took almost 44 per cent of the vote in a Sept 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, against 17 per cent for the CDU.
It fell three seats short of an absolute majority, and has started talks with other groups and MPs in an effort to form a state government. AFP
