Philippine ferry fire death toll jumps to 76
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:16:57 UTC
23:16:57 KST

The death toll from a Philippine ferry fire jumped to 76 on Saturday after the coast guard confirmed the discovery of 41 more bodies aboard the burnt-out vessel.
The remains will be transported to a port in Coron, Palawan, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said in a statement.
AFP watched hours earlier as disaster agency workers carried coffins to a cemetery in the resort town, intended for the temporary burial of victims of the fire that tore through the M/V June Aster on Wednesday.
The first 30 bodies arrived by sea earlier on Saturday as forensic specialists began the painstaking process of identifying the remains.
The confirmed death toll now stands at 76, including five bodies recovered in the immediate wake of the incident. The ship sits grounded about 7.5 kilometres (4.5 miles) off the coast.
One-metre (three-feet) deep graves have been dug to hold the victims' remains until DNA testing is completed, Kristine Ablana, a tourism official serving as an official spokesperson, told reporters on Saturday.
Relatives will be brought to identify personal items that may have belonged to family members.
"Once someone is able to verify... that this photo or these belongings are indeed those of their relative, they will be asked to provide a DNA sample," Ablana said.
Thirty passengers, including two Chilean nationals, and 13 crew have been rescued, according to the coast guard. Around a dozen people are believed to remain unaccounted for.
'Happened in seconds'
Cayabyab said in a radio interview that the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.
"From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly," she said of survivors' accounts.
"Everything happened in seconds," she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on life jackets.
Near the pier where the bodies were to be returned, an emotional Josenit Mayo, 40, told AFP her daughter had been aboard the ferry, returning from the capital Manila for a family visit.
"She told me 'Mom, I want to go home as I'm missing my siblings,'" Mayo said. "She insisted she was lonely."
Myra Cabilan told AFP she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.
"His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter," Cabilan said, fighting back tears.
"At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he's still missing. I have lost hope."
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog. The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas. Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country's more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.

BRICS nations urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:16:35 UTC
23:16:35 KST

Breadcrumb
BRICS nations urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East war
Members of the 11-nation BRICS group including China, Russia, Iran and India called for calm in the Middle East at a summit in New Delhi on Saturday, overcoming earlier divisions to issue a joint statement.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who joined Russian, Iranian, Indian and other leaders in the Indian capital, told the summit that the war in the Middle East "does not serve the common interests of the international community".
Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on 28 February.
But leaders issued a statement on Saturday after intense diplomatic efforts by host India, as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia," the joint statement said, adding the countries "call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation".
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
"We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders.
Modi, opening the two-day summit, called for a system "where every country has a voice, every member has a stake and humanity's development is at the centre of every effort".
He told leaders that BRICS nations "represent 50 percent of the world's population, 40 percent of global GDP and more than 25 percent of global trade".
But finding balance in the bloc is a tough diplomatic task.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
Iran's Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a "regional policeman", with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Pezeshkian met with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed on the summit sidelines.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
'Handling differences'
But the summit's other major focus is China.
Xi's visit is also being closely watched because it is his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses, and greeted with a handshake by Modi at the summit venue.
Xi and Modi later met, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported, without providing further details.
His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said ahead of his visit that it was "ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences".
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border with Tibet.
"They are looking for 'early and substantial harvest' when it comes to the border issue," said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
"You cannot have a build-up of your forces on the border... but at the same time say 'we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships'."
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday - exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 - waving placards against Xi's visit.

suspended metal grid ceiling meets translucent and reflective surfaces inside french café
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:15:38 UTC
23:15:38 KST

Raw Metal and Pale Blue Accents Give Mellow Cafe Its Identity
Mellow Cafe is an unbuilt interior concept for a compact takeaway coffee shop in Mulhouse, France. Developed by Wrong Door Studio, the project explores how a small commercial footprint can become a distinctive hospitality experience through a clear spatial strategy, expressive materials, and carefully integrated functional elements. The concept is built around efficiency and intuitive customer flow. Rather than filling the limited space with decorative elements, the design uses the architecture itself to organize the experience, from ordering and preparation to pick-up and product display. Functional zones are visually integrated into the interior, allowing the 31-sqm space to remain open, legible, and uncluttered.
The material palette combines raw industrial references with a softer, almost weightless atmosphere. Stainless steel forms the main working surfaces and custom counters, while textured metal panels and grid structures introduce depth without visually reducing the space. A suspended metal grid ceiling becomes one of the defining elements of the interior, integrating lighting and technical components into a single architectural system. Translucent and reflective surfaces interact with the predominantly neutral palette, while pale blue accents appear throughout the space in furniture, signage, shelving details, and graphic elements. These subtle interventions give Mellow Cafe its visual identity without competing with the functional character of the interior.
Lighting Becomes Part of the Architecture at Mellow Cafe
The designers at Wrong Door Studio treat lighting as part of the architecture rather than an additional decorative layer. Illuminated signage, linear lighting integrated into shelving, and luminous ceiling panels create a graphic rhythm across the space. A projected digital menu further reduces physical visual clutter and reinforces the deliberately minimal approach. The project also extends the spatial identity into smaller details, from the suspended speakers and product displays to the pick-up counter and branded packaging, creating a consistent experience across architecture, furniture, graphics, and customer touchpoints. Rather than attempting to disguise its compact dimensions, Mellow Cafe uses them as the starting point for the design. The result is a precise, contemporary hospitality concept where industrial materials, digital elements, and functional architecture come together to give a small takeaway space a strong and recognizable identity.

French officials investigate if malicious act caused train derailment
- Published
Officials in northern France are investigating whether the derailment of a passenger train on Friday evening was the result of a malicious act.
"At this stage, the leading theory is that a piece of rail was present on one of the tracks, potentially causing the derailment. The reason for its presence is unknown," prosecutor Sébastien Gallois said on Saturday.
Local media say 186 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.
Forty-four people were treated for injuries, including an 18-year-old woman who was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.
"The train's 'black box' has been seized. Several interviews are scheduled, and a court-appointed expert has been called in," prosecutor Gallois said in a press release.
"The main victim is still in hospital but her life is no longer in danger. The other victims have received care and treatment; they have either been discharged or are about to be."
The Rouen prosecutor's office earlier said the train driver had tested negative for drugs and alcohol.
The train derailed near Cléon, just south of Rouen, shortly before 20:00 (18:00 GMT), and some 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were immediately deployed to the crash scene.
"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, a passenger on the train, told ICI Normandie radio.
"I couldn't stay in my seat anymore. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I'm still shaking," he added.

PANDA child advocacy and rehabilitation center opens in Kyiv region
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
17:12:52 EEST
23:12:52 KST

The PANDA Center for the Protection, Advocacy and Recovery of Children, dedicated to the memory of staunch child rights advocate Denys Monastyrsky and established based on the Barnahus model, has begun operating in one of the communities of Kyiv region, the Kyiv Regional Military Administration and the Ministry of Justice reported.
"Children should not have to face war, cruelty or pain. But when tragedy strikes, our main human task is not simply to find those responsible, but to protect the child's psyche and not hurt them a second time. A warm, safe space has been created here, where psychologists, medical professionals, lawyers and law enforcement officers come together around the child," Kyiv Regional Military Administration Head Tymur Tkachenko, who attended the center's opening on Saturday, wrote on Telegram.
According to him, more than 13,000 children in Kyiv region have found themselves in difficult circumstances, and more than 11,000 of them have suffered as a result of the war.
National Police Deputy Head Andriy Nebytov also attended the opening of the center.
"At the center, police officers, medical professionals, psychologists and social workers will provide comprehensive assistance to children who have suffered from violence, human trafficking and war crimes. The center will operate according to the international Barnahus model: necessary investigative procedures and assistance will be provided in a single safe, child-friendly environment to prevent the child from being traumatized again," the National Police said in a statement on Telegram.
According to the National Police, about 800 children have suffered from sexual violence, rape, sexual harassment and sexual abuse this year alone. Another 65 children have been recognized as victims of human trafficking.
"We must not only ensure that those responsible are inevitably punished. It is fundamentally important to return the child to a normal life," Nebytov said.
Ukraine's Justice Minister Denys Maslov, who also attended the event, explained that one of the key problems in the child protection system for children who have experienced violence is that a child often has to recount their painful story again and again to different specialists – an investigator, doctor, psychologist, and so on.
According to him, Ukraine is working to change this approach. This involves implementing the Barnahus model, which makes it possible to bring the necessary procedural actions together in a single child-safe environment. The main principle is to minimize repeated traumatization and create conditions in which the child does not have to repeatedly recount what they experienced.
The PANDA Center has 30 places for the safe accommodation of children and is capable of assisting about 500 children per year. It is equipped with specialized rooms for interviewing children, observation and conducting forensic medical examinations.
"This model should become the standard. We are working on this together with the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, the Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine. The Ministry of Justice will also cooperate with the PANDA team to study this experience and further scale it up across Ukraine," Maslov said.
"For our region, this project is fundamental. Integrating the Barnahus model at our regional center for social and psychological rehabilitation is a joint decision and responsibility for the benefit of high-quality rehabilitation of children," Tkachenko stressed.

Why PLA’s laser-equipped Type 19 vehicle could matter in a Taiwan conflict
Images appear to show amphibious platform adapted with energy weapon and extra sensors for counter-drone defence
Unverified images posted on mainland Chinese social media on August 29 show a new variant of the Type 19 amphibious 8x8 combat vehicle featuring a turret-mounted laser weapon and extra sensors alongside its standard autocannon.
Janes, an open-source defence intelligence provider, reported in 2023 that vehicles from the Type 19 family had entered service with the 73rd Group Army under the Eastern Theatre Command, which includes amphibious brigades expected to play a major role in a potential Taiwan landing operation.
Assuming the new variant retains the base platform’s amphibious capability, it could accompany frontline units in a possible landing operation, providing defence against uncrewed surveillance and loitering munitions.
Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum and a former senior China analyst at Rand Corporation and for the US military, said it was difficult to know without more technical data whether the modifications affected the Type 19’s amphibious performance, but he believed operating the laser system while afloat “should be possible”.
The added weight could potentially be offset by reducing the crew size or other equipment, although the system would also need to be protected from salt water, he said.
Heath said that if those challenges could be overcome, the laser-based counter-drone system could be “very useful in a Taiwan conflict” in which Taiwanese forces might use drone swarms to target amphibious vehicles coming ashore.
The laser system’s low operating cost could make it particularly useful against such attacks, Heath added.

Feature: DR Congo's Bukavu grapples with grief after fire kills 29 students
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
22:00:01 CST
23:00:01 KST

BUKAVU, DR Congo, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Ten photographs from the same family were pinned side by side on a wall in the fire-hit Kadutu neighborhood of Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu Province in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Residents stopped before the portraits, speaking quietly among themselves. Others stood in silence, their eyes fixed on the faces of those who had died from Thursday's fire.
Around them, the scars of the tragedy were everywhere: blackened walls, homes reduced to ashes, sheets of metal twisted by the heat and personal belongings scattered among the debris.
The death toll has risen to 29, all of them students, according to a report released by local authorities late Thursday. Another 25 students were hospitalized, four of them in unstable condition. The blaze destroyed two schools and more than 300 homes in the neighborhood.
For residents of the affected area, the deepest loss is the children who will never return home.
Sitting amid the charred remains of her house, Maman Rachelle Munigi looked over what was left of her home. "Many people are grieving, not only because they have lost members of their own families, but also because they have lost students from this neighborhood," she told Xinhua.
Fires are not uncommon in Bukavu, but residents said they could not recall another blaze that had claimed the lives of so many children.
"Bukavu may have long been used to fires. We have seen many of them. But Bukavu had never lost so many innocent children in a fire, especially schoolchildren," said Bashengzei Chrispin, standing in front of the ruins of his home.
According to the local authorities' report, the two schools, both built largely of wood, were engulfed while students were in class. A stampede broke out as children, residents and parents who had rushed to collect their children tried to escape through a narrow passage.
Serge Chirimwami, a teacher at Furaha Primary School, one of the schools hit by the fire, recalled the panic as the flames spread.
"Most of the students died in the panic while they were inside the school and the gate was closed. By the time the teacher arrived, it was already too late for them," he said.
One teacher interviewed at the site said about 900 students were at the two schools when the fire broke out.
The cause of the blaze remains unclear. According to local authorities, fires were reported almost simultaneously at three separate locations about 500 meters apart. The exact circumstances have yet to be established.
On Friday, a day after the disaster, men, women and children were still combing through the debris.
Some lifted sheets of metal or cleared away charred remains, searching for anything that could still be salvaged -- clothes, cooking utensils or building materials that had survived the flames.
For many families, little was left.
Bahati Mushagalusa was among those who lost almost everything. His own home and another house he had been renting out were both destroyed.
"So many belongings went up in smoke," he said. "Everything was burned, including everything inside. We do not know where to sleep."
The March 23 Movement rebel group, which has controlled Bukavu since February 2025, declared three days of mourning across South Kivu Province on Friday following the tragedy.
A funeral for the victims is scheduled to be held next Monday. ■

Alutaguse National Park to expand by nearly 25,000 hectares
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Alutaguse National Park to expand by nearly 25,000 hectares
The government has approved amendments to the protection rules for Alutaguse National Park, aimed at merging existing protected areas and species habitats into a single functioning whole. The park will expand by 24,749 hectares, bringing its total area to 69,768 hectares.
"Alutaguse is Estonia's largest continuous forest‑and‑bog landscape and the only place where the flying squirrel still lives. Current protection is fragmented: small core areas in the middle of managed forest have not improved the species' status. With the expansion, we are connecting these isolated fragments into a functioning whole," said Minister of Energy and Environment Andres Sutt.
Linking the park's existing, separated parcels and nearly one hundred small core areas into an ecologically coherent forest mass is essential for strengthening protection of two umbrella species — the flying squirrel and the capercaillie.
The expansion takes place almost entirely on state land: of the newly protected areas, only 24 hectares — about 0.1 percent — are privately owned. This private land will fall under a limited‑management zone where forestry remains possible under certain conditions.
The national park will incorporate 97 previously separate species core areas totaling 7,506 hectares, and an additional 17,237 hectares will be protected for the first time. Most of this consists of valuable forest habitats. Protection will also extend to 3,040 hectares of previously unprotected bogs, including Virunurme bog and the Lemmaku, Kaasiku, Kassisaare, Õpetaja and Pikasilla bogs.
The flying squirrel's range in Estonia is limited to Alutaguse, and the species is in critical condition. Existing core areas are 25‑meter circles around nest trees. Because flying squirrels glide rather than fly, they require continuous canopy cover. If surrounding forest is cut, the protected circle becomes an island in an open clearing — leaving the animal without food sources or movement corridors. This isolates small populations that eventually die out. The same logic applies to capercaillie and other species dependent on old forests: what matters is not the number of patches but whether they are connected.
Capercaillie habitat will gain an additional 10,513 hectares of protection. Alutaguse is one of Estonia's most important capercaillie strongholds. In total, the expansion improves protection for 37 threatened or declining species.
Experience from neighboring countries such as Lithuania and Finland shows that expanding national parks has a positive impact on nature tourism and the service sector that depends on it.
Alutaguse features Estonia's only mainland dunes, the lake‑rich Kurtna landscape, the longest sandy beach on Lake Peipus, and Puhatu — one of Northern Europe's largest bog complexes. National‑park status signals internationally that the region has high‑quality visitor infrastructure for exploring natural values.
RMK is building Estonia's first treetop nature trail in Kauksi and renovating the Kauksi recreation area. A nature spa recently opened in Uusküla, and development activity has increased in the holiday‑home areas along Peipus's northern shore. Together with existing attractions and accommodation, the expansion supports longer visitor stays even outside the summer peak season.
The procedure was launched by the climate minister's directive on 17 October 2024, and the draft protection rules were publicly displayed from 18 June to 5 September 2025. Based on submitted proposals, restrictions in the capercaillie zone were eased, 1.7 hectares of residential land were removed from protection, and construction was permitted on yard land. The regulation enters into force on the tenth day after publication in the Riigi Teataja.
ERR reported in April that the expansion had been delayed. Nearly six years ago, the Estonian Fund for Nature proposed expanding the park. The state intended to finally make the long‑delayed decision — even without municipal support if necessary, as Alutaguse municipality had long opposed the expansion.
When then‑climate minister Yoko Alender launched the expansion at the Iisaku Nature Center in autumn 2024, the aim was to complete the process within six months.

The oldest evidence of regular psychoactive substance use has been found on an island in Indonesia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:40:07 EEST
22:40:07 KST

The oldest evidence of regular psychoactive substance use has been found on an island in Indonesia
Kyiv • UNN
Sulawesi hunter-gatherers may have consumed betel nuts 25,000 years ago. Scientists found traces of them on severely damaged teeth.
Hunter-gatherers on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi may have regularly consumed betel nuts as early as 25,000 years ago. This is indicated by research conducted by scientists from Griffith University, Live Science reports, writes UNN.
Details
Researchers examined heavily damaged teeth belonging to two people who lived on Sulawesi during different periods. One man died approximately 25,000–16,000 years ago, while the other person died around 7,600–6,300 years ago. Both were approximately 40–50 years old at the time of death.
The teeth displayed characteristic grooves, and analysis of the samples confirmed the presence of traces of betel nuts. The seeds of the Areca catechu palm contain arecoline, a neuroactive substance that affects the nervous system.
They may have used it as a painkiller
According to one of the study's authors, Adam Brumm, ancient people may have sucked on whole betel nuts to numb their mouths and ease toothache. At the same time, this practice likely only worsened the condition of their teeth.
On one of the teeth, the groove was so deep that it exposed the inner pulp cavity.
It must have been incredibly painful
Approximately 4,000 years ago, the inhabitants of Sulawesi were already mixing betel nuts with slaked lime to produce a stimulant. A similar practice still exists in parts of South Asia and Oceania.
It now seems likely that betel chewing in the form in which we know it developed from a much simpler and more ancient practice — sucking on a whole nut
The study's findings were published in the scientific journal Science Advances.

Nashville airport board unanimously approves name change to honor Dolly Parton

The Nashville airport is to be renamed after Dolly Parton, a board of commissioners voted on Friday, in tribute to the Smoky Mountain singer who is estimated to bring $1.8bn each year to Tennessee through her Dollywood theme park.
The decision ensures that Parton, who died last month at 80 years old, will be memorialized with her name on an airport, although the renaming process will take time to complete.
In her lifetime, Parton did not think the idea, which came about last year, would come to fruition.
“I think that’s probably more of a joke than anything,” Parton told the Tennessean. “I mean, it does sound like a lot of fun to say: ‘Your flight is departin’ from Nashville’s D Parton.’”
The move to rename gained traction last month when the Nashville mayor, Freddie O’Connell, and the Tennessee governor, Bill Lee, threw their support behind the name change.
“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said in a statement, recognizing what he called her “Volunteer spirit”.
“It is fitting that Nashville international airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith and kindness,” Lee added.
After the airport’s commissioners voted in favor of the change, Lee said it was an “important step to honor her remarkable legacy” as “Dolly has always helped the world fall in love with Tennessee”.
The name change is likely to be pricey since it will require new signage across the entire 4,500-acre (1,700-hectare) property, and updates to an airport monuments, merchandise, shuttle buses, uniforms, business cards, legal contracts and leases.
Although the new airport name in her honor has not been decided, Tennessean columnist Alejandro Ramos argued last month that the case for the change “is larger than music” because of her contributions to the state of Tennessee and to international literacy through her Imagination Library charity.
“Parton’s songs helped make Tennessee recognizable around the world. But her deepest legacy may be what she did with the success that followed. She accumulated the kind of fame, wealth and influence few people ever experience. Then she repeatedly turned those resources outward,” Ramos wrote.
The Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority said in a statement: “While a final name has not yet been determined, we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated”.

Gujarat earthquake, Nepal floods &amp; more: What is it about the date 26?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:40:01 UTC
22:40:01 KST

Gujarat, the tsunami, 26/11, and now Nepal. Some of the disasters etched deepest into public memory have one oddly specific thing in common: they happened on the 26th.The coincidence surfaced again after the August 26 catastrophe in Nepal, where a glacier collapse unleashed a wall of mud, rock and water through the Himalayan valleys, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving thousands missing. As images of the destruction spread, so did an old question: what is it about the 26th?But is the date really unusually deadly, or are we simply very good at finding patterns once we know where to look?
When nature struck on the 26th
The natural disasters alone would be enough to build a legend around this date. The Gujarat earthquake of January 26, 2001, Republic Day, struck Kutch with such force that it killed close to 20,000 people and injured more than 160,000, flattening entire towns like Bhuj and Anjar. Three years later, on December 26, 2004, a magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off Sumatra sent a tsunami crashing into the coastlines of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, part of a disaster that killed or left missing roughly 228,000 people across the Indian Ocean rim. The following July, on July 26, 2005, Mumbai received close to 944 mm of rainfall in 24 hours, a deluge that killed more than a thousand people across Maharashtra and brought the city to a standstill for days.
Gujarat earthquake of 2001
The pattern isn't confined to Indian soil, or even to this century. Turkey's Erzincan earthquake killed an estimated 32,700 people on December 26, 1939. The Skopje earthquake of July 26, 1963 killed around 1,070 and left 200,000 homeless. Iran's Bam earthquake, which levelled a 2,000-year-old citadel city, struck on December 26, 2003, killing roughly 31,000 people. Indonesia's Yogyakarta earthquake killed more than 5,700 on May 26, 2006, and the Hindu Kush earthquake of October 26, 2015 shook Afghanistan, Pakistan and parts of northern India simultaneously.
When the 26th turned man-made
Where the 26th gets stranger is that it isn't only earthquakes and floods, events with no human author. It has also coincided with some of the worst disasters humans have caused deliberately or through negligence.The most seared into Indian memory is November 26, 2008, when ten Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai, laying siege to the city for nearly three days and killing 166 people. It is remembered simply as 26/11, a date that needs no year attached to be understood. It wasn't an isolated instance of terrorism landing on this date, either, the Ahmedabad serial blasts of July 26, 2008, one of the deadliest terror strikes on Indian soil that year, fell on the same date. Outside India, the Kabul airport bombing of August 26, 2021, carried out during the US-led evacuation from Afghanistan, killed at least 183 people, including 13 American service members.
Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai
Industrial and nuclear disasters share the date too, and this is where the list stops looking like a coincidence confined to any one country or cause. Reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded during a botched safety test on April 26, 1986, in what remains the worst nuclear accident in history. More than four decades earlier, on April 26, 1942, a gas and coal-dust explosion at China's Benxihu colliery killed 1,549 miners through carbon monoxide poisoning, one of the deadliest mining disasters ever recorded.
Crashes, collisions and the 26th
Then there is a third category that rarely makes it into casual conversations about the 26th, but rounds out just how wide its reach is: ordinary transport disasters, the kind that don't need an earthquake or a bomb, just a broken rail or a failed engine part.India's Khanna rail disaster, a derailment and collision caused by a broken rail near Punjab's Khanna town, killed 212 people on November 26, 1998. The Aurangabad air crash, when flight IC-491 went down while approaching the Maharashtra airport, killed 55 of 118 people aboard on April 26, 1993. Overseas, Lauda Air Flight 004 crashed in Thailand on May 26, 1991, after an uncommanded thrust-reverser deployment sent the Boeing 767 out of control, killing all 223 people aboard.
The date that refuses to be just a number
Laid end to end, the list stops looking like a curated coincidence and starts looking almost deliberately comprehensive — quakes, tsunamis, floods, terror attacks, a nuclear meltdown, a mine explosion, a rail crash, an air crash. Nearly every disaster category a newsroom covers has, at some point, chosen the 26th.
So, is the 26th actually cursed?
There's a statistical explanation for this, and it's less exciting than a curse. The British statistician David Hand has spent years studying coincidences like this, he calls it the law of truly large numbers. Basically, if disasters are happening somewhere in the world almost every day, and a month only has 28 to 31 possible dates, some date was bound to end up looking busier than the rest. It just happened to be the 26th. It could as easily have been the 9th.Then there's confirmation bias, which does a lot of the heavy lifting here. Once you start looking for disasters on the 26th, you notice every one that fits and forget the ones that don't. Bhopal's gas leak, India's worst industrial disaster, happened on the night of December 2-3, 1984. The Uttarakhand floods were in June 2013. The Balasore train collision that killed nearly 300 people was on June 2, 2023. None of these are anywhere near the 26th. Nobody brings them up when the "jinx" comes up, because once you believe a pattern, you stop counting the exceptions.
Uttarakhand floods of 2013
Numerology adds a third layer, and in India this one actually sticks with people. Add up 2 and 6 and you get 8, a number some numerology traditions link to upheaval and karmic reckoning. For anyone who already believes in that system, a disaster landing on the 26th isn't a coincidence: it's confirmation.
There's no actual link between a calendar date and earthquakes, floods or violence. But belief doesn't need a mechanism. It just needs enough stories that fit, and the 26th has no shortage of those by now.
What the 'jinx' really tells us
So what does the list really tell us? Not that the date is cursed; just that disasters don't check the calendar, and over a long enough stretch of history, every date ends up with its own body count. The 26th's list happens to include some of the most consequential disasters of the last century, ones big enough that they changed building codes, early-warning systems, even how countries think about security. That's really why the date sticks in memory. Not the number itself, but what it forced people to rebuild afterward.

When Statecraft Becomes Transaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Executive Order (EO) 14422, signed Aug. 27, 2026, counts icebreakers. The US Coast Guard supplies nine of the 11 icebreaking vessels on the Great Lakes and clears the commercial lanes without charge, the order observes; the United States has spent nearly four billion dollars on the freshwater ecosystem in a decade, and Canada far less. From that ledger the order draws its conclusion. Because the deepest water lies on the American side, “the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume.” Lake Ontario “becomes” Lake America.
Read the inference slowly, because it does not hide: contribution establishes ownership; ownership licenses the name.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The EO presents the inference as settled policy, restating a January 2025 EO on names as a commitment to recognize “the extraordinary contributions of the American people” by naming landmarks for shared achievements.
The earlier EO’s stated policy said nothing like that. Instead, it spoke of honoring “visionary and patriotic Americans” in the nation’s past. In the older document, contribution names what a patriot gave; in the newer one, what a nation has paid in.
Ten days after the lake order, President Trump began posting maps of New Mexico with “Mexico” struck through in red, an image the White House amplified and the state’s governor refused to entertain. No constitutional route exists for renaming a state, and none was attempted.
Russia’s War in Ukraine Has Cost Poland’s Economy More than €100 bln, Estimate Shows
                                                                                                                                                                         
But naming has never been only about names. It announces who holds the standing to say what a thing is.
None of this argues against bargaining: diplomacy bargains, as it must. European governments underinvested in their own defense for three decades, and an administration that forces allies to buy usable capacity rather than rent American cover is right about that. I grant that fully, and once, because what follows does not depend on denying it. What follows depends on a distinction between a method and a metaphysics.
An alliance, though, is not a subscription willy-nilly reducible to a method. Its worth lies partly in goods that never appear on an invoice: interoperability built over decades, intelligence relationships unavailable at market, and the deterrence produced when an adversary believes a commitment will hold under pressure.
The last item is the strange one. It exists only in the enemy’s mind, and it thins the moment the enemy suspects that the commitment itself is subject to continual repricing.
On assistance to Ukraine, at least, the ledger has shifted decisively. NATO’s Ankara Declaration of July 8, 2026 records that European allies and Canada now finance the vast majority of security assistance to Ukraine and pledges €70 billion ($81 billion) in equipment, assistance, and training for 2026, with at least equivalent levels promised for 2027. Burden-shifting has produced substantial results. The strategic question it was supposed to answer sits exactly where it sat.
Territory is one object of the war in Ukraine – it is not the war itself. The Charter of the United Nations treats the territorial integrity and political independence of states as constitutive of international order rather than as negotiable holdings, and the Secretary-General has called Russia’s full-scale invasion a clear violation of it.
Putin’s own account of his aims will not fit inside a real-estate frame. At the St. Petersburg forum on June 20, 2025, he grounded a claim on a premise about peoplehood: Russians and Ukrainians being one people, and so “all of Ukraine is ours.” Putin then supplied the operative rule: “wherever a Russian soldier sets foot, that’s ours.”
Set that beside the Lake Ontario EO… and something uncomfortable surfaces: because the largest constituent of the Russian Empire was Russia, because both Russia and Ukraine have a shared history, then “all of Ukraine is ours.”
Of course, one cannot justifiably claim that Trump’s EO and Putin’s nationalism are moral equivalents – that would be grotesque. However, the grammar of naming based on power and “possession” is the same. Each converts a prior claim (contribution in one case and kinship in the other) into title. In the Lake Ontario EO, title then licenses a name; in Putin’s historical argument, naming and genealogy serve as evidence of title.
What separates them is what each is prepared to do to make the title hold. Russia invaded a sovereign state, annexed its territory, and denies its separate political existence; nothing in an executive order about a lake belongs to that category, and an argument that blurred the distinction would deserve to fail. Yet the parallel is narrow. It is also instructive, because the same grammar deceives its user in both cases.
Putin’s longer argument, set out in his 2021 essay on the historical unity of Russians and Ukrainians, rests on genealogy – and carries its own refutation. The essay concedes that the medieval word behind Ukraine’s name appears in 12th-century sources “referring to various border territories.” Various: plural, relative to more than one center. Having granted that the word named several frontiers, the essay proceeds as though it had named one, and as though naming a frontier settled who owns it.
I decline to litigate whether Kyiv’s baptism under St. Volodymyr in 988 outranks Moscow’s first appearance in the chronicles in 1147. Why? To litigate is to concede the premise: that antiquity conveys title. Sovereignty is not an inheritance, and etymology is not a deed.
A negotiating framework of this kind fails here, and it fails on its own terms. If a rational actor accepts a sufficiently good offer, then everything turns on what counts as good, and instrumental rationality supplies no common scale. Putin need not be deranged to refuse terms Washington considers generous. A leadership may rank strategic depth, imperial standing, and the denial of a neighbor’s independent existence above sanctions relief and reconstruction contracts and rank them consistently for 20 years. A negotiator can handle the priceable dimensions of such a conflict with skill and still be working on the wrong problem. A scale calibrated for one quantity returns a number for anything you set on it. The number is not false; it is beside the point.
Early on Sept. 8, 2026, ending a three-day pause on strikes observed while American envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv, Russian ballistic and cruise missiles and drones struck Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing and injuring civilians and damaging more than 50 sites in the capital, among them residential buildings, dormitories, and schools.[12]Later that day, the Kremlin’s readout of an hour-long call described Trump pressing for a swift end to the war, which would open “impressive and far-reaching” prospects for restored relations, with particular benefit to trade.
Ukraine’s foreign minister answered in 10 words: “His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.” An offer denominated in trade normalization reached a party that had spent that same morning demonstrating what it values more.
Rhetorical domination compounds the difficulty, and its record can be checked. George C. Edwards III, surveying Trump’s public discourse, catalogs the branding and delegitimizing of opponents, the fueling of fear, and the stoking of division, and arrives at a finding easy to skip past: the rhetoric diminished the president’s capacity to govern.
Consider the clearest instance: on July 31, 2025, Dmitry Medvedev, answering a warning from Trump, invoked the “Dead Hand,” the Cold War-era system reputed to launch automatically should Russia’s leadership be destroyed – though he called it fabled even as he brandished it. The following day, Trump announced on Truth Social that he had ordered two nuclear submarines repositioned. That is, a social-media post moved strategic assets.
Whatever that is, it is not the pricing of interests; it is a contest over who is seen to yield, conducted with the instruments of nuclear deterrence. The same instinct shows in Vice President JD Vance’s assigned part, which Reuters described in 2025 as an attack-dog role, exercised in Munich and then in the Oval Office against President Zelensky.
Any comparison with Medvedev stops well short of equivalence: Vance has not invoked a doomsday system.
Moscow, meanwhile, has folded nuclear risk into the bargaining environment. The doctrine Putin approved on Nov. 19, 2024 reserves the right to answer with nuclear weapons a conventional attack creating a “critical threat” to Russian or Belarusian sovereignty or territorial integrity, where the 2020 formulation had spoken of a threat to the state’s very existence.
Analysts read the change differently: the Arms Control Association sees a lowered and blurred threshold, while the United States Institute of Peace argues the amendments codify guidance already operative and mark no real departure. Either reading serves the point, since ambiguity is the instrument.
A negotiator who prices deliverables cannot price this, because its worth to Moscow lies in its staying unresolved. Beijing repeats that nuclear weapons must not be used and nuclear war must not be fought. The statement matters and may constrain Moscow. It also remains a Chinese position serving Chinese interests, and expecting Beijing to enforce Western assumptions about tolerable Russian conduct would reproduce the original error at a higher level.
The danger begins not with bargaining but with the elevation of a partial truth into a master category. The objects of statecraft are not homogeneous: political communities have histories, identities, jurisdictions, and common goods; alliances embody commitments and serve strategic goods; sovereignty is a juridical status, not merely possession of territory. None is commensurable without remainder in a single metric.
Putin’s characteristic move is civilizational absorption: Ukraine’s independent political identity is subordinated to an alleged antecedent unity of peoplehood, history, and imperial space.
The Trump administration’s recurrent vocabulary is different (assets, leverage, contributions, burdens, and deals), but it raises an analogous question: does bargaining remain an instrument ordered toward political goods that exceed exchange value, or does the logic of the bargain become the measure of those goods themselves? Treat an alliance as a subscription, and its members learn to calculate cancellation.
Sovereignty includes territory and exceeds it, the way a marriage may include a shared address without being constituted by it. Each of these realities has a transactional dimension; none is exhausted by one. The error lies not in using a category that captures something real, but in allowing a partial category to become an exhaustive ontology. At that point, the category no longer merely guides policy; it governs what its user can see.
Which returns us to the issue of Lake Ontario. Federal maps will print the new name, since an executive order can compel that much, and the water will keep crossing a border that no order can move. There is the difficulty in miniature: a name can be assigned; the thing declines to be renamed.
Washington may yet win real concessions from Moscow, and nothing here forecloses it. But a settlement built on the assumption that Moscow must eventually want what Washington would want in its place is the same category mistake, now committed where the cost of error is counted in cities.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Russia Launches Large-Scale Missile and Drone Attack Across Ukraine, Killing at Least Four
Russia launched a large-scale overnight missile and drone attack across Ukraine on September 12, killing at least four people and injuring civilians in Odesa, Kryvyi Rih, Zaporizhzhia, and the Kyiv region.
Odesa and the surrounding region were the primary target of the attack, the Ukrainian Air Force reported. We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Emergency and municipal crews were deployed to the damaged building, while an operational headquarters was established to assist residents.
In Kryvyi Rih, a Russian ballistic missile struck an industrial facility, killing one person and injuring two others, according to Dnipropetrovsk regional authorities. Another man was reported missing. The two injured men, aged 54 and 58, were hospitalized, with one reported in serious condition and the other in moderate condition.
Five apartment buildings, a primary healthcare center, three educational facilities, and several businesses were also damaged in Kryvyi Rih. The city was later targeted by attack drones.
Russia also struck a residential area of Zaporizhzhia with a drone, destroying at least one house and starting fires, regional defense officials reported. Rescue workers recovered the bodies of a 64-year-old woman and a 37-year-old man from the rubble. A 59-year-old woman was injured.

Damage was recorded in the Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil, and Vyshhorod districts. At least 15 sites were affected, including seven private homes, vehicles, warehouses, hangars, and a power line.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force on September 12, Russia began the overnight attack at around 6 p.m. the previous evening and used ballistic missiles, eight sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles, and 129 drones.
The drones included Shahed-type attack UAVs, S8000 Banderol drones, and decoys. They were launched from areas around Kursk and Oryol in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk region and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
Russian ballistic missiles were launched from Russia’s Voronezh and Rostov regions and from temporarily occupied Crimea, while the Kalibr missiles were fired from the Black Sea.
As of 8:30 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 110 aerial targets, including six Kalibr cruise missiles, two Kh-59/69 missiles, one S8000 Banderol drone, and 101 Shahed-type and other drones, the Air Force said.
Russian missiles and attack drones were recorded hitting 20 locations across Ukraine, while debris from intercepted targets fell at four additional sites.
Ukraine used combat aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare systems, unmanned systems, and mobile fire groups to repel the attack. The Air Force said Russian drones remained in Ukrainian airspace after the initial interception figures were released.
Earlier, on September 11, Russian drones struck gas stations in Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts, injuring at least two people. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also reported a second strike on a gas station in the Obolonskyi district.

He noted that Russia recruits about 1,000 service members every day, and sometimes this figure reaches 1,200 people. At the same time, according to him, the losses of the occupation forces are significantly higher.
Russia recruits approximately 1,000 people every day, sometimes 1,200. But look at these losses. Yesterday — 1,410, the day before yesterday — 1,551. Of these, 835, about 60%, were killed in action
— Ivashchenko noted.
According to him, the average life expectancy of a Russian recruit after arriving on the battlefield is between 20 and 30 minutes.
Ivashchenko also spoke of the low morale of Russian service members and the unwillingness of a significant portion of the population of the Russian Federation to fight.
The enemy's morale is very low because no one wants to fight. And the state of Russia's population is the same: most people actually do not want war
— said the Chief of the Defence Intelligence Directorate.
What the Defence Intelligence Directorate says about a new mobilization in the Russian Federation
The generals of the Russian occupation army asked the Kremlin to mobilize 800,000 people after the so-called elections in September. At the same time, Russia is suffering significant losses on the front, while the average life expectancy of a recruit after arriving on the battlefield may be between 20 and 30 minutes. This was reported by Lieutenant General Oleh Ivashchenko, Chief of the Defence Intelligence of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, in an exclusive interview with the British newspaper The Times, UNN reports.
According to Ivashchenko, Russia's military leadership appealed to Russian President Vladimir Putin with a request to mobilize 800,000 people after the September elections.
At the same time, the Chief of the Defence Intelligence Directorate questioned Russia's ability to mobilize such a number of people simultaneously.

Russia raised payments to millions, but there were fewer contract soldiers. From January to August 2026, 234,000 people signed contracts with Russia's Ministry of Defence — 10% fewer than last year. Payments reach 3.4 million rubles.

Houthi advance in Yemen puts US in a new bind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:16:18 UTC
22:16:18 KST

Houthi advance in Yemen puts US in a new bind
WASHINGTON – A lightning offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis has put the militants in a position to control a crucial Middle East waterway, creating a major new problem for US President Donald Trump as his war with Iran grinds on in its seventh month.
Widening the Middle East conflict, Houthi fighters have advanced south along Yemen’s coast, increasing their ability to choke off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – the “Gate of Tears” at the mouth of the Red Sea – giving Tehran potential leverage over both of the region’s main oil-shipping corridors.
The militants reached the island of Perim on Sept 11, in the middle of the strait between Yemen and Africa.
That is bad news for Saudi Arabia, which has been shipping much of its oil from Red Sea ports since the war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
It also comes at a difficult time for Trump, who is already grappling with record-low approval ratings and searching for a way out of the conflict, most recently by announcing an economic pressure campaign designed to force concessions from Iran’s government.
High US petrol prices driven by the conflict have jeopardised his Republican Party’s chances of keeping control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Iran remains defiant despite being hurt militarily and economically.
“Just weeks ago, Trump adopted a strategy of squeezing Iran’s economy while keeping military conflict at levels too low to squeeze the American economy,” said Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
“The Houthis have shattered Trump’s plan.”
Danger of joining the fight
The US administration cannot afford to have the Houthis close the strait, driving up energy prices and disrupting global trade.
But at the same time, entering a fight with a foe that has withstood previous attacks by Saudi Arabia and the US would be a dangerous new mission for a US military already stretched by the fighting in Iran.
Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, called Trump on Sept 10 and asked for US military help fighting the Houthis, three sources told Reuters. He was told Washington would not intervene directly for now, but would help with intelligence, the sources said.
Trump confirmed on Sept 12 that he had spoken to the Crown Prince and said the Houthis had also called his administration and asked Washington not to become directly involved in the conflict.
A senior Trump administration official declined to address specific questions, but said the US is focused on national security interests such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea “while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges”.
Saudi Arabia, Iran and the Houthis did not respond to a request for comment.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Sept 10 that the Yemen conflict could not be solved by blockade or military action against the Houthis and called for dialogue, without addressing Iran’s own role.
A second key strait
Iran responded to US and Israeli attacks earlier in 2026 by disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, the outlet to the Gulf through which around a fifth of global oil supplies flowed before the war.
If the Houthis close the Bab el-Mandeb, that would deal another economic blow, constraining another 7 per cent of global petroleum supplies and about 12 per cent of global trade.
“This was always the worst-case scenario, that the Iranians exert control not only of Strait of Hormuz but Bab el-Mandeb, two of the leading energy choke points in the world,” said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near East affairs during Trump’s first term and is now at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think-tank.
“It’s an enormous amount of leverage that (the Iranians) have in hand.”
Analysts and former officials say Trump now faces a choice: devote US forces and scarce air-defence munitions to pushing back the Houthis, or leave Saudi Arabia and its allies, a Yemeni government based in the south, to confront them alone.
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital 12 years ago, and a Saudi-led military intervention has failed to dislodge them since.
Taking on the Houthis would effectively end a deal Trump struck in 2025 in which the US would stop bombing the group in exchange for a halt to strikes on Red Sea shipping. That would be likely to expose US forces to missile attacks from Yemen.
A stretched US military
It would also be another burden for the US military.
US officials say a fight with the Houthis could require significant naval and aerial resources and divert US intelligence assets, given the need to pinpoint Houthi positions that have changed since 2025.
If US Navy vessels and aircraft have to start shooting down Houthi drones and missiles, it could also worsen diminished stockpiles of US munitions and air-defence interceptors.
The senior administration official denied that the US was concerned about its resources being stretched.
“The US military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the commander-in-chief’s strategic goals and beyond,” the official said.
Tim Lenderking, who served as US special envoy on Yemen under former US president Joe Biden and is now a principal at law firm Squire Patton Boggs, said that with Trump signalling an unwillingness to get directly involved militarily against the Houthis, the US needs to do more to share intelligence with the Saudis for their air campaign and step up diplomatic and material support for Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“This administration came in asking the question, ‘What can Yemen do for us?’” Lenderking said, during a webcast sponsored by the Middle East Institute think-tank in Washington.
“Well, Yemen can spoil our day.” REUTERS

Quzlu: A stepped village offering a glimpse of rural Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:15:34 UTC
22:15:34 KST

Quzlu: A stepped village offering a glimpse of rural Iran
TEHRAN - The stepped village of Quzlu, nestled in the mountainous landscape of northwestern Iran, offers travelers a chance to experience traditional rural architecture, unspoiled nature and a time-honored cultural heritage.
Located in Zanjan province, Quzlu is among the rural settlements that reflect the longstanding relationship between human habitation and the natural environment. Its hillside homes, built into the mountain landscape, provide a distinctive setting for visitors seeking an alternative to conventional tourist destinations.
Quzlu’s most striking feature is its stepped architecture, in which the roof of one house serves as the courtyard of the home above it. The arrangement follows the contours of the mountainside and creates a compact settlement that blends with its surroundings.
Traditional construction materials, including stone and wood, are part of the village’s architectural character. The buildings and their relationship with the surrounding landscape offer visitors an opportunity to observe a form of rural architecture rooted in local conditions.
Preserving this architectural fabric could help maintain Quzlu’s identity while creating opportunities for heritage tourism and traditional-style accommodation.
The landscape surrounding Quzlu adds another dimension to a visit. Mountain scenery, green pastures and springs are among the natural features described as attractions of the area.
The village and its surroundings offer potential for nature-based activities, including walking, photography and exploring the rural landscape. Seasonal changes in vegetation and scenery provide different experiences throughout the year.
For travelers interested in quieter destinations, Quzlu presents an opportunity to spend time in a mountainous environment away from the bustle of major cities.
Quzlu is part of Mahneshan county, an area known for its distinctive geological formations and historical sites.
Among the region’s notable attractions are the formations known as the “Jinn’s Chimneys,” volcanic rock structures that rise dramatically from the landscape. The ancient Behestan Castle, also known as Takht-e Div or the “Devil’s Throne,” is another landmark that adds historical interest to the area.
The combination of unusual geological features, ancient fortifications and traditional villages gives Mahneshan potential for both geotourism and cultural travel.
Experts say development of tourism in Quzlu could also create opportunities for the local community. Proposals include restoring traditional homes for use as eco-lodges, improving walking routes and providing training for residents who wish to host visitors.
Such initiatives could help introduce travelers to local food, handicrafts and agricultural products while creating additional sources of income for villagers.
The development of rural tourism, however, would need to be managed carefully to ensure that visitor numbers and new infrastructure do not undermine the village’s architectural character or natural environment.
Stepped villages: where architecture meets the mountains
Iran’s stepped villages offer travelers a rare chance to experience places where architecture, nature and traditional life have developed together over centuries. Built into hillsides and mountain slopes, these settlements are more than scenic destinations. They are living examples of how communities adapted to challenging landscapes while preserving their cultural identity.
One of the best-known examples is Masuleh in Gilan province, northern Iran. Its distinctive houses rise one above another along the green mountainside, creating a remarkable architectural landscape. In many parts of the village, the roof of one house serves as the courtyard or passageway of the house above it. Narrow lanes, stone steps and traditional buildings give Masuleh a character that is difficult to find elsewhere.
The charm of stepped villages lies partly in their close relationship with the surrounding environment. Steep slopes, flowing streams, forested mountains and changing weather create a constantly shifting backdrop. Mist drifting through Masuleh, for example, can transform its streets and rooftops into an atmospheric landscape.
Other Iranian villages, including Kandovan in East Azarbaijan and Abyaneh in Isfahan province, offer different interpretations of traditional mountain settlement. Kandovan is known for its homes carved into volcanic rock, while Abyaneh is recognized for its historic architecture and distinctive red-earth buildings.
These villages also provide opportunities to discover local customs, handicrafts, regional food and traditional ways of life. Walking through their lanes allows visitors to see how residents have maintained a connection with their surroundings.
For travelers seeking more than conventional sightseeing, Iran’s stepped villages offer a rewarding experience. They combine striking scenery with history, architecture and cultural heritage, making them valuable destinations for those interested in discovering the country’s diverse landscapes and living traditions.

Iranian women showcase traditional crafts at BRICS exhibition in New Delhi
TEHRAN – A group of female Iranian artisans highlight skills at a handicraft’s exhibition being held on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi.
The five-day exhibition, titled BRICS Bazaar, runs from Sept. 10 to 15. It brings together handicrafts from BRICS member countries in an effort to strengthen cultural and artistic cooperation, as well as broader economic and political ties.
The exhibition was designed as a symbol of cultural links among the participating countries, according to IRNA’s correspondent in the Indian capital.
At the entrance, handmade carpets from member countries are arranged in a circle in a range of colors, highlighting the cultural, ethnic and religious diversity of the BRICS grouping.
Talking to IRNA, Ameneh Sedighi, an artisan from Iran’s northern Gilan province, said her participation aimed to introduce Iranian traditional embroidery, particularly Rashti-doozi, to international visitors.
She said the craft dates back between 330 and 550 years before Christ and was historically practiced by men, but is now carried out by women.
Rashti-doozi is produced using natural silk thread from Gilan and a special hook, Sedighi, who teaches the craft, said.
“We were able to showcase the distinguished art of Rashti-doozi and our country’s traditional arts to visitors at this exhibition,” she said.
Sedighi said foreign visitors, particularly Indians, had shown strong interest in Iranian handicrafts and praised the host government’s cooperation with Iranian artisans.
The exhibition also highlights the similarities between the handicrafts of Kashmir and Iran. A representative from Kashmir attributed the resemblance to the close cultural ties between the two peoples, IRNA said.
The BRICS grouping, whose name derives from its original members Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, was established in 2009. It has since expanded beyond its founding membership.

ECB rate hike could push loan payments higher next spring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

ECB rate hike could push loan payments higher next spring
The European Central Bank's latest rate hike is already reflected in the six‑month Euribor that shapes most Estonians' loan payments, meaning borrowers are unlikely to see higher monthly costs this year — but a spring increase could still push payments up.
Financial markets currently believe that Thursday's ECB rate hike to 2.5 percent will not be the last this year.
"Market expectations put euro‑area base rates at around 2.8 percent by year‑end, and by next spring they are expected to rise to about 3.2 percent. Euribor, which moves mainly according to market expectations, stands at 2.8 percent today," said Rain Leesi, head of investments at Avaron, an investment management firm.
Since the six‑month Euribor affecting Estonians' loan payments is already at 2.8 percent, the next rate hike is considered priced in and should not raise loan payments. A further rise in Euribor is more likely later on.
"If we look at the level at which Euribor can be fixed for the next five years, today it can be fixed at 3.5 percent — the same high rate as in 2023, when ECB interest rates were around four percent," Leesi said.
Most Estonian home‑loan contracts use floating Euribor, meaning any rise in Euribor directly affects monthly payments.
"If today the six‑month Euribor is 2.8 percent and it rises by half a percentage point, then for a €100,000 loan balance the monthly payment increases by €30, and for €150,000 by €45," said Sille Hallang, head of retail banking at SEB.
So far, rising Euribor has not dampened Estonians' appetite for home loans.
"We do not see a decline in borrower activity — quite the opposite. The home‑loan market is very active and growing compared with last year, so there is no visible direct impact at the moment," Hallang said.
According to Hallang, SEB's volume of new home loans has grown more than 10 percent over the past year.
Ülo Kaasik, governor of Eesti Pank and member of the ECB Governing Council, said he understands why markets expect further rate hikes, noting that they depend on global developments and energy‑price movements.
"Whether we need to raise rates further depends on how future developments unfold and how inflation pressures play out. The main concern now is that risks are increasing, especially geopolitical risks, where events can shift in either direction at any moment," Kaasik said.

Deliberate targeting of passenger rail network
The strikes in Fastiv, Lutsk, and across Sumy region follow a string of coordinated attacks against Ukrainian passenger trains earlier in the week, marking an escalation in Russian operations directed against civilian transport corridors.
Between Sept. 8 and Sept. 9, Russian forces attacked four separate passenger trains in northern and eastern Ukraine, killing three people and injuring at least 20 others.
On Sept. 8, Russian attack drones struck a Kyiv-Sumy passenger train in the Sumy region. Early warnings enabled approximately 90 passengers and crew members to evacuate before the locomotive was hit and caught fire; two injured women later died in the hospital.
On the same day, an evacuation was ordered for a Dnipro-Zaporizhzhia passenger train before it was hit, though a female attendant was killed after re-entering the train.
Later on Sept. 8, consecutive drone strikes hit a suburban diesel train in the Sumy region, injuring 10 civilians. On Sept. 9, Russian jet-powered drones struck a passenger electric train at a railway station in the Izium district of Kharkiv region, injuring eight people and setting two passenger cars ablaze.
Pertsovskyi previously described the systematic assaults as a deliberate campaign against passenger rail traffic. Rail operations have served as the country’s primary transportation backbone since Ukraine closed its civil airspace following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

New Russian tanks arrive with upgraded protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:09:22 UTC
22:09:22 KST

- Uralvagonzavod delivered another undisclosed batch of T-90M and T-72B3M tanks to the Russian Army for Tank Crew Day, marking the holiday's 80th year.
- Independent researchers estimate Russia has lost more than 3,700 main battle tanks since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine began.
Russia’s state-owned tank manufacturer Uralvagonzavod has delivered another batch of T-90M “Proryv” and T-72B3M tanks to the Russian Army, the company said, timed to coincide with Russia’s Tank Crew Day.
As with previous shipments, Uralvagonzavod did not disclose how many tanks were included in the batch or where they are headed.
The company said the delivered vehicles carry improved all-around protection, part of what it describes as continuous work to upgrade armor on its tanks. Footage released with the announcement shows a T-90M fitted with an all-round protection kit Uralvagonzavod says took roughly two years to develop, covering the turret with a screen built from woven steel cable, adding armor over the running gear, and protecting the hull sides with rubber strips mounted on spring-loaded supports. Recent Uralvagonzavod shipments have also included nets meant to intercept first-person-view drones before impact and electronic-warfare equipment built to jam drone signals, though the company did not specify which of those additional features, if any, appear on this particular delivery.
Tank Crew Day marks its 80th observance this year. The holiday, established in the Soviet Union in 1946 and held on the second Sunday of September, has become a recurring occasion for Uralvagonzavod to publicize tank deliveries, alongside Victory Day each May.
“The Tank Crew holiday symbolizes the unbreakable link between production and the battlefield,” said Alexander Potapov, general director of Uralvagonzavod. He credited today’s tank crews and factory workers with carrying forward what he called the legacy of the T-34, the Soviet tank credited with helping win World War II, and thanked both groups for their service.
A driver-testing engineer at the plant described reliability as the most important quality in a combat vehicle, noting that Uralvagonzavod runs each tank through at least a 100 km (62 mile) test drive, along with checks of its weapons, navigation equipment and other onboard systems, before it ships to the military.
The T-90M is the most advanced and expensive tank in Russia’s T-72/T-90 lineage, built around a newly designed welded turret with Relikt reactive armor and a remotely operated machine gun mount that lets the crew engage targets without exposing themselves outside the vehicle. Russia has fielded it as an interim upgrade while its newer T-14 Armata tank remains stuck in prolonged trials years after it was first unveiled. The T-72B3M is a modernized rebuild of the far older, mass-produced T-72 platform, valued for being cheaper and more readily available than the T-90M even as it offers less advanced protection and fire control.
Independent researchers at Oryx, an open-source group that tracks visually confirmed equipment losses, estimate Russia has lost more than 4, 400 main battle tanks since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, more than the size of the tank fleet it invaded with. Those losses have pushed Uralvagonzavod to refurbish older tanks pulled from storage alongside new production, and claims from Russian officials describing their tanks as the best in the world have been disputed by Ukrainian officials and Western defense analysts.
